  • Compliance with Union laws (Art 256): a State must use its executive power to ensure that laws made by Parliament are obeyed; the Union may give directions for this. States' police and revenue staff enforce central laws such as the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the National Food Security Act.
  • Not impeding the Union (Art 257(1)): State executive power must not obstruct the Union's executive power.
  • Communications and railways (Art 257(2)–(3)): when directed, States must maintain means of communication of national or military importance and protect railways in their territory; the Union pays any extra cost (Art 257(4)).
  • Election duty (Art 324(6)): the Governor must make staff available to the Election Commission, which is why State officials conduct Lok Sabha polls.

2. Duties towards other States and the nation

  • Full faith and credit (Art 261): public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State must be recognised throughout India.
  • Inter-State cooperation: States implement river-water tribunal awards (Art 262) and work through the Inter-State Council (Art 263, set up in 1990) and the Zonal Councils.
  • Fiscal discipline (Art 293): a State indebted to the Union needs its consent to borrow; States have Fiscal Responsibility laws, such as the AP FRBM Act 2005.
  • Shared decisions (Art 279A): States sit in the GST Council to keep one national market.

3. Social and democratic duties

  • Directive Principles (Art 37): "fundamental in the governance" of the country, for example panchayats (Art 40), public health (Art 47) and environment (Art 48A).
  • Weaker sections: promote the interests of SCs and STs (Art 46) and follow Union directions on schemes for STs (Art 339(2)).
  • Local democracy (Parts IX and IXA): hold panchayat and municipal elections through a State Election Commission and set up a State Finance Commission every five years.

In return, the Union must protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance (Art 355).

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh executes the Polavaram project, a national project under Section 90 of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, on the Union's behalf; its State Disaster Management Authority works with the NDRF during cyclones, and it sits in the Southern Zonal Council.

The Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions stressed consultation over coercion: when States perform these duties willingly and the Union respects their autonomy, national unity and State autonomy reinforce each other.
free.g1m-2020-p4-1a:
Make in IndiaPLI schemesEase of doing businessIndustrial corridors

Manufacturing's share in India's GVA has stayed at roughly 15–17% for three decades, well below the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. A weak factory sector means too few jobs for workers leaving farms and a large import bill for electronics and machinery. Since Make in India (September 2014), the government has combined a better investment climate, output-linked incentives and logistics reform to make India a manufacturing hub linked to global value chains.

1. Improving the investment climate

  • Make in India (2014): a campaign covering 25 focus sectors; FDI was liberalised, with the automatic route allowed up to 100% in most sectors and up to 74% in defence (2020).
  • Corporate tax cut (2019): the rate fell to 22% for existing companies and 15% for new manufacturing units set up by March 2024, bringing India in line with competing Asian economies.
  • Regulatory reform: the National Single Window System (2021) for approvals, the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 (minor offences decriminalised), and the four Labour Codes, in force from 21 November 2025, which replace 29 central labour laws.
  • Competitive federalism: State rankings under the Business Reform Action Plan push States to compete for investors.

2. Incentives for scale and technology

  • Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes: 14 sectors with an outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore, including mobiles, pharma, auto, batteries, solar modules, textiles and food. Because support is tied to actual sales, firms are rewarded only when they produce more in India.
  • Semiconductors and electronics: the India Semiconductor Mission (₹76,000 crore, 2021) for fabs and assembly-testing units, and the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (2025) to deepen the supply chain.
  • National Manufacturing Mission (Union Budget 2025-26): policy support and a roadmap for small, medium and large industry.
  • PM MITRA parks (2021): seven integrated textile parks to give the textile chain scale from fibre to fashion.

3. Infrastructure and logistics

  • PM Gati Shakti (2021): a GIS-based master plan that coordinates roads, railways, ports and gas lines; the National Logistics Policy (2022) aims to cut logistics costs.
  • Dedicated Freight Corridors move cargo faster between the hinterland and ports.
  • Industrial smart cities: 12 new ones under the National Industrial Corridor Programme (August 2024), with ready plots.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

  • Two of these 12 nodes, Orvakal (Kurnool) and Kopparthy (YSR Kadapa), are in AP.
  • The electronics cluster at Sri City, Kia's plant at Penukonda and the State's Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) complement the national effort.

The results are visible: smartphones are now among India's largest exports. Raising manufacturing's share further, for Viksit Bharat@2047, needs better skills, more R&D, lower logistics costs and MSMEs linked to global value chains.
free.g1m-2020-p4-1b:
Agricultural productivityFragmented holdingsRain-fed farmingInput and market constraints

Agriculture employs about 46% of India's workers (PLFS 2023-24) but produces less than one-fifth of GVA, which shows low productivity per hectare and per worker. Yields of rice, wheat and pulses are well below those of China and the world leaders. The Green Revolution raised yields mainly in irrigated pockets, while large dryland areas lagged. The causes are structural, technological and institutional, and they reinforce one another.

1. Structural factors

  • Small, fragmented holdings: the average holding is 1.08 ha, and 86% of holdings are small or marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16). Tiny, scattered plots make tractors, harvesters and borewells uneconomical.
  • Population pressure: too many people depend on the land, so disguised unemployment keeps output per worker low.
  • Insecure tenancy: oral leases leave tenants without bank credit, crop insurance or input subsidies, and without any incentive to invest in land improvement.
  • Low capital formation: public investment in irrigation, drainage and rural infrastructure has lagged behind spending on input subsidies.

2. Technological factors

  • Dependence on the monsoon: nearly half of the net sown area is rain-fed, so a delayed or weak monsoon lowers yields across the dryland belt.
  • Poor inputs: low seed replacement rates, and urea-biased fertiliser use (driven by the subsidy) that is far from the recommended 4:2:1 NPK balance and degrades soil health.
  • Weak research and extension: low spending on agricultural R&D and too few extension workers, so new varieties and practices spread slowly.
  • Low mechanisation on small farms, and little use of precision or protected cultivation.

3. Institutional and market factors

  • Inadequate institutional credit: small and tenant farmers still depend on moneylenders at high interest.
  • Post-harvest losses and volatile prices: poor storage and cold chains, and price crashes that discourage investment in better inputs.
  • Climate change: heat waves, erratic rain and new pests reduce and destabilise yields.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

The Godavari–Krishna deltas have some of India's highest paddy yields, but rain-fed Rayalaseema, especially drought-prone Anantapur, has low yields. Many delta farmers are tenants, so the AP Crop Cultivators Rights Act, 2019 gives them cards to obtain credit.

Way forward: micro-irrigation (PMKSY, "more crop per drop"), Soil Health Cards, quality seeds, digital agriculture (AgriStack), FPOs and climate-resilient varieties can raise productivity sustainably, a second Green Revolution that is also ecologically sound.
free.g1m-2020-p4-2a:
Tax baseTax-GDP ratioInformal economyExemptions and evasion

The tax base is the set of people, incomes and transactions that actually pay tax. India's base is narrow: the combined (Centre and States) tax-GDP ratio is about 18%, against an OECD average of about 34%, and the Centre's gross tax revenue for 2026-27 (BE), ₹44.04 lakh crore, is only about 11% of GDP. A narrow base forces higher rates on the few who comply and limits spending on health, education and infrastructure.

1. Economic factors

  • Large informal economy: nearly 90% of workers are informal, and small cash-based enterprises stay outside the income tax and GST net.
  • Low incomes and a high threshold: most households earn below the taxable level. Since Budget 2025-26, income up to ₹12 lakh pays no tax under the new regime, so few of India's 140 crore people pay income tax.
  • Untaxed agriculture: agricultural income is exempt from central income tax, and the States, which alone can tax it (Entry 46, State List), hardly do. The exemption is also misused to show other income as farm income.

2. Policy factors

  • Exemptions and deductions: deductions, area-based exemptions and sector incentives shrink the effective base; the Budget's statement of revenue forgone shows their cost.
  • Gaps in GST: petroleum products, alcohol for human consumption and electricity are outside GST, and exemptions and composition thresholds keep many small firms out.
  • Weak local taxes: urban local bodies collect very little property tax because valuations are outdated and collection is lax.

3. Administrative and behavioural factors

  • Evasion: under-reporting of income, cash deals in real estate, benami holdings and shell companies.
  • Complexity and litigation: frequent changes and disputes raise compliance costs and lower tax morale.

4. Steps taken to widen the base

  • Data and technology: PAN-Aadhaar linking, wider TDS/TCS, the Annual Information Statement and faceless assessment track transactions and reduce discretion.
  • Simpler laws and rates: GST rate rationalisation (September 2025) and the simpler Income-tax Act, 2025 (in force from April 2026).
  • Formalisation: GST e-invoicing and digital payments bring small firms into the record and make their turnover visible.

AP angle: Agriculture is about a third of AP's economy and is largely untaxed. The State depends on SGST, excise, stamps and vehicle taxes, and heavily on central transfers.

The base should be widened rather than rates raised, as the Kelkar Task Force (2002) and the Tax Administration Reform Commission (2014) urged, through formalisation and the use of data.
free.g1m-2020-p4-2b:
Public debtArticle 292Internal and external debtDebt-GDP ratio

Public debt is the money the Union Government borrows against the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits that Parliament may fix by law (Article 292; no such law has been made so far). Together with "other liabilities" in the Public Account, it makes up the Centre's total liabilities. Since the 2018 amendment of the FRBM Act, the debt-GDP ratio has become the main anchor of India's fiscal policy.

1. Components of public debt

  • Internal debt (the bulk): dated G-secs, Treasury Bills (91, 182 and 364 days), Sovereign Gold Bonds, and special securities (to the National Small Savings Fund, for bank recapitalisation, oil bonds). It is in rupees and held mostly by banks, insurers and the RBI.
  • External debt (small): multilateral (World Bank, ADB) and bilateral (Japan) loans, shown at historical exchange rates, mostly long-term and concessional.
  • Other liabilities: small savings, provident funds, reserve funds and deposits in the Public Account, which the government must also repay.

2. Trends since 2010

  • 2010–2019, consolidation: after the 2008-09 stimulus, the Centre's debt eased to around 50% of GDP. The 2018 FRBM amendment (N.K. Singh Committee) made debt the anchor: 40% of GDP for the Centre and 60% for general government.
  • 2020-21, the COVID-19 shock: revenue fell and relief spending rose, so the fiscal deficit reached about 9.2% of GDP and central debt crossed 60%.
  • Since then, a glide path: the fiscal deficit fell to 4.8% (2024-25), 4.4% (2025-26 RE) and 4.3% (2026-27 BE). Debt fell to 56.1% and then 55.6% of GDP, with a new target of 50±1% by 2030-31.
  • Quality of debt: it is mostly domestic, in rupees and long-dated, so currency and rollover risks are low. But interest takes more than a third of the Centre's revenue receipts.

3. Concerns

  • Interest burden: high interest payments crowd out capital and social spending and limit room for the next crisis.
  • State debt: State debt adds to the overall burden; AP's liabilities are about 36% of GSDP (2026-27 BE). The 16th Finance Commission projects combined Centre and State debt to fall from 77.3% of GDP (2026-27) to 73.1% (2030-31).

Steady fiscal consolidation, borrowing mainly for capital spending, and faster growth will lower the debt ratio and create fiscal space.
free.g1m-2020-p4-3a:
Revenue deficitFiscal deficitDebt-GSDP ratioPost-bifurcation finances

After bifurcation on 2 June 2014, residual Andhra Pradesh received 58.32% of the population and of the debt but lost Hyderabad's revenues. With a weak revenue base and large committed spending, the 14th Finance Commission treated it as a revenue-deficit State for 2015-20. Its finances since 2014-15 show a revenue deficit every year, a fiscal deficit near the 3% FRBM limit, and debt that doubled in five years.

1. Year-wise position, 2014-15 to 2019-20

  • 2014-15 (10 months): revenue deficit (RD) ₹13,776 crore (2.62% of GSDP); fiscal deficit (FD) ₹20,745 crore (3.95%); debt ₹1.49 lakh crore.
  • 2015-16: FD ₹21,863 crore; debt about 29% of GSDP.
  • 2016-17: FD ₹30,909 crore, including ₹8,256 crore of DISCOM debt taken over under UDAY. Without UDAY, FD was 3.26% of GSDP. Debt reached ₹2.01 lakh crore.
  • 2017-18: debt about ₹2.25 lakh crore (RE), 28% of GSDP.
  • 2018-19: RD ₹13,899 crore (1.51%); FD ₹35,441 crore (3.86%); debt ₹2.58 lakh crore.
  • 2019-20 (RE): RD ₹26,647 crore (2.47%); FD ₹40,493 crore (3.75%); debt about ₹3.02 lakh crore.

2. Assessment

  • Persistent revenue deficit: borrowed money partly financed salaries, pensions, interest and welfare rather than assets, against the "golden rule" of borrowing only for investment.
  • Fiscal deficit near the limit: the FD hovered around the 3% FRBM ceiling and crossed it in some years.
  • Debt doubled: from ₹1.49 lakh crore to about ₹3.02 lakh crore in five years. The debt ratio stayed near 28% only because nominal GSDP grew fast.
  • Hidden liabilities: guaranteed borrowing by State corporations grew outside the budget.
  • Causes: loss of Hyderabad's revenues, a high share of committed spending, expanding welfare, capital needs for a new capital and for Polavaram, and slow central assistance.

3. Latest position

  • In 2024-25 the RD was 3.8% and the FD 5.1% of GSDP. The AP Budget 2026-27 targets 1.1% and 3.8%.
  • Liabilities are about 36% of GSDP, and guarantees total ₹1.77 lakh crore (PRS), so the debt overhang remains the main fiscal risk.

Higher own revenue, quality capital spending and an end to off-budget borrowing (as the 16th Finance Commission advises) can put AP on a path of fiscal sustainability.
free.g1m-2020-p4-4a:
14th Finance CommissionLocal body grantsFiscal deficit limitsFRBM reform

The 14th Finance Commission (chair: Dr. Y.V. Reddy; award period 2015-20) raised the States' share of the divisible pool of central taxes from 32% to 42%, the largest increase ever, and so gave States far more untied money. Alongside devolution, it made important recommendations on grants to local governments, on fiscal deficit limits for the Centre and the States, and on reform of the FRBM Act.

1. Grants to local governments

  • Size: a total of ₹2,87,436 crore for 2015-20: ₹2,00,292 crore for gram panchayats and ₹87,144 crore for municipalities.
  • Who receives it: only duly constituted gram panchayats (not intermediate or district panchayats) and municipalities. The grant was shared among States by population (90%) and area (10%).
  • Basic and performance grants: split 90:10 for gram panchayats and 80:20 for municipalities. Performance grants required audited accounts and higher own revenue, which rewards better local governance.
  • Purpose: basic services such as water supply, sanitation, drainage, solid waste management, street lights and local roads.

2. Fiscal deficit

  • Centre: a fiscal deficit (FD) of 3% of GDP.
  • States: an FD of 3% of GSDP, with extra room for prudent States, as shown below. This flexibility applied only if the State had no revenue deficit, so it rewarded low debt and low interest burdens.
  • Effect: the rule-based limit made State borrowing predictable, while higher devolution let the Centre restructure centrally sponsored schemes and lower its share in many of them.

3. FRBM Act

  • Revenue deficit: drop the "effective revenue deficit" target and aim to eliminate the revenue deficit itself.
  • Fiscal Council: create an independent body to assess budgets and fiscal risks in advance.
  • Escape clause: define the "exceptional circumstances" in which targets may be relaxed; States to amend their FRBM Acts on the same lines.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

  • AP received 4.305% of devolution.
  • It also received a revenue-deficit grant of ₹22,113 crore for 2015-20, recognising its post-bifurcation gap.

Latest position: The 16th Finance Commission (2026-31) recommends ₹7,91,493 crore for local bodies, in an 80:20 basic-to-performance split with entry conditions. It keeps the States' FD limit at 3% of GSDP and the Centre's FD path to 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31.

The 14th FC strengthened fiscal autonomy and grassroots democracy; its lasting lesson is that more untied money must come with accountability and rule-based fiscal discipline.
free.g1m-2020-p4-4b:
Revenue deficitFiscal deficitPrimary deficitDeficit financing

A deficit arises when government spending exceeds its own (non-borrowed) resources. The FRBM Act, 2003 uses three measures, each telling a different story about the quality of spending and the burden of past debt. How the gap is financed, by market borrowing or by new money from the RBI, decides whether deficit financing supports growth or fuels inflation.

1. Differences between the three deficits

  • Revenue deficit (RD) = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. It is borrowing for current spending (salaries, interest, subsidies), that is, government dissaving.
  • Fiscal deficit (FD) = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts such as loan recoveries and disinvestment). It equals total borrowing.
  • Primary deficit (PD) = FD − interest payments. It shows the current fiscal stance after removing the burden of past debt.
  • Reading them together: a zero primary deficit means the government borrows only to pay interest; a large revenue deficit within the FD signals poor quality of spending.
  • Example: in the Union Budget 2026-27 the FD is 4.3% and the RD 1.5% of GDP, so about 2.8% of GDP of borrowing funds capital outlay.

2. Deficit financing

Traditionally it meant borrowing from the RBI, that is, creating new money. Ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997, and the FRBM Act bars RBI primary purchases of government bonds except under the escape clause. Today the deficit is financed mainly by market borrowing through dated securities and Treasury Bills, and by small savings, so its effects work mostly through interest rates rather than money creation.

3. Positive effects

  • Resources for development: it mobilised funds for heavy industry in the Mahalanobis-era Plans.
  • Counter-cyclical support: it sustains demand in recessions, as during COVID-19 (FD about 9.2% in 2020-21).
  • Crowding in: deficit-funded roads, railways and power can attract private investment.

4. Negative effects

  • Inflation: when the deficit is monetised, more money chases the same goods.
  • Crowding out: heavy borrowing raises interest rates and squeezes private investment.
  • Debt trap: interest takes more than a third of the Centre's revenue receipts.
  • Twin deficits: a high FD widens the current account deficit (as before the 1991 crisis) and hurts credit ratings.

Andhra Pradesh angle: AP's 2026-27 FD of 3.8% of GSDP is above the 3% norm. Interest of ₹37,281 crore absorbs about 16% of revenue receipts.

Deficits help when they finance productive capital spending (the golden rule) and hurt when they fund consumption, so the FRBM glide path should be followed.
free.g1m-2020-p4-5a:
AP Reorganisation Act, 2014Special Category StatusRevenue-deficit grant14th Finance Commission

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 gave residual AP 58.32% of the population but not Hyderabad's revenues, leaving the new State with a large resource gap. The Act therefore placed special obligations on the Centre, and the 14th Finance Commission (FC) added rule-based transfers, including a revenue-deficit grant. These are the two main channels of central assistance to AP.

1. Under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014

  • Section 46: grants to cover the 2014-15 resource gap, and a backward-area package of ₹50 crore per district per year for seven districts: four in Rayalaseema plus Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam.
  • Section 90: Polavaram declared a national project, with the Centre funding its irrigation component.
  • Section 93 and the Thirteenth Schedule: institutions such as IIT and IISER Tirupati, NIT Tadepalligudem, IIM and IIPE Visakhapatnam, AIIMS Mangalagiri, the Central University (Anantapur) and the Tribal University (Vizianagaram); also a new railway zone, airport upgrades, the Vizag–Chennai Industrial Corridor, and feasibility studies for a Kadapa steel plant and for metro rail.
  • Section 94: tax incentives, and support for the new capital's Raj Bhavan, High Court, Secretariat and Legislature.

2. Special Category Status and the Special Assistance Measure

  • Special Category Status (SCS) was promised in 2014 but was not written into the Act.
  • The Centre argued that the 14th FC had ended the distinction between special and general category States, and instead gave a Special Assistance Measure (2016) that funded externally aided projects.
  • Why it matters: SCS would have meant a higher central share in centrally sponsored schemes and tax incentives for industry, so the demand remains politically and economically important for the State.

3. Under the 14th Finance Commission

  • Tax devolution: AP's share was 4.305% of the divisible pool, which itself rose to 42%.
  • Revenue-deficit grant: ₹22,113 crore for 2015-20, to cover the post-bifurcation gap.
  • Local bodies: grants for gram panchayats and municipalities for basic services such as drinking water, sanitation and street lights.
  • Assessment: the Act's education institutions have been set up, but big-ticket items such as Polavaram, the capital and industrial incentives have moved slowly.

Latest position: Amaravati support, the steel plant package and a slightly higher 16th FC share show continuing central help, but several promises remain incomplete.

Special Category Status and a central steel plant at Kadapa remain pending; timely fulfilment, in the spirit of cooperative federalism, is essential.
free.g1m-2020-p4-5b:
AP Budget 2020-21NavaratnaluFiscal deficitCOVID-19 shock

Andhra Pradesh's Budget 2020-21 was presented on 16 June 2020, delayed by the COVID-19 lockdown. Total expenditure was ₹2,24,789 crore, 28.6% above 2019-20 (RE). Built around the Navaratnalu welfare programmes, it tried to protect household incomes in a pandemic year in which revenues were falling sharply, and its fiscal deficit rose well above the FRBM limit.

1. Major features

  • Welfare-centred: YSR Pension Kanuka ₹16,000 crore (now NTR Bharosa pensions), YSR Aasara ₹6,300 crore, Amma Vodi ₹6,000 crore (replaced in 2025 by Thalliki Vandanam), Rythu Bharosa ₹3,615 crore (now Annadata Sukhibhava). Most were paid as direct benefit transfers, and the new village and ward secretariats handled enrolment and doorstep delivery.
  • Agriculture: a ₹3,000 crore Price Stabilisation Fund and ₹4,000 crore for nine hours of free daytime power to farms.
  • Nadu-Nedu: ₹3,000 crore for schools and ₹1,528 crore for hospitals, to upgrade public infrastructure.
  • Optimistic receipts: ₹1,62,558 crore of non-debt receipts, 41% above 2019-20, in a lockdown year.

2. Fiscal deficit situation

  • Deficits: revenue deficit ₹18,434 crore (1.82% of GSDP); fiscal deficit ₹48,296 crore (4.78% of GSDP), well above the 3% FRBM limit; primary deficit 2.76%.
  • Debt: liabilities to rise to 34.6% of GSDP, from 28%.
  • Interest: payments of ₹20,383 crore, a large committed charge.
  • Central relaxation: for 2020-21 the Centre raised States' borrowing limit to 5% of GSDP: 3.5% unconditional, 1% linked to four reforms (One Nation One Ration Card, ease of doing business, power, urban local body revenues) and 0.5% for meeting three of them.

3. Assessment

  • Strength: it protected household incomes, especially of women, the elderly and farmers, during the pandemic.
  • Weakness: committed revenue spending, low capital outlay and rising debt narrowed fiscal space for the future.
  • Revenue realism: receipts assumed 41% growth in a lockdown year, so any shortfall had to be met by more borrowing or by cutting capital spending.

Latest position: The AP Budget 2026-27 (₹3,32,205 crore) targets a revenue deficit of 1.1% and a fiscal deficit of 3.8% of GSDP, with liabilities at about 36% (PRS).

Balancing welfare with capital spending and revenue mobilisation is the key to fiscal sustainability.
free.g1m-2020-p4-6a:
Rural–urban povertyTendulkar estimatesMultidimensional Poverty IndexRegional disparity

Poverty in Andhra Pradesh has fallen steadily on both consumption-based (Tendulkar) and multidimensional measures, and the State has long been below the national average. Official State-wise consumption poverty estimates stop at 2011-12, so later trends come from NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI). On every measure, poverty remains concentrated in rural, tribal and drought-prone areas, and rural poverty has been roughly twice the urban rate.

1. Trends

  • Tendulkar method (undivided AP): rural poverty fell from 32.3% (2004-05) to 10.96% (2011-12), and urban poverty from 23.4% to 5.81%. The overall rate fell to 9.2%, far below the national 21.9%. Rural poverty was nearly twice the urban rate.
  • NITI Aayog's MPI: AP's poverty headcount fell from 11.77% (NFHS-4, 2015-16) to 6.06% (NFHS-5, 2019-21), against 24.85% to 14.96% for India. Rural deprivation in nutrition, cooking fuel, housing and schooling remains much higher than urban.
  • Regional pattern: poverty is highest in the tribal agency areas (Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam) and drought-prone Rayalaseema, and lowest in the irrigated deltas.

2. Causes of rural poverty

  • Rain-fed farming: dependence on the monsoon and repeated droughts in Rayalaseema make farm incomes unstable.
  • Heavy debt: 93.2% of agricultural households are indebted, with an average debt of ₹2.45 lakh, the highest in India (NSS Situation Assessment Survey 2019).
  • Landlessness and tenancy: tenants and agricultural labourers, many of them SC/ST, have insecure, seasonal incomes.
  • Isolation of agency areas: poor health, education and connectivity keep tribal families poor, and seasonal migration from Srikakulam and Vizianagaram is common.
  • Disasters: cyclones such as Hudhud (2014) and Titli (2018) destroy crops, boats and houses and push families back into poverty.

3. Causes of urban poverty

  • Informal jobs: low-paid, insecure work in construction, transport and street vending, with slum housing and low skills among migrants.
  • Low urbanisation: about 29% (Census 2011), which limits the creation of non-farm jobs and the pull of cities.

4. Measures

  • Livelihoods: SERP's self-help-group model and MGNREGS provide credit and wage work.
  • Safety nets: PDS, and NTR Bharosa pensions (₹4,000 a month from 2024).
  • New approach: the P4 "Zero Poverty" initiative (2025), in which better-off families mentor poor families.

Ending residual poverty needs irrigation for dry regions, non-farm jobs, and better health and education in tribal areas, in line with SDG 1 (no poverty).
free.g1m-2020-p4-6b:
Public Distribution SystemNFSA 2013Targeting and leakageDoorstep delivery

The Public Distribution System (PDS) delivers subsidised foodgrains under the National Food Security Act, 2013. In Andhra Pradesh it covers about 2.68 crore people under the NFSA and, with State-funded cards, over 4 crore people. It works through about 1.5 crore rice cards and about 29,000 fair price shops (FPS) (2025), and NFSA rice is free under PMGKAY. It is a vital safety net, but it faces problems of targeting, leakage, delivery and nutrition.

1. Targeting errors

  • NFSA design: the Act covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, with 35 kg a month for Antyodaya families and 5 kg per person for priority households; the State-wise ceiling is based on Census 2011.
  • Beyond the NFSA ceiling: rice cards far exceed the NFSA ceiling, so the State carries the extra cost (rice subsidy of ₹3,344 crore in the 2026-27 budget).
  • Inclusion and exclusion: ineligible cardholders are reported, while some genuine poor and migrant families are left out.

2. Leakage and diversion

  • Resale and recycling: many beneficiaries sell PDS rice, and it is recycled into the open market or exported.
  • Kakinada racket: seizures at Kakinada port in 2024 exposed diversion of PDS rice to exports.
  • National picture: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) estimated that about 46% of PDS grain leaked out before reaching households.

3. Delivery model

  • Mobile units: doorstep delivery by 9,260 Mobile Dispensing Units (from 2021) proved costly and leaky.
  • Return to shops: from 1 June 2025 the State returned to FPS, keeping home delivery for those aged 65 and above and persons with disabilities.

4. Other issues

  • Authentication failures: ePoS biometric checks fail for elderly and manual workers, and connectivity is poor in agency areas.
  • Nutrition: a rice-centred basket with few pulses or millets, despite high anaemia; fortified rice is only a partial answer.
  • Fiscal burden: procurement, storage and transport costs keep rising.
  • Dealer viability: low margins for fair price shop dealers encourage short weighing and diversion.

Reforms under way: One Nation One Ration Card portability, Aadhaar-seeded ePoS, smart rice cards (distributed from August 2025) and GPS tracking of vehicles aim to plug these gaps.

PDS must remain a food safety net, with better targeting through e-KYC, millets and pulses for nutrition, and strict action against diversion; the Shanta Kumar Committee's idea of gradual cash transfers in large cities can be tested where markets work well.
free.g1m-2020-p4-7a:
e-NAMOne Nation One MarketAPMC reformPrice discovery

The National Agriculture Market (e-NAM), launched on 14 April 2016, is a pan-India electronic trading portal that links existing APMC mandis into a unified national market for farm produce. The Small Farmers' Agri-Business Consortium (SFAC) implements it for the Ministry of Agriculture. Its aim is transparent price discovery, better prices for farmers and, ultimately, "One Nation, One Market".

1. Features

  • Online auctions: transparent bidding, with direct payment into farmers' bank accounts.
  • Market reforms built in: assaying (quality testing) facilities, a single State-wide trading licence, and a single-point levy of market fee.
  • New modules: warehouse-based trading, an FPO module and the "Platform of Platforms" (2022) linking private platforms.
  • Coverage (PIB, March 2026): 1,656 mandis in 23 States and 4 UTs, over 1.8 crore farmers and 4,724 FPOs registered, and trade of about ₹4.84 lakh crore since 2016.

2. Expected benefits

  • For farmers: more bidders, transparent prices and quick online payment, which reduce the hold of local commission agents.
  • For traders and buyers: access to produce from many mandis through one licence.
  • For policy: real-time data on arrivals and prices, useful for procurement and for managing price volatility.

3. Challenges in implementation

  • Legal reform: States must amend their APMC Acts to allow e-trading, unified licences and single-point levies. The Model APLM Act, 2017 has been adopted only partly.
  • Little inter-mandi or inter-State trade: most e-NAM transactions are local auctions, and physical trade continues alongside.
  • Quality and logistics: few assaying labs, no standard grading, and weak transport and dispute settlement, so distant buyers hesitate to bid on produce they cannot see.
  • Resistance from commission agents and trader cartels, who lose their hold on local auctions.
  • Farmer readiness: low digital literacy, poor internet in rural areas, a preference for cash, and small lot sizes.
  • Too few markets: far below the Swaminathan Commission's norm of a market within 5 km.
  • Political sensitivity: the 2020 farm laws, which sought to allow trade outside APMC yards, were repealed in 2021, so market reform now rests largely with the States.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

Several AP market yards trade on e-NAM. Village-level Rythu Seva Kendras (formerly Rythu Bharosa Kendras) and FPOs could help with aggregation, grading and digital trade, so that small farmers reach distant buyers.

Way forward: farm-gate assaying, FPO aggregation, interoperable platforms and APMC reforms through cooperative federalism can realise "One Nation, One Market".
free.g1m-2020-p4-7b:
Rainbow RevolutionAgricultural diversificationNutritional securityAllied sectors

The Rainbow Revolution means developing all parts of agriculture together: crops, horticulture, livestock, fisheries and poultry. Each sub-sector is symbolised by a colour. The National Agriculture Policy (2000) emphasised it to raise agricultural growth above 4% a year. It marks a shift from the cereal-centred Green Revolution to diversified, high-value farming that serves changing diets.

1. Components

  • Green: high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertilisers made India self-sufficient in wheat and rice, but mainly in irrigated regions.
  • White: village dairy cooperatives on the Anand pattern linked milk producers directly to urban consumers.
  • Blue: inland aquaculture, marine fisheries, harbours and cold chains, with a focus on fishers' incomes.
  • Yellow: the Technology Mission sharply raised oilseed output in the early 1990s, though imports later rose again.
  • Other colours: silver for eggs and poultry, pink for onions and prawns, and round for potatoes.
  • Common thread: each revolution combined technology, institutions (cooperatives, missions) and markets.

2. Objectives

  • Higher incomes: diversify from cereals into high-value products such as milk, fish, fruits and vegetables, whose demand rises with income.
  • Nutritional security: add proteins, fats and vitamins to diets, and reduce imports of edible oils and pulses.
  • Employment: generate jobs for small, landless and women farmers, since livestock and fisheries need little land.
  • Value addition: encourage agro-processing, cold chains and exports, and attract private investment.
  • Sustainability: use land, water and genetic resources sustainably.

3. Discussion

  • Achievements: India is the world's largest milk producer and the second-largest producer of fish and of fruits and vegetables.
  • Gaps: dependence on edible oil imports, weak cold chains and processing, regional imbalance, and groundwater stress from input-intensive farming.
  • Equity: gains have gone more to irrigated and market-connected regions than to dryland farmers.
  • Continuing support: PM Matsya Sampada Yojana, the edible-oil missions and the Dairy Processing and Infrastructure Development Fund (2017) carry the rainbow approach forward with investment in processing and cold chains.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

AP is a true "rainbow" State. It leads India in fish and shrimp production (the country's aqua hub), oil palm and chillies, and is among the top producers of eggs and fruits such as banana, papaya and mango. In AP, allied sectors such as livestock and fisheries drive agricultural growth.

A rainbow approach, linked to FPOs, food processing and climate-resilient practices, can raise farm incomes sustainably and make agriculture nutrition-sensitive.
free.g1m-2020-p4-8a:
Agricultural growthFarm incomesAllied sectorsIndebtedness

Agriculture and allied sectors produce about a third of Andhra Pradesh's GVA and support most rural households. The State reported double-digit growth in this sector in 2014-19, led largely by fisheries, livestock and horticulture rather than field crops. The real test is whether this output growth became income growth for farmers, and the evidence shows a mixed picture: incomes rose, but debt and inequality among farmers remain high.

1. Positive impact on incomes

  • Above-average income: according to the NSS Situation Assessment Survey 2019 (2018-19), an AP agricultural household earned ₹10,480 a month on average, slightly above the national ₹10,218.
  • High-value activities: aquaculture, horticulture (banana, papaya, mango) and dairy brought high returns to farmers in the deltas and to women in dairy.
  • Direct income support: YSR Rythu Bharosa (₹13,500 a year, 2019-24), and now Annadata Sukhibhava–PM-KISAN (₹20,000 a year from 2025). Free crop insurance and zero-interest crop loans also helped.
  • Diversified sources: livestock and wage incomes cushion households when crops fail.
  • Shift in land use: many delta farmers moved low-return paddy land into fish and shrimp ponds, raising incomes, though with costs to soil, water and food-grain output.

2. Why incomes did not rise as fast as output

  • Debt: 93.2% of AP agricultural households were indebted, with an average debt of about ₹2.45 lakh, the highest in India (SAS 2019). Rising input costs and interest absorbed the gains.
  • Uneven growth: much of the growth came from capital-intensive aquaculture and livestock, while rain-fed crop farmers in Rayalaseema stagnated.
  • Tenant farmers: they cultivate much of the delta land but pay high rents and often miss institutional credit, insurance and subsidies.
  • Price volatility: crashes in tomato, onion and chilli prices, and limited procurement at MSP.
  • Climate shocks: droughts and cyclones such as Michaung (2023) cause crop losses.

3. Way forward

  • Collective strength: FPOs can buy inputs in bulk and sell in larger lots, improving prices for small farmers.
  • Value addition: food processing near production centres captures more of the consumer rupee.
  • Risk management: price stabilisation, timely insurance claims and tenancy reform that gives tenants access to credit.
  • Lower costs: low-cost natural farming (APCNF) reduces spending on chemicals and so reduces debt.

Output growth must become income growth; this is central to the "Swarna Andhra@2047" vision.
free.g1m-2020-p4-8b:
Rythu BharosaVillage-level extensionCrop insuranceNatural farming

Agriculture is the backbone of Andhra Pradesh's economy. Since 2019 the State has built a support system that reaches farmers at every stage, from income support and inputs to village-level extension, risk cover and markets. The aim is to cut cultivation costs, reduce risk and bring services to the village. The main schemes as of 2020 are given below, with later changes noted.

1. Income and input support

  • YSR Rythu Bharosa–PM-KISAN (2019): ₹13,500 a year per farm family, including landless tenant farmers from weaker sections. It was replaced in 2025 by Annadata Sukhibhava–PM-KISAN (₹20,000 a year).
  • Inputs: subsidised seeds, soil testing, and farm machinery through YSR Yantra Seva custom hiring centres, so small farmers need not buy costly machines.

2. Village-level extension

  • Rythu Bharosa Kendras (RBKs, 2020): over 10,000 village one-stop centres for inputs, advice, e-crop booking and procurement, staffed by village agriculture and horticulture assistants. Farmers can order certified seeds and fertilisers at a kiosk and receive them in the village. They have since been renamed Rythu Seva Kendras.
  • e-Crop (e-Panta) booking: a digital record of crops that links farmers to insurance, input subsidy and MSP procurement.

3. Risk cover and credit

  • YSR Free Crop Insurance (2019): farmers paid no premium; the State bore the cost, and crops booked in e-Crop were covered.
  • YSR Zero-Interest Crop Loans: interest relief on crop loans of up to ₹1 lakh repaid on time.
  • Price Stabilisation Fund (₹3,000 crore): market intervention when prices crash.

4. Irrigation and power

  • Free power: nine hours of free daytime power to farm pumps.
  • Water: YSR Jala Kala (free borewells for small farmers), micro-irrigation through the AP Micro Irrigation Project to save water in dry regions, and Polavaram and other projects to expand canal irrigation.

5. Sustainability and quality

  • AP Community-Managed Natural Farming (APCNF, 2016): run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, it covers lakhs of farmers and is among the world's largest agro-ecology programmes.
  • Integrated Agri Labs test seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, protecting farmers from spurious inputs.

6. Assessment

  • Strengths: the schemes reduce cost and risk, and the village-level network brings services, data and procurement close to the farmer.
  • Gaps: fiscal sustainability, inclusion of tenants who lack records, weak market linkages beyond procurement, and the need for climate resilience in dryland Rayalaseema.

Farming becomes profitable only when such support is matched by better prices, lower costs and stable incomes.
free.g1m-2020-p4-9a:
Industrial Policy 1980Industrial Policy 1991Small-scale reservationInvestment limits

Both the Industrial Policy Statement, 1980 and the 1991 policy (with its separate statement on Small, Tiny and Village Enterprises, August 1991) saw small industry as vital for jobs and for spreading industry to backward areas. But 1980 protected small units within the licence regime, while 1991 sought to make them competitive in an open, liberalised economy.

1. Industrial Policy Statement, 1980

  • Higher limits: investment limits raised to ₹2 lakh for tiny units, ₹20 lakh for small-scale units and ₹25 lakh for ancillary units.
  • Nucleus plants: introduced in industrially backward districts, to develop ancillary and small units around them.
  • Reservation: continued reserving items for exclusive small-scale production, with District Industries Centres (1978) providing support at the district level.
  • Protection: promoted "economic federalism" and shielded small units from large-scale competition.

2. 1991 policy for small enterprises

  • Higher limits: ₹5 lakh for tiny units irrespective of location, ₹60 lakh for small-scale units, and ₹75 lakh for ancillary and export-oriented units.
  • Equity participation: other industrial firms, including foreign firms, could hold up to 24% of the equity in small units, to bring in capital and technology.
  • Credit: priority lending to tiny units, SIDBI refinance, factoring, and the Delayed Payments Act, 1993.
  • New focus: from subsidies to marketing, technology upgrading and quality.
  • Dereservation: reserved items were gradually removed (fully by 2015), exposing small firms to competition.

3. Contrast

  • Philosophy: 1980 was protective and location-based; 1991 was market-oriented and focused on competitiveness and quality.
  • Role of the state: guardian in 1980, using reservation and licensing to keep large firms out; facilitator in 1991, using credit, technology and marketing support.
  • Access to capital: 1980 relied on the units' own resources and state support; 1991 opened the door to equity from other firms.
  • Result: reservation kept many units small and technologically backward, as the Abid Hussain Committee (1997) later noted; after 1991 small firms faced competition but gained access to capital, credit and technology.

4. Present position

Under the MSMED Act, 2006, the 2025 limits are: micro ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover, small ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore, and medium ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore. Andhra Pradesh's MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy (2024-29) promotes "One Family, One Entrepreneur".

Competitiveness backed by credit, technology and markets remains the right path.
free.g1m-2020-p4-9b:
Public sectorCommanding heightsMaharatna and NavratnaEfficiency

The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 gave the public sector the "commanding heights" of the economy. Central public sector enterprises (CPSEs) grew from 5 units with ₹29 crore of investment in 1951 to several hundred. They built India's industrial base when private capital was scarce, but their record on efficiency is mixed, so a critical examination must weigh both sides.

1. Achievements

  • Infrastructure and heavy industry: SAIL (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur), BHEL, ONGC, NTPC and Coal India built the core sectors and reduced import dependence.
  • Balanced regional development: plants were located in backward areas, such as the Bhilai and Rourkela steel plants and the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (RINL).
  • Social goals: employment, reservations, and stable prices for essentials such as fuel and fertilisers.
  • Revenue: dividends and taxes (about ₹75,000 crore of CPSE dividends expected in 2026-27).
  • Global firms: Maharatna and Navratna companies such as NTPC, ONGC and IOC compete globally. Public sector banks returned to profit after recapitalisation and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

2. Weaknesses

  • Low returns: returns on capital below those of private firms, and chronic loss-makers such as BSNL, MTNL and Air India (before 2022).
  • Technology lag: outdated plants and slow decisions left many units uncompetitive once markets opened after 1991.
  • Governance: political interference, overstaffing, soft budget constraints and little autonomy, with multiple layers of accountability slowing decisions.
  • Banking stress: public sector bank bad loans peaked at about 14.6% in March 2018.

3. Reforms

  • Autonomy: the MoU system (1986, after the Arjun Sengupta Committee), Navratna (1997) and Maharatna (2010) status.
  • Disinvestment: since 1991, and the New Public Sector Enterprise Policy (2021) to keep a minimum presence in strategic sectors.
  • Privatisation: the sale of Air India (January 2022).

4. Critical assessment

  • Context matters: in the 1950s private capital and technology were scarce, so the public sector was a necessity, not a choice.
  • Mixed record: a few enterprises became world-class, while many sick units survived only on budget support.
  • Changing role: today the state's role is shifting from owner to regulator, keeping a presence only in strategic sectors.

Andhra Pradesh angle: RINL, after years of losses, received a ₹11,440 crore revival package in January 2025. NTPC Simhadri and the Dredging Corporation of India are other key CPSEs in the State.

Judgement: The public sector served its developmental purpose but lagged in efficiency; a lean, professional public sector in strategic areas is the way forward.
free.g1m-2020-p4-10a:
DisinvestmentStrategic saleValuation and transparencyStakeholder interests

Disinvestment is the sale of government equity in public sector enterprises, either a minority stake or a strategic sale with transfer of management. It began in 1991-92 and was guided by the Rangarajan Committee (1993), the Disinvestment Commission (1996) and now DIPAM (2016) and the New Public Sector Enterprise Policy (2021). Past sales show that success depends on preparing the ground first.

1. Clarity of purpose

  • Clear objective: decide whether the aim is efficiency or revenue, and separate strategic sectors (minimum presence) from non-strategic ones (exit).
  • Use of proceeds: proceeds should fund capital assets (National Investment Fund, 2005), not the revenue deficit, since selling family silver to pay running costs leaves the state poorer.
  • Method: choose between minority sales (offer for sale, IPOs such as LIC's in 2022) and strategic sales, depending on whether management control should change.

2. Process issues

  • Fair valuation and transparency: value land and brands properly, use open competitive bidding with independent valuers, and avoid controversies like BALCO (2001) and Centaur Hotel.
  • Timing and investor interest: BPCL's strategic sale was dropped in 2022 after bidders withdrew.
  • Restructuring before sale: Air India's debt was moved to a special-purpose vehicle before its sale to the Tata group (January 2022).
  • Avoid sales between PSUs, such as ONGC buying HPCL (2018), which only move money between government pockets.
  • Institutional oversight: a Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment and a ministerial Alternative Mechanism oversee strategic sales, which adds checks and credibility.

3. Stakeholders and safeguards

  • Public and regional sentiment: enterprises with strong regional or emotional value need consultation with the State and the public before a sale is announced.
  • Employees: job security, VRS, pensions and reservations, with union consultation; resistance is lower when workers are assured of their rights in the sale agreement.
  • Regulation: sector regulators and the Competition Commission must prevent public monopolies from becoming private monopolies, so that consumers gain from efficiency.
  • Legal clearances: the Supreme Court (2003) held that HPCL and BPCL, nationalised by law, could be privatised only with Parliament's approval.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

The strategic sale of the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, approved in principle in 2021, met strong resistance because the plant is tied to the 1966 "Visakha Ukku – Andhrula Hakku" movement. In January 2025 the Centre approved an ₹11,440 crore revival package instead. The case shows that public sentiment and regional history must be weighed along with balance sheets.

Disinvestment should be a transparent, consultative means to efficiency, not an end in itself.
free.g1m-2020-p4-11a:
Food processingValue additionFarm-to-fork chainsFiscal incentives

Andhra Pradesh produces surpluses of rice, fruits, chillies, oil palm, milk and shrimp, but only a small share is processed, so farmers lose value and post-harvest losses stay high. Food processing links agriculture with industry: it raises value addition, stabilises farm prices and creates rural jobs. The State has therefore made it a thrust sector, with the AP Food Processing Society as the nodal agency.

1. Policy and incentives

  • Policy continuity: the AP Food Processing Policy 2015-20, followed by the 2020-25 policy and now the Food Processing Policy 2024-29.
  • Fiscal incentives: capital subsidy on plant and machinery, interest subvention, and reimbursement of stamp duty, power cost and SGST, with extra support for SC/ST, BC and women entrepreneurs.
  • Non-fiscal support: single-desk clearances, land in industrial and food parks, and private "plug-and-play" parks where small units can start quickly.

2. Infrastructure and value chains

  • Mega food parks under the PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana, such as Srini Food Park (Chittoor), plus food processing parks with common facilities.
  • Farm-gate infrastructure: primary processing centres, cold storages and pack-houses, partly financed by the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020), which offers loans with interest subvention.
  • Aggregation: Rythu Seva Kendras (formerly Rythu Bharosa Kendras) and FPOs aggregate produce for processors, so small farmers can supply in bulk.

3. Sector-specific initiatives

  • Aquaculture: the AP State Aquaculture Development Authority Act, 2020 regulates farms, seed and feed, supporting shrimp processing and exports.
  • Micro units: PMFME (2020) gives a 35% credit-linked subsidy, up to ₹10 lakh, under "One District One Product".
  • Natural farming (APCNF): chemical-free produce for premium domestic and export markets.
  • Exports: mango pulp, chillies, shrimp and spices, which need certification and traceability.
  • Oil palm and horticulture: AP leads India in oil palm, so crushing mills and pack-houses near plantations and orchards keep value within the State.

4. Challenges

  • Fragmented supply: small, scattered farms make steady, uniform supply difficult.
  • Cold-chain gaps: too few reefer vehicles and cold storages near farms.
  • Incentive delays: late payment of incentives hurts small processors.
  • Export standards: certification, residue limits and traceability for global markets, where shrimp consignments face strict testing.
  • Credit and skills: small processors find it hard to raise working capital and to meet food-safety (FSSAI) norms.

Linking farmers, FPOs and processors in farm-to-fork chains can raise incomes, cut wastage and create rural jobs, as Swarna Andhra@2047 envisages.
free.g1m-2020-p4-11b:
Marginal cost pricingNatural monopolyAllocative efficiencyTwo-part tariff

Public utilities such as electricity, water, railways and gas are natural monopolies: their fixed costs (plants, grids, pipes, tracks) are very high and their running costs low, so one supplier serves the market most cheaply. How such a utility should price its output is a classic problem. The Marginal Cost Pricing (MCP) rule, associated with Hotelling (1938), says a utility should charge a price equal to the marginal cost of supply (P = MC).

1. The rule explained

  • Efficiency: at P = MC, what consumers will pay for the last unit equals the cost of producing it. Output is allocatively efficient, with none of the deadweight loss of monopoly pricing (P > MC).
  • Signal to users: consumers use more only when the value to them exceeds the cost to society, so scarce capacity is not wasted.
  • Peak-load pricing: a variant that charges more at peak times, so that peak users bear the cost of capacity built for them. For example, an extra unit of electricity at night costs little because plants are idle, while at the evening peak it may need costly generation.

2. Problems with the rule

  • Losses: when average cost (AC) falls as output rises, MC is below AC, so P = MC means a loss, covered by subsidies from distortionary taxes.
  • Measurement: joint costs and lumpy investments make MC hard to estimate; short-run and long-run MC can differ widely.
  • Second best: if other sectors do not price at MC, applying the rule in one sector may not raise welfare (Lipsey–Lancaster, 1956).
  • Equity: the rule ignores ability to pay, so poor households may be priced out of essentials such as water.
  • Investment: no surplus is left for maintenance and expansion, and subsidies weaken cost discipline.

3. Practical alternatives

  • Average-cost pricing: the utility breaks even, at some loss of efficiency.
  • Two-part tariffs: a fixed charge recovers capacity costs, and a per-unit charge close to MC keeps the efficiency signal.
  • Ramsey pricing: higher mark-ups where demand is less elastic.
  • Time-of-day tariffs: mandatory for commercial and industrial consumers from April 2024.

Andhra Pradesh angle: The AP Electricity Regulatory Commission sets two-part tariffs with cross-subsidies, and the State budget funds free farm power. The Tariff Policy, 2016 seeks tariffs within ±20% of the average cost of supply.

The best approach combines efficiency (MC signals), viability (fixed charges) and equity (targeted subsidies).
free.g1m-2020-p4-12a:
Public-Private PartnershipsRisk sharingKelkar CommitteeHybrid Annuity Model

Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) are long-term contracts in which a private partner finances, builds or operates public infrastructure and bears agreed risks, in return for user charges or government payments. They combine private capital and efficiency with public goals. India built many highways, ports, airports and power plants through PPPs, but in the 2010s many projects stalled, adding to bank bad loans (the "twin balance sheet" problem).

1. Problems faced

  • Aggressive bidding: over-optimistic traffic and revenue forecasts made many projects unviable from the start.
  • Delays and risk transfer: delays in land acquisition and clearances, with risks loaded onto private partners that they could not control.
  • Rigid contracts: no framework for renegotiation when conditions changed, and slow dispute resolution.
  • Fear of decision-making: officials hesitated to settle disputes for fear of investigations.
  • Financing mismatch: short-term bank loans for long-term projects, and a shallow corporate bond market.
  • Regulatory gaps: no independent regulator in sectors such as roads to settle tariff and performance disputes.
  • Narrow spread: few PPPs in health, education and urban services, where user charges cannot cover costs.

2. Recommendations

  • Better preparation: value-for-money studies, at least 80% of land acquired and clearances obtained before bidding, and a published PPP project pipeline (Union Budget 2025-26).
  • Fair risk sharing: the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016), where the government pays 40% of cost during construction, and Toll-Operate-Transfer and InvITs for existing assets. Each risk should rest with the party best able to manage it.
  • Institutions (Kelkar Committee, 2015): a "3P India" institute, a PPP review committee for renegotiation, an infrastructure adjudication tribunal, and independent regulators.
  • Legal protection: the 2018 amendment to the Prevention of Corruption Act protects bona fide decisions.
  • Long-term finance: NIIF (2015), NaBFID (2021), deeper bond markets, and Viability Gap Funding (revamped in 2020 with more support for social infrastructure).
  • Capacity: updated model concession agreements and PPP cells in States and cities.

3. Andhra Pradesh angle

The AP Infrastructure Development Enabling Act, 2001 was one of India's first State PPP laws. Krishnapatnam and Gangavaram ports and the Bhogapuram airport (design-build-finance-operate-transfer) are PPP examples, and the P4 model extends the partnership idea to people.

A second generation of PPPs, with balanced risks and credible dispute resolution, can mobilise private capital for Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2020-p4-13a:
Smart Cities MissionArea-based developmentSpecial Purpose VehiclesUrban governance

The Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25 June 2015 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. It aimed to give citizens core infrastructure, a clean and sustainable environment and a decent quality of life through "smart solutions". India's cities produce a large and growing share of output, but they suffer from congestion, poor services and weak municipal finances, which the Mission sought to address through model projects.

1. Initiatives

  • City Challenge: 100 cities were selected competitively in four rounds (2016–2018), a new way of choosing cities by the quality of their plans.
  • Funding: ₹48,000 crore of central assistance (about ₹100 crore per city per year), matched by States and urban local bodies, plus convergence with other schemes and PPPs.
  • Special Purpose Vehicles under the Companies Act carry out the projects, to allow quick decisions.
  • Smart solutions: e-governance, smart water and power meters, intelligent traffic management and better solid-waste management, to make services efficient and transparent.
  • Two components: area-based development (retrofitting, redevelopment, greenfield) and pan-city ICT solutions. Integrated Command and Control Centres run in all 100 cities and proved useful during COVID-19.
  • Outcome: about 8,000 projects worth about ₹1.6 lakh crore, over 90% completed when the Mission closed on 31 March 2025.
  • Related missions: AMRUT 2.0, SBM-Urban 2.0, PMAY-Urban 2.0 and the ₹1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund (2025-26).

2. Challenges

  • Governance: SPVs bypass elected urban bodies, diluting the 74th Amendment.
  • Narrow focus: area-based development covers a small part of each city, which raises equity concerns, as slums and peripheral areas gain little.
  • Finance: weak municipal revenues, limited PPP interest and few municipal bonds.
  • Delays: the deadline was extended from 2020 to 2025.
  • Basics and climate: urban floods and heat waves show that sensors cannot replace drains.
  • Data and capacity: many cities lack trained staff and reliable data to run ICT systems after the projects end.

3. Andhra Pradesh angle

Visakhapatnam and Kakinada were selected in the first round (2016), and Tirupati and Amaravati later. Visakhapatnam's command centre is a notable outcome, used for traffic, surveillance and disaster response.

The next phase must empower urban local bodies, strengthen their own revenues and plan for climate resilience, so that cities drive inclusive growth.
free.g1m-2020-p4-13b:
Industrial Development Policy 2015-20Sunrise AP Vision 2029Single Desk PortalInvestment incentives

Andhra Pradesh's first post-bifurcation Industrial Development Policy 2015-20 sought to make AP "a progressive and highly industrialised state" and a centre of technology and innovation. It was part of the Industry Mission of Sunrise AP Vision 2029 and aimed to rebuild an industrial base weakened by the loss of Hyderabad, using the State's coast, corridors and land through a corridor-and-cluster approach.

1. Objectives and targets (by 2020)

  • Ranking: be among the top three States for industrial investment by 2022.
  • Structural change: raise manufacturing's share of GSDP from 9.95% (2013-14) to 15%, and industry's share from 20.7% to 25%.
  • Investment and jobs: attract ₹2 lakh crore of investment and create 10 lakh jobs.

2. Strategy

  • Corridors and clusters: Vizag–Chennai Industrial Corridor nodes (Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Gannavaram–Kankipadu, Srikalahasti–Yerpedu), Krishnapatnam on the Chennai–Bengaluru corridor, the Visakhapatnam–Kakinada petrochemicals region (PCPIR), and manufacturing zones (NIMZs) in Chittoor and Prakasam.
  • Land bank: a target of 10 lakh acres, allotted on 99-year leases, so that investors find ready land.
  • Single Desk Portal: clearances within 21 working days, with deemed approval, which reduced the discretion and delays that investors fear.
  • Ten thrust sectors with their own policies (food processing, life sciences, textiles, electronics, aerospace, automobiles and others).

3. Incentives

  • Costs: 100% reimbursement of stamp duty, and power cost reimbursement of ₹1 per unit for five years.
  • Tax: reimbursement of net VAT or SGST: 100% for five years for micro and small units; 75% for medium and 50% for large units, for seven years.
  • Inclusion: SC/ST and BC entrepreneurs get a 35% investment subsidy (45% for women); first-generation women entrepreneurs get 25%.
  • Mega projects: tailor-made packages for projects of ₹500 crore or 2,000 jobs.

4. Outcome and assessment

  • Gains: AP topped the national ease-of-doing-business rankings and attracted Kia, Isuzu and Sri City units.
  • Limits: incentive arrears built up and were partly cleared by the ReSTART package (2020).
  • Lessons: the targets for manufacturing's share and jobs were ambitious for a State that had just lost its main industrial centre, and investment commitments did not always turn into projects on the ground.

Its corridor-and-cluster approach continued in the 2020-23, 2023-27 and 4.0 (2024-29) policies, showing the policy's lasting influence on industrial strategy.
free.g1m-2020-p4-14a:
Power sector reformDISCOM financesRenewable energyIntegrated Clean Energy Policy 2024

Andhra Pradesh was a pioneer in power reform. The AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998 split the State Electricity Board into separate generation, transmission and distribution companies, and in 2014 AP was among the first States in the "24x7 Power for All" programme. Yet the sector still faces financial and technical stress, even as it moves towards a large renewable-energy future. Cheap, reliable power is central to the State's plans for industry, agriculture and green hydrogen.

1. Challenges

  • Distribution company (DISCOM) finances: tariffs below the cost of supply and heavy reliance on State subsidy for free farm power, often paid late, have caused accumulated losses.
  • High power purchase costs: costly long-term contracts, including early renewable energy contracts at high tariffs. The 2019 attempt to renegotiate them hurt investor confidence.
  • True-up charges: fuel and power-purchase cost adjustments passed on to consumers after the fact, which causes public resentment.
  • Integrating renewables: variable solar and wind supply, curtailment, and the need for storage and stronger transmission.
  • Rising demand from cities, industry and farm pumps, and cyclone damage to the grid (Hudhud, 2014).
  • Smart metering under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, which some consumers oppose.

2. Vision targets

  • As of 2020: 24x7 quality power for all, nine hours of free daytime power to farms, a 10,000 MW solar project for farm supply, lower losses, and energy efficiency through LED programmes.
  • Current (Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, a five-year policy): over 160 GW of new renewable and pumped-storage capacity (78.5 GW solar, 35 GW wind, 22 GW pumped storage) plus 25 GWh of battery storage, and 1.5 million tonnes a year of green hydrogen, with about ₹10 lakh crore of investment and 7.5 lakh jobs.
  • Consumers and costs: lower power purchase costs, rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar, and NTPC's green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka.

3. Way forward

  • DISCOM reform: timely subsidy payment, cost-reflective tariffs and lower losses.
  • Competitive procurement: transparent bidding for new capacity and storage.
  • Grid strength: green energy corridors and cyclone-resilient networks along the coast.
  • Demand side: smart meters, time-of-day tariffs and energy efficiency to flatten the evening peak.

DISCOM reform, competitive procurement and storage-backed renewables can give AP affordable, reliable green power, in line with India's net-zero goal for 2070.
free.g1m-2020-p4-14b:
Vision 2020Second Green RevolutionDiversificationAgro-processing

"Vision 2020" refers to India's long-term development visions prepared around 2000: Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's Technology Vision 2020 (TIFAC) and his book India 2020 (1998), and the Planning Commission's India Vision 2020 (2002, S.P. Gupta Committee). Kalam named agriculture and food processing as the first of five core areas for a developed India, along with education and healthcare, information technology, infrastructure and critical technologies.

1. Major initiatives highlighted

  • A second Green Revolution: higher productivity through better seeds, biotechnology and precision farming, extended to rain-fed and eastern regions left out of the first.
  • Water management: irrigation, watershed development, drip and sprinkler systems, and dryland farming, since water is the main constraint.
  • Diversification: horticulture, floriculture, dairy, poultry and fisheries, which give higher incomes per hectare.
  • Agro-food processing: value addition, cold chains, fewer post-harvest losses, and exports.
  • Market reforms: freer domestic trade, contract farming, warehousing and rural roads.
  • Institutions: land records, tenancy reform, rural credit, research and extension.
  • IT for farmers: weather, price and advisory services delivered to villages.
  • Rural non-farm jobs to absorb surplus farm labour and raise rural incomes.
  • Rural infrastructure: roads, power, storage and communication, which Kalam's PURA idea (Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas) sought to bring together in village clusters.

2. Outcomes

  • Taken up by programmes: many of these ideas were taken up through national programmes, as the table shows.
  • Production: foodgrain output now exceeds 350 million tonnes (2024-25), and India leads in milk and is second in fruits, vegetables and fish.
  • Unfinished agenda: productivity in rain-fed areas, groundwater stress, small holdings, weak market reform and low farm incomes remain challenges.
  • Processing gap: only a small share of farm produce is processed, so post-harvest losses remain high.

3. Andhra Pradesh angle

The State's "Swarna Andhra Pradesh: Vision 2020" (1999) stressed agricultural growth, watershed programmes (Neeru-Meeru) and agro-processing, and Rythu Bazars (1999) let farmers sell directly to consumers. Swarna Andhra@2047 carries this forward.

Latest position: PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (for 100 low-productivity districts), the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, and digital agriculture continue the agenda, showing that the vision's priorities of productivity, water and markets still guide policy.

The Vision 2020 goal of a productive, diversified and market-linked agriculture remains relevant for Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2020-p4-15a:
PMEGPSelf-employmentMargin money subsidyKVIC

The Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) is a credit-linked subsidy scheme launched in 2008-09 by merging the PM Rozgar Yojana (1993) and the Rural Employment Generation Programme (1995). The Ministry of MSME runs it, with the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) as national nodal agency, and with State KVIBs and District Industries Centres as implementing agencies. It aims to turn job-seekers into job-creators through new micro-enterprises.

1. Objectives

  • Employment: create jobs in rural and urban areas through new micro-enterprises in manufacturing and services.
  • Self-employment: bring traditional artisans and unemployed youth into self-employment near their homes.
  • Stability: provide sustained employment, reduce rural-to-urban migration and raise artisans' earnings.

2. Eligibility and benefits

  • Who can apply: any individual above 18 years, for new units only; for projects above ₹10 lakh in manufacturing or ₹5 lakh in services, at least Class VIII pass. SHGs, societies and trusts can also apply.
  • Project size: up to ₹50 lakh for manufacturing and ₹20 lakh for services.
  • Margin money subsidy: for general applicants, 15% in urban and 25% in rural areas. For special categories (SC, ST, OBC, minorities, women, ex-servicemen, persons with disabilities, and the North-East, hill and border areas), 25% urban and 35% rural.
  • Own contribution: 10% for general applicants and 5% for special categories. Banks lend the rest, with CGTMSE guarantee cover, so no collateral is needed for smaller loans.
  • Second loan: up to ₹1 crore to upgrade a unit, with a 15% subsidy (20% in the North-East and hill States).

3. Achievements

  • Scale: from 2008-09 to December 2025 the scheme assisted over 10.7 lakh micro-enterprises, employing an estimated 87 lakh people (Lok Sabha, December 2025).
  • Funding: it was approved for 2021-22 to 2025-26 with ₹13,554 crore. In August 2026 the government told the Rajya Sabha that an extension beyond March 2026 was under consideration.

4. Concerns

  • Access: bank rejections and delays in sanctioning loans.
  • Survival: units that close after the subsidy is adjusted, and weak market links.

Andhra Pradesh angle: In AP the scheme runs through KVIC, the State Khadi Board and District Industries Centres. Units assisted rose from 2,477 in 2021-22 to 5,577 in 2023-24 (Lok Sabha, August 2024), and the scheme complements "One Family, One Entrepreneur".

Post-start-up support, market links and mentoring can make PMEGP a stronger engine of self-employment.
free.g1m-2023-p4-1a:
New Age reformsPublic goodsFormalisationPotential growth

The Economic Survey 2022-23 used the term 'New Age' reforms for the changes made since 2014, which shifted policy from one-time liberalisation to building public goods, formalising the economy and trust-based governance. The Survey compared them with the 1998-2002 reforms that paid off in the 2003-08 boom, and argued that India's medium-term potential growth would rise as their benefits matured.

1. Impact of the reforms

  • Digital public infrastructure: JAM (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile), Direct Benefit Transfer and UPI (2016) cut leakages and brought millions into formal finance; UPI crossed 20 billion transactions a month in 2025.
  • Tax reform: GST (2017) unified the national market, and the 2019 cut in corporate tax to 22% (15% for new manufacturing units) made India competitive with its Asian peers.
  • Balance-sheet repair: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) and the 4R strategy (recognition, resolution, recapitalisation, reform) cut banks' gross NPAs from 11.2% (March 2018) to about 2.3% (March 2025), reviving credit growth.
  • Macro stability: flexible inflation targeting (2016) and a fiscal glide path helped India absorb COVID-19 and the 2022 commodity shock without a crisis.
  • Investment and ease of business: a public capex push, PM Gati Shakti (2021), PLI schemes (2020), the Jan Vishwas Act 2023 and four Labour Codes (in force from November 2025).

2. Growth potential, 2023-30

The Survey expected average real growth of about 6.5% in the medium term and said potential growth could rise to 7-8% as the reforms pay off. Outcomes so far beat this baseline: 7.4% in 2025-26 (NSO first advance estimate) and an RBI projection of 7.1% for 2026-27 (October 2026).

  • Demographic dividend: a young workforce, if skilled and employed, can lift savings, investment and consumption through the decade.
  • Infrastructure and logistics: record public capex (₹12.2 lakh crore in 2026-27) and Gati Shakti lower logistics costs and crowd in private investment.
  • Global shifts: China-plus-one supply chains, services exports and the digital economy widen the base of growth.
  • Constraints: weak private investment, low female labour force participation (41.7%, PLFS 2023-24), skill gaps, global protectionism and climate risks.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Swarna Andhra@2047 vision likewise counts on ports, industrial corridors, the Amaravati capital and technology-driven governance for high growth.

Sustaining 7-8% growth needs second-generation reforms in land, labour, power and skills, and stronger state capacity: the path to Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2023-p4-1b:
Managed floatRupee depreciationImported inflationForex intervention

India follows a managed float. After the dual-rate LERMS of March 1992, the rupee became market-determined in March 1993; the current account was made fully convertible in August 1994, while the capital account remains only partly convertible, as the Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006) advised a cautious path. So the market sets the rate, but the RBI smooths sharp moves.

1. Is the rupee fully market-determined?

  • In principle, yes: there is no official target or band; the rate reflects trade flows, capital flows (FDI, FPI, ECBs), remittances and the interest-rate gap with the US.
  • In practice, managed: the RBI intervenes in spot, forward and offshore (NDF) markets to curb excessive volatility, though it does not defend any particular level.
  • Other levers: capital-account controls, ECB and FPI limits and large reserves (about $700 billion) also shape the rate. The RBI watches the 40-currency REER to judge competitiveness.
  • Verdict: market-determined in principle, managed in practice.

2. Effects of depreciation (from about ₹60 per dollar in 2014 to beyond ₹90 in December 2025)

  • Costlier imports: India imports over 85% of its crude oil, besides edible oils, fertilisers and electronics, so imported inflation and subsidy bills rise.
  • Debt and capital: unhedged firms' foreign borrowings cost more to service, and FPI outflows can become self-reinforcing.
  • Gains: IT services, textiles, pharma and marine exports become more competitive, and remittances (India is the world's largest recipient) are worth more in rupees.
  • Limits: the high import content of exports such as electronics and gems, and the J-curve effect, delay any improvement in the trade balance.

3. Role of the RBI in defending the rupee

  • Direct intervention: selling dollars from reserves in spot and forward markets, and buy-sell swaps to manage the resulting rupee liquidity.
  • Interest rates: the repo rate was raised by 250 bps in 2022-23 and again to 5.50% in October 2026; besides fighting inflation, this narrows the rate gap that drives outflows.
  • Attracting inflows: in 2013 a special FCNR(B) swap window drew about $34 billion; in July 2022 the RBI relaxed interest caps on FCNR(B) and NRE deposits, raised the ECB limit and eased FPI norms.
  • Less dollar dependence: rupee trade settlement through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (2022) and a local-currency arrangement with the UAE (2023).

AP angle: a weaker rupee helps Andhra Pradesh's shrimp and rice exporters but raises costs for Visakhapatnam's crude-importing refinery and pharma units that import raw materials.

The RBI should smooth volatility, not defend a level; lasting rupee stability needs a lower current account deficit, stronger exports and steady capital inflows.
free.g1m-2025-p4-1a:
Current Account DeficitBalance of PaymentsTrade deficitRupee depreciation

The Balance of Payments (BoP) records all of India's transactions with the rest of the world. Its current account covers trade in goods and services, income and transfers; a Current Account Deficit (CAD) arises when payments exceed receipts and must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing down reserves. India's CAD was about 0.6% of GDP in 2025-26 (US$25.2 billion, RBI), but a much wider goods deficit and volatile capital flows kept the BoP under pressure.

1. Factors contributing to the CAD

  • Large merchandise trade deficit: India imports over 85% of its crude oil, besides gold, electronics, coal and fertilisers; the goods deficit (BoP basis) widened to US$337.3 billion in 2025-26 from US$286.9 billion in 2024-25 (RBI).
  • Narrow export base: weak manufacturing competitiveness, a small role in global value chains and a trade deficit of about US$99 billion with China (2024-25).
  • External shocks: volatile crude prices (West Asia conflict, 2026) and US tariff actions in 2025 hurt exports such as shrimp, textiles and gems.
  • Primary income outflows: interest on external debt, and dividends and profits repatriated by foreign firms.

2. Why the BoP turned unfavourable

  • Weak capital inflows: in 2025-26, net FPI outflows of US$16.4 billion and net FDI of only US$6.9 billion left the CAD unfinanced, so foreign-exchange reserves fell by US$23.6 billion on a BoP basis (RBI).
  • Rupee depreciation: the rupee breached ₹90 per US dollar in December 2025.
  • Cushions: a large services surplus (US$216.6 billion in 2025-26, from IT and Global Capability Centres) and record remittances (about US$135 billion in 2024-25) keep the CAD far smaller than the goods deficit.

3. Implications for the Indian economy

  • Imported inflation: a weaker rupee and costlier crude raise fuel and input costs; rising inflation led the RBI to raise the repo rate to 5.50% in October 2026.
  • Reserves and liquidity: RBI's dollar sales to steady the rupee use up reserves and tighten domestic liquidity; external borrowing becomes costlier to service.
