  • Sustainability: a CAD below about 2.5% of GDP is considered manageable; the 4.8% CAD of 2012-13 left India exposed in the 2013 taper tantrum, and the 1991 crisis followed a collapse of reserves.
  • Twin deficits: a high fiscal deficit adds to import demand and widens the CAD.

AP angle: AP's merchandise exports were ₹1.59 lakh crore in 2025-26 (DGCI&S data), with marine products at 18%, so US tariffs on shrimp directly hurt the State's aquaculture farmers.

Export diversification through FTAs (India–UK CETA, 2025; India–EFTA TEPA), PLI-led manufacturing and an energy transition that cuts oil imports can make India's external sector resilient.
free.g1m-2025-p4-1b:
ManufacturingInfrastructure bottlenecksLogistics costPM Gati Shakti

Manufacturing contributes only about 17% of India's GVA, well short of the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. Factories compete on cost and time, and both depend on infrastructure: power, transport, ports, land and water. Costly and unreliable infrastructure therefore acts as a hidden tax that keeps Indian firms small and less competitive than rivals in East and South-East Asia.

1. How infrastructure bottlenecks hinder manufacturing

  • High logistics cost: estimated at 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT, for 2021-22); freight is road-heavy and railways carry only about 27% of it, raising costs for bulk goods such as steel and cement.
  • Power: industrial tariffs carry cross-subsidies for farm and household users; DISCOM losses and interruptions push firms to costly captive power and diesel back-up.
  • Ports and last-mile links: congestion, weak hinterland rail and road links and slow multimodal transfer raise turnaround time and inventory costs, hurting time-sensitive exports.
  • Land: difficult acquisition, fragmented holdings and few plug-and-play industrial parks delay projects for years.
  • Other gaps: water scarcity, urban congestion, and weak testing, certification and R&D facilities for MSMEs.

2. Impact on the sector

  • Small scale: high costs keep most firms small and informal, unable to reap economies of scale.
  • Weak exports: costs and delays limit India's integration into global value chains.
  • Low investment: uncertainty over land and power deters private capex and FDI in labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and footwear.
  • Lost jobs: labour-intensive factories need cheap logistics and reliable power; where these are lacking, investment goes to competitors such as Vietnam and Bangladesh, a lost opportunity for India's young workforce.

3. Steps to address them

  • States' role: land and water are State subjects and power is distributed by State DISCOMs, so single-window clearances, land banks and DISCOM reforms are essential.
  • Regulatory ease: decriminalisation under the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 and faster dispute resolution remove non-physical bottlenecks.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh hosts two of the new industrial smart cities, Orvakal and Kopparthy; the Visakhapatnam–Chennai and Chennai–Bengaluru industrial corridors and new ports at Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam and Mulapeta aim to cut logistics costs for its industries.

Cheap and reliable power, seamless multimodal logistics and ready industrial land, planned jointly by the Centre and the States, can lift manufacturing's share and make India a global manufacturing hub.
free.g1m-2020-p5-1a:
Life expectancy at birthMortality declineHealth transitionPublic health

Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if the age-specific death rates of a given period stayed unchanged throughout its life. It summarises the health of a whole population rather than predicting any one person's lifespan. Globally it has risen from about 32 years in 1900 to 73.3 years in 2024 (UN World Population Prospects 2024); India's rose from about 32 years in 1951 to a little over 70 years today.

1. Why it matters as an indicator

  • Captures deaths at every age: a death in infancy removes many potential years, so falling child mortality lifts the average far more than gains in old age.
  • Measure of development: it is one of the three dimensions of the UNDP's Human Development Index and reflects nutrition, sanitation and health care together.

2. Factors behind the improvement

  • Vaccines and control of infections: smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 and India became polio-free in 2014; the Universal Immunisation Programme (1985) and Mission Indradhanush protect children from measles, diphtheria, tetanus and severe forms of TB.
  • Clean water and sanitation: sewers and chlorinated water cut cholera and typhoid in 19th-century Europe; in India, Swachh Bharat (2014) and the Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water in about 82% of rural homes by July 2026) play the same role.
  • Medicines and medical technology: antibiotics after penicillin (1928), oral rehydration salts for diarrhoea, anti-malarials and TB drugs, and later treatment for heart disease, diabetes and cancer.
  • Better nutrition and food security: the Green Revolution, the public distribution system, the National Food Security Act (2013) and mid-day meals prevented famines and reduced child undernutrition.
  • Mother-and-child care and wider development: institutional deliveries (about 89% of births, NFHS-5) and newborn care have brought India's infant mortality to 24 per 1,000 and maternal mortality to 87 per lakh live births (SRS); income growth, female literacy and smaller families reinforce these gains.

3. Challenges that remain

  • Quality of years: non-communicable diseases now cause about two-thirds of deaths in India; air pollution and drug resistance threaten healthy years.
  • Inequality: infant mortality ranges from 8 in Kerala to 36 in Chhattisgarh (SRS 2024), and rural rates exceed urban ones.
  • Shocks: COVID-19 cut global life expectancy in 2020–21; it has returned to pre-pandemic levels in nearly all countries since 2022 (UN, 2024).
  • Ageing: more elderly people need pensions, geriatric care and long-term support.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's maternal mortality ratio of 30 (2021–23) is the joint lowest in India with Kerala; Dr NTR Vaidya Seva gives cashless hospital care, and a Universal Health Policy approved in 2025 aims to widen it.

The doubling of life expectancy owes more to public health (vaccines, water, food and safe births) than to hospitals alone. The next goal is to add healthy years, through prevention of chronic disease, clean air and universal health coverage.
free.g1m-2020-p5-2a:
UIDAIAadhaarDirect Benefit TransferJAM trinity

The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) is a statutory body under the Ministry of Electronics and IT, created by the Aadhaar Act, 2016; it began in 2009 under the Planning Commission. It issues the 12-digit Aadhaar number, linked to a resident's fingerprints, iris scans, photograph and basic details, and runs online authentication. Over 145 crore Aadhaar numbers have been generated (2026), making Aadhaar the identity layer of India's digital public infrastructure.

1. Functions of UIDAI

  • Enrolment and de-duplication: biometric matching ensures one person gets only one number; Aadhaar proves identity, not citizenship.
  • Authentication and e-KYC: service providers get a yes/no answer through fingerprint, iris, face or OTP; with consent, e-KYC shares verified details instantly.
  • Privacy safeguards: virtual ID, biometric locking and masked Aadhaar. In Puttaswamy (2018) the Supreme Court upheld Aadhaar for welfare but struck down its use by private firms (Section 57).

2. Harnessing IT for targeted delivery (DBT)

  • JAM trinity: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile phones let the government pay benefits straight into a beneficiary's account; DBT began on 1 January 2013.
  • Cleaning beneficiary lists: seeding lists with Aadhaar removed ghost and duplicate names in LPG subsidy (PAHAL), ration cards, scholarships, MGNREGS wages and pensions.
  • Digital payment rails: the Public Financial Management System tracks funds, and NPCI's Aadhaar Payments Bridge routes money to the account linked to an Aadhaar number, so the beneficiary need not even give account details.
  • Portable rations: Aadhaar authentication on ePoS machines at fair-price shops lets migrants draw rations anywhere under One Nation One Ration Card.
  • Scale: over ₹52 lakh crore has been transferred through more than 900 schemes and over ₹5 lakh crore saved by plugging leaks (PIB, August 2026).

3. Aadhaar in financial transactions

  • Last-mile banking: the Aadhaar-enabled Payment System (AePS) lets bank correspondents serve villages without branches, which helped women and the elderly draw benefits during the Covid-19 lockdown.
  • Financial inclusion: easy KYC made it possible to open crores of Jan Dhan accounts and bring small savers into insurance and pension schemes.

4. Concerns

  • Exclusion: worn fingerprints of manual workers and the elderly, poor connectivity and seeding errors can deny rations or pensions; Aadhaar cannot be made compulsory for opening bank accounts or getting SIM cards (Puttaswamy).
  • Fraud and privacy: AePS frauds using cloned fingerprints and data leaks; biometric locking and the DPDP Act, 2023 add safeguards.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats use Aadhaar authentication to deliver pensions and welfare at the doorstep, and the Real Time Governance Society monitors delivery.

Aadhaar has turned welfare from a leaky pipeline into targeted delivery. Face authentication, offline and assisted options, and quick grievance redress can make it fully inclusive.
free.g1m-2020-p5-2b:
CybercrimePhishingCyber stalkingVictim support (1930)

Cybercrime is any crime in which a computer, phone or network is the target or the tool: hacking, online fraud, harassment, data theft or attacks on systems. Such offences are punished mainly under the IT Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. NCRB's Crime in India 2024 recorded 1,01,928 cyber crime cases, up 17.9% over 2023, with fraud as the motive in about 73% of them.

1. Phishing

  • How it works: a message that looks official (a bank asking for "KYC update", an "unpaid electricity bill", a parcel or job offer) carries a link to a fake site or asks the victim to share an OTP. Vishing uses calls and smishing uses SMS.
  • Examples: a fake bank page captures net-banking passwords and the money is moved within minutes through mule accounts; fake customer-care numbers on search engines; QR codes sent "to receive money" that actually pay the fraudster.
  • Variant: in "digital arrest" scams, callers pose as police or CBI on video calls and frighten victims into transferring money; no such procedure exists in Indian law.

2. Cyber stalking

  • How it works: repeated unwanted messages, tracking a person's location through stalkerware, creating fake profiles, morphing photographs and threatening to publish them.
  • Example: a rejected acquaintance creates a fake profile of a college student, posts morphed images and messages her friends. This attracts BNS Section 78 and IT Act provisions on privacy (66E) and obscene content (67).
  • Impact: fear, depression and dropping out of studies or work; women and minors are the main targets.

3. How the government helps victims

  • Quick reporting: helpline 1930 and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in), run by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), MHA. A complaint made in the "golden hour" lets banks freeze the stolen money; this system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026.
  • Women and children: the portal accepts anonymous complaints about child sexual abuse material; under the IT Rules, 2021, platforms must remove non-consensual intimate images within 24 hours of a complaint.
  • Telecom tools: Sanchar Saathi blocks lost phones and fraudulent SIMs; its Chakshu facility takes reports of suspected fraud calls and messages.
  • Organisations: CERT-In guides recovery from ransomware, and the Cyber Swachhta Kendra offers free malware-cleaning tools.
  • Investigation and counselling: cyber police stations and forensic labs, and the Tele-MANAS helpline (14416) for victims under stress.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's 2026-27 budget provides for a cybercrime police station in every district; an earlier ransomware attack on the power utilities of AP and Telangana showed that public utilities are also targets.

Laws alone cannot stop cybercrime. Cyber hygiene (no OTP sharing, strong passwords, updated software), fast reporting and well-trained police together offer the best protection.
free.g1m-2020-p5-3a:
ISROVikram SarabhaiMangalyaanChandrayaan-3

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), formed on 15 August 1969, is the research and development arm of the Department of Space (1972) and is headquartered in Bengaluru. Founded on Dr Vikram Sarabhai's vision of using space for national development (communication, weather and resource mapping), it has grown from working out of a church at Thumba to missions to the Moon, Mars and the Sun.

1. A brief history

  • Beginnings (1962–72): the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) chose Thumba, near the magnetic equator, for rocket research; ISRO followed in 1969, and the Space Commission and Department of Space in 1972.
  • Building capability (1975–90): Aryabhata (1975); the SITE experiment (1975–76) beamed educational TV to about 2,400 villages; SLV-3 (1980, project director A.P.J. Abdul Kalam) made India a launching nation; the INSAT and IRS series began.
  • Operational launchers (1990s–2010s): PSLV became the workhorse, GSLV flew with an indigenous cryogenic stage from 2014, and a PSLV placed 104 satellites in one flight (2017).
  • Exploration and reform (2008–2026): Chandrayaan-1, Mangalyaan, Aditya-L1 and SpaDeX docking (2025); NSIL (2019), IN-SPACe (2020) and the Indian Space Policy, 2023 opened space to private firms, and Skyroot's Vikram-1 became India's first private orbital rocket (July 2026). Gaganyaan's uncrewed G1 mission had not flown by October 2026; a crewed flight is targeted for 2027.

2. Three ISRO centres and their locations

3. Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)

  • Launched by PSLV-C25 on 5 November 2013, it entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the first in the world to do so at the first attempt.
  • It cost about ₹450 crore, far less than comparable missions. Designed for six months, it worked for about eight years until contact was lost in 2022, studying the Martian surface and atmosphere.

4. Chandrayaan missions

  • Chandrayaan-1 (2008): its instruments, including NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper, helped find water molecules on the Moon.
  • Chandrayaan-2 (2019): the orbiter still works, though the lander crashed.
  • Chandrayaan-3 (2023): the Vikram lander touched down near the south pole on 23 August 2023 (Shiv Shakti point), making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near its south pole; the Pragyan rover confirmed sulphur in the lunar soil. 23 August is now National Space Day.
  • Next: Chandrayaan-4 to bring back lunar samples (targeted for 2028) and LUPEX with Japan.

AP angle: every Indian orbital launch so far has lifted off from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota (Tirupati district), where a Third Launch Pad was approved in January 2025; NARL at Gadanki studies the atmosphere.

From carrying the APPLE satellite on a bullock cart (1981) to landing near the lunar south pole, ISRO shows the power of frugal innovation; reliable launchers and private partners will shape its next phase.
free.g1m-2020-p5-3b:
Satellite orbitsGeostationary orbitSun-synchronous orbitPSLV and GSLV

A satellite stays in orbit because its forward speed balances Earth's gravity; the higher the orbit, the lower the speed needed and the longer the orbital period. Orbits are grouped by height and path into LEO, MEO, GEO and SSO. ISRO, which crossed 100 satellites in 2018 and has also launched over 400 foreign satellites, chooses the orbit to suit the job and the rocket to suit the orbit.

1. LEO and MEO

  • Low Earth orbit: closest to Earth, so satellites move at about 7.8 km/s and circle Earth in roughly 90 minutes. Low height gives sharp images and quick signals, but each satellite sees only a small area, so large constellations are needed; LEO is also the most crowded with debris.
  • Medium Earth orbit: suits navigation, because a few dozen satellites can cover the globe; GPS satellites take about 12 hours per orbit. India's regional NavIC instead uses geostationary and inclined geosynchronous satellites to cover India and about 1,500 km around it.

2. GEO: the "fixed" satellite

  • A satellite at 35,786 km over the equator, moving eastward, takes one sidereal day to orbit and so appears fixed over one spot. Fixed dish antennas can point at it, and three such satellites can cover almost the whole Earth except the poles.
  • It suits TV, DTH, VSAT banking links and weather watch (INSAT-3D series). A geosynchronous orbit with some tilt has the same period but traces a figure-of-eight; only the zero-tilt one over the equator is geostationary.

3. SSO: the imaging orbit

  • A near-polar orbit (inclined about 98°) whose plane turns about one degree a day, keeping pace with Earth's motion around the Sun. The satellite therefore crosses each place at the same local solar time, giving uniform lighting for comparing images over seasons and years.
  • ISRO's remote-sensing fleet (Cartosat, Resourcesat, Oceansat and the radar satellite EOS-04) uses it for crop, forest, water and disaster mapping.

4. PSLV and GSLV launches

  • PSLV became ISRO's workhorse for Sun-synchronous and low orbits, and for deep-space missions on a budget. It suffered back-to-back third-stage failures in PSLV-C61 (May 2025) and C62 (January 2026); a failure analysis committee reported in June 2026.
  • GSLV carries heavier satellites to transfer orbit using a cryogenic upper stage, indigenous since 2014. GSLV-F16 launched NISAR (July 2025), and GSLV-F17 placed EOS-05 (September 2026), India's first imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit.

AP angle: all these launches lift off from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, close to the equator on the east coast, so rockets gain from Earth's eastward spin and spent stages fall into the sea.

Matching the right orbit to each mission underpins communication, navigation and Earth observation. Restoring PSLV's reliability and readying the reusable NGLV are ISRO's next priorities.
free.g1m-2020-p5-4a:
Nuclear fissionThree-stage programmeNPTNSG waiver

Nuclear energy is the energy released when the nucleus of a heavy atom such as uranium-235 splits (fission) or when light nuclei join (fusion). In a reactor a controlled chain reaction heats water into steam that drives a turbine. India runs 24 reactors with 8,780 MW (about 3.1% of electricity in 2024-25) and aims at 100 GW by 2047.

1. Then and now: reactors under construction

The units being built at the end of 2019 included the first 700 MWe PHWRs at Kakrapar and Rawatbhata, the PFBR and Kudankulam 3–4; most are now complete or nearly so. Newer units (Kudankulam 5–6, Gorakhpur 1–2, Kaiga 5–6) are under construction, and NPCIL counted 17 reactors (about 13 GW) under implementation in September 2026.

2. Advantages for India

  • Clean, firm power: near-zero carbon emissions and round-the-clock supply that balances solar and wind.
  • Energy security: India's large thorium reserves (monazite sands of Kerala, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and AP) can be tapped through Homi Bhabha's three-stage programme; the PFBR opens stage II.
  • Small footprint: very high energy density needs little land per unit of power.
  • New momentum: the SHANTI Act, 2025 allows private Indian companies into nuclear power, and the Nuclear Energy Mission (₹20,000 crore) aims at five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033.

3. Disadvantages

  • Cost and delay: high capital cost and long gestation; the PFBR, begun in 2004, reached criticality only in 2026.
  • Fuel dependence: domestic uranium is limited and low-grade, so imports are needed.
  • Safety and waste: the risk of accidents (Fukushima, 2011) and long-lived high-level waste that must be vitrified and stored for centuries.
  • Social and legal hurdles: land acquisition, local protests (Kudankulam, Jaitapur) and earlier liability concerns that kept foreign vendors away.

4. The NPT and its impact on India

  • What it is: the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968; in force 1970) recognises only the five states that tested before 1 January 1967 as nuclear-weapon states; all others must forgo weapons and accept IAEA safeguards. India, Pakistan and Israel never joined.
  • India's stand: the treaty is discriminatory, freezing a nuclear "haves and have-nots" order with no disarmament timetable.
  • Costs: after Pokhran-I (1974) the Nuclear Suppliers Group denied technology and fuel, sanctions followed Pokhran-II (1998), and uranium shortages kept reactors below capacity.
  • Gains: isolation forced self-reliance in PHWRs, fast breeders and enrichment. The 2008 NSG waiver and the Indo-US 123 Agreement then opened uranium imports, and India joined the MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement and Australia Group.
  • Continuing limits: NSG membership is blocked, chiefly by China, which cites India's non-membership of the NPT.

AP angle: NPCIL plans six 1,208 MW reactors at Kovvada (Srikakulam) with US technology, and UCIL mines uranium at Tummalapalle (YSR Kadapa).

Nuclear power is no silver bullet, but as a low-carbon base load it complements renewables. Standardised fleets, an independent regulator and fuel security can make it a pillar of energy security.
free.g1m-2020-p5-5a:
2030 AgendaSustainable Development GoalsSDG India IndexLeave no one behind

In September 2015 all 193 UN member states adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 169 targets that replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals. Built on the promise to "leave no one behind", the goals join the economic, social and environmental pillars of development. India's composite score in NITI Aayog's SDG India Index rose from 57 (2018) to 71 (2023-24).

1. SDG 1: No poverty

  • Jobs-led growth: labour-intensive manufacturing, MSME credit and skilling to absorb farm and informal workers.
  • Social protection: free foodgrains under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, PM-KISAN income support, 125 days of rural wage work under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (which replaced MGNREGA in July 2026), housing (PMAY) and Jan Dhan-linked insurance and pensions.
  • Target lagging regions: focus on high-poverty States and aspirational districts, tribal and minority groups.

2. SDG 3: Good health and well-being

  • Primary care first: about 1.82 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for maternal care, immunisation and NCD screening.
  • Financial protection: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (₹5 lakh per family); raise public health spending towards the 2.5% of GDP goal of the National Health Policy, 2017.
  • Disease programmes: TB Mukt Bharat, malaria elimination by 2030, Mission Indradhanush and the HPV vaccine.

3. SDG 6: Clean water and sanitation

  • Finish and sustain: complete the Jal Jeevan Mission (extended to December 2028) and keep villages ODF Plus through solid and liquid waste management.
  • Source sustainability and quality: groundwater recharge, water budgeting, removing fluoride and arsenic, and treating and reusing urban wastewater (Namami Gange, AMRUT).

4. SDG 7: Affordable and clean energy

  • Renewables with storage: reach 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 with battery and pumped storage and green energy corridors.
  • Households and farms: PM Surya Ghar rooftop solar, PM-KUSUM solar pumps, Ujjwala LPG for clean cooking, and energy-efficiency drives such as LED lighting.

5. Enablers: localising the goals

Progress depends on States and panchayats, on reliable data (MoSPI's National Indicator Framework), on finance (green bonds, CSR) and on partnerships with civil society.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh is a Front Runner in the SDG India Index; its maternal mortality ratio of 30 (2021–23) already beats the SDG target, its Clean Energy Policy (2024) serves SDG 7, and its natural-farming programme serves SDGs 2 and 15.

With barely four years left, India can meet these goals only if growth stays inclusive and green, States and panchayats lead implementation, and data track the last mile, so that truly no one is left behind.
free.g1m-2020-p5-5b:
Plate tectonicsElastic reboundEarthquake early warningDisaster response

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground caused by the release of strain energy stored in rocks. The energy travels as seismic waves from the focus (hypocentre) underground; the point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre. About 59% of India's land is prone to moderate to severe earthquakes, as Latur (1993) and Bhuj (2001) showed.

1. What causes earthquakes

  • Plate tectonics: most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries where plates collide, separate or slide past one another. The Indian Plate moves north by about 4–5 cm a year into the Eurasian Plate, building stress along the Himalaya and the North-East.
  • Faulting and elastic rebound: rocks bend under stress until they suddenly break and slip along a fault, releasing the stored energy.
  • Intraplate earthquakes: old weak zones inside a plate can reactivate, as at Latur and in the Kutch region (Bhuj).
  • Volcanic and human-induced quakes: magma movement; filling of large reservoirs (Koyna, 1967), deep mining and fluid injection.
  • Measurement: magnitude (energy released, on a logarithmic scale) differs from intensity (damage at a place); India's National Center for Seismology (MoES) monitors earthquakes.

2. Can we prevent or predict them?

  • Prevention: natural earthquakes cannot be prevented; only human-induced ones can be reduced by regulating reservoir filling, mining and injection.
  • Prediction: science cannot yet predict the exact time, place and size of an earthquake. It can only forecast where strong shaking is likely, through seismic zoning (BIS Zones II–V; the 2025 code's Zone VI was withdrawn in March 2026), fault mapping and the study of "seismic gaps".
  • Early warning: sensors that detect the fast but weak P-waves can warn of strong shaking a few seconds to tens of seconds in advance, enough to stop trains and lifts; IIT Roorkee runs such a system in Uttarakhand, and SACHET added cell-broadcast alerts in 2026.
  • The real answer is mitigation: "earthquakes do not kill, buildings do", so seismic building codes (IS 1893, IS 13920), retrofitting of schools and hospitals, and microzonation of cities matter most.

3. Relief after an earthquake: inland and coastal regions

  • Common steps: search and rescue in the first 72 hours by NDRF and SDRF teams; triage and field hospitals; safe water, food, tents and toilets to prevent epidemics; checks on damaged buildings before people return; and psychosocial care. NDMA, SDMAs and DDMAs coordinate under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.

AP angle: most of Andhra Pradesh lies in the lower-hazard Zones II and III, but its 1,053 km coast was hit by the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. INCOIS, Hyderabad, now issues tsunami alerts, and the NDRF's 10th Battalion is based at Vijayawada.

Earthquakes cannot be stopped or precisely predicted, but deaths can be prevented. Safer buildings, early warning and trained communities, in line with the Sendai Framework, turn a natural hazard into a manageable event rather than a disaster.
free.g1m-2020-p5-6a:
Solid wasteSource segregationWaste hierarchySanitary landfill

Solid waste is any discarded solid or semi-solid material from homes, markets, industries, farms, hospitals and construction sites. Indian cities generate about 1.6 lakh tonnes of municipal waste a day (CPCB, 2020-21), and the quantity rises with urbanisation and consumption. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 (in force from 1 April 2026) make four-stream segregation at source the foundation of scientific management.

1. Classification of solid waste

  • By nature: roughly half of Indian city waste is wet organic matter, which suits composting and biogas rather than burning; dry waste includes recyclables and inert material.
  • By risk: hazardous, biomedical, e-waste and battery waste are handled under separate rules, because of toxicity or infection.

2. Steps to manage solid waste

  • Reduce at source: extended producer responsibility (EPR) for plastics, e-waste and batteries, and the ban on identified single-use plastics (1 July 2022).
  • Segregation and collection: households separate wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste; bulk generators must process wet waste on site; covered, compartmentalised vehicles and transfer stations carry the rest to processing plants.
  • Processing: composting and vermicomposting, biomethanation to biogas or bio-CNG (Indore), material recovery facilities that send dry waste to recyclers, and refuse-derived fuel for cement kilns.
  • Waste-to-energy and disposal: incineration only for non-recyclable dry waste; inert rejects go to an engineered landfill.
  • Legacy dumps: biomining under Swachh Bharat Mission–Urban 2.0 had cleared 1,048 of 2,476 dumpsites by November 2025.

3. Landfills: advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages: simple and cheap for waste that cannot be processed; a sanitary landfill with a liner, leachate collection and daily soil cover limits pollution; landfill gas (methane) can be captured for energy; closed sites can become parks.
  • Disadvantages: it needs large areas of scarce urban land; leachate can poison groundwater; methane is a potent greenhouse gas and causes fires (Ghazipur, Delhi; Brahmapuram, Kochi, 2023); it breeds flies and rodents and harms waste-pickers; and it buries resources that could be recovered. Most Indian "landfills" are open dumps without liners.

AP angle: under Swachh Andhra, the State aimed to clear about 86 lakh tonnes of legacy waste by 2 October 2025, runs waste-to-energy plants at Visakhapatnam and Guntur, and saw Vijayawada, Guntur and Tirupati enter the Super Swachh League (2024-25).

Following the waste hierarchy (reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and only then landfill) turns waste into a resource and moves cities towards a circular economy.
free.g1m-2020-p5-6b:
Soil erosionLand degradationAgents of erosionSoil conservation

Soil erosion is the detachment and removal of the fertile topsoil by water, wind and other agents faster than new soil can form, which takes centuries. It is the main form of land degradation in India: ISRO's Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (2021) found 97.85 million hectares (29.7% of India) degraded in 2018-19, with water erosion the biggest cause.

1. Agents of soil erosion

  • Running water: raindrops, surface run-off and rivers; the most widespread agent, especially during intense monsoon showers on bare slopes.
  • Wind: lifts and drifts fine, dry soil in arid and semi-arid areas such as the Thar and parts of Rayalaseema.
  • Waves, ice and gravity: sea waves erode coasts; glaciers scour Himalayan valleys; landslides strip hill slopes.
  • Biotic agents: people and animals, through deforestation, overgrazing, shifting cultivation, mining and ploughing up and down slopes.

2. Stages of soil erosion

Every erosion event has three stages: detachment of particles, their transport by water or wind, and deposition elsewhere, often in rivers and reservoirs. Water erosion grows through five forms:

3. Effects of soil erosion

  • Lower farm output: loss of topsoil, organic carbon and nutrients reduces yields and raises fertiliser costs.
  • Silting: reservoirs, canals and tanks lose storage capacity; river beds rise and floods worsen.
  • Desertification and landslides in dry and hilly areas; water pollution from sediment and farm chemicals.
  • Social costs: falling incomes, farm distress and migration.

4. Factors affecting soil erosion

  • Climate: intensity and amount of rainfall and wind speed.
  • Soil: texture, structure and organic matter; loose sandy or silty soils erode easily.
  • Topography: steeper and longer slopes speed up run-off.
  • Vegetation cover: roots bind soil and canopy breaks the force of rain.
  • Human practices: tillage, cropping pattern, grazing and mining. Together these factors make up the Universal Soil Loss Equation (A = R × K × LS × C × P: rainfall, soil erodibility, slope, cover and practice).

5. Measures to conserve soil

AP angle: wind erosion and drought threaten Anantapur; shifting (podu) cultivation erodes Eastern Ghats slopes; sea erosion has eaten into Uppada village near Kakinada; casuarina shelter belts guard the coast, and natural farming (APCNF) keeps soil covered through pre-monsoon dry sowing and mulching.

Soil is a slowly renewable resource that is lost in a few rainy seasons. A watershed approach that combines vegetation, simple structures and farmers' participation is the surest way to conserve soil for future generations.
free.g1m-2020-p5-7a:
Gene therapyTransgenic organismsGenome editingBioethics

Yes, the three differ in aim and method, though all alter genetic material. Gene therapy treats a patient's disease by adding, silencing or correcting genes in his or her cells. A transgenic organism carries a gene from another species, introduced by recombinant DNA technology. Genome editing (such as CRISPR-Cas9, 2012) makes precise changes in an organism's own DNA; used beyond treating disease, to improve normal traits, it becomes gene enhancement.

1. Ethical concerns in gene therapy

  • Safety: viral vectors can trigger severe immune reactions or insert into the wrong place and cause cancer; a US trial volunteer, Jesse Gelsinger, died in 1999.
  • Cost and equity: some therapies cost crores of rupees per patient; India's NexCAR19 shows cheaper local options are possible.
  • Consent: patients are often children or desperate adults, so informed, voluntary consent needs special care.

2. Ethical concerns with transgenic organisms

  • Biosafety: gene flow to wild relatives, harm to non-target insects and resistant pests (pink bollworm now resists Bt cotton).
  • Farmers and markets: seed monopolies, debt and the right to save seed; consumer choice and labelling of GM food.
  • Animal welfare: transgenic animals used as "bioreactors" or disease models suffer.
  • Governance: in India the GEAC must approve release; Bt brinjal has been under a moratorium since 2010, and GM mustard awaits a Supreme Court ruling.

3. Ethical concerns with genome editing and enhancement

  • Germline editing: changes in embryos pass to future generations, who cannot consent. In 2018 a Chinese scientist, He Jiankui, edited twin embryos and was jailed in 2019.
  • Enhancement and inequality: editing for height, intelligence or looks revives eugenics and could create a genetic divide between rich and poor.
  • Unknown risks: off-target cuts and mosaicism; gene drives could alter wild populations irreversibly; dual-use (bioweapon) fears.

4. When can genome editing be considered ethical?

  • In medicine, editing a patient's own cells to treat a grave disease (as Casgevy and India's BIRSA 101 do for sickle cell disease) meets these tests; India's ICMR guidelines (2019) prohibit germline gene therapy.
  • In crops, edits without foreign DNA (SDN-1 and SDN-2) are exempt from GM rules since March 2022, but still need biosafety checks and transparency.

AP angle: India's first genome-edited rice varieties (May 2025) were developed from Samba Mahsuri, bred at Bapatla, and MTU 1010, bred at Maruteru.

Genetic technologies are tools, not ends. Guided by bioethics, strong regulation and public dialogue, genome editing can relieve suffering without crossing into designer babies.
free.g1m-2020-p5-7b:
CRISPR-Cas9Bacterial immunityGuide RNAGenome editing

The 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna for developing CRISPR-Cas9, the "genetic scissors" that can cut DNA at almost any chosen site. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is a stretch of bacterial DNA that, together with Cas (CRISPR-associated) proteins, forms a natural immune system against viruses that infect bacteria (bacteriophages).

1. How CRISPR functions in nature

  • Memory (adaptation): when a phage attacks, Cas proteins snip a short piece of its DNA and insert it as a spacer between the repeats of the bacterium's CRISPR array, a genetic record of past infections.
  • Expression: the array is copied into RNA and cut into short CRISPR RNAs; in the Cas9 system a second RNA, tracrRNA (discovered by Charpentier), pairs with each of them.
  • Interference: on a fresh attack, the RNA guides Cas9 to the matching viral DNA, and Cas9 cuts both strands, disabling the virus. A short "PAM" sequence next to the target tells Cas9 that the DNA is foreign, so the bacterium does not cut its own array.

2. Adaptation for research

  • Programmable scissors (2012): Charpentier and Doudna fused the two RNAs into a single guide RNA. By changing its 20-letter sequence, scientists can send Cas9 to any gene in any organism.
  • Repair does the editing: the cell mends the cut either by joining the ends, which often disables (knocks out) the gene, or by copying a supplied template, which makes a precise correction or insertion.
  • Wider toolkit: "dead" Cas9 switches genes on or off without cutting; base and prime editors change single letters; Cas12a and Cas13 target DNA and RNA.
  • Uses: finding gene functions, making disease models in mice and organoids, screening drug targets and breeding crops: India's genome-edited rice varieties Kamala and Pusa DST Rice 1 (May 2025).

3. Clinical and diagnostic applications

  • Casgevy reactivates fetal haemoglobin, freeing many patients from regular blood transfusions; it was the world's first approved CRISPR medicine.
  • In-body editing delivers CRISPR directly to the liver or eye and is in clinical trials abroad.

4. Concerns

  • Off-target cuts and incomplete editing; very high cost (Casgevy costs over US$2 million in the USA).
  • Germline editing is banned in India; the 2018 gene-edited babies in China showed the danger.
  • Patent disputes and biosafety of gene drives in the wild.

AP angle: the genome-edited Kamala rice was derived from Samba Mahsuri, bred at Bapatla, and sickle cell disease, common among tribal communities including those of AP's Agency areas, is the first target of India's CRISPR therapy.

From a bacterial defence to a medicine, CRISPR shows how basic research becomes precision medicine. Affordable access and strict ethical oversight will decide its benefits.
free.g1m-2020-p5-8a:
Communicable diseasesTuberculosisMalariaAvian influenza

Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa or worms) that spread through air, water, food, insect vectors or contact with infected animals. India has eliminated polio (2014) but still carries about 25% of the world's tuberculosis cases, a shrinking malaria burden and recurring zoonotic threats such as bird flu. Three are discussed here: tuberculosis, malaria and avian flu.

1. Tuberculosis

  • Causes: the bacterium discovered by Robert Koch (1882) spreads through the air when a person with lung TB coughs; undernutrition, HIV, diabetes, smoking and crowded, ill-ventilated homes raise the risk.
  • Treatment: diagnosis by sputum tests and rapid molecular machines (including India's own Truenat); free drugs under the National TB Elimination Programme (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), and the short BPaLM regimen for drug-resistant TB.
  • Prevention: BCG vaccine, preventive treatment for household contacts, Ni-kshay Poshan nutrition support and Ni-kshay Mitras; TB incidence fell 21% between 2015 and 2024.

2. Malaria

  • Causes: Plasmodium parasites, mainly P. vivax and the more dangerous P. falciparum (cerebral malaria), carried by the female Anopheles mosquito, which breeds in clean, stagnant water; forest and tribal belts are hit hardest.
  • Treatment: confirm by rapid test or microscopy; chloroquine with 14 days of primaquine for vivax; artemisinin-based combination therapy for falciparum.
  • Prevention: long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor residual spraying, Gambusia and guppy fish, and source reduction. WHO has recommended two vaccines (RTS,S and R21), and ICMR's AdFalciVax is under development. India's cases fell by 80.5% between 2015 and 2023; it left WHO's High Burden to High Impact group in 2024 and targets elimination by 2030.

3. Avian flu (bird flu)

  • Causes: highly pathogenic influenza A(H5N1), carried by migratory birds to poultry; humans catch it rarely, through close contact with sick birds or raw poultry, but it can be fatal. Sustained human-to-human spread has not been seen.
  • Treatment: early oseltamivir (Tamiflu), oxygen and intensive care, with isolation of the patient.
  • Prevention: culling of birds near an outbreak, disinfection and surveillance with compensation to farmers; protective gear for cullers; cooking chicken and eggs thoroughly; One Health surveillance linking human and animal laboratories (ICMR-NIV Pune; NIHSAD Bhopal).

AP angle: in March 2025 a two-year-old girl from Narasaraopet (Palnadu) died of H5N1 at AIIMS Mangalagiri (confirmed by ICMR-NIV Pune), after bird-flu outbreaks in poultry in the State; malaria in AP is concentrated in the tribal Agency areas.

Early diagnosis, complete treatment and vector and animal surveillance are common to all three. A One Health approach can make TB Mukt Bharat and malaria elimination achievable.
free.g1m-2020-p5-8b:
Recombinant DNARestriction enzymesCloning vectorsGenetic engineering

Recombinant DNA (rDNA) is DNA made by joining pieces of DNA from two different sources, usually a gene of interest and a carrier DNA called a vector, so that the gene can be copied and expressed in a host cell. In 1973 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer first placed a gene into a bacterial plasmid and multiplied it in E. coli, laying the foundation of genetic engineering.

1. Steps in creating rDNA

  • Isolation: DNA is extracted from cells (enzymes break cell walls, proteins and RNA are removed, DNA is precipitated with chilled ethanol); the desired gene may be amplified by PCR.
  • Cutting: the gene and the vector are cut with the same restriction enzyme, so their ends match.
  • Joining: DNA ligase seals the gene into the opened vector, forming rDNA.
  • Transformation: the rDNA enters host cells through calcium chloride treatment and heat shock, electroporation, microinjection, a gene gun or Agrobacterium.
  • Selection and expression: only cells carrying the vector survive on antibiotic medium; they are grown in bioreactors, and the product is purified (downstream processing).

2. Role of restriction enzymes

  • "Molecular scissors": bacteria make them to cut the DNA of invading viruses, while protecting their own DNA by methylation.
  • Specific sites: each enzyme recognises a short palindromic sequence; EcoRI cuts GAATTC between G and A.
  • Sticky ends: a staggered cut leaves single-stranded overhangs that pair with any DNA cut by the same enzyme, which is what allows the gene and vector to be joined. Some enzymes leave blunt ends.
  • Mapping and fingerprinting: the pieces they produce are separated by gel electrophoresis for gene mapping and DNA fingerprinting.

3. Role of vectors

  • Vehicles: vectors carry the foreign gene into the host and make it multiply there. Common ones are plasmids (such as pBR322), bacteriophages, the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium for plants, and disabled viruses for animal cells and gene therapy.
  • Features of a good vector: an origin of replication (ori) so it copies itself, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene to identify transformed cells, unique cloning sites for restriction enzymes, and small size.
  • Expression vectors also carry a promoter so that the host makes the protein.

4. Examples of rDNA technology

  • Human insulin: genes for its two chains were placed in E. coli; recombinant insulin (Humulin, approved in 1982) was the first rDNA medicine and largely replaced insulin from animal pancreas.
  • Others: the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (made in yeast), Corbevax, growth hormone, and Bt cotton, whose cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis kills bollworms.

AP angle: Bt cotton (approved in 2002) dominates the cotton fields of Guntur, Kurnool and Prakasam; and Andhra Pradesh's bioeconomy (US$13.74 billion, 2025) ranks fifth among the States.

rDNA technology turned living cells into factories for medicines, vaccines and better crops. Used with sound biosafety rules, it remains the backbone of modern biotechnology.
free.g1m-2020-p5-9a:
Intellectual propertyCopyright, patent, trademarkInventor's exclusive rightsParis, PCT and TRIPS

Intellectual property (IP) means creations of the mind: inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, brand names and symbols. The law gives their creators exclusive rights, usually for a limited time, so that they can recover the cost of creating them; in return, society gains the knowledge, because a patent must disclose the invention in full. The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) groups IP into industrial property (patents, trademarks, designs, geographical indications) and copyright.

1. Copyright, patents and trademarks: the differences

  • Copyright protects expression, not the idea: anyone may write another story about a farmer's struggle, but may not copy the text or the film of an existing one.
  • A patent protects how a thing works: even someone who invents the same thing independently cannot use it without a licence.
  • A trademark protects identity, not the product: others may sell butter, but not under a confusingly similar name or logo.

2. Rights of an inventor

  • Exclusive right (Section 48, Patents Act): to stop others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the patented product, or using the patented process, in India without consent.
  • Right to exploit: to license, assign or mortgage the patent, earn royalties and be named as the inventor.
  • Right to sue: for an injunction, damages or an account of profits against infringers.
  • Limits: the right lasts 20 years, is territorial, needs annual renewal fees and must be worked in India; compulsory licences (Natco–Bayer, 2012), government use and research exemptions balance it with the public interest.

3. How rights are gained and enforced globally

  • No "world patent": rights are granted country by country. The Paris Convention (1883) gives a 12-month priority right, and the Patent Cooperation Treaty (India joined in 1998) allows one international application. Trademarks use the Madrid Protocol (India, 2013); copyright is automatic in all Berne Convention countries.
  • Enforcement: through national courts and customs, such as the Delhi High Court's IP Division. The WTO's TRIPS Agreement (1995) sets minimum standards and requires effective remedies; disputes between states go to the WTO, and private disputes can go to WIPO's Arbitration and Mediation Center.

India's National IPR Policy (2016), "Creative India; Innovative India", seeks to raise both the creation and the enforcement of IP; patent filings reached 1,10,375 in 2024-25, 62% by Indian residents. A balanced IP regime that rewards inventors while protecting access is the way forward.
free.g1m-2020-p5-10b:
Satellite educationSITE and EDUSATPM eVIDYA DTH channelsSatellite broadband

The Covid-19 lockdowns of 2020–21 shut schools and colleges for months and exposed India's digital divide: online classes needed a smartphone and data, which many rural, tribal and poor students lacked. Satellites can reach every village at once, without cables. India's space programme has used this power for education since the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE, 1975–76), and it can now help restore and widen access to learning.

1. A legacy of space-based education

  • SITE beamed lessons on health, farming and schooling to villages in six States and proved that satellite TV could teach.
  • EDUSAT linked studios with thousands of virtual classrooms for interactive teaching and teacher training.

2. Role during and after the pandemic

  • PM eVIDYA (May 2020): "One Class, One TV Channel", now 200 DTH TV channels for classes 1–12 in about 30 Indian languages, including an Indian Sign Language channel; it reaches homes with no internet.
  • SWAYAM Prabha: DTH channels for college-level courses linked to the SWAYAM platform.
  • Free reach: the channels are uplinked by BISAG-N, Gandhinagar, and carried on free-to-air DTH platforms such as DD Free Dish, so a dish and a TV set are enough.
  • Blended with online platforms: DIKSHA and SWAYAM served students with internet, while satellite TV covered those without it.

3. How space can expand access further

  • Satellite broadband: high-throughput satellites such as GSAT-N2 (2024) and private low-orbit constellations can connect schools in tribal hills, islands and Ladakh, where fibre is costly, complementing BharatNet.
  • Interactive classrooms: two-way satellite networks on the EDUSAT model allow live doubt-clearing, virtual labs and teacher training at scale.
  • Earth-observation learning: ISRO's Bhuvan geoportal and the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's online outreach courses teach geography, GIS and disaster management.
  • Inspiring STEM: Chandrayaan-3 (2023), National Space Day (23 August) and ISRO's YUVIKA programme for school students draw young people to science.

4. Challenges

  • One-way broadcasts lack interaction; many homes lack TVs, power or devices; content must be local and in the mother tongue; satellite bandwidth is costly; and teachers need training to blend broadcast and classroom teaching.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh was one of SITE's six States, ISRO's first telemedicine link (2001) reached Aragonda in Chittoor district, and AP Fibernet carries BharatNet to panchayats; satellite classrooms can serve tribal schools of the Eastern Ghats.

Blending satellite TV, satellite broadband and classroom teaching can make Indian education pandemic-proof and truly inclusive.
free.g1m-2020-p5-11a:
NeGP and e-KrantiDigital IndiaJAM trinityBharatNet

The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP), approved in May 2006, aimed to make all government services accessible to the common man in his locality, efficiently, transparently and at affordable cost. It combined Mission Mode Projects (MMPs) with shared digital infrastructure. Under Digital India (launched on 1 July 2015) it was revamped as e-Kranti, "NeGP 2.0", one of the programme's nine pillars.

1. NeGP under Digital India

  • Mission Mode Projects: 27 MMPs at first (later 31) in central, State and integrated categories, such as passports, income tax, MCA21, land records, e-District and e-Procurement; e-Kranti raised the list to 44, adding education, health, agriculture and others.
  • Core infrastructure: State Wide Area Networks, State Data Centres and Common Services Centres (CSCs) in villages.
  • Approach: "centralised initiative, decentralised implementation"; e-Kranti added principles such as "transformation, not translation", mobile first and cloud by default.
  • Digital India's three vision areas: digital infrastructure as a utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment of citizens.

2. Role of three projects

  • Jan Dhan Yojana: the account is the "J" of the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile), which carries Direct Benefit Transfer of LPG subsidy, scholarships, wages and PM-KISAN money, cutting out middlemen and ghost beneficiaries. About 56% of accounts belong to women and 78% are in rural or semi-urban areas; during the 2020 lockdown, cash support went straight into women's Jan Dhan accounts.
  • DigiLocker: a cloud wallet of authentic e-documents such as Aadhaar, driving licences, vehicle papers and marksheets, legally equal to the originals (2016 rules). It is the "paperless" layer of the India Stack, cutting queues, forgery and repeated verification.
  • BharatNet: the broadband highway of rural India. Phase I reached 1 lakh panchayats (2017); the amended programme (August 2023) extends fibre to all villages in a ring network. It powers CSCs, e-District services, PM-WANI Wi-Fi, telemedicine and online classes.

3. The other projects in brief

  • The National Digital Literacy Mission, followed by PMGDISHA (target: 6 crore rural citizens), builds the skills needed to use these services, while e-Bhasha sought e-content in Indian languages, a goal now carried forward by Bhashini (2022).

AP angle: AP Fibernet carries BharatNet to panchayats, about 15,000 village and ward secretariats deliver services at the doorstep, and Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance offered 1,126 services by July 2026.

NeGP's journey into Digital India marks a shift from computerising offices to citizen-centric digital public infrastructure; closing the digital divide and protecting data under the DPDP Act, 2023, are the next steps.
free.g1m-2020-p5-11b:
BiofuelsEthanol blending (E20)National Policy on BiofuelsEnergy security

Biofuels are liquid or gaseous fuels made from biomass, such as bioethanol, biodiesel, compressed biogas (CBG) and sustainable aviation fuel. Unlike fossil fuels they are renewable, since they recycle carbon that plants absorbed recently. For India, which imports about 89% of its crude oil, they are a home-grown substitute; ethanol blending in petrol reached E20 (20%) in 2025.

1. Types of biofuels

  • Gaseous biofuels: biogas and CBG from cattle dung, press mud, crop residue and city waste (GOBARdhan, SATAT).

2. Importance to India's economy

  • Energy security and foreign exchange: blending since 2014 has saved about ₹1.4 lakh crore of foreign exchange, a cushion during oil shocks such as the 2026 Hormuz crisis.
  • Farm incomes: farmers have received about ₹1.2 lakh crore, and sugar mills earn from surplus cane and molasses, which eases cane-price arrears.
  • Waste to wealth: 2G ethanol and CBG turn stubble, dung and urban waste into fuel, reducing stubble burning and methane.
  • Rural jobs and investment: distilleries and CBG plants (over 130 commissioned by November 2025, against a target of 5,000) create rural employment.
  • Climate and clean air: lower carbon emissions support the Panchamrit goals; India also launched the Global Biofuels Alliance during its G20 presidency (2023).

3. National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 (amended 2022)

  • Categories: "basic" biofuels (1G ethanol, biodiesel) and "advanced" biofuels (2G ethanol, CBG, drop-in fuels), with extra incentives for the latter.
  • Wider feedstocks: cane juice, B-heavy molasses, damaged grains, maize and cassava; surplus food grains only with the approval of the National Biofuel Coordination Committee.
  • Targets: the 2022 amendment advanced E20 from 2030 to 2025-26, and it was achieved in 2025; the 2018 policy also aimed at 5% biodiesel in diesel by 2030.
  • Support: PM JI-VAN (2019) funds 2G bio-refineries and SATAT (2018) assures purchase of CBG; the amendment also allows production in SEZs and export units.
  • Next steps: standards for E22–E30 petrol were notified in May 2026, though no higher blending target had been fixed by October 2026; sustainable aviation fuel is to make up 1% of fuel for international flights by 2027.
  • Concerns: food-versus-fuel trade-offs, water-hungry sugarcane and mileage complaints from older vehicles call for a faster shift to 2G feedstocks and flex-fuel vehicles.

AP angle: Reliance laid the foundation of the first of 500 planned CBG plants in Andhra Pradesh in the Kanigiri area of Prakasam district (April 2025), a ₹65,000-crore programme using Napier grass grown on wasteland.

Balanced with food and water security, biofuels can turn farm and urban waste into energy self-reliance.
free.g1m-2020-p5-12a:
Scientific publicationsIndia's research outputR&D spending (GERD)ANRF

Science and engineering (S&E) publications are a common measure of a country's research output. The table shows world output rising from about 17.6 lakh articles in 2008 to 25.6 lakh in 2018, a growth of 3.83% a year. It reveals a shift of research power towards Asia: China overtook the USA, and India climbed to third place with the fastest growth among the top five, although its share of world output stayed small.

1. Interpreting the data

  • China overtook the USA: China more than doubled its output to become the largest producer (20.67%), while US output was almost flat.
  • India's rapid rise: India's output grew about 2.8 times, the fastest among the top five (10.73% a year), and it overtook Germany and Japan to become third.
  • But a small share: India's 5.31% share is about a quarter of China's; China published about 3.9 articles for every Indian article.
  • Low output per person: Germany, with about one-sixteenth of India's population, published about three-quarters as many articles.
  • Concentration: the top three produced 42.52% of world output, while Japan's output actually fell.

2. One factor: low investment in research

  • Low spending: India's gross expenditure on R&D (GERD) is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24) against China's 2.58%; the 2% target set in 2003 is still unmet.
  • Few researchers: 354 per million people (2023-24), a fraction of the level in advanced economies.
  • Weak university research: most State universities do little research, and competitive extramural grants are only about 1.4% of GERD.
  • Result: research is concentrated in a few elite institutions such as IISc, the IITs and CSIR labs, so India cannot match China's scale, and quality and citations lag behind quantity.

3. Policy measure: fund research through ANRF and raise GERD

  • Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023): about ₹50,000 crore over 2023–28; its PAIR programme links top institutions with State universities as hubs and spokes.
  • Private R&D: the ₹1 lakh crore RDI scheme (2025) gives long-term, low-cost finance for research in sunrise sectors.
  • Access and quality: One Nation, One Subscription (2025) opens journals to public institutions; grants should reward quality (citations, patents, licences) rather than paper counts.
  • Road map: a time-bound path to 2% of GDP, with tax credits for industry R&D and more PhD fellowships.

Update and AP angle: India remained third in publications in 2022, with a 6.2% share (DST). In Andhra Pradesh, IIT and IISER Tirupati, NARL Gadanki and the Amaravati Quantum Valley can lift research if State universities are linked to them through PAIR-type partnerships.

India has the quantity momentum; sustained funding and a focus on quality can turn it into scientific leadership.
free.g1m-2020-p5-12b:
Forest coverRecorded forest areaIndia State of Forest ReportTrees outside forests

Forest cover and forest area (recorded forest area) are two different measures, both reported every two years by the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, in the India State of Forest Report (ISFR). Forest cover describes what is actually on the ground, as seen from satellites; recorded forest area describes the legal status of land in government records. So a piece of land can be forest in one sense but not in the other.

1. Forest cover vs recorded forest area

  • Overlap, not identity: much forest cover lies inside recorded forests, but some recorded forest land has no trees, and some forest cover (plantations, orchards, agroforestry) lies outside it.
  • Tree cover is a separate measure: patches of trees smaller than 1 ha outside recorded forests. Scrub, with canopy below 10%, is not forest cover.

2. What the graph shows (FSI, 2001–2017)

  • Forest cover rose steadily: from 675,538 sq km (2001) to 708,273 sq km (2017), a gain of about 32,700 sq km (4.8%), or from about 20.6% to 21.5% of India's geographical area.
  • Forest area stayed almost flat: between about 764,600 and 774,700 sq km, ending slightly below its 2001 level; the legal forest estate barely changed, with small shifts from updated State records and diversion of forest land for projects.
  • The gap narrowed: from about 92,900 sq km to about 59,100 sq km, because tree canopy grew faster than the legal forest estate.
  • Why cover rose: plantations and afforestation (CAMPA, Green India Mission), agroforestry and Joint Forest Management, and partly finer satellite resolution and better interpretation, so not all of the gain is new forest.
  • Caution: a canopy-based count includes orchards and coconut or rubber plantations, so it can rise even while dense natural forest is lost.

3. The latest position (ISFR 2023)

  • Forest cover is 7,15,343 sq km (21.76% of the geographical area) and tree cover 1,12,014 sq km (3.41%), together 25.17%, against the 33% goal of the National Forest Policy, 1988.
  • Recorded forest area is still larger than forest cover, at a little under a quarter of the geographical area; a sizeable part of forest cover lies outside recorded forests, while part of the recorded forest land has little or no tree canopy.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's forest cover is about 30,085 sq km (18.46%), down about 139 sq km since 2021, and its 421 sq km of mangroves are fourth in the country.

Rising canopy over a static legal forest estate is welcome, but forest quality, meaning dense, natural and biodiverse forest, matters more than canopy counts.
free.g1m-2020-p5-13a:
Climate justiceCBDR-RCLoss and damageClimate finance

Climate justice treats climate change as a question of fairness, not only of science: those who did least to cause warming, and can least afford to adapt, should not bear its heaviest costs. It applies between countries (historical polluters versus the Global South), within countries (the poor, women, farmers, fishers, tribal people) and across generations. Its legal anchor is the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) in the UNFCCC (1992).

1. Why it is a question of justice

  • Historical responsibility: since 1850 the USA has emitted about a fifth of cumulative CO2; India, home to about 18% of humanity, about 3%.
  • Unequal emissions today: India's per-capita emissions are less than half the world average.
  • Unequal impacts: small islands, deltas and drylands face sea-level rise, cyclones and heat with the least money to cope.
  • Broken promises: the US$100 billion a year pledged at Copenhagen (2009) was first met only in 2022, and the USA's second exit from the Paris Agreement took effect in January 2026.

2. Coverage in news media and publications such as Time

  • Youth and future generations: Time named the 16-year-old Swedish activist Greta Thunberg its Person of the Year for 2019, the youngest ever, putting the "Fridays for Future" school strikes and the rights of future generations on front pages worldwide.
  • New vocabulary: several newsrooms, such as The Guardian (2019), switched to "climate crisis", and hundreds of outlets joined the Covering Climate Now partnership (2019).
  • Loss and damage stories: reporting on Pakistan's floods (2022), Pacific islands and Indian heat waves framed disasters as unjust costs borne by those who polluted least; the ICJ advisory opinion (July 2025) on states' climate duties made headlines.
  • Gaps: coverage peaks around disasters and COPs and then fades, and Global North voices dominate over affected communities.

3. Measures aligned to climate justice

  • Climate finance as grants: deliver the new goal of US$300 billion a year by 2035 (COP29) mainly as grants and cheap loans, not debt.
  • Loss and Damage Fund: agreed at COP27 and launched at COP28 (2023); it must be fully funded and reach affected communities quickly.
  • Adaptation and just transition: COP30 (Belém, 2025) agreed to triple adaptation finance by 2035 and set up a just transition mechanism.
  • Technology and fair carbon space: affordable transfer of clean technology and earlier net zero by rich countries.
  • Justice at home: Mission LiFE (2022), heat action plans and social protection for informal workers.

AP angle: fishers and farmers on AP's cyclone-prone coast and in drought-hit Rayalaseema are on the front line; AP Community Managed Natural Farming, a joint winner of the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity (2024), shows a people-led adaptation path.

Climate justice turns the climate debate from charity to equity; COP31 (Antalya, November 2026) must translate it into money, technology and protection for the most vulnerable.
free.g1m-2020-p5-13b:
Ozone layerGround-level ozoneOzone-depleting substancesMontreal Protocol

The graphic shows how ozone (O3) varies with height. Near the ground its concentration is very low; it rises sharply above about 15 km, peaks at nearly 8 parts per million at about 35 km in the stratosphere, and falls to almost nothing above about 70 km in the mesosphere. This band is the ozone layer, which holds about 90% of the atmosphere's ozone and absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV-B) rays.

1. What the graphic shows

  • Formation: in the stratosphere, short-wave UV splits oxygen molecules (O2) into atoms, which join other O2 molecules to form O3; ozone then absorbs UV-B and splits again, turning UV energy into heat. This is why temperature rises with height in the stratosphere.
  • The peak: lower down there is too little short-wave UV to split oxygen; higher up the air is too thin to make much ozone.
  • Troposphere: ozone here is a secondary pollutant, a small but harmful part of smog.

2. (a) How human activity affects ozone

  • Thinning the "good" ozone: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from refrigerators, air-conditioners and aerosol sprays, halons from fire extinguishers, carbon tetrachloride and methyl bromide drift up to the stratosphere. UV frees chlorine and bromine atoms, and one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
  • The ozone hole: each spring (September–October), polar stratospheric clouds speed up this destruction over Antarctica; the 2024 hole peaked at 22.4 million sq km.
  • Repair through treaties: the Montreal Protocol (1987), the first treaty ratified by every country, has phased out about 99% of controlled ozone-depleting substances; the layer should recover to 1980 levels by about 2040 (about 2066 over Antarctica). The Kigali Amendment (2016), ratified by India in 2021, phases down HFCs, the ozone-safe but heat-trapping substitutes; India's freeze comes in 2028.
  • Adding "bad" ozone near the ground: nitrogen oxides (NOx) from vehicles and power plants and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from fuels, solvents and biomass burning react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone, which is highest on sunny afternoons.

3. (b) How ozone affects human health

  • Loss of the shield: more UV-B causes skin cancers, including melanoma, cataracts, sunburn and weaker immunity; it also harms plankton and crops.
  • Breathing ozone: ground-level ozone is a strong oxidant that inflames the airways, causes cough and chest pain, reduces lung function and triggers asthma attacks; children, older people and outdoor workers are most at risk. It also lowers wheat and rice yields, and it is one of the eight pollutants in India's Air Quality Index.

AP angle: the MST (Mesosphere–Stratosphere–Troposphere) radar at NARL, Gadanki, near Tirupati, studies the very layers shown in the graphic.

Ozone is "good up high, bad nearby"; the Montreal Protocol's success shows that global cooperation works, and the same resolve is needed for clean air at ground level.
free.g1m-2020-p5-14a:
Particulate matterIndoor air pollutionNational Air Quality IndexCPCB

Air pollution is India's biggest environmental health risk: it was linked to about 1.67 million deaths in 2019, nearly 18% of all deaths (Lancet Planetary Health, 2020). Pollutants come from vehicles, industry, power plants, dust and open burning outdoors, and from cooking fuels and household products indoors. The Air Quality Index (AQI) turns many measurements into one number that citizens can understand.

1. Common and hazardous pollutants and their health effects

  • Outdoor: PM2.5 is the most dangerous, because these fine particles reach the alveoli and the bloodstream.
  • Indoor: smoke from solid fuels in poorly ventilated kitchens exposes women and children to high levels of PM and CO; tobacco smoke, mould and mosquito-coil smoke add to the load. Ujjwala (over 10 crore LPG connections) tackles the main source.

2. What is AQI, and who monitors it

  • National AQI: "One Number, One Colour, One Description". It covers eight pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and lead) in six bands: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500).
  • Method: each pollutant's concentration becomes a sub-index; the highest sub-index is the AQI, and that pollutant is the "prominent pollutant". At least three pollutants, one of them PM2.5 or PM10, are needed.
  • Who monitors: the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), with State Pollution Control Boards and UT committees, under the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP) of manual stations, plus Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) that show real-time AQI on CPCB's portal and the Sameer app; CPCB issues a daily AQI bulletin. SAFAR (IITM Pune) forecasts air quality for major cities.

3. Contribution of PM to AQI

  • PM usually decides the AQI: PM levels exceed their standards by far larger margins than the gases, so PM2.5 or PM10 is the "prominent pollutant" on most days in most Indian cities.
  • Winter peaks: in north India, stubble burning, firecrackers and cold, still air push PM-driven AQI into the "Severe" band; ozone becomes prominent on some summer days.
  • Policy follows: the National Clean Air Programme (2019) targets PM10 (a cut of up to 40% by 2025-26), yet only 14 of 130 cities met the PM10 standard in 2025-26.

AP angle: the AP Pollution Control Board monitors the State's air; Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and other AP cities are NCAP non-attainment cities, and AP declared itself "smoke-free" in 2017 with LPG for every household (Deepam).

Because PM dominates the AQI, cleaner fuels, dust control and regional airshed planning will improve air quality the most.
free.g1m-2020-p5-14b:
SARS-CoV-2Droplet and aerosol spreadRapid antigen testAntibody tests (ELISA)

Covid-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) is a respiratory illness caused by SARS-CoV-2, a new coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. WHO declared it a public-health emergency of international concern in January 2020 and a pandemic on 11 March 2020; the emergency ended in May 2023. WHO has recorded over 7 million deaths worldwide; India reported about 4.5 crore cases and 5.3 lakh deaths.

1. What Covid-19 is

  • The virus: an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus (a betacoronavirus). Its spike (S) protein binds the ACE2 receptor on cells of the airways, lungs, blood vessels and gut; the nucleocapsid (N) protein packs its RNA.
  • The disease: after an incubation of about 2–14 days come fever, cough, fatigue and loss of smell or taste; severe cases develop pneumonia, low oxygen, blood clots and an overactive immune response (a "cytokine storm"). Older people and those with diabetes, hypertension or obesity are most at risk.
  • Variants: mutations produced Alpha, Delta (behind India's deadly second wave of 2021) and the highly infectious Omicron (late 2021).

2. How it spreads

  • Main route: respiratory droplets and fine aerosols at close range; aerosols linger in poorly ventilated rooms, so ventilation matters.
  • Silent spread: people can transmit the virus a day or two before symptoms, or without ever having symptoms, which made it hard to contain.
  • Minor route: contaminated surfaces and hands.
  • Control: masks, distancing, ventilation, testing and isolation, and vaccination (over 220 crore doses in India, recorded on CoWIN).

3. Immuno-diagnostic methods and their uses

Immuno-diagnostic tests use the specific binding of an antibody to an antigen, made visible by a colour change, gold particles or emitted light.

  • Rapid antigen tests: monoclonal antibodies on a strip capture viral protein; they are quick and cheap for screening but miss more cases than RT-PCR, so symptomatic people who test negative need an RT-PCR test.
  • Antibody tests: IgM appears about a week after infection and IgG later, so these tests show past infection, not current disease. India's indigenous COVID Kavach ELISA (NIV Pune, 2020) was used in ICMR's national serosurveys; the fourth round (June–July 2021) found antibodies in about two-thirds of Indians.
  • Other uses: checking antibody levels after vaccination and choosing donors for convalescent plasma. In April 2020 ICMR stopped the use of some imported rapid antibody kits because of poor accuracy, which showed the need for validation.

Covid-19 showed that fast, affordable diagnostics, together with genomic surveillance (INSACOG) and a One Health approach, are the first line of pandemic preparedness.
free.g1m-2020-p5-15a:
Active immunityImmunological memorySmallpox and polioMission Indradhanush

A vaccine is a preparation of a weakened or killed microbe, a part of it, an inactivated toxin or its genetic code, which trains the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease. It produces active immunity and long-lasting immunological memory. Since Edward Jenner's smallpox vaccine (1796), vaccines have saved more lives than almost any other health measure.

1. Mechanism of action

  • Primary response: the first dose produces antibodies slowly; boosters strengthen and prolong the memory.
  • Secondary response: when the real microbe arrives, memory cells respond within days and neutralise it before it causes illness.
  • Types: live attenuated (BCG, measles–rubella), inactivated (IPV, Covaxin), subunit (hepatitis B, HPV), toxoid (tetanus), conjugate (Hib, pneumococcal), viral vector (Covishield), mRNA, and DNA (ZyCoV-D, 2021, the world's first human DNA vaccine).
  • Herd immunity: when enough people are immune, transmission stops and even the unvaccinated are protected; measles needs about 95% coverage.

2. Diseases eradicated from India by vaccines

  • Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated worldwide; India succeeded through "search and contain" vaccination around every case.
  • Polio: India, once home to the largest number of cases, was certified polio-free in 2014. Maternal and neonatal tetanus was also eliminated (2015) by vaccinating mothers.

3. Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) 2011–2020

  • What: a WHO-led framework for the "Decade of Vaccines", endorsed by the World Health Assembly's 194 member states in 2012, with UNICEF, Gavi and the Gates Foundation as partners.
  • Goals: a polio-free world; 90% national and 80% district coverage for every vaccine; elimination of measles, rubella and maternal and neonatal tetanus; new vaccines; and fewer child deaths.
  • Outcome: progress on polio and new vaccines, but most targets were missed, as global DTP3 coverage stalled at about 85%. Its successor, the Immunization Agenda 2030, aims to halve the number of "zero-dose" children.

4. Mission Indradhanush

  • Launch: 25 December 2014, to vaccinate children and pregnant women left out of the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP); named after the rainbow's seven colours for the seven diseases first targeted; goal: 90% full immunisation.
  • Reach: 12 phases of Mission Indradhanush and Intensified Mission Indradhanush (from 2017) up to 2023 vaccinated 5.46 crore children and 1.32 crore pregnant women.
  • Results: full immunisation coverage reached 93.5% in 2023-24, and zero-dose children fell from 26 lakh (2013) to 16 lakh (2023).
  • Now: the UIP covers 12 diseases, and the U-WIN registry (2024) and HPV vaccine for 14-year-old girls (2026) strengthen it.

Vaccines have wiped smallpox and polio out of India; reaching the last zero-dose child, countering hesitancy and adding new vaccines will decide the next victories.
free.g1m-2020-p5-15b:
Hepatitis C virusChronic liver diseaseDirect-acting antiviralsNo vaccine

The 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Harvey J. Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles M. Rice "for the discovery of Hepatitis C virus". Their work explained the mysterious "non-A, non-B" hepatitis that followed blood transfusions, made blood screening possible and led to drugs that now cure the infection. Yet hepatitis C still affects about 47 million people worldwide (WHO, 2026).

1. The Nobel-winning discovery

  • Harvey Alter (US National Institutes of Health, 1970s) showed that unexplained transfusion hepatitis was caused by an unknown virus that could be passed to chimpanzees.
  • Michael Houghton (Chiron, 1989) isolated the virus's genetic sequence, and it was named the hepatitis C virus (HCV).
  • Charles Rice (1997) proved that HCV alone causes hepatitis, by injecting its engineered genetic material into a chimpanzee.

2. The virus and the disease

  • Virus: a small, enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of the flavivirus family (genus Hepacivirus); error-prone copying creates many genotypes and fast-changing variants within each patient.
  • Spread through blood: unsafe injections and medical procedures, unscreened transfusions and shared needles among people who inject drugs; less often from mother to baby or through sex. It does not spread through food, water, breast milk or casual contact.
  • A "silent" disease: most new infections cause no symptoms. About 30% of people clear the virus within six months; the rest develop chronic infection, and 15–30% of them get cirrhosis within 20 years, which can lead to liver failure and liver cancer.
  • Burden (WHO, 2026): about 0.9 million new infections a year and about 239,000 deaths in 2024; only about a third of infected people know their status.
  • Diagnosis and cure: an antibody test is followed by an HCV RNA test to confirm infection. Oral direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), such as sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or velpatasvir, cure more than 95% of patients in 12–24 weeks. India's National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (2018) provides free testing and DAA treatment with low-cost Indian generics.

3. Is there a vaccine?

No. As of 2026, WHO states that there is no effective vaccine against hepatitis C, unlike hepatitis A and B.

  • Why it is hard: HCV has many genotypes and mutates quickly, hiding its envelope proteins from antibodies; natural infection does not give lasting protection, so people can be re-infected; and good animal models are lacking.
  • Trials so far: a viral-vector vaccine tested in the USA did not prevent chronic infection (2021); research continues.
  • Prevention today: safe injections (auto-disable syringes), screening of all donated blood, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and "test and treat", since cure also stops further spread.

HCV went from discovery to cure in three decades; without a vaccine, WHO's goal of eliminating hepatitis C as a public-health threat by 2030 depends on screening, cheap DAAs and safe injections.
free.g1m-2023-p5-1a:
Knowledge creation vs consumptionScientific Social ResponsibilityLab-to-society gapScientific temper

India creates knowledge at scale: it is third in the world in scientific publications and received over 1.1 lakh patent applications in 2024-25. Yet much of this stays in journals and laboratories, unused by farmers, small industries, schools or policymakers.
