Scientific Social Responsibility (SSR), the duty of scientists to share knowledge, facilities and skills with society, was formalised by DST's SSR Guidelines, 2022. The statement is largely valid, with one caveat.

1. Stand: largely agree, with a caveat

  • Lab-to-market gap: much publicly funded research ends as papers; university patents are rarely licensed, and MSMEs and farmers seldom use technologies that already exist.
  • Lab-to-society gap: superstition, quackery, vaccine hesitancy and misinformation persist despite the fundamental duty to develop scientific temper (Article 51A(h)), so knowledge is not "consumed" by society.
  • But creation also lags: R&D spending is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24) against China's 2.58%, and India has just 354 researchers per million people. SSR complements, but cannot replace, more research funding.

2. How SSR can remedy the situation

  • Knowledge sharing: scientists give public lectures, train teachers, mentor students and explain research in local languages; the guidelines ask for at least 10 days of SSR a year, credited in performance appraisal.
  • Sharing facilities: laboratories open costly instruments to colleges, start-ups and MSMEs that cannot afford them.
  • Demand-driven research: contact with farmers, fishers and local bodies helps scientists pick real problems; the CSIR Aroma Mission (Vigyan Team award, 2025) took aromatic crops and distillation to farmers.
  • Trust and scientific temper: CSIR's Jigyasa (student–scientist connect) and Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (institutions adopting villages) build a culture of inquiry.

3. Challenges in implementing SSR

  • Non-binding guidelines: SSR is voluntary, so institutions apply it unevenly.
  • Incentives and workload: promotions still reward papers and grants; teaching-heavy state universities have little spare time.
  • No dedicated funds: travel, outreach and instrument-sharing costs lack a budget line.
  • Measuring impact: counting hours is easy, judging real social benefit is hard, so SSR risks becoming box-ticking.
  • Language and access: most science is in English, while rural and tribal users need field-level, local-language communication.

AP angle: APCOST (Vijayawada), IIT and IISER Tirupati, NARL Gadanki and ANGRAU can anchor SSR through school adoption, farmer outreach and shared laboratories, with the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub (2025) linking them to start-ups.

SSR turns science from an ivory-tower activity into a public good. Backed by funds, appraisal credit and impact measures, and by higher R&D spending through ANRF, it can make India both a creator and a user of knowledge.
free.g1m-2023-p5-1b:
Digital healthAyushman Bharat Digital MissionTelemedicineAI in healthcare

India's health system faces a triple challenge: too few doctors and specialists in rural areas, a rising burden of non-communicable diseases alongside TB and infections, and high out-of-pocket spending, because public spending is still below the 2.5% of GDP target of the National Health Policy, 2017. Technology, from digital health IDs and telemedicine to AI, genomics and drones, can stretch scarce resources and bring care closer to people.

1. Matching technology to India's health challenges

2. How technology is transforming healthcare

  • Access: e-Sanjeevani offers doctor-to-doctor and online OPD consultations where specialists are absent; Tele-MANAS (14416) gives 24×7 mental-health support in many languages.
  • Continuity and efficiency: the ABHA ID lets records follow the patient; ABDM's Scan and Share OPD tokens (over 23 crore by June 2026) cut registration waits from about an hour to a few minutes.
  • Public-health intelligence: CoWIN managed over 220 crore COVID-19 doses, U-WIN records routine immunisation, and the Integrated Health Information Platform tracks outbreaks.
  • Precision and lower costs: the government's AI strategy for healthcare (SAHI) and the BODH benchmarking platform (February 2026), Genome India's 10,000 genomes and indigenous devices cut costs and import dependence.
  • Financial protection: PM-JAY's IT platform runs cashless, portable treatment: over 48.5 crore Ayushman cards and 13.25 crore admissions by August 2026.

3. Limitations and concerns

  • Digital divide: only about half of women used a mobile phone of their own (NFHS-5); the elderly, poor and tribal people need assisted access.
  • Privacy and security: health data are highly sensitive; the DPDP Act, 2023 must be enforced, and the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi (2022) showed the risk.
  • No substitute for staff: teleconsultation needs working health centres, drugs and tests; AI must be validated on Indian data, with clear accountability for errors.
  • Uneven adoption: many private providers are yet to link records, and high-end therapies remain costly.

AP angle: AIIMS Mangalagiri, the AP MedTech Zone at Visakhapatnam (India's first medical-devices park, 2016), the cashless Dr NTR Vaidya Seva network and the proposed Universal Health Policy (2025) can use digital records and telemedicine to reach tribal and Rayalaseema areas.

Technology is a force multiplier, not a replacement, for doctors, nurses and public spending. With stronger primary care, data protection and digital literacy, it can carry India towards universal health coverage (SDG 3.8) by 2030.
free.g1m-2025-p5-1b:
Internet of ThingsSmart homeHome automationCyber security

The Internet of Things (IoT), a term coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999, is a network of everyday objects fitted with sensors, chips and internet connectivity that collect data and act on it with little human input. In homes, it links electricity meters, lights, locks, cameras, pumps and appliances to phones, voice assistants and the cloud, turning a house into a smart home. Cheap sensors, home broadband and 5G (launched October 2022) have spread it rapidly in India.

1. How home automation works

2. Impact on household systems

  • Energy: prepaid smart meters show real-time use, end manual meter reading and allow mobile recharges; smart plugs and timers cut waste. India had installed 7.24 crore smart meters by 30 June 2026, 5.73 crore of them under the RDSS (Rajya Sabha reply, July 2026).
  • Safety and security: app-linked CCTV, video doorbells, smart locks and smoke or gas-leak sensors raise instant alerts, even when the family is away.
  • Water: level sensors start and stop motor pumps, ending overflowing tanks, while soil-moisture sensors water gardens only when needed.
  • Health and elderly care: wearables track heart rate, sleep and falls and alert relatives or doctors, helping elderly people live independently.
  • Convenience: voice assistants control lights, fans and TVs; robot vacuum cleaners and scheduled washing machines save time.

3. How everyday tasks have evolved

4. Concerns: an evaluation

  • Privacy: cameras, speakers and meters record voices, images and daily habits; the DPDP Act, 2023 (Rules notified November 2025, most duties from May 2027) gives users rights over such data.
  • Cyber security: devices with default passwords are easy to hack; in 2016 the Mirai botnet hijacked cameras and routers to knock major websites offline. CERT-In and the Cyber Swachhta Kendra help detect and clean such infections.
  • Cost and digital divide: smart homes are mostly urban and affluent and need reliable power and internet.
  • Interoperability and e-waste: devices of different brands often do not work together, and short-lived gadgets add to e-waste.
  • Over-dependence: a server or network outage can lock users out of their own devices.

AP angle: by 30 June 2026 Andhra Pradesh had installed about 32.8 lakh of the 59.2 lakh smart meters sanctioned under RDSS, about 31.4 lakh of them at consumers' premises, and AP Fibernet carries low-cost broadband and IPTV to homes.

On balance, IoT has moved household work from manual, reactive chores to automated, data-driven services that save energy, time and even lives. Secure-by-design devices, strong data protection and affordable access must go with it, so that smart homes are also safe homes.
free.g1m-2023-p2-2a:
Uttaramerur inscriptionsSabha and urKudavolaiVillage autonomy

The Cholas (c. 850–1279 CE) combined a powerful monarchy with remarkable local self-government. Two inscriptions of Parantaka I (919 and 921 CE) on the Vaikuntha Perumal temple at Uttaramerur, near Kanchipuram, lay down how the village sabha was constituted, who could serve on it and how its committees worked: a written constitution of village autonomy more than a thousand years old.

1. Village assemblies under the Cholas

  • Ur: the general assembly of tax-paying landholders in ordinary villages.
  • Sabha (mahasabha): the assembly of Brahmana landholders in brahmadeya villages such as Uttaramerur.
  • Nagaram: the assembly of merchants in trading centres.
  • Nadu: above the village, the assembly of a group of villages dealt with revenue and local matters.

2. Rules laid down at Uttaramerur

  • Wards: the village was divided into 30 wards (kudumbus), each sending one member.
  • Qualifications: ownership of at least a quarter veli of tax-paying land, a house on one's own site, age between 35 and 70, and knowledge of Vedic texts.
  • Disqualifications: those who had served on a committee in the previous three years, those who had failed to submit accounts and their relatives, and persons guilty of crimes or 'sins' were barred.
  • Selection by lot (kudavolai): names of eligible men were written on palm-leaf tickets, put in a pot and drawn by a young boy before the whole assembly.
  • Committees (variyams): the thirty members formed the annual (samvatsara), garden (thotta) and tank (eri) committees; a gold (pon) committee was also chosen. Members served for one year.

3. Contribution to village autonomy

  • Wide functions: the assemblies assessed and collected land revenue, maintained tanks, roads and temples, managed endowments, kept land records and settled disputes.
  • Financial power: they owned common land, received endowments and recorded sales and gifts of land in inscriptions.
  • Accountability: one-year terms, rotation, compulsory audit of accounts and the lot system prevented concentration of power and corruption.
  • Light royal control: royal officers attended mainly as observers, and the crown respected the assemblies' decisions, so villages ran their own affairs even through wars.

4. Limitations

  • Narrow membership: it was confined to propertied, learned Brahmana men; women, the landless and lower castes were excluded.
  • Oligarchic character: it was self-rule by a village elite, not democracy in the modern sense.

AP angle: medieval Andhra had a parallel tradition of village self-sufficiency, the ayagar system of twelve village functionaries (karanam, reddi, talari and artisans) paid with shares of the harvest.

Uttaramerur shows the deep roots of local self-government in India, an ideal later written into Article 40 and given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment (1992).
free.g1m-2023-p2-2b:
Market controlPrice regulationStanding armyBarani's account

Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) introduced a set of market regulations in Delhi in the early 1300s, after repeated Mongol invasions had reached the outskirts of the capital. Our main source is Ziauddin Barani's Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, supplemented by Amir Khusrau. The aim was to keep the prices of essential goods low and fixed, so that a large army could be maintained cheaply.

1. Objectives

  • Military: maintain a large standing army on modest cash salaries (Barani mentions 234 tankas a year for a cavalryman) without emptying the treasury.
  • Economic: check hoarding, profiteering and price rise in the capital.
  • Food security of Delhi: keep the capital supplied with grain even in years of drought.

2. Main features

  • Separate markets: a grain market (mandi); the Sarai-i-Adl for cloth, sugar, dry fruits and oil; a market for horses, slaves and cattle; and a general market for daily goods.
  • Fixed prices: wheat at 7½ jitals and barley at 4 jitals per man; prices of cloth, horses and slaves were also fixed.
  • Assured supply: land revenue in the Doab was raised to half the produce and collected in kind to stock royal granaries; grain carriers (karwanis) were registered and made to sell at fixed rates; Multani merchants were given advances to bring cloth.
  • Rationing and permits: grain was rationed in times of scarcity, and costly fabrics could be bought only with a permit (parwana).
  • Enforcement: the Shahna-i-Mandi (market superintendent), the Diwan-i-Riyasat and spies (barids, munhiyans) watched traders; short-weighing was punished by cutting flesh from the trader's body.

3. Impact

  • Positive: prices stayed stable even in drought years; the large army repulsed the Mongols and financed campaigns in the Deccan and the south.
  • On peasants: heavy revenue and compulsory sale of grain at low prices left them little surplus.
  • On merchants: profits were squeezed and trade discouraged; the system rested on espionage and terror.
  • Short-lived: largely confined to Delhi, it collapsed soon after his death in 1316.

AP angle: the army these regulations sustained carried Malik Kafur's expedition (1309–10) to Warangal, forcing the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra II, whose kingdom included much of present Andhra, to pay tribute.

4. Assessment

  • Source problem: Barani admired the results but wrote decades later with a moral purpose, so his account may be exaggerated.
  • Nature: the reforms were military-fiscal measures, not welfare measures for the people.

It was a remarkable medieval experiment in price control and state procurement, though driven by military needs and enforced by coercion rather than welfare.
free.g1m-2023-p2-3a:
Indo-Islamic synthesisCharbagh and double domeTrabeate elementsAkbar and Shah Jahan

Mughal architecture (16th–17th centuries) blended Persian-Timurid forms with indigenous Rajput, Gujarati and Hindu building traditions. It began with Humayun's Tomb, matured in red sandstone under Akbar, and reached its peak in white marble under Shah Jahan, producing an Indo-Islamic synthesis that reflected the composite culture of the empire.

1. Features of Mughal architecture

  • Timurid-Persian forms: bulbous double domes, iwans (lofty arched portals) and the charbagh garden divided into four by water channels; Humayun's Tomb (architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas) set the model.
  • Materials: red sandstone under Akbar (Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri); white marble with pietra dura inlay under Jahangir and Shah Jahan (Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb, Taj Mahal).
  • Symmetry and ornament: perfect symmetry and axial planning, tall minarets, calligraphy, floral and geometric ornament, and pierced stone screens (jalis).
  • Garden setting: unlike Humayun's Tomb, which stands at the centre of its charbagh, the Taj Mahal stands at the river end of the garden on the Yamuna, flanked by a mosque and a guest house.
  • Fort-palaces and cities: Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza; Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid.
  • Decline: under Aurangzeb building slowed; the Bibi-ka-Maqbara at Aurangabad is a modest imitation of the Taj.

2. Influence of Hindu and indigenous elements

  • Trabeate construction: pillars, beams and brackets dominate Fatehpur Sikri, as in Jodha Bai's palace, the Diwan-i-Khas with its carved central pillar, and the tiered, pillared Panch Mahal.
  • Rajput features: chhatris (domed kiosks), chhajjas (sloping eaves) and serpentine brackets were drawn from Rajput and Gujarati palaces.
  • Hindu motifs: the kalasha finial and the inverted lotus crown the domes of Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal; lotus motifs and carved Hindu-style brackets appear in the Jahangiri Mahal, Agra Fort.
  • Craftsmen and policy: Akbar's sulh-i-kul, Rajput alliances and the employment of Gujarati and Rajasthani craftsmen made this synthesis possible.

3. Assessment

  • Phases of synthesis: the Hindu element was strongest under Akbar; under Shah Jahan Persian elegance dominated, but chhatris and lotus finials remained.
  • Legacy: Mughal forms shaped later Rajput palaces and, much later, the colonial Indo-Saracenic style.

Deccan/AP angle: the Qutb Shahis of Golconda, who also ruled coastal Andhra, developed a parallel Indo-Islamic style; Mughal influence spread after Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687.

Mughal architecture embodies India's composite culture; Humayun's Tomb, the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri and the Red Fort Complex are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
free.g1m-2023-p2-3b:
SwarajyaAshtapradhanPeasant welfareReligious tolerance

Shivaji (1630–1680), crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674, carved the Maratha Swarajya out of Bijapur and Mughal territories. Historians often describe his state as inclusive and peasant-friendly. The statement can be tested against his recruitment, revenue, religious and military policies, remembering that 'welfare state' and 'egalitarian' are modern concepts applied to a 17th-century monarchy.

1. Egalitarian features

  • Open recruitment: Mavale peasants and men of many castes rose through merit; Muslims held high posts, such as the commander Siddi Hilal and the admiral Daulat Khan.
  • Curbing hereditary power: deshmukhs and jagirdars were brought under control, and most officers were paid in cash rather than through jagirs.
  • Religious tolerance: he made grants to temples and also to mosques and dargahs; even the critical chronicler Khafi Khan noted that his soldiers were forbidden to harm mosques, the Quran or women.

2. Welfare features

  • Revenue reform: Annaji Datto surveyed land with a measuring rod (kathi); assessment was fixed at about 30 per cent of produce, raised to 40 per cent when other cesses were abolished, and collected directly from peasants.
  • Peasant relief: loans for seed and cattle, remission in bad seasons and incentives to cultivate waste land.
  • Protecting the people: soldiers were forbidden to damage standing crops or take women to camp, and his orders told officers not to take even a blade of grass from peasants without paying.
  • Ordered administration: the Ashtapradhan council ran departments, the Nyayadhish dispensed justice, each fort was held jointly by three officers of equal rank (havaldar, sabnis and sarnobat) who checked one another, and a navy with sea forts such as Sindhudurg protected the coast.

3. Limitations

  • Hierarchy remained: the varna order continued; his coronation by Gaga Bhatta required a Kshatriya genealogy, and Brahmanas dominated civil posts.
  • Burden on neighbours: chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (an additional one-tenth) were levied on neighbouring territories, and Surat was raided.
  • Priorities of war: survival against the Mughals and Bijapur shaped policy more than welfare.
  • Dependence on the ruler: the system rested on Shivaji's personal vigilance and weakened under the Mughal onslaught after his death in 1680.

AP angle: during his Karnataka expedition (1677) Shivaji allied with Abul Hasan Qutb Shah of Golconda and visited Srisailam.

By seventeenth-century standards, Shivaji's state was markedly inclusive and peasant-oriented, a proto-welfare state, though not egalitarian in the modern sense.
free.g1m-2023-p2-4a:
Permanent SettlementRyotwariMahalwariCommercialisation of agriculture

After obtaining the Diwani of Bengal (1765), the East India Company treated land revenue as its main source of income and experimented with ways of collecting it. Three systems emerged: the Permanent Settlement (about 19% of British Indian territory), Mahalwari (about 30%) and Ryotwari (about 51%). All aimed at maximum, assured revenue, and together they transformed India's agrarian economy.

1. The land revenue systems

  • Permanent Settlement (1793): zamindars, earlier only collectors, became hereditary owners; the State's demand was fixed forever, and an estate was auctioned if dues were not paid by sunset of the due date (Sunset Law). Peasants became mere tenants at the zamindar's mercy.
  • Ryotwari: the State dealt directly with each cultivator, who became the registered owner and paid the revenue himself; but the demand was high and periodically raised, so the State itself acted as a giant landlord.
  • Mahalwari: the village or estate (mahal) was assessed as a unit and the headman (lambardar) collected the dues; the system recognised joint village ownership.

2. Impact on the Indian economy

  • Land as a commodity: land became saleable and mortgageable; rural indebtedness and land alienation to moneylenders grew, provoking the Deccan Riots (1875), the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) and the Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900).
  • Forced commercialisation: rigid cash demands pushed peasants towards indigo, cotton, jute and opium, weakening food security.
  • Stagnant agriculture: absentee landlordism, subinfeudation and rack-renting spread in zamindari areas, while neither State nor landlord invested in improvement.
  • Famines and the drain: demands collected even in bad years deepened distress in famines; R.C. Dutt blamed over-assessment of land revenue for famines, and with Dadabhai Naoroji traced India's poverty to the drain of wealth.
  • New landlords: many old zamindari families lost their estates at auctions under the Sunset Law, and the buyers were often urban merchants and moneylenders with no tie to the land.
  • Revolts: the Indigo Revolt (1859–60), Pabna (1873–76) and later Kisan movements.
  • Side-benefits: land surveys, records of rights and legal titles.

AP angle: the Permanent Settlement was extended to the Northern Circars (coastal Andhra) in 1802, creating zamindaris such as Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram, while Munro introduced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema). The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 ended zamindari in Andhra.

Colonial revenue systems maximised extraction and impoverished the peasantry; post-independence land reforms, from zamindari abolition to tenancy laws, sought to reverse this legacy.
free.g1m-2023-p2-4b:
Muslim reform movementsRevivalism and modernismAligarh movementSir Syed Ahmad Khan

After 1857 Indian Muslims faced British suspicion, the loss of Persian as court language (1837) and backwardness in English education and government jobs. Nineteenth-century reform among Muslims took two forms: revivalist movements that sought to purify Islam, and modernist movements, led above all by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, that sought to reconcile Islam with Western science and education.

1. Revivalist movements

  • Wahabi movement: inspired by Shah Waliullah, Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli preached a return to pure Islam and waged armed struggle, first against the Sikhs (he died at Balakot in 1831) and later against the British; it was crushed by the 1870s.
  • Faraizi movement: Haji Shariatullah stressed the obligatory duties of Islam; under his son Dudu Miyan it became a peasant movement against zamindars and indigo planters.
  • Deoband: Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi trained ulema in orthodox theology; anti-British, it later supported the Congress.

2. Modernist movements

  • Early modernists: the Mohammedan Literary Society urged Muslims to take up English education.
  • Later currents: the Ahmadiyya favoured Western education, and the Nadwat-ul-Ulama tried to blend tradition with modern learning.

3. Contributions of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817–1898)

  • Modern education: he opened schools at Moradabad (1859) and Ghazipur (1863); his Scientific Society (1864) translated Western works into Urdu; the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (1875) became Aligarh Muslim University (1920).
  • Spreading the message: the Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) carried the Aligarh movement across India and produced a modern Muslim middle class.
  • Religious rationalism: he interpreted the Quran in the light of reason and science; his journal Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870) attacked superstition, polygamy and the rigid purdah system.
  • Political ideas: Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1859) explained the causes of 1857 and urged Indian representation in the councils. He is widely quoted as describing Hindus and Muslims as the 'two eyes' of India; he reconciled Muslims with the British, but he later opposed the Congress, a stance criticised as encouraging separatism.

4. Assessment

  • Revivalists strengthened anti-colonial feeling but resisted modern education and women's rights.
  • Modernists spread education but were elitist and loyalist; both streams emphasised a separate identity that later fed communal politics.
  • Aligarh's graduates went on to lead many political currents, from the Khilafat movement to the Muslim League.

Sir Syed laid the foundation of modern Muslim education, though his political loyalism left a contested legacy.
free.g1m-2023-p2-5a:
Agrarian distressKisan SabhasGandhian satyagrahasMass nationalism

Colonial land revenue systems, rack-renting and indebtedness made peasant discontent endemic in British India. From local, spontaneous revolts in the 19th century, peasant movements became organised and linked with nationalism in the 20th, culminating in the All India Kisan Sabha (1936). They gave the freedom struggle its mass base and its agrarian agenda.

1. Factors behind peasant movements

  • Revenue and rent burden: heavy land revenue and rents, illegal cesses and evictions by zamindars and planters.
  • Forced commercial cropping: under the tinkathia system in Champaran, tenants had to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land.
  • Indebtedness: rural debt led to the transfer of land to moneylenders, as in the Deccan.
  • Economic shocks: famines and the Great Depression (1929–33), which halved farm prices while the revenue demand stayed fixed.
  • Forest laws: restrictions on grazing, firewood and podu cultivation.
  • Political awakening: Gandhian mass movements, Kisan Sabhas, socialist ideas and the vernacular press.

2. Phases

  • 19th century: spontaneous and local revolts against planters, zamindars and moneylenders, aimed at immediate grievances rather than colonial rule.
  • Gandhian phase: satyagrahas at Champaran, Kheda and Bardoli linked peasant grievances with the Congress.
  • Kisan Sabha phase: class organisations under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati and N.G. Ranga demanded the abolition of zamindari.

3. Impact on the national movement

  • Mass base: Champaran made Gandhi a national leader, and peasants filled the ranks of Non-Cooperation, the no-tax campaigns of Civil Disobedience and Quit India.
  • New leaders: Bardoli made Vallabhbhai Patel 'Sardar', and contact with Awadh peasants radicalised Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Radical agenda: the Karachi resolution (1931) and the Faizpur session (1936) adopted the reduction of rent and revenue and relief from debt; the Congress ministries of 1937–39 passed tenancy and debt-relief laws.
  • Tensions: the Congress restrained no-rent campaigns to retain landlord support, as in the Bardoli resolution (1922) after Chauri Chaura.
  • Legacy: zamindari abolition and land reforms after 1947.

AP angle: the Palnadu forest satyagraha and the Pedanandipadu no-tax campaign (1921–22) linked peasant grievances with Non-Cooperation; N.G. Ranga founded the Indian Peasants' Institute at Nidubrolu (1933) and became the first general secretary of the All India Kisan Sabha.

Peasant movements turned nationalism into a mass movement and placed agrarian justice at the heart of independent India's agenda.
free.g1m-2023-p2-5b:
CommunalismDivide and ruleSeparate electoratesPartition

Communalism is the belief that people following a religion share common secular interests that differ from, and finally oppose, those of other religious groups (Bipan Chandra). It grew from the late 19th century, was encouraged by colonial policy, and culminated in the Partition of 1947. It did help the British, mostly indirectly, by dividing the national movement.

1. Did communalism help the British?

  • Divide and rule: the Partition of Bengal (1905) and the Simla deputation (1906) prepared the way for separate electorates under the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), extended in 1919 and by the Communal Award (1932).
  • Weakened united front: communal parties (Muslim League, 1906; Hindu Mahasabha, 1915) mostly stayed away from mass struggles such as Civil Disobedience and Quit India; the League observed a 'Deliverance Day' (1939) when the Congress ministries resigned.
  • Excuse for delay: the British posed as neutral arbiters and cited communal disagreement, as at the Round Table Conferences, to delay self-government.
  • Not merely a British creation: middle-class competition for jobs and seats, religious revivalism and uneven development also fed it; the British exploited existing divisions.

2. Indicative traits of communalists

  • Religion as a political unit: the religious community was treated as a single political and economic group.
  • Social base: mainly landlords and sections of the urban middle classes competing for jobs, seats and patronage.
  • Distorted history: history was rewritten as perpetual religious conflict, and religious symbols and slogans were used for mobilisation.
  • Loyalism: reliance on British patronage and hostility to the Congress's composite nationalism.
  • Fear psychosis: the constant cry of 'religion in danger', which hardened into extreme communalism in the late 1930s and 1940s.

3. Impact on modern Indian history

  • Violence: riots in the 1920s and after Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) in Calcutta, Noakhali and Bihar.
  • Failed settlements: constitutional negotiations, from the Nehru Report (1928) to the Cabinet Mission (1946), foundered on communal demands.
  • Partition: the two-nation theory led to the Lahore Resolution (1940) and Partition (1947), which displaced an estimated 10–15 million people and took several hundred thousand lives.
  • Legacy: lasting mistrust, which made secularism central to the Constitution (Articles 25–28; part of the basic structure, S.R. Bommai, 1994) and fraternity a value of the Preamble.

Communalism served colonial interests and divided the freedom struggle; fraternity and constitutional secularism remain its antidote.
free.g1m-2023-p2-6b:
Eastern Chalukyas of VengiImmigration and agraharasCaste mobilityTelugu awakening

The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (c. 624–1076 CE), founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakesin II, ruled coastal Andhra from Vengi (Pedavegi) and later Rajamahendravaram. Over four centuries, immigration from Karnataka and the Tamil country, caste mobility in an age of war, and a new Telugu literary consciousness restructured the region's society and religion.

1. Impact of immigration

  • Karnataka connection: the dynasty came from Badami, bringing officials, warriors, Brahmana families and Jaina monks.
  • Agraharas: immigrant Brahmanas settled on land grants (agraharas) spread Vedic learning, Sanskrit and the varna ideal across the Godavari–Krishna delta.
  • Spread of settled agriculture: new agraharas and temple villages extended cultivation in the deltas and drew local cultivators, artisans and service groups into a Brahmanical village order.
  • Chola ties: Vimaladitya and Rajaraja Narendra married Chola princesses, bringing Tamil influence; Kulottunga I united the Vengi and Chola crowns in 1070.

2. Caste mobility

  • Warrior-cultivators rise: long wars, especially with the Rashtrakutas, allowed cultivating and warrior groups to rise through military and village service.
  • Village headmen: the rattagudi (the root of 'Reddi') and nayakas gained status.
  • Regional groups: groups from regions such as Kammanadu and Velanadu later crystallised into landed castes; merchants and artisans gained prestige through temple endowments.

3. Religious restructuring

  • Decline of Buddhism: once dominant in the Krishna valley, Buddhism faded; Jainism enjoyed early patronage, with basadis at Vijayawada and Ramatirtham and grants by kings such as Ammaraja II.
  • Rise of Shaivism: Pashupata and Kalamukha teachers made Shaivism dominant; Chalukya Bhima I is credited with the Draksharama and Kumararama (Samalkot) temples of the Pancharamas, and Gunaga Vijayaditya III's age saw the Biccavolu temples.
  • Temple as centre: Vaishnavism and Brahmanical temple worship grew, and temples became centres of land, learning, dance and charity.

4. Social awakening

  • Telugu in inscriptions: Pandaranga's Addanki inscription (9th century) and Yuddhamalla's Bezawada inscription contain early Telugu verse.
  • Adikavi Nannaya: under Rajaraja Narendra (1019–1061), Nannaya, assisted by Narayana Bhatta, began the Andhra Mahabharatam, the first Telugu kavya, earning the title Adikavi.
  • Identity: Telugu became a language of courts and temples, fostering a distinct Telugu identity alongside Sanskrit.

The Eastern Chalukya age thus laid the foundations of Telugu society, culture and literature, a synthesis of immigrant traditions and local vitality.
free.g1m-2023-p2-8a:
KanyasulkamSocial reform through literatureVyavaharika bhashaTelugu renaissance

Gurajada Venkata Apparao and Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy, both from north coastal Andhra, led the modern Telugu renaissance. Gurajada used drama, poetry and the short story to attack social evils, while Gidugu fought to replace the archaic granthika style with the people's spoken vyavaharika Telugu in education and writing. Together they took literature and learning to the common people.

1. Gurajada Apparao (1862–1915): social reform through literature

  • Kanyasulkam: first staged in 1892 and revised in 1909, this first great social play in spoken Telugu satirised bride-price, the marriage of young girls to old men and the hypocrisy of orthodox elders and fake reformers such as Girisam, while supporting widow remarriage.
  • Reform through laughter: unlike didactic reformers, he used humour and realistic characters, such as the orthodox Agnihotravadhanlu and the old miser Lubdhavadhanlu, to make audiences laugh at their own customs.
  • Dignity for the marginalised: the courtesan Madhuravani is portrayed with intelligence and dignity, challenging moral stereotypes.
  • Reformist poetry: poems such as Purnamma, on a child bride, written in his new mutyala saralu metre, carried reformist themes to ordinary readers.
  • Short story: Diddubatu (1910) is regarded as the first modern Telugu short story.
  • Humanist patriotism: 'Desamante matti kadoyi, desamante manushuloyi' (a country is its people, not its soil) made people, not territory, the measure of patriotism.

2. Gidugu Ramamurthy (1863–1940): the vyavaharika bhasha movement

  • Core argument: education and writing should use spoken Telugu instead of the archaic granthika style, so that literacy could reach the masses.
  • Launch: he began the movement in the early 1900s with Gurajada and the school inspector J.A. Yates.
  • Scholarship and debate: he debated orthodox scholars, showed that classical poets themselves used spoken forms, and ran the monthly journal Telugu.
  • Tribal education: he worked for the Savara tribe, preparing a Savara grammar and dictionary and opening schools; he received the Kaisar-i-Hind medal.
  • Outcome: spoken Telugu gradually entered textbooks, newspapers and administration; his birthday, 29 August, is observed as Telugu Language Day in Andhra Pradesh.

AP angle: both worked in the Vizianagaram–Srikakulam region, and their joint effort made coastal Andhra the cradle of modern Telugu prose, drama and reform.

Together they democratised Telugu literature and learning, linking language reform with social reform.
free.g1m-2023-p2-9a:
Rampa rebellionAlluri Sitarama RajuTribal resistanceGuerrilla warfare

Alluri Sitarama Raju (1897–1924) led the Rampa or Manyam rebellion (1922–24) in the Godavari and Visakhapatnam Agency tracts of the Eastern Ghats. Combining tribal grievances against forest laws and forced labour with the nationalist spirit of Non-Cooperation, it became one of the most important tribal uprisings of India's freedom struggle.

1. Causes

  • Forest laws: the Madras Forest Act (1882) restricted podu (shifting) cultivation, grazing and the collection of forest produce, threatening tribal livelihoods.
  • Forced labour: vetti for road-building under officials such as the tahsildar Bastian, and exploitation by contractors and moneylenders.
  • Loss of traditional authority: traditional muttadars (hill chiefs) were displaced by colonial officials; Rampa had already risen in revolt in 1879–80.
  • Nationalist climate: the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) raised hopes of swaraj among the hill people.

2. Raju as leader

  • Mobilisation: an ascetic figure, he won the trust of Koya and Konda Dora tribals; inspired by Non-Cooperation, he preached temperance and panchayat justice before turning to armed revolt.
  • Strategy: he waged guerrilla warfare in the hills, raided the Chintapalli, Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi police stations in August 1922 to seize arms, and ambushed police parties.
  • Organisation: lieutenants such as Gam Gantam Dora and Gam Mallu Dora led bands, while villagers provided shelter, food and intelligence.
  • Suppression: the British deployed the Malabar Special Police and Assam Rifles under a special commissioner; Raju was captured and shot at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924, and the revolt ended.

3. Assessment

  • Strengths: charismatic leadership, mastery of the terrain and the fusion of tribal grievances with nationalism kept the revolt alive for nearly two years against a far stronger force.
  • Limitations: it was localised, with limited arms, no Congress support for armed struggle and isolation from the plains.
  • Means and ends: though he used arms, unlike the Congress, his aim of swaraj and dignity for the hill people matched the national goal.

4. Legacy

  • Folk hero: remembered as 'Manyam Veerudu', he inspired later tribal and national struggles.
  • Honours: Andhra Pradesh named the Alluri Sitharama Raju district (2022, headquarters Paderu) after him, and his 125th birth anniversary was celebrated nationally in 2022.

Raju's sacrifice shows that tribal resistance was an integral part of the freedom struggle; the fight for forest rights he led finds an echo in the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
free.g1m-2023-p2-9b:
Telugu Dalit literatureSelf-respectAnti-caste ideologyAmbedkarite poetry

Telugu Dalit literature is writing by and about Dalits that rejects caste hierarchy and asserts self-respect, dignity and equality. It evolved from early 20th-century protest poetry by pioneers such as Gurram Jashuva and Boyi Bhimanna into an assertive, Ambedkarite movement after the Karamchedu massacre of 1985, offering a counter-narrative to Brahmanical aesthetics.

1. Early pioneers

  • Gurram Jashuva (1895–1971): Gabbilam (1941), in which an untouchable barred from the temple sends his plea to Lord Shiva through a bat, is a landmark critique of untouchability; he also wrote Firdousi and Kreestu Charitra (Sahitya Akademi Award) and received the Padma Bhushan.
  • Boyi Bhimanna (1911–2005): his play Paleru, on a bonded farm servant, urged Dalits to seek education and break free; his poetry collection Gudiselu Kalipotunnai ('the huts are burning') won the Sahitya Akademi Award.
  • Their approach: humanist and reformist, they appealed to the conscience of society while exposing the humiliation of caste.

2. Assertive phase (after 1985)

  • Response to atrocities: the Karamchedu (1985) and Chunduru (1991) massacres provoked a wave of poetry; anthologies such as Chikkanavutunna Pata (1995) gave the movement a collective voice.
  • New poets: Kalekuri Prasad, Endluri Sudhakar, Satish Chandar, Shikhamani, Madduri Nagesh Babu and Katti Padma Rao drew on Ambedkar's ideas.
  • Gender: Dalit women writers such as Challapalli Swaroopa Rani and Joopaka Subhadra exposed the double oppression of caste and gender.

3. Contributions of the Dalit poets

  • Ideological: they replaced pity with self-respect and questioned Brahmanical aesthetics as well as the neglect of caste in leftist literature.
  • Identity and dignity: they celebrated Dalit labour, culture and history; the Mala and Madiga experiences found a literary voice.
  • Counter-history: they retold myth and history from the Dalit point of view, as Jashuva did by making a bat, a creature thought impure, the messenger to Shiva.
  • Language: everyday speech, songs and oral forms broadened the Telugu literary canon.
  • Social impact: their writing strengthened movements for land, education and reservation, and for protection under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

AP angle: the landmarks of this literature lie in Andhra: Jashuva was born at Vinukonda, and the Karamchedu (then Prakasam district) and Chunduru (then Guntur district) massacres that sparked the assertive phase took place in coastal Andhra.

Telugu Dalit poets turned literature into an instrument of social justice, echoing the constitutional values of equality (Article 14), abolition of untouchability (Article 17) and fraternity.
free.g1m-2023-p2-10a:
AP Reorganisation Act 2014Assets and liabilitiesPopulation ratioRevenue deficit

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 created Telangana on 2 June 2014. Residuary Andhra Pradesh got about 58% of the population but lost Hyderabad, the hub of revenue, industry and state-level institutions. The Act's mixed rules for dividing assets and liabilities (location for some items, population for others, headquarters for still others) left AP with more debt than assets and a long tail of disputes.

1. Inconsistencies in apportionment

  • Mixed principles: land and immovable assets pass to the state where they are located, but debt and pensions are divided broadly on the population ratio; with most state-level assets in Hyderabad, AP got more liabilities than assets.
  • Headquarters rule: assets of Schedule IX companies and corporations (about 90 bodies) are linked to their headquarters, mostly in Hyderabad; disputes over what 'headquarters' covers stalled the division, and the Sheela Bhide expert committee's recommendations were only partly implemented.
  • Schedule X gap: for these institutions (over 100) the Act provided only for continuing their services for a limited period, with no clear rule on assets; the dispute over the funds of the AP State Council of Higher Education reached the Supreme Court.
  • Need ignored: dividing liabilities by population took no account of revenue capacity, so the State with the smaller tax base carried the larger debt.
  • Revenue mismatch: Hyderabad's large tax base went to Telangana while AP inherited a larger pension and debt burden, leading to a revenue deficit from the first year that required central grants.

2. Other adverse effects

  • Power dues: dues for electricity supplied by AP Genco to Telangana's discoms (2014–17) remained disputed despite a Union Power Ministry direction in 2022.
  • Capital: Hyderabad was the common capital only for ten years (till June 2024), while AP had to build Amaravati from scratch with central support under Section 94.
  • Rebuilding institutions: AP had to recreate a secretariat, universities and corporations, relying on the promises of the Thirteenth Schedule, such as new national educational institutions.

3. Way forward

  • Time-bound settlement: the Union Home Ministry can facilitate negotiations, building on the official-level committees the two states formed in 2024.
  • Neutral resolution: expert arbitration for unresolved Schedule IX and X cases, instead of prolonged litigation.
  • Fiscal support: Finance Commission grants and central assistance to offset the revenue loss.

A cooperative-federal approach can settle these bifurcation legacies and let both states grow.
free.g1m-2023-p2-10b:
Schedule XIRiver Management BoardsApex CouncilInter-state water sharing

Part IX (Sections 84–91) of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 governs Krishna and Godavari waters after bifurcation. It creates an Apex Council of the Union Water Resources (now Jal Shakti) Minister and both Chief Ministers (Section 84) and two River Management Boards (Section 85), the KRMB and the GRMB, which must function on the principles laid down in the Eleventh Schedule.

1. Principles in the Eleventh Schedule

  • Existing rights protected: tribunal allocations of assured water to the undivided state's regions stay unchanged, and future allocations of excess flows by tribunals bind both states.
  • Priority of use: drinking water first, then irrigation, then power.
  • Operation: the Union Water Resources Ministry's operation protocol binds both states; the boards' orders on operating head works, including hydel projects, are binding, and the boards advise on floods and droughts.
  • New projects: these need board appraisal and technical clearance plus Apex Council sanction; the state where a project lies executes it.
  • Ongoing projects: six (Handri-Neeva, Telugu Ganga, Galeru-Nagari and Veligonda in AP; Kalwakurthy and Nettempadu in Telangana) are to be completed as planned by the undivided state.
  • Penalties: a state that does not comply faces financial and other penalties from the Centre.

2. Functioning of the boards

  • Delayed jurisdiction: the Union notified the boards' jurisdiction only in July 2021, seven years after bifurcation, and the handover of the Srisailam and Nagarjunasagar outlets became contentious.
  • Recurring disputes: over power generation at Srisailam, which AP said lowered the water level needed for its Rayalaseema canals, and over new lift schemes on both sides; central forces were deployed at Nagarjunasagar dam after a November 2023 stand-off.
  • Apex Council and tribunal: the Council met in 2016 and 2020; in October 2023 the Centre gave the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II (whose term was extended under Section 89) further terms of reference.
  • Dependence on states: the boards rely on the two states for funds, staff and data, which limits their independence.

3. AP's concerns

  • Lower riparian: AP depends on fair and timely releases from upstream reservoirs for its deltas and drinking water.
  • Polavaram: declared a national project under Section 90, it is central to AP's water security.

4. Way forward

  • Board control and telemetry: give the boards effective control of the common outlets, as the Act envisages, and install telemetry for transparent water accounting.
  • Regular Apex Council meetings and data-sharing to settle disputes before they escalate.

Schedule XI provides a sound rule-based framework; faithful implementation through empowered boards can make river management cooperative rather than confrontational.
free.g1m-2023-p2-11a:
Climatic controlsMonsoon mechanismRelief and HimalayasJet streams

Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period (about 30 years). The factors that determine it are climatic controls; NCERT lists six major ones: latitude, altitude, pressure and wind system, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief. In India these act together with upper-air jet streams to produce a distinct monsoon climate with marked regional variations.

1. Latitude and altitude

  • Latitude: the Tropic of Cancer divides India; the south is tropical with high temperatures throughout the year, while the north is sub-tropical with a large annual range.
  • Altitude: temperature falls by about 6.5°C per 1,000 m, so hill stations stay cool and Ladakh is a cold desert.

2. Relief

  • Himalayas: they block cold Central Asian winds and trap the monsoon winds, forcing them to shed rain over the subcontinent.
  • Western Ghats: they cause heavy orographic rain on the windward side and a rain shadow over the Deccan.
  • Aravallis: lying parallel to the monsoon winds, they fail to stop them, leaving western Rajasthan dry; the funnel-shaped Khasi hills give Mawsynram its very heavy rain.

3. Pressure, winds and jet streams

  • Summer: intense heating creates a low over north-west India; the south-east trades cross the equator and become the south-west monsoon.
  • Winter: high pressure over the land produces dry north-east winds; western disturbances, steered by the subtropical westerly jet, bring winter rain to north-west India.
  • Tropical cyclones and depressions: low-pressure systems from the Bay of Bengal bring much of the rain to the east coast, both during the monsoon and after it.
  • Onset: the northward shift of the westerly jet and the tropical easterly jet over the peninsula influence the monsoon's onset; the retreating monsoon brings rain to the Coromandel coast.

4. Distance from the sea and ocean conditions

  • Continentality: coastal places have an equable climate, while interior places have an extreme one.
  • Ocean conditions: El Niño tends to weaken the monsoon, while a positive Indian Ocean Dipole strengthens it.

AP angle: coastal Andhra receives both south-west and north-east monsoon rain and faces Bay of Bengal cyclones (Hudhud 2014, Michaung 2023); Rayalaseema lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, making Anantapuramu one of India's driest districts.

Climate change is now altering these controls, demanding climate-resilient agriculture and better forecasting.
free.g1m-2023-p2-12a:
SagarmalaPort-led developmentCoastal Economic ZonesLogistics cost

Sagarmala is the Union Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways' flagship programme for port-led development, approved by the Union Cabinet in March 2015. It seeks to use India's long coastline (about 11,099 km as re-measured), 12 major and over 200 non-major ports and some 14,500 km of potentially navigable waterways to cut logistics costs and drive industrial growth.

1. Objectives

  • Lower logistics costs: reduce costs for EXIM and domestic cargo by optimising the modal mix towards coastal shipping and inland waterways, which are cheaper and cleaner than road transport.
  • Port-led industrialisation: locate industries near ports to cut transport time and costs for bulk cargo.
  • Export competitiveness: cut the time and cost of moving export cargo through more efficient ports.
  • Coastal communities: develop fisheries, skills and jobs in coastal areas.

2. Key features

  • Five pillars: port modernisation and new port development; port connectivity by road, rail and pipelines; port-led industrialisation through Coastal Economic Zones; coastal community development; and coastal shipping and inland water transport.
  • Institutions: the National Sagarmala Apex Committee (2015) for policy, and the Sagarmala Development Company (2016), restructured in 2025 as Sagarmala Finance Corporation Ltd, India's first maritime-focused NBFC.
  • Community development: fishing harbours and skilling of coastal youth under DDU-GKY.
  • Next phase: a Sagarmala 2.0 phase is proposed, aligned with Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047.

3. Why it is important

  • Trade: about 95% of India's trade by volume and 70% by value moves by sea, so port efficiency directly shapes competitiveness.
  • Logistics reform: lower logistics costs complement PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy (2022).
  • Efficiency gains: major ports handled a record 915 million tonnes in 2025-26.
  • Blue economy and security: shipbuilding, fisheries and coastal tourism create jobs, while stronger ports add to maritime security in the Indian Ocean.
  • Green growth: shifting cargo from road to water cuts fuel use and emissions.

4. Challenges

  • Land acquisition, coastal ecology and the livelihoods of fishing communities; dependence on private investment; and slow hinterland connectivity.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's long coastline, Visakhapatnam port and the new Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam and Mulapeta ports make the State a major beneficiary of port-led growth.

Timely execution, private investment and environmental safeguards will decide whether Sagarmala makes India a global maritime hub.
free.g1m-2023-p2-13a:
Demographic dividendWorking-age populationDependency ratioHuman capital

Demographic dividend is the economic growth potential that arises when the share of the working-age population (15–64 years) rises relative to dependants (UNFPA). India, the world's most populous country since 2023, with a median age of about 28, is in this window, which UNFPA expects to last until about 2055. Whether it becomes a dividend or a burden depends on jobs, skills and health.

1. Indian context

  • Large working-age base: Census 2011 found about 60% of the population aged 15–59 years, and the dependency ratio is falling.
  • Peak ahead: the Economic Survey 2018-19 projected that the working-age share would peak around 2041.
  • Fertility below replacement: the total fertility rate (TFR) has fallen to 2.0 (NFHS-5, 2019-21), below the replacement level of 2.1.
  • Regional asymmetry: southern states are ageing early (AP's TFR is 1.7, NFHS-5), while Bihar and Uttar Pradesh remain young, so the dividend will come mainly from the northern states.

2. Opportunities

  • Workforce and savings: a larger workforce with fewer dependants can raise savings, investment and growth, as it did in East Asia.
  • Market and talent: a vast domestic market and a global supply of skilled workers in IT, health care and services.
  • Fiscal space: a falling dependency ratio frees resources for investment in infrastructure and human capital.

3. Challenges

  • Jobs: the Economic Survey 2023-24 estimated that about 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs are needed every year until 2030.
  • Skills and education: formal skilling is low and learning gaps persist; about 90% of workers are informal.
  • Women: female labour force participation, though rising, was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Health: 35.5% of children under five are stunted (NFHS-5), which lowers future productivity.
  • A closing window: as fertility falls, India will begin to age before it becomes rich unless growth speeds up.

4. Policy responses

  • Skills and education: Skill India Mission (2015) and NEP 2020.
  • Jobs: PLI and employment-linked incentive schemes.
  • Health and nutrition: Ayushman Bharat and Poshan Abhiyaan.

AP angle: with fertility well below replacement, Andhra Pradesh faces early ageing; in November 2024 it removed the two-child norm for local body candidates. Skilling through the AP State Skill Development Corporation is key to using its shrinking dividend.

Without investment in health, education and jobs, the dividend could turn into a demographic burden; human capital is the key.
free.g1m-2023-p2-13b:
Rural settlementsClustered and dispersedSettlement patternsSite factors

A rural settlement is a group of dwellings whose people depend mainly on primary activities such as farming, fishing, forestry and herding. NCERT classifies Indian rural settlements into four types, clustered, semi-clustered, hamleted and dispersed, while their shape (pattern) depends on relief, water, transport routes, security and social structure.

1. Types of rural settlements

  • Clustered: found on fertile plains where intensive farming, social cohesion and defence favour living together; in dry areas, scarce water also draws people together.
  • Semi-clustered: results from the segregation of a large village or from groups moving to its edge, often along caste lines.
  • Hamleted: social and ethnic factors split a village into physically separate units (hamlets) that keep a common name.
  • Dispersed: rugged terrain, dense forests and small patches of cultivable land force families to live apart.

2. Factors affecting rural settlements

  • Physical: relief, altitude, soil fertility, climate, drainage and the availability of water decide where people settle; wet-point sites lie near rivers, tanks and springs, and dry-point sites stand on raised ground above flood level.
  • Cultural and ethnic: caste structure, religion and tribal customs shape layout; segregation produces semi-clustered and hamleted forms.
  • Security: defence against raiders and wild animals favoured compact, walled or hilltop villages.
  • Economic: intensive farming favours clusters, while plantations, ranching and shifting cultivation favour scattered homesteads.
  • Transport: roads, railways and canals attract new settlements and shape linear patterns.
  • Planning: canal colonies and resettlement colonies have planned, regular layouts.

3. Rural settlement patterns in India

  • Linear: along roads, rivers, canals and coasts, as on the Kerala coast and along delta canals.
  • Rectangular: on plains and wide valleys, with roads crossing at right angles.
  • Circular: around lakes and tanks, or arranged in a ring for defence.
  • Star-like: where several roads converge on a village.
  • T, Y or cross-shaped: at road junctions.
  • Double village: on both banks of a river, linked by a bridge or ferry.

AP angle: compact villages are typical of the deltas and Rayalaseema; linear villages line the canals and the coast; tribal hamlets (gudems) are dispersed in the Eastern Ghats agency, and names ending in -palli and -gudem reflect hamlet origins.

Schemes such as PMAY-Gramin, SVAMITVA (2020) and the Rurban Mission (2016) aim to make rural settlements planned and sustainable.
free.g1m-2023-p2-14a:
Forest conservationForest (Conservation) ActJoint Forest ManagementGreen India Mission

As per the India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023, forest cover is 21.76% and forest plus tree cover 25.17% of India's geographical area, against the National Forest Policy 1988 goal of 33%. To close this gap and protect biodiversity, India combines legal, participatory, afforestation, judicial and technological strategies of forest conservation.

1. Constitutional and legal strategies

  • Constitution: Articles 48A and 51A(g) make environmental protection a duty of the State and of citizens; the 42nd Amendment (1976) moved forests and wildlife to the Concurrent List.
  • Laws: the Indian Forest Act 1927; the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972; the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, which requires central approval for diverting forest land, amended and renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023; the Forest Rights Act 2006; and the Compensatory Afforestation Fund (CAMPA) Act 2016.
  • Protected areas: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and tiger, elephant and biosphere reserves protect the richest forests.

2. Judicial strategies

  • Godavarman case: T.N. Godavarman (1996) extended protection to all forests in the dictionary sense, whatever their ownership.
  • Recent order: in February 2024, hearing challenges to the 2023 amendment, the Supreme Court ordered that this wide definition continue.

3. Participatory strategies

  • Joint Forest Management (1990): forest departments and village committees share protection duties and benefits; van panchayats, community forest resource rights under the FRA and sacred groves add to this.
  • People's movements: Chipko (1973) and Appiko (1983) showed the power of local communities.

4. Afforestation, monitoring and international commitments

  • Programmes: social forestry, the National Agroforestry Policy (2014), the Green India Mission (2014), MISHTI for mangroves (2023) and 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam' (2024).
  • Monitoring: Forest Survey of India satellite mapping and forest-fire alerts.
  • Commitments: restoring 26 million hectares of degraded land and creating an additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent, both by 2030.

Challenges: diversion for mining and infrastructure, encroachment, forest fires, invasive species such as Lantana, monoculture plantations counted as forest cover, and weak FRA implementation.

AP angle: Vana Samrakshana Samithis, a special task force against red sanders smuggling in the Seshachalam hills, and mangrove restoration at Coringa; notified forests cover over a fifth of the State, but actual forest cover is about 30,085 sq km, roughly 18.5% of its area (ISFR 2023).

Combining strict protection with community rights and scientific restoration can secure India's forests and its climate goals.
free.g1m-2023-p2-15a:
Environment Impact AssessmentEIA Notification 2006Public consultationSustainable development

Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) is a process to predict and evaluate the environmental and social impacts of a proposed project before approval and to suggest ways to reduce them. In India it began with river valley projects in 1976–77, became mandatory under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 through the EIA Notification 1994, and is now governed by the EIA Notification 2006. It applies the precautionary principle at the planning stage.

1. Meaning and process

  • Categories: Category A projects are appraised at the Centre by the Expert Appraisal Committee; Category B projects by State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities, and B2 projects need no full EIA report.
  • Stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal, followed by a decision and post-clearance monitoring, all now handled through the PARIVESH portal.

2. Evaluation: strengths

  • Integrated planning: EIA brings environmental and social concerns into project design (Rio Principle 17).
  • People's voice: public hearings give affected people a say; in Niyamgiri (2013) the Supreme Court left the mining decision to gram sabhas.
  • Mitigation: clearance conditions on pollution control, green belts and rehabilitation can be enforced and challenged before the National Green Tribunal.

3. Evaluation: weaknesses

  • Conflict of interest: consultants paid by project proponents prepare EIA reports, leading to poor baseline data and copied reports.
  • Weak participation: public hearings are often perfunctory, and many projects are exempted or placed in lighter categories; the draft EIA Notification 2020 drew wide criticism for proposing post-facto clearance and shorter consultation.
  • Weak monitoring: post-clearance compliance is rarely checked.
  • Capacity gaps: State authorities and pollution control boards lack the staff and expertise to appraise and monitor thousands of projects.
  • Ex post facto clearances: the Supreme Court in Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) called them contrary to environmental law.
  • AP angle: the LG Polymers styrene gas leak at Visakhapatnam (May 2020), which killed at least 12 people, exposed a plant operating without a valid environmental clearance.

4. Suggestions to make it effective

  • Independent regulator: a national environmental regulator, as urged by the Supreme Court in Lafarge (2011), and accredited consultants paid from a common fund.
  • Wider scope: strategic and cumulative EIA, with carrying-capacity studies for river basins and industrial clusters.
  • Accountability: make consultants and proponents liable for false or copied data, with blacklisting and penalties.

A transparent, participatory EIA is essential to reconcile development with sustainability.
free.g1m-2023-p3-2a:
Article 163Discretionary powersSpecial responsibilitiesConstitutional head

The Governor is the constitutional head of a State and, as a rule, acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 163(1); Shamsher Singh, 1974). But Article 163(1) itself excepts functions the Governor exercises "in his discretion", and under Article 163(2) his decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion is final. Certain Articles also give him special responsibilities, where he consults ministers but decides on his own judgement.

1. Constitutional discretion

  • Reserving Bills (Article 200): he may reserve a Bill for the President's consideration; reservation is compulsory when a Bill would endanger the position of the High Court.
  • President's Rule (Article 356): his report to the President on the failure of constitutional machinery is his own assessment.
  • Adjoining Union Territory: as its administrator (Article 239(2)), he acts independently of his State ministry.
  • Sixth Schedule: in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, he decides the share of mining royalties payable to autonomous district councils.
  • Seeking information (Article 167): he can call for information from the Chief Minister on administration and proposals for legislation.

2. Situational discretion

  • Appointing a Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority, or when a Chief Minister dies in office with no obvious successor.
  • Dismissing a ministry that has lost its majority, and dissolving the Assembly in such a case.
  • Judicial limits: S.R. Bommai (1994) made the floor test decisive; Rameshwar Prasad (2006) held the 2005 dissolution of the Bihar Assembly unconstitutional; Nabam Rebia (2016) held that the Governor's discretion is narrow and cannot be used to advance the House's session on his own.

3. Special responsibilities

4. Judicial position and reforms

  • Assent to Bills: after State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025) fixed timelines, the Supreme Court's opinion on the Presidential Reference (November 2025) held that courts cannot impose timelines or "deemed assent", though prolonged, unexplained inaction is open to limited judicial review.
  • Reform proposals: the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended an eminent, non-partisan Governor, consultation with the Chief Minister on appointment, and sparing use of discretion.

AP angle: Section 8 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 gave the Governor special responsibility for the security of life, liberty and property of residents of Hyderabad, the common capital, for up to ten years (until June 2024).

Discretion is a constitutional safety valve, not a parallel centre of power; exercised in good faith and within judicial limits, it protects both responsible government and the federal balance.
free.g1m-2023-p3-2b:
NEP 202042nd AmendmentConcurrent ListCooperative federalism

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, based on the Kasturirangan Committee draft, replaced the 1986 policy. Some States see it as centralising: a uniform 5+3+3+4 school structure, the three-language formula, common entrance tests, a proposed single higher-education regulator and Samagra Shiksha funds linked to PM SHRI agreements. The debate goes back to the 42nd Amendment (1976), which, on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, moved education and four other subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List.

1. What was transferred

2. Rationale behind the transfer

  • National standards: a concurrent role in education complements the Union's power to coordinate and determine standards in higher education and research (Entry 66, List I).
  • National integration and mobility: the Kothari Commission (1964-66) favoured a national system of education with a common structure, and common norms ease recognition of degrees and movement of students and teachers across States.
  • Funding and planning: the Union could legislate and fund on a national scale, as in the RTE Act, 2009 (under Article 21A) and Centrally Sponsored Schemes such as Samagra Shiksha.
  • Ecology: forests and wildlife cross State boundaries; the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023, followed.
  • Context: the transfer was made during the Emergency without wide consultation with the States, which is one reason the autonomy debate persists.

3. Does the NEP denude State autonomy?

  • Concerns: under Article 254 a Union law prevails over a repugnant State law, and conditional grants pressure States to adopt central models.
  • Diversity: uniform entrance tests and the language formula may not suit every State's needs, and a single higher-education regulator could reduce the role of State universities and State councils of higher education.
  • Counterpoint: the NEP is a policy, not a law; it leaves States room to adapt language, curriculum and pace, and States still run and fund most government schools and universities.
  • Federal safeguard: the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions advised the Union to consult States before legislating on Concurrent subjects.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh has adopted NEP-aligned steps such as foundational-stage school restructuring and PM SHRI schools, showing room for State-specific implementation within a national framework.

Cooperative federalism, with the Union setting minimum standards, flexible rather than conditional funding, and the States free to innovate after genuine consultation, can reconcile national quality with State autonomy in education.
free.g1m-2023-p3-3a:
73rd and 74th AmendmentsWomen's reservationProxy leadershipPolitical empowerment

The 73rd Amendment (1992) reserved at least one-third of seats and chairperson posts in Panchayats for women (Article 243D); the 74th Amendment reserved one-third of seats in municipalities (Article 243T), leaving chairpersons' reservation to State law. Twenty-one States, including Andhra Pradesh, and two UTs reserve 50%, and about 15 lakh women, around 46% of the 32 lakh elected panchayat representatives, hold office (Ministry of Panchayati Raj). This makes local bodies a major arena of women's political empowerment.

1. Scope

  • Grassroots leadership: women preside over panchayats and Gram Sabhas, bringing their concerns into local planning.
  • Gender-sensitive priorities: Chattopadhyay and Duflo (2004) found that women pradhans invested more in drinking water, a key need of women.
  • Better oversight of services: elected women monitor anganwadis, schools, sanitation, health and nutrition more closely.
  • Social inclusion: reservation within SC and ST seats has brought Dalit and Adivasi women into public office, challenging both caste and gender hierarchies.
  • A pipeline to higher office: local experience complements the 106th Amendment (2023), which reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats for women.

2. Challenges

  • Proxy leadership: male relatives ("sarpanch-pati") often run affairs while the elected woman only signs.
  • Social barriers: patriarchy, caste hierarchy and low literacy limit women's voice in meetings and Gram Sabhas.
  • Rotation of reserved seats every term breaks continuity and discourages long-term work.
  • Weak devolution of funds, functions and functionaries leaves even capable leaders with little real power.
  • Domestic burden, harassment and violence deter women from contesting again.

3. Enhancing empowerment in rural and urban local bodies

  • End proxy leadership: a Ministry of Panchayati Raj advisory committee (report, 2025) recommended exemplary penalties, women's ombudspersons and a federation of women leaders for peer support.
  • Capacity building: training under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, including digital literacy and financial management.
  • Continuity and voice: rotation after two terms, Mahila Sabhas before Gram Sabhas, and women's ward committees in cities.
  • Real devolution: gender budgeting, safety measures and child-care support.
  • Collective strength: linking elected women with self-help group federations gives them networks, information and confidence.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's self-help group movement (DWCRA from 1982, SERP in rural and MEPMA in urban areas) has produced confident women leaders who contest local elections and manage public resources.

Moving from representation to real power needs capacity, devolution and social change, so that women lead local governance in their own right.
free.g1m-2023-p3-3b:
Article 280Finance CommissionFiscal democracyDevolution

The Finance Commission (FC) is a quasi-judicial body constituted by the President every five years under Article 280 to recommend the sharing of Union taxes and grants-in-aid. It is not a permanent body: it dissolves after submitting its report. Yet its rule-based, consultative method has made it the most trusted pillar of fiscal federalism. The 16th FC (Chairman Arvind Panagariya, constituted 31 December 2023) covers 2026-27 to 2030-31; its report was tabled with the Union Budget 2026-27.

1. Why its credibility endures

  • Independent experts: a Chairperson and four members, with qualifications laid down by the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951, consult the Union, every State and local bodies.
  • Transparency: formulae, weights and reasons are published, and the report is laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum (Article 281).
  • Convention of acceptance: although advisory, its tax-devolution recommendations are accepted by the Union.
  • Institutional memory: each Commission builds on the data and methods of its predecessors, which keeps transfers predictable.

2. Promoting fiscal democracy

Fiscal democracy here means that citizens of every State, whatever its revenue capacity, get comparable public services, and that transfers are decided through an open, consultative and rule-bound process rather than discretion.

  • Vertical balance: the States' share of the divisible pool rose to 42% (14th FC) and is 41% under the 15th and 16th FCs.
  • Equity: the income-distance criterion (42.5% weight under the 16th FC) gives more to poorer States.
  • Incentives: demographic performance, forest and ecology, and the 16th FC's new "contribution to GDP" criterion (10%) reward good performance.
  • Third tier: grants to panchayats and municipalities and disaster response funds carry resources to the grassroots.

3. Limitations

  • Terms of reference are set by the Union and can tilt the outcome.
  • Cesses and surcharges stay outside the divisible pool, so the States' effective share is lower than 41%.
  • No permanent secretariat monitors implementation between Commissions.
  • Bypass routes: Centrally Sponsored Schemes and discretionary grants (Article 282) move large sums outside the FC framework.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's share rises from about 4.05% (15th FC) to about 4.2% (16th FC). After bifurcation AP relied on revenue-deficit grants under the 14th and 15th FCs; the 16th FC has discontinued such grants, making own-revenue growth vital.

A permanent secretariat, a smaller share of cesses and closer consultation with States on the terms of reference would further strengthen this credible, temporary institution of fiscal federalism.
free.g1m-2023-p3-4a:
MotionsResolutionsParliamentary procedureExecutive accountability

A motion is a formal proposal made by a member for eliciting a decision of the House. No discussion on a matter of general public importance can take place in Parliament except on a motion moved with the consent of the presiding officer. Motions are thus the main procedural tools through which the House debates issues, expresses its will and holds the government to accountability.

1. Kinds of motions

  • Substantive motion: a self-contained, independent proposal, such as the motion for impeachment of the President or removal of a judge.
  • Substitute and subsidiary motions: a substitute motion replaces an original motion on a policy or situation; subsidiary motions (ancillary, superseding, amendments) depend on or relate to another motion.
  • Closure motion: cuts short a debate; it may be simple, compartment, kangaroo or guillotine.
  • Calling attention motion: an Indian innovation (1954) to draw a minister's attention to an urgent matter and seek an authoritative statement.
  • Other motions: cut motions (policy, economy and token cuts) to reduce demands for grants, and No-Day-Yet-Named motions, admitted by the presiding officer but without a date fixed for discussion.

2. Motions and resolutions: the difference

  • Relationship: a resolution is a particular kind of substantive motion; every resolution is a motion, but not every motion is a resolution.
  • Voting: every resolution must be put to vote, whereas many motions, such as calling attention or short-duration discussions, end without a vote.
  • Purpose: a resolution records the opinion or decision of the House on a matter of general public interest; a motion may be only a procedural step.
  • Types of resolutions: private members' resolutions, government resolutions and statutory resolutions, such as those approving a Proclamation of Emergency or President's Rule.

3. Significance and concerns

  • Accountability: motions keep the executive answerable on a daily basis, the essence of parliamentary government.
  • Voice of the Opposition: adjournment, censure and no-confidence motions give minorities in the House a structured way to raise issues and force a debate.
  • Decline in use: frequent disruptions and fewer sittings mean that many admitted motions are never discussed.

AP angle: in July 2018 a no-confidence motion moved in the Lok Sabha by a member from Andhra Pradesh, over special category status for the State, was debated and defeated. In January 2020 the Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed a resolution under Article 169 seeking abolition of the Legislative Council, and withdrew it by another resolution in November 2021, showing how a resolution records a House's formal decision.

Motions and resolutions are the instruments of deliberation in a parliamentary democracy; more sittings and fewer disruptions would let legislatures use them to the full.
free.g1m-2023-p3-4b:
Legislative CouncilArticles 168-171BicameralismArticle 169

Under Articles 168-169, a State may have a Legislative Council as a second chamber. Six States have one: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Its strength cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly's or fall below 40 (Article 171), and its members are partly elected by local bodies, graduates, teachers and MLAs and partly nominated by the Governor. The Council is a revising chamber that stands equal to the Assembly in some matters and clearly unequal in others.

1. Matters in which the Council is equal

  • Ordinary Bills may be introduced in either House.
  • Ordinances issued by the Governor (Article 213) must be laid before both Houses.
  • Ministers, including the Chief Minister, may be drawn from either House.
  • Reports of the State Finance Commission, the State Public Service Commission and the CAG are considered by both Houses.
  • Enlarging the jurisdiction of the State Public Service Commission needs approval of both Houses.

2. Matters in which the Council is unequal

  • Money Bills and Budget: a Money Bill is introduced only in the Assembly; the Council can only make recommendations within 14 days (Article 198), and the Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Article 199). The Council discusses the Budget but cannot vote on demands for grants.
  • Ordinary Bills: the Council can delay a Bill passed by the Assembly for at most three months the first time and one month the second (Article 197); there is no joint sitting, so the Assembly prevails. A Bill originating in the Council and rejected by the Assembly simply ends.
  • Ministerial responsibility: the Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Assembly (Article 164(2)).
  • Elections: only elected MLAs vote in the elections of the President and of Rajya Sabha members.
  • Survival: Parliament creates or abolishes a Council by law on an Assembly resolution passed by a special majority (Article 169).

3. Assessment

  • Merits: graduates, teachers and nominated experts bring knowledge to debates, and the Council gives a second look at hasty legislation.
  • Criticism: it can only delay, adds to cost, and is sometimes used to accommodate those who lose elections.

AP angle: AP's Council has 58 members. The timeline shows its dependence on the Assembly: it has been created, abolished, revived and nearly abolished again by Assembly resolutions under Article 169.
