Consolidation is on track at the Centre; sustainability now needs higher tax buoyancy, better spending quality and stricter State-level discipline.
free.g1m-2023-p4-5a:
Budgetary policyReallocation of resourcesSocial servicesAP Budget 2023-24

Budgetary policy uses taxes, spending, borrowing and transfers to steer resources where markets alone would not send them. In Musgrave's terms it performs the allocation, distribution and stabilisation functions. For a State like Andhra Pradesh, which carries most social-sector responsibilities under the Seventh Schedule, the budget is the main instrument of human development.

1. Importance of budgetary policy in reallocation

  • Correcting market failures: the budget supplies public and merit goods such as education, health and sanitation, which markets under-provide.
  • Redistribution: progressive taxes, subsidies and direct benefit transfers move resources to the poor, women and weaker sections.
  • Regional and sectoral balance: spending can be steered to lagging regions (Rayalaseema, north coastal and tribal areas) and to priority sectors such as irrigation and MSMEs.
  • Growth: capital spending builds future capacity, while revenue spending sustains consumption and human capital.
  • Stabilisation: higher spending in downturns and restraint in booms smooth the cycle, though this is mainly a Union role.

2. Social services in AP Budget 2023-24 (₹2,79,279 crore; fiscal deficit 3.8% of GSDP)

  • Welfare of SC, ST, BC and minorities: ₹51,292 crore, 19.8% of spending against a States' average of 3.5% (PRS); sub-plans of ₹20,000 crore (SC), ₹6,929 crore (ST) and ₹38,605 crore (BC).
  • Direct benefit transfers: ₹54,228 crore across 22 schemes, including YSR Pension Kanuka (₹21,434 crore) and YSR Aasara for SHG women (₹6,700 crore).
  • Education: ₹32,658 crore (12.6%, below the 14.8% States' average), including Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu school upgrades.
  • Health, nutrition and housing: health ₹16,207 crore; social welfare and nutrition ₹11,230 crore, including YSR Sampoorna Poshana (₹1,073 crore); housing ₹5,600 crore (Pedalandariki Illu). Rural development received ₹16,159 crore.

3. Assessment

  • Strengths: strongly redistributive and women-centred; DBT reduced leakages and middlemen.
  • Weaknesses: committed spending and DBT left little for capital outlay, and education stayed below the States' average.
  • Missing link: outlays were tracked more than outcomes such as learning levels, anaemia or employment.

4. Latest trend (AP Budget 2026-27, ₹3.32 lakh crore)

NTR Bharosa pensions (formerly YSR Pension Kanuka) get ₹27,719 crore; Thalliki Vandanam (replacing Amma Vodi) ₹8,456 crore; education, sports and culture ₹35,673 crore; and health ₹19,630 crore. Capital outlay rises by 47%, signalling a shift towards investment alongside welfare.

Budgets should balance welfare with human-capital and physical investment, and track outcomes, not just outlays.
free.g1m-2023-p4-5b:
Gender budgetingChild budgetingGender Budget StatementOutcome budgeting

Gender budgeting applies a gender lens to the whole budget cycle, from planning to audit, tracking how much spending reaches women and girls and with what effect; it began with Australia's women's budget (1984). Child budgeting tracks spending on children (0-18) for health, education, development and protection. Neither is a separate budget: both are analytical statements within the main budget.

1. Gender and child budgeting in India

  • Gender Budget Statement: carried in the Union Budget since 2005-06, with Part A (schemes 100% for women), Part B (30-99%) and, since 2024-25, Part C (below 30%).
  • Gender budget cells: set up in Union ministries to review schemes and spending from a gender angle.
  • Child budget: the Union has published a statement on allocations for children since 2008-09.
  • Purpose: both make the budget accountable for those who have little voice in it.

2. Does Andhra Pradesh follow them?

Yes. Andhra Pradesh has presented separate Gender Budget and Child Budget statements since 2021-22, counting the full cost of exclusive schemes and a beneficiary share of general ones.

  • Gender Budget 2023-24: about ₹77,914 crore (roughly 28% of the budget): Part A ₹31,826 crore (PMAY-U housing, YSR Cheyutha, Aasara, Amma Vodi) and Part B ₹46,089 crore (pensions, Rythu Bharosa, rice subsidy).
  • Child Budget 2023-24: about ₹20,593 crore (₹16,748 crore in 2021-22), mostly education (Nadu-Nedu, Samagra Shiksha, Vidya Deevena) and nutrition (ICDS, Sampoorna Poshana).
  • Latest: the statements continue (for example 2025-26) with renamed schemes, such as Thalliki Vandanam in place of Amma Vodi, along with Stree Shakti free bus travel for women (from August 2025).

3. Evaluation

  • Strengths: greater transparency; women are the main recipients of DBT; house-site pattas are issued in women's names.
  • Weaknesses: Part B inflates totals by apportioning general schemes (pensions, rice subsidy) on assumptions; there are no gender audits or outcome indicators; child protection gets little (Mission Vatsalya about ₹118 crore).
  • Outcomes lag: NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 58.8% of AP women anaemic and 31.2% of under-five children stunted.
  • Process gaps: the statements are compiled after allocations are decided, so they rarely shape priorities, and local bodies do not yet prepare their own.

AP follows both in form; in substance it should move from accounting to outcome budgeting, with sex- and age-disaggregated data, gender audits and local-level gender budgeting.
free.g1m-2023-p4-6a:
Differentiated bankingSmall Finance BanksPayments BanksDigital banking

Differentiated banking means licensing specialised, niche banks with limited activities, rather than only full-service universal banks. Following the Nachiket Mor Committee (2014), the RBI gave in-principle licences to 11 payments banks and 10 small finance banks in 2015 to reach the unbanked and underserved at low cost. Together with digital rails, they are the backbone of India's financial inclusion strategy.

1. Scope for financial inclusion

  • Small Finance Banks: lend to small farmers, micro enterprises and the unorganised sector, with minimum capital of ₹200 crore, 75% priority-sector lending and at least half of loans up to ₹25 lakh. Licensing is on tap since 2019; many grew out of microfinance institutions and brought their village reach into regulated banking.
  • Payments Banks: accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer and offer payments and remittances but cannot lend; India Post Payments Bank uses the postal network for doorstep service.
  • Complementary lenders: RRBs, cooperative banks, NBFC-MFIs and MUDRA loans fill the remaining gaps in rural and micro credit.
  • Limits: thin margins, risky small-ticket loans and payments banks' reliance on fees; several payments-bank licensees gave up their licences.

2. Potential of digital banking

  • JAM base: over 55 crore Jan Dhan accounts with Aadhaar e-KYC give almost every household an account.
  • UPI: about 20 billion transactions a month (2025), with UPI 123PAY for feature phones and credit lines on UPI.
  • Last mile: Aadhaar-enabled payments (AePS), business correspondents and 75 Digital Banking Units (2022) serve villages without branches.
  • Credit: Account Aggregators and the Unified Lending Interface allow cash-flow-based, collateral-free loans to MSMEs and farmers.
  • Result: the RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose to 67.0 (March 2025).

3. Challenges

  • Skills and access: low digital literacy and patchy connectivity in remote areas.
  • Safety: rising cyber fraud and mis-selling erode trust; data protection depends on the DPDP Act 2023.
  • Gender gap: only 33% of women had ever used the internet (NFHS-5).
  • Usage: many accounts stay dormant, so access has not always meant use.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats, SHG women working as banking correspondents and Stree Nidhi carry digital services to villages; under 'One State-One RRB' its four RRBs became the Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank (sponsored by Union Bank of India) from 1 May 2025.

Differentiated banks plus digital rails can deliver 'phygital' inclusion; the focus must now shift from accounts to usage, credit and consumer protection.
free.g1m-2023-p4-6b:
Women entrepreneurshipCollateral gapCare burdenCredit and market access

Women own only about one-fifth of MSMEs (NSS 73rd round) and 13.76% of establishments (Sixth Economic Census). Female labour force participation has risen to 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), but much of it is unpaid or subsistence work. Raising women entrepreneurship is therefore central to inclusive growth and to the goal of women-led development.

1. Challenges faced by women entrepreneurs

  • Finance: little collateral, since few women hold land or property titles, along with lender bias and small loan sizes, keeps women in micro enterprises.
  • Care burden and social norms: women spend about 299 minutes a day on unpaid domestic work against 97 for men (Time Use Survey 2019); limits on mobility and safety restrict travel to markets and suppliers.
  • Markets and networks: weak links to buyers, mentors, investors and value chains.
  • Skills and technology: gaps in business, financial and digital skills, and limited access to modern equipment.
  • Compliance burdens: registration, tax and licensing procedures weigh most on very small firms.

2. Schemes and initiatives of the Government

  • Credit: MUDRA (2015), with about 68% of loans going to women; Stand-Up India (2016), with loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for greenfield units of women and SC/ST entrepreneurs; higher CGTMSE guarantee cover and PMEGP subsidy for women.
  • Recent budgets: term loans up to ₹2 crore for 5 lakh first-time women, SC and ST entrepreneurs (2025-26).
  • SHG-based: DAY-NRLM, Lakhpati Didi (target 3 crore) and Namo Drone Didi (15,000 drones) turn self-help groups into enterprise platforms.
  • Market access: Mahila e-Haat (2016), GeM's 'Womaniya' and a 3% public-procurement target for women-owned micro and small enterprises.
  • Ecosystem: NITI Aayog's Women Entrepreneurship Platform (2018) and Startup India support for women founders.

3. Gaps that remain

  • Scale: most loans are small, so few women-led units grow beyond the micro stage.
  • Care infrastructure: creches, safe transport and working women's hostels are still scarce.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's SHG movement (SERP, Stree Nidhi) is among India's strongest. YSR Cheyutha (2020-24) gave ₹18,750 a year to women aged 45-60 from weaker sections, with retail tie-ups for small businesses. The MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) aims at 'One Family, One Entrepreneur'.

Collateral-free credit, care infrastructure, mentoring and market links can turn women micro-borrowers into growth entrepreneurs, the essence of women-led development.
free.g1m-2023-p4-7a:
Agricultural creditKisan Credit CardInstitutional sourcesInterest subvention

Agricultural credit finances crop production, farm investment and marketing. India follows a multi-agency approach, with commercial banks, regional rural banks and cooperatives lending to farmers and NABARD (1982) providing refinance. Yet small, tenant and marginal farmers still depend on moneylenders, so the access and cost of credit remain central to farm incomes.

1. Types of agricultural credit

  • By duration: short-term crop loans (up to 15 months), medium-term loans (1-5 years) and long-term loans (over 5 years), each with its own uses and lenders (see table).
  • By purpose: production credit, investment credit and marketing credit, such as loans against warehouse receipts.
  • By security: secured loans against land or gold, and unsecured group loans to SHGs and joint-liability groups.

2. Sources of agricultural credit

  • Institutional: commercial banks (the largest share), RRBs (1975), cooperatives (StCB-DCCB-PACS for short-term and ARDBs for long-term credit), NBFCs and MFIs.
  • Non-institutional: moneylenders, traders, commission agents, landlords and relatives, often at high interest and tied to the sale of produce.
  • Dependence: about 70% of farm households' outstanding loans are institutional, but moneylenders still hold about 20% (NSS 77th round, 2019). Andhra Pradesh has the highest share of indebted farm households (93.2%) and the highest average debt (about ₹2.45 lakh).

3. Initiatives to improve access

  • Kisan Credit Card (1998): extended to animal husbandry and fisheries (2018-19); loans at 7% interest, effectively 4% on prompt repayment, under the Modified Interest Subvention Scheme, with the limit raised from ₹3 lakh to ₹5 lakh (Budget 2025-26).
  • Priority sector lending: 18% of bank credit must go to agriculture, including 10% to small and marginal farmers; the collateral-free limit was raised to ₹2 lakh (RBI, January 2025).
  • Stronger cooperatives: computerisation of 63,000 PACS and model bye-laws that let PACS take up dairy, fisheries, storage and other businesses.
  • Infrastructure and income support: the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (₹1 lakh crore, 3% interest subvention), the Kisan Rin Portal (2023) and PM-KISAN to curb distress borrowing.

AP angle: the AP Crop Cultivators Rights Act, 2019 gives tenant farmers Crop Cultivator Rights Cards for bank loans; Rythu Seva Kendras (formerly RBKs) link farmers to banks; and Annadata Sukhibhava (from 2025, replacing YSR Rythu Bharosa) gives ₹20,000 a year, ₹14,000 from the State plus ₹6,000 PM-KISAN, easing working-capital needs.

The priorities now are credit for tenants and small farmers, more investment credit for capital formation, and safe digital lending.
free.g1m-2023-p4-7b:
Sustainable agricultureNatural farmingSoil healthFarm incomes

Sustainable agriculture meets present food and income needs without degrading soil, water and biodiversity for future generations: it must be economically viable, ecologically sound and socially fair. In India it answers falling groundwater, fertiliser-driven soil fatigue and climate risk, the legacies of input-intensive Green Revolution farming in regions such as Punjab and Haryana.

1. Sustainable practices and systems in India

  • Organic and natural farming: PKVY (2015), MOVCDNER in the North-East, and Sikkim as the first fully organic State (2016). The National Mission on Natural Farming (November 2024, ₹2,481 crore) targets 1 crore farmers on 7.5 lakh ha through 15,000 clusters.
  • Resource conservation: micro-irrigation under PMKSY ('Per Drop More Crop'), zero tillage, crop-residue management, SRI in paddy and rainwater harvesting save water and energy.
  • Soil health: Soil Health Cards (2015), neem-coated urea, integrated nutrient and pest management, and PM-PRANAM (2023) to cut chemical fertiliser use.
  • Diversified systems: integrated crop-livestock-fish farming, agroforestry, millets (International Year of Millets 2023) and climate-resilient varieties (NICRA), under the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture.

2. AP angle: Community-managed Natural Farming

  • Model: Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming (APCNF, since 2016), run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, uses bio-stimulants (jeevamrutham, beejamrutham), 365-day green cover and pre-monsoon dry sowing.
  • Results: it has cut input costs, covers lakhs of farmers, is among the world's largest agroecology programmes, and won the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity (2024).
  • Transition challenges: possible yield dips in the first years, labour needed to prepare bio-inputs, and the lack of separate markets and prices for natural produce slow adoption.

3. Suggestions to improve incomes

  • Certification and branding: low-cost PGS-India certification and branding open premium domestic and export markets.
  • Collective marketing: FPOs can aggregate produce, add value through processing and sell directly to consumers.
  • Lower costs: village bio-input enterprises can replace purchased chemicals and create rural jobs.
  • New income streams: carbon credits and payments for ecosystem services can reward farmers for soil carbon and water conservation.
  • Price support and risk cover: MSP and procurement for millets and pulses, crop insurance and MGNREGS-built farm ponds can protect farmers during the transition, when yields may dip.

Sustainable farming pays when lower costs, premium markets and risk cover come together; it is essential for SDG 2 (zero hunger) and for climate adaptation.
free.g1m-2023-p4-8a:
Farm mechanisationCustom Hiring CentresYSR Yantra SevaSmall holdings

Farm mechanisation is the use of machines, from tractors and transplanters to combine harvesters and drones, to replace or supplement human and animal power in farm operations. India's mechanisation level is about 47%, well below that of developed countries. With small holdings, the Custom Hiring Centre (CHC) model, which rents machines rather than selling them, suits India and Andhra Pradesh best.

1. Scope and benefits

  • Timeliness: faster sowing and harvesting allow multiple cropping and reduce weather risk at harvest.
  • Input efficiency: precise placement saves seed, fertiliser and water; drones spray evenly and keep workers away from chemicals.
  • Productivity: higher yields and a lower unit cost of cultivation.
  • Labour: machines offset farm-labour scarcity caused by migration and MGNREGS, and reduce drudgery, especially for women.
  • Lower losses and new enterprise: threshers, dryers and graders cut post-harvest losses, while custom hiring, repair and drone-pilot services create rural jobs.

2. Central support

The Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation (2014-15) funds Custom Hiring Centres, farm machinery banks and hi-tech hubs, and subsidises machines for individual farmers; Namo Drone Didi gives 15,000 drones to women SHGs for spraying services. Kisan drones and custom hiring through farmer producer organisations extend modern machines to small farmers.

3. Implementation in Andhra Pradesh

  • YSR Yantra Seva Pathakam (2021): CHCs at every Rythu Bharosa Kendra (RBK) and cluster-level CHCs with combine harvesters in paddy areas. Farmer groups paid 10%, the State gave a 40% subsidy and banks lent 50%.
  • Access: small farmers hire tractors, rotavators, sprayers and harvesters at notified rates, booked through the RBK, reducing dependence on private owners who charge high peak-season rents.
  • After 2024: RBKs became Rythu Seva Kendras; mechanisation continues under SMAM and State plans, with subsidies to individuals and groups and drone-based CHCs for spraying.

4. Issues

  • Small holdings: the average holding in AP is only 0.94 ha (Agriculture Census 2015-16), so individual ownership rarely pays.
  • Peak demand: every farmer needs the same machine in the same fortnight.
  • Operation: under-used equipment in the off-season, poor maintenance, scarce trained operators and slow group loan repayment.
  • Fit: machines suited to tank-fed paddy, horticulture and dry-land crops in Rayalaseema are still limited.

CHCs suit AP's small-farm structure; digital booking, operator training, crop-specific machines and FPO-run hubs can make mechanisation affordable and sustainable.
free.g1m-2023-p4-9a:
Strategic disinvestmentDIPAMOffer for SaleAsset monetisation

Strategic disinvestment is the sale of a substantial government stake in a central public sector enterprise (usually 50% or more) together with transfer of management control to a strategic buyer; in minority disinvestment the government stays in control. In 2016 the Department of Disinvestment (set up in 1999) was renamed the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), widening its role to managing public investment for value.

1. Methods of disinvestment since 2016

  • IPOs and FPOs: listing CPSEs on stock exchanges, for example LIC (May 2022, about ₹21,000 crore, then India's largest IPO).
  • Offer for Sale (OFS): quick sale of government shares in listed CPSEs through the stock-exchange mechanism.
  • Exchange Traded Funds: the CPSE ETF (2014) and Bharat-22 ETF (2017) sold diversified baskets of CPSE shares to retail and institutional investors.
  • Strategic and inter-CPSE sales: sales with transfer of control (Air India, NINL) and sales to other CPSEs (HPCL to ONGC, 2018; REC to PFC, 2019).
  • Capital restructuring: DIPAM's 2016 guidelines push CPSEs to pay higher dividends and use buybacks and bonus shares.
  • Policy frameworks: the New PSE Policy (2021) keeps a minimal presence in four broad strategic sectors and privatises or closes CPSEs elsewhere; the National Monetisation Pipeline (2021) leases operating assets.

2. Achievements and outcomes

  • Air India: sold to Talace (Tata group) in January 2022 for ₹18,000 crore; it is now expanding with record aircraft orders, showing efficiency gains after privatisation.
  • Neelachal Ispat Nigam: sold to Tata Steel Long Products (2022, ₹12,100 crore) and revived.
  • Shortfalls: receipts mostly missed targets (2021-22: ₹1.75 lakh crore budgeted, about ₹13,500 crore realised); the BPCL sale was called off (2022), and the Shipping Corporation and CONCOR sales stalled.
  • Shift in approach: DIPAM now stresses dividends and value creation; the 2026-27 target is ₹80,000 crore (₹47,000 crore in 2025-26 BE).

AP angle: the Dredging Corporation of India (Visakhapatnam) was sold to four port trusts (2019). Rashtriya Ispat Nigam (Visakhapatnam Steel Plant) was approved for strategic sale in 2021, but in January 2025 the Centre approved an ₹11,440 crore revival package.

Disinvestment should aim at efficiency and better use of public capital, not just deficit-filling, with transparent valuation and protection for workers, so that the public gets fair value for its assets.
free.g1m-2023-p4-9b:
Industry 4.0Cyber-physical systemsProduction-Linked IncentiveManufacturing

Industrial Revolution 4.0, a term popularised by Klaus Schwab of the World Economic Forum (2016), is the fusion of physical, digital and biological systems in production through AI, the Internet of Things, robotics, 3D printing and cyber-physical 'smart factories'. It grew out of Germany's 'Industrie 4.0' strategy (2011) and is changing where and how goods are made.

1. Likely impact on India's manufacturing

  • Productivity and quality: predictive maintenance, real-time quality control and mass customisation lower costs and defects.
  • New industries: semiconductors, EVs and batteries, drones and electronics, backed by the India Semiconductor Mission (2021) and the IndiaAI Mission (2024).
  • Supply chains: digital traceability helps Indian firms join global value chains as China-plus-one sourcing grows.
  • Jobs: automation threatens routine low-skill work in garments and auto assembly while raising demand for skilled technicians, risking 'premature deindustrialisation' with manufacturing still about 15-17% of GVA.
  • MSME divide: small firms lack capital, skills and cyber-security; SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 hubs demonstrate smart-factory tools to them.
  • Green manufacturing: smart energy management and 3D printing cut waste, helping exporters meet carbon rules such as the EU's carbon border adjustment.

2. Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes

  • Design: launched in 2020 for mobile phones and extended to 14 sectors with an outlay of nearly ₹2 lakh crore; incentives are paid on incremental sales over a base year.
  • Sectors: electronics, IT hardware, pharma, medical devices, autos, ACC batteries, solar modules, textiles, food processing, white goods, specialty steel, telecom and drones.
  • Outcomes: over ₹2.4 lakh crore of actual investment and over 14 lakh jobs by March 2026 (PIB); India is the second-largest mobile phone maker, and smartphone exports reached ₹2.62 lakh crore (about $28 billion) in 2025.
  • Concerns: uneven uptake (textiles, specialty steel), low domestic value addition in assembly and delayed payouts; the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (2025) targets deeper value addition.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh hosts Google's planned $15 billion AI hub at Visakhapatnam (announced 2025) and the Sri City electronics cluster, backed by its Electronics Manufacturing Policy 4.0 (2024-29); skilling its youth for these jobs is the key task.

PLI, combined with skilling, R&D and MSME digitalisation, can make Industry 4.0 a source of jobs rather than a threat to them, and help manufacturing drive Viksit Bharat.
free.g1m-2023-p4-10a:
MSMEsDr. YSR NavodayamReSTARTLoan restructuring

Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), defined under the MSMED Act, 2006, are Andhra Pradesh's largest non-farm employers and the base of its manufacturing. In a farm-heavy economy they link agriculture with industry and services. Two State programmes, Dr. YSR Navodayam (2019) and ReSTART (2020), sought to keep them afloat during credit stress and the COVID-19 lockdown.

1. (i) Importance of MSMEs in Andhra Pradesh's economy

  • Jobs: they provide local employment for rural youth, women and artisans at a low capital cost per job.
  • Value addition to farm output: rice mills, aqua and seafood processing, and chilli, turmeric and cotton processing raise farm incomes.
  • Exports: marine products, pharma intermediates, granite and handlooms reach global markets.
  • Ancillaries: they supply large units, such as Kia's vendor base at Penukonda and electronics firms at Sri City.
  • Heritage and balance: crafts and handlooms spread industry across regions and support SC, ST and women entrepreneurs.
  • Formalisation: Udyam registration links units to priority-sector credit, public procurement preferences and the MSME Samadhaan portal for delayed payments.

2. (ii) Scope and implementation of Dr. YSR Navodayam and ReSTART

  • Dr. YSR Navodayam (2019): the State's drive under the RBI's January 2019 scheme for one-time restructuring of stressed but standard MSME loans with total exposure up to ₹25 crore, without downgrading them to NPAs. Units had to be GST-registered unless exempt, so the scheme also nudged formalisation. District Industries Centres and banks identified eligible units and helped them apply.
  • ReSTART (22 May 2020): a COVID-19 relief package that released ₹905 crore of pending industrial incentives in two instalments, waived fixed power demand charges for three lockdown months (₹188 crore), set up a ₹200 crore low-interest working-capital fund, and committed government purchase of about 360 MSME products with payment in 45 days.
  • Assessment: both eased liquidity and saved jobs at a critical time, but depended on banks' willingness to lend, reached mainly registered units, and arrears of incentives recurred.

3. Present position

Both programmes were time-bound and have ended. Support now runs under the AP MSME and Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29), with its aim of 'One Family, One Entrepreneur', MSME parks across constituencies and the World Bank-backed RAMP programme.

Timely credit, regular payment of incentives and cluster infrastructure are the keys to a resilient MSME sector that can make AP's growth broad-based.
free.g1m-2023-p4-11a:
Digital Public InfrastructureIndia StackDigital divideBharatNet

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) means open, interoperable, population-scale digital systems built as public goods, on which government and private firms can build services. India's 'India Stack' covers identity (Aadhaar), payments (UPI), data (DigiLocker, Account Aggregators) and services (ONDC, ABDM, CoWIN, GeM, FASTag). Its reach has made India a model for the Global South, recognised at the G20 summit (2023).

1. Impact on socio-economic development

  • Financial inclusion: over 55 crore Jan Dhan accounts; UPI handles about 20 billion transactions a month, making India the world leader in real-time payments.
  • Governance: DBT removed duplicate and fake beneficiaries, saving over ₹3 lakh crore (government estimate), and delivered relief quickly during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
  • Formalisation and credit: digital trails enable loans for street vendors and MSMEs (PM SVANidhi, Account Aggregators), and GeM opens public procurement to small sellers.
  • Services: DigiLocker, e-Sanjeevani telemedicine, DIKSHA for school content, e-NAM for farmers and e-Shram for unorganised workers widen access to public services.
  • Global influence: the G20 New Delhi Declaration (2023) endorsed a DPI framework, and India shares its tools through the Global DPI Repository.

2. Steps to accelerate digital infrastructure and reduce the digital divide

  • Connectivity: BharatNet to all gram panchayats (amended programme of about ₹1.39 lakh crore, 2023), a fast 5G rollout (from October 2022), PM-WANI public Wi-Fi and the Digital Bharat Nidhi for remote areas.
  • Skills and access: PMGDISHA rural digital literacy (6 crore target), Common Service Centres as assisted access points, and Bhashini tools for Indian languages.
  • Trust and security: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and its Rules (2025), CERT-In and the Telecommunications Act 2023.
  • Closing the gender gap: only about 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5), so women's digital literacy through SHGs and Common Service Centres is a priority.

3. Concerns

  • Exclusion risks: authentication failures can deny rations or pensions to the elderly and to manual workers.
  • Privacy and fraud: large databases and rising cyber fraud demand strong data protection and grievance redress.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh has AP Fibernet, about 15,000 village and ward secretariats delivering services at the doorstep, the Real Time Governance Society and 'Mana Mitra' WhatsApp governance (2025).

DPI has made inclusion real; affordable devices, local-language content and digital skills must now ensure that no one is left offline.
free.g1m-2023-p4-11b:
Smart Cities MissionArea-based developmentMunicipal financeLand value capture

The Smart Cities Mission (25 June 2015) selected 100 cities through a challenge (2016-18) for area-based development (retrofitting, redevelopment and greenfield projects) plus pan-city ICT solutions, executed by city Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs). It closed on 31 March 2025 with over 90% of projects completed, leaving lessons for urban financing.

1. Features of a smart city

A smart city provides core infrastructure and a decent quality of life through smart solutions. Its elements include assured water and electricity, sanitation and solid-waste management, efficient public transport, affordable housing, robust IT connectivity and e-governance, safety of women, children and the elderly, health, education and a sustainable environment. An Integrated Command and Control Centre, now working in all 100 cities, manages traffic, utilities and emergencies with real-time data.

2. Role in economic development

  • Agglomeration: cities produce most of India's GDP; better infrastructure raises productivity and draws investment.
  • Ease of living and business: better mobility, utilities and digital services cut costs for households and firms.
  • Jobs: construction, services, tourism and start-ups grow with improved urban infrastructure.
  • Efficiency: data-driven management of traffic, water and energy saves resources and money.

3. Challenges in financing

  • Grant dependence: the Centre gave about ₹48,000 crore (about ₹100 crore per city a year), with matching State and ULB shares, so projects leaned on grants.
  • Weak municipal finances: low property-tax collection, poor user charges and low credit ratings limit borrowing.
  • Little private capital: PPPs and bonds formed only a small share of funding.
  • Institutional friction: SPVs bypassing elected urban local bodies, and delays in land and clearances.

4. Solutions

  • Own revenue: property-tax reform with GIS mapping and floor rates (a 15th FC condition), and cost-recovering user charges.
  • Market borrowing: municipal and green bonds, as with the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation's ₹80 crore bond (2018) and APCRDA's ₹2,000 crore Amaravati bonds (2018).
  • Land value capture (MoHUA framework, 2017), PPPs with viability gap funding, and pooled financing for smaller cities.
  • New funds: the Urban Infrastructure Development Fund and the ₹1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund (Budget 2025-26).

AP angle: Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Tirupati and Amaravati were Andhra Pradesh's smart cities; the Visakhapatnam and Amaravati bonds show how AP cities have tapped markets.

Financially strong, accountable ULBs, in the spirit of the 74th Amendment, can make smart-city gains outlast the mission.
free.g1m-2023-p4-12a:
Export Promotion Policy 2022-27PUSH strategyValue additionDistrict export hubs

Andhra Pradesh's Export Promotion Policy 2022-27 aims to make the State an export hub and double exports in five years, shifting from raw commodities to value-added products. Its core is the 'PUSH' strategy, built on four pillars: value addition, better infrastructure and institutions, streamlined processes and digital technology. District-level committees and port-led development along the State's long coastline, the third longest in India, support it.

1. The PUSH strategy

  • Promote value addition: move from exporting raw shrimp, rice and chilli to processed and branded products that earn more per tonne.
  • Upgrade infrastructure and institutions: ports, logistics and testing labs, with District Industries Centres (DICs) acting as export facilitators.
  • Streamline processes: faster customs and State clearances through single-window approvals.
  • Harness digital technology: a dedicated trade portal, market intelligence and e-commerce exports for small firms.

2. Challenges of the export sector

  • Concentration: a few products (shrimp, rice, pharma) and markets; US tariff hikes (2025), anti-dumping and countervailing duties and Ecuadorian competition hit AP's shrimp exporters.
  • Quality barriers: antibiotic-residue rejections and strict EU and US standards, with few accredited testing labs.
  • Logistics costs: gaps in cold chains, port connectivity and last-mile roads raise costs.
  • MSME constraints: weak awareness of export procedures, costly export credit and insurance, and little branding.
  • Volatility: currency swings and global demand shocks.

3. Support extended by the AP Government

  • District focus: District Export Promotion Committees with district export action plans, aligned with the Districts as Export Hubs and One District One Product initiatives.
  • Facilitation: a State Export Promotion Committee, and Export Facilitation Cells at State level and in DICs for handholding and capacity building.
  • Partnerships: engagement with 34 Export Promotion Councils for handholding support.
  • Infrastructure: port-led development (Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam, Mulapeta, Kakinada Gateway), industrial corridors and fishing harbours.
  • Convergence: with RoDTEP, the Export Promotion Mission (2025) and MPEDA schemes.

4. Way forward

  • Quality first: more accredited testing labs near aqua and spice clusters, and residue monitoring at the farm level, to cut rejections.
  • Diversification: new markets through India's trade agreements, and new products such as ready-to-eat seafood, formulations and electronics.
  • Branding: a common AP brand for GI-tagged products such as Guntur chilli and handlooms.

As India's leading shrimp-exporting State, AP needs quality infrastructure, branding and diversification of products and markets to make its long coastline a true gateway to global markets.
free.g1m-2023-p4-13a:
Global stagflationImported inflationInflation targetingMonetary Policy Committee

In 2022-23 the world faced stagflation-like conditions: after the Russia-Ukraine war, global inflation rose to 8.7% (2022) and stayed at 6.8% (2023, IMF), while global growth slowed to about 3%. Sharp rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve and other central banks carried these shocks to emerging economies like India through trade, prices and capital flows.

1. Effects on India's growth and inflation

  • Exports: merchandise exports fell from about $451 billion (2022-23) to $437 billion (2023-24) as world demand slowed.
  • Imported inflation: costlier crude, edible oils and fertilisers pushed CPI inflation to 7.8% (April 2022) and 6.7% on average in 2022-23.
  • Capital flows: US Fed hikes caused FPI outflows and rupee depreciation; the RBI raised the repo rate by 250 bps (May 2022-February 2023).
  • Resilience: domestic demand and public capex sustained growth; inflation eased to 5.4% (2023-24) and 4.6% (2024-25), and growth is estimated at 7.4% for 2025-26 (NSO).
  • Now: with crude volatility, weather risks and CPI at 4.8% (August 2026), the RBI raised the repo rate to 5.50% (October 2026), projecting 2026-27 growth at 7.1% and inflation at 5.2%.

2. Methods to control inflation

  • Monetary policy manages demand-pull inflation and expectations, while fiscal and supply-side measures tackle cost-push shocks in food and fuel that interest rates cannot fix quickly.
  • AP example: Rythu Bazaars in Andhra Pradesh sell subsidised tomatoes and onions during price spikes.

3. Inflation targeting

  • Framework: on the Urjit Patel Committee's (2014) advice, the RBI Act was amended in 2016 (Sec. 45ZA) to set a CPI target of 4% ±2%, fixed by the Union government every five years.
  • Monetary Policy Committee: six members, three from the RBI (the Governor has a casting vote) and three external experts, decide the repo rate by majority.
  • Accountability: if inflation stays outside the band for three straight quarters, the RBI must report the reasons and remedies to the government, as it did in November 2022.
  • Assessment: it has anchored expectations and brought inflation down, though food and supply shocks, which make up a large part of the CPI basket, limit its reach.

Credible inflation targeting, fiscal prudence and supply-side reforms such as storage and cold chains offer the durable answer to imported shocks.
free.g1m-2023-p4-13b:
Foreign Direct InvestmentConsolidated FDI PolicyAutomatic routeFDI equity inflows

Foreign investment includes FDI, a lasting interest usually of 10% or more of a company's equity, and portfolio investment below that level; it brings capital, technology, management skills and market access. India's FDI regime rests on FEMA, 1999, the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019, and the DPIIT's Consolidated FDI Policy, updated through Press Notes.

1. Factors that spur foreign investment

  • Market: a large, fast-growing economy and a young, increasingly skilled workforce.
  • Liberal policy: most sectors are open under the automatic route, and caps have been eased in defence, telecom, insurance and space.
  • Manufacturing push: Make in India, PLI schemes, the semiconductor mission and China-plus-one shifts in supply chains.
  • Business climate: GST, the IBC, the National Single Window System, PM Gati Shakti and macroeconomic stability.
  • Trade deals: the India-EFTA TEPA with a $100 billion investment commitment (in force October 2025), the UAE CEPA, and GIFT City as an international financial centre.

2. Major features of the Consolidated FDI Policy

  • Issuing authority: DPIIT issues the consolidated circular (latest effective 15 October 2020) and updates it through Press Notes, under FEMA and the Non-Debt Instruments Rules 2019.
  • Two routes: the automatic route needs no prior approval; the government route uses the Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal, after the FIPB was abolished in 2017.
  • Sectoral caps: set by sector (see table), with conditions such as minimum capitalisation and local sourcing in some sectors.
  • Prohibited sectors: lottery, gambling, chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business, cigarette manufacturing and atomic energy.
  • Security screening: under Press Note 3 (2020), investment from countries sharing a land border with India needs government approval.

3. Present situation of FDI equity inflows (DPIIT)

  • Inflows: FDI equity inflows in 2025-26 were $58.84 billion, up 18%; total FDI was $94.5 billion.
  • Sources and destinations: Singapore, the US (more than doubled) and Mauritius lead as sources; Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat lead among States.
  • Concern: net FDI was weak in 2024-25 owing to high repatriation and Indian firms' outward investment.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh has drawn big proposals such as Google's $15 billion AI hub at Visakhapatnam and the proposed AM/NS steel plant at Anakapalli.

Predictable regulation, stable taxes and faster contract enforcement can turn proposals into lasting, job-rich investment.
free.g1m-2023-p4-14a:
Public debtFiscal deficitDebt sustainabilityInterest-growth differential

Public debt is the government's total outstanding internal and external liabilities. It rose sharply after COVID-19; central government debt is 56.1% of GDP (2025-26 RE). Debt is sustainable when it can be serviced without ever-rising taxes, default or inflation, which depends on the gap between growth and interest rates and on the primary balance.

1. Reasons for higher public debt

  • Persistent deficits: revenue deficits mean the government borrows even to meet current spending, not only to build assets.
  • COVID-19 shock: the Centre's fiscal deficit hit 9.2% of GDP in 2020-21 as revenue fell and relief spending rose.
  • Low tax base: a general-government tax-GDP ratio of only about 18%, a narrow income-tax base and many exemptions.
  • Committed spending: interest takes nearly 40% of the Centre's revenue receipts, besides salaries, pensions (including old-pension revival in some States) and subsidies.
  • Off-budget and contingent liabilities: loans of State corporations and SPVs, guarantees, and discom losses (the UDAY takeover, 2015).

2. Scope for debt sustainability: favourable factors

  • r < g: nominal growth (about 10% assumed for 2026-27) exceeds the effective interest rate, so the debt ratio can fall even with a small primary deficit (the Domar condition).
  • Safe structure: debt is mostly domestic, rupee-denominated and long-maturity, so currency and rollover risks are low.
  • Captive demand: large domestic savings and banks' SLR holdings provide steady buyers for government bonds.
  • Credible path: the fiscal deficit falls to 4.3% in 2026-27, with a debt anchor of 50±1% of GDP by March 2031.

3. Risks

  • Heavy interest burden: interest crowds out development spending on health, education and infrastructure, and keeps pressure on India's sovereign credit ratings.
  • Adverse shocks: the IMF (2023) warned that general government debt could exceed 100% of GDP under adverse shocks, a view the government disputed.
  • States: rising State liabilities, guarantees and freebies add to general-government debt, which is much higher than the Centre's debt alone.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's outstanding liabilities are about 36% of GSDP (2026-27 BE), plus guarantees and corporation borrowings flagged by the CAG; interest and pensions take a large share of its revenue.

India's debt is sustainable if growth stays high and deficits keep falling; a credible debt path, better tax buoyancy and productive capex are essential.
free.g1m-2023-p4-14b:
Women-led developmentEducationSkillingMicrofinance

'Women-led development', a theme India championed during its G20 presidency (2023), treats women as leaders and drivers of growth, not passive beneficiaries of welfare. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023), reserving one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for women, symbolises this shift from women's development to women's agency.

1. Education

  • Progress: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015), Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas under Samagra Shiksha and NEP 2020's Gender Inclusion Fund raised girls' enrolment. Female GER in higher education (28.5%) now exceeds male GER (AISHE 2021-22), and women are about 43% of STEM graduates.
  • Shift: the aim has moved from access to quality and leadership; DST's Vigyan Jyoti, for example, encourages girls to take up science.
  • Gaps: few women in STEM jobs, research and leadership; dropouts among poor and tribal girls remain high.

2. Skilling

  • Progress: Skill India and PMKVY, women's ITIs, Namo Drone Didi (15,000 drones to SHG women) and Lakhpati Didi (target 3 crore) are turning women into skilled earners and service providers.
  • Gaps: mismatch between training and jobs, mobility limits and the care burden; female LFPR has risen to 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), but much of it is unpaid or self-employed work.

3. Microfinance

  • Progress: the SHG-bank linkage programme (NABARD, 1992) and DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women in SHGs) turned savings groups into enterprise platforms; women hold about 68% of MUDRA loans, over 80% of Stand-Up India loans and over half of Jan Dhan accounts.
  • Shift: credit is now tied to enterprise and income; a 'Lakhpati Didi' is an SHG member with an annual household income of at least ₹1 lakh.
  • Gaps: small loan sizes and pockets of microfinance over-indebtedness (2024-25).

AP angle: undivided Andhra Pradesh pioneered DWCRA (1982-83) and the SERP-Velugu model; Stree Nidhi gives SHG women quick credit, while Thalliki Vandanam (aid to mothers for schooling) and Stree Shakti free bus travel (2025) strengthen women's agency.

4. Assessment

The statement largely holds: policy has moved from welfare to agency, and women are now designers and leaders of programmes such as SHG federations. Yet women-led development also needs care infrastructure, safe workplaces and transport, equal pay and more women in decision-making.

Turning education and credit gains into quality jobs and leadership is central to Viksit Bharat.
free.g1m-2023-p4-15a:
Rainbow RevolutionAllied sectorsFood processingAgro-industrial value chains

The Rainbow Revolution, envisaged in the National Agriculture Policy 2000, seeks holistic growth across all farm sub-sectors rather than foodgrains alone. It brings together earlier colour-coded revolutions in crops, milk, fish, oilseeds, horticulture and poultry, aiming at diversification, nutrition security and higher farm incomes.

1. Impact of the Rainbow Revolution

  • Food security: a record foodgrain output of over 350 million tonnes (2024-25) supports free grain under PMGKAY for about 81 crore people.
  • Milk: India is the largest producer (about 239 million tonnes, 2023-24), thanks to Operation Flood and cooperatives.
  • Fish: India is the second-largest producer (about 184 lakh tonnes, 2023-24), now led by inland aquaculture.
  • Horticulture and eggs: horticulture output exceeds foodgrains; India is second in fruits and vegetables and among the top egg producers.
  • Incomes and nutrition: livestock and fisheries grow faster than crops, diversifying incomes for small and landless farmers and women.
  • Exports: India is the largest rice exporter and a major exporter of marine products and spices.
  • Gaps: over half of edible-oil needs are still imported; groundwater and soil depletion and regional imbalance persist.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh leads in fish and shrimp, is the largest oil-palm grower, a leading egg producer and a major chilli producer (Guntur), with strong horticulture: a model 'Rainbow' State.

2. Scope for industrial transformation of agriculture

  • Food processing: PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana, PLI for food processing and PMFME for micro units (One District One Product), since only a small share of fruits and vegetables is processed.
  • Value chains: 10,000 FPOs, cold chains, Operation Greens and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund link farms to factories.
  • Agri-tech: the Digital Agriculture Mission and AgriStack (2024), drones, precision farming and agri start-ups.
  • Bio-economy: ethanol from cane and grain (E20 achieved in 2025), bio-fertilisers and the BioE3 policy.
  • Allied industries: dairy and poultry are already organised like industries, and feed, vaccines, packaging and processing create non-farm rural jobs.
  • Constraints: small holdings, weak cold chains, low processing levels and limited credit for agro-entrepreneurs slow this transformation.
  • AP example: the AP Food Processing Policy (2024-29), aqua-processing units, spice parks and port-linked agri exports.

The next phase is moving from production to processing and markets, sustainably, so that farmers capture more of the value chain.
free.g1m-2023-p4-15b:
APMC regulatione-NAMFarmer-market linkageOne Nation One Market

Agricultural marketing is a State subject ('markets and fairs', Entry 28, State List). Regulated markets began with the cotton markets of colonial Berar and were recommended for all of India by the Royal Commission on Agriculture (1928). Each State now has an APMC Act; Andhra Pradesh's is the AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966.

1. Regulation of agricultural markets

  • Working: Agricultural Produce Market Committees notify produce and market areas, license traders and commission agents, levy market fees, and are meant to ensure open auction, fair weighing and prompt payment.
  • Reforms: the Model APMC Act 2003, the Model APLM Act 2017 (single State market area, private markets, e-trading) and the Model Contract Farming Act 2018. The three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021, so reform is now State-led.
  • Problems: too few markets (the National Commission on Farmers sought one within 5 km of every farmer), trader cartels, high fees and commissions, poor grading and storage, and fragmented State markets.

2. e-National Agriculture Market (e-NAM)

  • Platform: launched on 14 April 2016 with SFAC as lead agency, e-NAM links over 1,400 mandis in 23 States and 4 UTs on one electronic platform.
  • Features: a single licence, e-auction, quality assaying, online payment, an FPO trading module and warehouse-based trading (e-NWR).
  • Benefits: transparent prices, more buyers and less collusion among traders; farmers can see prices on their phones before deciding where and when to sell.
  • Limits: little inter-mandi and inter-State trade, weak assaying and internet infrastructure, trader resistance, and slow State adoption of unified licences.

3. Other farmer-market linkages

  • Collectives: FPOs under the 10,000 FPO scheme give small farmers bargaining power and scale.
  • Direct and digital channels: contract farming, Gramin Agricultural Markets, ONDC and warehouse receipts widen choices beyond the mandi.
  • Price support: PM-AASHA protects farmers of pulses and oilseeds when prices fall below MSP.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Rythu Bazaars (since 1999) link farmers directly to consumers; Rythu Seva Kendras with e-Crop booking support procurement; and AP mandis trade on e-NAM, though most trade still happens within the same mandi.

Unified State markets, assaying, warehouse-based trade and strong FPOs can make 'One Nation, One Market' real and raise the farmer's share of the consumer's rupee.
free.g1m-2023-p5-2a:
Citizen-centric governanceDigital public infrastructureAccountabilityE-governance bottlenecks

E-governance is the use of ICT to deliver services and information between government, citizens and businesses. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (11th report, 2008) set the goal of SMART governance: simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent. India's digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, UMANG) has made many services faceless, paperless and trackable, but technical, economic and social bottlenecks still limit its reach.

1. How digital platforms improve quality and accountability

  • Speed and convenience: UMANG offers about 2,575 services on one app (July 2026); DigiLocker's 72 crore+ users hold e-documents legally equal to originals.
  • Leak-proof delivery: Direct Benefit Transfer through the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) pays beneficiaries directly, weeding out fake and duplicate names.
  • Transparent spending: GeM for procurement, PFMS for fund flows and e-Office for files leave a digital audit trail.
  • Faceless processes: online passports, faceless tax assessment and e-courts reduce discretion, delays and petty corruption.
  • Grievance redress and feedback: CPGRAMS and state helplines track every complaint against a deadline; dashboards show officials and citizens how departments perform.

2. Citizen-centric governance: Andhra Pradesh examples

  • RTGS: a command centre tracks schemes, grievances and weather in real time from a state data lake.
  • Mana Mitra (January 2025): WhatsApp governance with 1,126 services from 35 departments by July 2026.
  • Village and ward secretariats: about 15,000 doorstep service centres, with AP Fibernet carrying broadband to panchayats.

3. Technical, economic and social bottlenecks

  • Exclusion risk: when the digital window is the only window, a failed fingerprint or a server outage hits the poorest hardest, such as elderly pensioners and manual workers.
  • Weak local capacity: panchayats and small towns lack trained IT staff, and projects are often designed without asking users, so service quality varies widely across States.

4. Way forward

  • Assisted and offline options: CSCs and secretariat staff as human help desks, with a grievance channel for every digital service.
  • Trust and safety: enforce the DPDP Act, 2023, CERT-In audits and open standards that prevent vendor lock-in.
  • Inclusion: Bhashini for Indian languages, PMGDISHA for digital literacy, accessible design for persons with disabilities.

Digital platforms make governance faster and more accountable, but technology must include, not exclude. Being digital by default, human by choice, with strong data protection, will make e-governance truly citizen-centric.
free.g1m-2023-p5-2b:
Atmanirbhar BharatPLI and semiconductorsDigital public infrastructureGlobal technology hub

Atmanirbhar Bharat (launched in May 2020) seeks self-reliance by making India a trusted link in global supply chains, not by closing the economy. In IT and electronics it marks a shift from a services-led model, built on software exports, to products, hardware and deep tech: phones, chips, AI and digital platforms. Production-linked incentives (PLI), the India Semiconductor Mission and digital public infrastructure are its main tools.

1. The big change in India's IT and electronics sector

  • Electronics manufacturing: PLI schemes for mobile phones (2020) and IT hardware (2023) made India the world's second-largest mobile phone maker; electronics production reached about ₹13.1 lakh crore in 2025-26, nearly seven times the 2014-15 level, and exports crossed ₹4 lakh crore.
  • From assembly to chips: the component scheme (2025) targets parts; ISM approved 12 units worth over ₹1.64 lakh crore, and ISM 2.0 adds equipment and materials.
  • Home-grown platforms: UPI (about 242 billion transactions in 2025-26), Aadhaar and DigiLocker show software self-reliance and are offered to other countries.
  • IT services move up the value chain: the tech industry earned about US$315 billion in 2025-26 (NASSCOM estimate) and employs about 59.5 lakh people; Global Capability Centres now do R&D, not just back-office work.
  • Strategic missions: IndiaAI for GPU compute and Indian foundation models, the National Quantum Mission, and data-centre capacity up from 375 MW (2020) to about 1,575 MW (2026).

2. Gaps that remain

  • Low value addition: most chips and many components are still imported.
  • Low R&D: spending is 0.84% of GDP, and India has few product companies of global scale.
  • Jobs and skills: AI automation threatens entry-level IT jobs; chip-design and AI skills are scarce.

3. Steps to make India a global technology hub

  • Research and deep tech: use the ₹1 lakh crore RDI scheme and ANRF to push R&D towards 2% of GDP, with a Deep-Tech Fund of Funds for start-ups.
  • Chips and supply chains: design-linked incentives, fabs and packaging, trusted partners (Quad, the EU) and critical minerals.
  • Talent: AI and semiconductor courses, reskilling of IT workers, and bringing diaspora researchers home.
  • Infrastructure and rules: green-powered data centres (Budget 2026-27 offers a tax holiday till 2047 to foreign cloud firms serving global customers from India) and stable data rules under the DPDP Act.
  • Standards and IP: Indian standards for digital public infrastructure and a stronger patenting and licensing culture.

AP angle: AP's IT & GCC Policy 4.0 (December 2024), Google's 1 GW AI hub and data centre at Visakhapatnam (₹1.35 lakh crore) and the Amaravati Quantum Valley (foundation stone, February 2026) position the State as a deep-tech destination.

Atmanirbhar Bharat is moving India from the "back office of the world" towards a product and platform nation. Sustained R&D, talent and trusted supply chains will decide whether India becomes a true global technology hub by 2047.
free.g1m-2023-p5-3a:
Space debrisKessler syndromeSpace situational awarenessProject NETRA

Space junk (orbital debris) is any human-made object in orbit that no longer serves a purpose: dead satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments from explosions, collisions and anti-satellite (ASAT) tests. ESA's Space Environment Report 2025 counts about 40,000 tracked objects, only about 11,000 of them active satellites, and estimates over 1.2 million fragments larger than 1 cm. Rising launches and mega-constellations are crowding low Earth orbit.

1. Sources of space junk

  • Spent stages and dead satellites: left in orbit once missions end.
  • Fragmentations: fuel or battery explosions and collisions, such as the Iridium–Kosmos crash of 2009; break-ups in 2024 alone added over 3,000 tracked fragments (ESA).
  • ASAT tests: China's 2007 test created thousands of long-lived fragments, and Russia's 2021 test forced the ISS crew to shelter. India's Mission Shakti (2019) hit a target at about 300 km, so most of its debris decayed quickly.
  • Mega-constellations: thousands of broadband satellites raise the risk of close approaches.

2. Challenges and potential risks

  • Collision risk: at about 7–8 km/s, even a centimetre-sized fragment can disable a satellite.
  • Kessler syndrome: each collision creates more debris and more collisions; ESA warns debris would keep growing even with no new launches, making some orbits unusable.
  • Threat to services and astronauts: navigation, communication, weather and earth-observation satellites, and crewed missions such as the ISS and India's planned Gaganyaan and Bharatiya Antariksh Station.
  • Operating costs: ISRO made 18 collision-avoidance manoeuvres for its Earth-orbiting satellites in 2025 (ISSAR 2025); each one uses fuel and shortens satellite life.
  • Governance gaps: intact satellites or rocket bodies now fall back to Earth more than three times a day on average (ESA), and no binding treaty requires debris removal; the Outer Space Treaty (1967) only makes states responsible and liable.

3. Project NETRA

  • What: NETRA (Network for space object Tracking and Analysis) is ISRO's space situational awareness system to track debris and warn Indian satellites of close approaches.
  • Components: an optical telescope being built at Hanle (Ladakh) and a tracking radar being designed; it works under IS4OM (2022), ISRO's unit for safe and sustainable space operations.
  • Aims: reduce dependence on foreign tracking data, protect India's satellites and feed ISRO's annual Space Situational Awareness Report.
  • Link to India's goals: supports Debris-Free Space Missions by 2030 and safe human spaceflight.

4. Way forward

Design satellites and rocket stages to de-orbit (ISRO already lowers spent PSLV fourth stages so that they re-enter), develop active debris removal, follow IADC and UN COPUOS guidelines, and work for a global ban on destructive ASAT tests.

Space is a shared, finite resource. With NETRA, Debris-Free Space Missions and global rules, India can help keep orbits usable, because space sustainability now matters as much as exploration.
free.g1m-2023-p5-3b:
Space sector reformsIN-SPACePrivate investmentSpace economy

The question's premise needs a correction: ISRO is a government research agency under the Department of Space, not a PSU; its commercial arms, Antrix (1992) and NewSpace India Ltd (NSIL, 2019), are the public sector companies. ISRO has performed brilliantly, from Mangalyaan to Chandrayaan-3 (2023), yet India holds only about 2% of the global space economy (about US$8 billion). The 2020 reforms invite private investment to grow it to US$44 billion by 2033.

1. Why private investment is needed despite ISRO's success

  • Demand beyond one agency's capacity: demand for launches, broadband and earth-observation data is soaring, but ISRO's launch rate is limited; after PSLV failures in May 2025 and January 2026, GSLV-F17 (September 2026) was ISRO's only successful launch of 2026 up to mid-October.
  • Budget limits: public funds cannot build all the rockets, satellites, ground stations and applications a US$44 billion economy needs; private and foreign capital can.
  • Let ISRO focus on frontier science: Gaganyaan (crewed flight planned for 2027), the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (first module 2028), the reusable NGLV and a crewed Moon landing by 2040 need ISRO's full attention, while routine production moves to industry.
  • Innovation and lower costs: start-ups bring 3D-printed engines, small satellites and launch-on-demand, as the global "NewSpace" wave has shown.
  • Jobs and exports: a wider supply chain creates skilled jobs and earns foreign exchange.

2. Reforms that opened the sector

  • Indian Space Policy 2023 opened every space activity to private firms.
  • Liberal FDI (2024): automatic route up to 74% for satellites, 49% for launch vehicles and 100% for components, plus a ₹1,000 crore venture fund (2024).
  • Technology transfer: about 75 ISRO technologies were transferred through IN-SPACe by 2024, and an HAL–L&T consortium is building PSLVs under an NSIL contract.

3. Early results

  • A growing ecosystem: about 440 space start-ups were active in 2026.
  • Global customers: NSIL launched 72 OneWeb satellites (2022–23) and AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird (December 2025).

4. Concerns to manage

  • Safety and liability: clear licensing, insurance and liability rules for private launches.
  • Security and debris: control over sensitive data and responsible use of crowded orbits.

AP angle: SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota hosts Agnikul's private launch pad and launched Vikram-1; a Third Launch Pad (₹3,984.86 crore) is coming up, and AP Space Policy 4.0 (2025) plans space cities at Lepakshi and near Tirupati.

Private investment does not replace ISRO; it multiplies it. With ISRO as the scientific anchor and industry as the workhorse, India can turn its space success into a large, globally competitive space economy.
free.g1m-2023-p5-4a:
No First UseCredible minimum deterrenceAssured second strikeNuclear doctrine 2003

India's nuclear doctrine, adopted on 4 January 2003 after Pokhran-II, rests on credible minimum deterrence and No First Use (NFU): nuclear weapons will be used only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or Indian forces anywhere, and that retaliation will be massive enough to inflict unacceptable damage. A hostile two-front environment has revived calls to drop NFU, yet India has kept it, for sound strategic reasons.

1. Circumstances pressing for a review

  • Two nuclear neighbours: China's fast-growing arsenal and China–Pakistan collusion raise the risk of a two-front crisis.
  • Pakistan's first-use posture: Pakistan rejects NFU and has built short-range "tactical" weapons such as Nasr to deter Indian conventional action; critics ask whether massive retaliation against a small tactical strike is credible.
  • Nuclear signalling in crises: Pakistan's threats around Operation Sindoor (May 2025) led India to declare that it would not tolerate "nuclear blackmail".
  • Official remarks: in 2019 the Defence Minister said NFU holds "till today" but that the future "depends on circumstances"; some strategists prefer deliberate ambiguity.
  • Erosion of global arms control: treaties are lapsing and some powers are lowering their nuclear thresholds, as Russia did in its 2024 doctrine.

2. Why India remains committed to NFU

  • Deterrence does not need first use: the nuclear triad of Agni missiles (Agni-5 tested with MIRV in 2024), aircraft and submarines (INS Arihant and INS Arighaat) assures a survivable second strike.
  • Conventional options: India can respond below the nuclear threshold, as at Balakot (2019) and in Operation Sindoor (2025).
  • Stability and cost: NFU avoids a costly arms race, hair-trigger alerts and accidental war, keeping the arsenal truly "minimum".
  • Diplomatic capital: restraint and a clean record earned the 2008 NSG waiver, the Indo-US 123 Agreement and membership of the MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement and Australia Group.
  • Consistency and flexibility: NFU fits India's call for universal, non-discriminatory disarmament (1988 Action Plan), and the doctrine already keeps the nuclear option against a major biological or chemical attack.

3. Way forward

  • Survivability: more ballistic-missile submarines, longer-range K-series missiles, and robust command, control and early warning under the Nuclear Command Authority.
  • Clarity, not ambiguity: review the doctrine periodically in private, while keeping the public message consistent.
  • Risk reduction: hotlines and confidence-building measures with Pakistan and China, and support for a global NFU treaty.

AP angle: the Arihant-class submarines, the sea leg that makes NFU credible, are built at the Ship Building Centre in Visakhapatnam, home of the Eastern Naval Command.

NFU is not weakness but confidence in a survivable second strike. Backed by credible capabilities and clear political will, it keeps India a responsible nuclear power while deterring both adversaries.
free.g1m-2023-p5-5a:
Climate emergency1.5 °C thresholdClimate-smart agricultureResilience

Climate change, the long-term warming driven mainly by human greenhouse-gas emissions, is now "unequivocal" (IPCC AR6). 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 °C (about 1.55 °C, WMO), and atmospheric CO₂ reached 423.9 ppm in 2024. Because its impacts cross borders and grow with every tonne emitted, it demands urgent collective action. For India, where nearly half the workforce depends on farming, climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is central to the response.

1. Why urgent intervention is needed

  • A closing window: keeping warming to 1.5 °C needs a 43% cut in global emissions by 2030 from 2019 levels (IPCC); delay locks in more warming.
  • Tipping points: Arctic sea-ice loss, permafrost thaw and ice-sheet collapse can make warming self-reinforcing and irreversible.
  • Rising extremes: longer heat waves, intense downpours and rapidly intensifying cyclones; the 2022 heat wave hit India's wheat harvest and led to export curbs.
  • Food, water and health security: heat and erratic monsoons cut yields, especially in rainfed areas; glaciers retreat and vector-borne diseases spread.
  • Justice and the global commons: emissions anywhere harm everyone, but poor countries and small farmers suffer most, so action under the Paris Agreement cannot wait.

2. Climate-smart agriculture

CSA, defined by the FAO (2010), has three pillars: sustainably raise productivity and incomes, adapt and build resilience, and reduce or remove emissions.

3. How CSA softens the effects of climate change

  • Resilient varieties: 109 high-yielding, climate-resilient and biofortified varieties of 61 crops were released in August 2024, and genome-edited Pusa DST Rice 1 (May 2025) yields more on saline soils.
  • Research and extension: ICAR's NICRA (2011) demonstrates climate-resilient practices in vulnerable districts through Krishi Vigyan Kendras, and IMD's agro-advisories guide sowing and spraying.
  • Lower emissions: water-saving rice methods cut methane, and balanced fertiliser use and natural farming cut nitrous oxide and input costs.
  • Risk transfer: PMFBY (2016) protects incomes after droughts, floods and cyclones.
  • Conserving the resource base: the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture under the NAPCC and the National Mission on Natural Farming (2024) protect soil and water.

AP angle: AP Community Managed Natural Farming (RySS, 2016; over 10 lakh farmers; Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity, 2024) uses pre-monsoon dry sowing for year-round green cover, holding moisture in drought-prone Rayalaseema, while delta farmers face cyclones such as Michaung (2023) and creeping salinity.

Climate change is a threat multiplier that cannot wait. Climate-smart agriculture, backed by research, finance and farmer institutions, lets Indian farming adapt and mitigate at once, protecting food security while lowering emissions.
free.g1m-2023-p5-6a:
Paris Agreement Article 6Carbon Credit Trading SchemeCarbon creditsNDC

A carbon credit is a tradable certificate for one tonne of CO₂-equivalent reduced or removed. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (2015) lets countries cooperate to meet their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) by trading such reductions, succeeding the Kyoto-era Clean Development Mechanism, in which India was a leading host of projects. India is building a domestic carbon market and a set of mitigation programmes that generate the reductions to trade.

1. The Paris framework and India's steps

  • Selective trading: India allows international sale mainly for advanced technologies (green hydrogen, offshore wind, storage-linked renewables, sustainable aviation fuel, carbon capture), so cheaper reductions stay for its own NDC.

2. Mitigation activities that lower CO₂ emissions

  • Renewables: about 299 GW (September 2026), with 50% non-fossil capacity reached in June 2025; PM Surya Ghar rooftop solar and PM-KUSUM for farmers.
  • Green hydrogen: the National Green Hydrogen Mission (₹19,744 crore) targets 5 million tonnes a year by 2030.
  • Energy efficiency: PAT for heavy industry (2012), UJALA's 36 crore+ LED bulbs, appliance star labels and building codes.
  • Cleaner fuels and transport: E20 ethanol blending achieved in 2025, compressed biogas (SATAT, GOBARdhan) and support for electric vehicles.
  • Nuclear and sinks: the SHANTI Act (2025) opens nuclear power to private firms, towards 100 GW by 2047, and the Green India Mission expands forest carbon sinks.

3. Domestic carbon market: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme

  • Legal basis: the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 enabled the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS, June 2023), run by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE).
  • Compliance mechanism: emission-intensity targets were first notified for seven sectors (aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp and paper in October 2025; refineries, petrochemicals and textiles in January 2026), covering about 490 units, with 2023-24 as the baseline.
  • Trading: units that beat targets earn carbon credit certificates, and laggards must buy and surrender them; CERC's 2026 regulations provide for trading them on power exchanges.
  • Offset mechanism: voluntary projects outside the obligated sectors can also earn credits, and the Green Credit Programme (2023) rewards actions such as planting trees on degraded land.

4. Targets and challenges

  • Targets: the updated NDC (2022) promises a 45% lower emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 (versus 2005), and NDC 3.0 (March 2026) 47% and 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035, with net zero by 2070.
  • Challenges: avoiding double counting, robust measurement and verification, stable carbon prices, and the EU's carbon border tax (CBAM, from January 2026).

AP angle: NTPC's green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka and the Kakinada green-ammonia complex use green hydrogen and green ammonia, both on India's 2023 list of activities open to Article 6.2 cooperation.

India is turning climate action into a market opportunity: a domestic carbon market plus selective Article 6 trading can attract finance for clean technology while protecting its own NDC, in line with CBDR-RC and net zero by 2070.
free.g1m-2023-p5-6b:
Municipal solid wasteSegregation at sourceWaste processingCPCB action plan

Municipal solid waste (MSW) is the everyday waste from homes, shops, markets and offices in towns. Urban India generates about 1.66 lakh tonnes a day (MoHUA, December 2025), and the share processed has risen from 16% in 2014 to about 80% under Swachh Bharat Mission–Urban. Yet big cities still struggle with mixed waste, overflowing dumps and fires. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 (in force from 1 April 2026) now govern the system.

1. Challenges in disposing of massive amounts of MSW

  • Mixed waste: without segregation at source, wet waste spoils recyclables, and wet, low-calorie waste burns poorly in waste-to-energy plants.
  • Land and legacy dumps: cities are running out of landfill sites, and less than half of India's roughly 2,500 legacy dumpsites had been fully cleared by early 2026.
  • Pollution and health: open dumps leak leachate into groundwater, emit methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and catch fire, as at Delhi's Ghazipur.
  • Collection and transport: irregular door-to-door collection, open trucks and poorly kept bins.
  • Finance and institutions: weak municipal finances, low user fees, loss-making plants and an informal recycling sector outside the system.
  • Changing composition: more plastics, e-waste and sanitary waste.

2. Action plan for cities generating more than 500 tonnes a day

CPCB's Action Plan for Management of MSW, prepared on the National Green Tribunal's direction in the Almitra Patel case and aligned with the 2016 Rules, groups cities by waste quantity. For the largest (above 500 TPD, such as Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune) it suggests:

  • Combine technologies: a single technology cannot handle such quantities; cities above 1,000 TPD will need high-capacity options such as waste-to-energy, with segregation ensuring enough calorific value.
  • Private participation and finance: private operators for collection and processing, with user fees, tipping fees and spot fines.
  • Monitoring: committees at State, district and city levels review progress.

3. Strengthened framework: SWM Rules, 2026

  • Four-stream segregation: wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste.
  • Bulk generators (for example, those producing 100 kg or more a day) must process wet waste on site or buy EBWGR certificates.
  • Less landfill, more fuel: landfills take only inert rejects, and cement and other solid-fuel industries near RDF plants must replace a rising share of their fuel with RDF, reaching 15% within six years.
  • Accountability: an online tracking portal and environmental compensation for violations.

AP angle: Vijayawada, Guntur and Tirupati entered the Super Swachh League (Swachh Survekshan 2024-25), and waste-to-energy plants at Visakhapatnam and Guntur and a legacy-waste clearance drive under Swachh Andhra show the plan at work.

For big cities the answer is to segregate, decentralise, process and landfill only the residue. The CPCB plan, the 2026 Rules, user fees and the inclusion of waste-pickers together can build a circular economy of urban waste.
free.g1m-2023-p5-7a:
BiotechnologyGenetic engineeringBiosafety and bioethicsDual-use risks

Biotechnology uses living cells, organisms and their molecules to make useful products and processes. Since recombinant DNA (1973) and CRISPR genome editing (Nobel Prize, 2020), it has transformed medicine, farming and industry, and India's bioeconomy reached about US$195 billion in 2025. But the same power to rewrite life raises concerns of biosafety, ethics, inequity and misuse.

1. Blessings of biotechnology

  • Health: recombinant insulin and vaccines (India makes nearly 60% of the world's vaccines, including Covaxin and the HPV vaccine CERVAVAC), India's own CAR-T therapy NexCAR19 (2023), the CRISPR-based sickle-cell therapy BIRSA 101 (2025) and rapid diagnostics.
  • Agriculture: Bt cotton (2002) cut bollworm sprays; the world's first genome-edited rice varieties (May 2025) give higher yields and salt tolerance; tissue culture supplies disease-free banana and sugarcane plants; biofertilisers and biopesticides reduce chemicals.
  • Environment and energy: bioremediation of oil spills (TERI's Oilzapper), second-generation ethanol from crop residue, and biogas.
  • Industry: enzymes, bioplastics and biomanufacturing under the BioE3 Policy (2024).
  • Forensics and genomics: DNA fingerprinting solves crimes, and Genome India's 10,000 genomes support precision medicine.

2. Curses and risks

  • Biosafety: gene flow from GM crops to wild relatives, superweeds and resistant pests; pink bollworm now resists Bt cotton, and herbicide-tolerant cotton is sown illegally.
  • Ethics: germline editing raises the spectre of "designer babies", as with the gene-edited twins born in China in 2018.
  • Dual use and biosecurity: gain-of-function research and synthetic biology could produce bioweapons or cause lab leaks; the Biological Weapons Convention (1972) has no verification system.
  • Inequity and corporate control: costly therapies, seed monopolies and patents, and biopiracy of Indian knowledge such as turmeric, neem and basmati.
  • Genetic privacy: DNA data can be misused by insurers, employers or the state.

3. Balancing promise and risk

  • Regulation: the 1989 Rules under the Environment (Protection) Act work through IBSCs, the RCGM and the GEAC; simpler genome edits (SDN-1 and SDN-2) were exempted in 2022, and the Supreme Court's split verdict on GM mustard (2024) asked for a national GM-crop policy.
  • Ethics and law: germline editing is not permitted in India; the Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols, the Biological Diversity Act (amended 2023) and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library guard against harm and biopiracy, and the DPDP Act protects genetic data.
  • Public trust: open biosafety data, labelling and public consultation.

AP angle: both genome-edited rice varieties were derived from AP-bred rice, Samba Mahsuri (Bapatla) and MTU 1010 (Maruteru), and AP's bioeconomy, about US$13.74 billion in 2025, is fifth among States.

Biotechnology is neither blessing nor curse by itself; its effect depends on governance. A science-based, transparent and ethical regulatory system can maximise its benefits while keeping biosafety and justice in view.
free.g1m-2023-p5-8a:
Antimicrobial resistanceAntibiotic misuseOne HealthNAP-AMR

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) arises when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites evolve to survive the drugs meant to kill them, so common infections become hard or impossible to treat. Bacterial AMR directly caused about 12.7 lakh deaths worldwide in 2019 (Lancet, 2022). India, among the world's largest consumers of antibiotics, is a hotspot, and has adopted a One Health approach linking human, animal and environmental health.

1. Why antibiotic resistance is getting worse in India

  • Over-the-counter sales and self-medication: antibiotics are bought without prescription and taken for viral fevers, colds and diarrhoea.
  • Irrational prescribing: few rapid diagnostics, patient pressure, irrational fixed-dose combinations, and heavy use of WHO "Watch" antibiotics.
  • Incomplete courses and substandard drugs: they leave the toughest bacteria alive to multiply.
  • Hospital infections: crowded wards and weak infection control spread resistant strains; ICMR surveillance reports resistance even to carbapenems, the drugs of last resort.
  • Animals and environment: antibiotics used in poultry and aquaculture, untreated pharmaceutical effluent and hospital sewage, and poor sanitation spread resistance genes.
