  • Empty pipeline: very few new antibiotics are being developed worldwide.

2. India's strategies and action plans

  • National Action Plan on AMR (2017): six priorities under One Health: awareness, surveillance, infection prevention, rational use in humans and animals, research and investment, and India's leadership.
  • NAP-AMR 2.0 (2025–29): launched in November 2025 to update and accelerate the plan.
  • Regulation: Schedule H1 (2014) requires a prescription register for key antibiotics, the Red Line marks prescription-only antibiotic packs, and colistin was banned as an animal growth promoter (2019).
  • Surveillance and hospitals: ICMR's AMR surveillance network tracks resistance, and stewardship and infection-control programmes (Kayakalp awards for clean hospitals) curb misuse.
  • New drugs and States: nafithromycin (2024), developed in India with BIRAC support, treats resistant pneumonia; Kerala's KARSAP (2018) was the first state action plan.

3. Way forward

  • Enforcement: strict prescription-only sales and audits of chemists and hospitals.
  • Prevention: vaccines (typhoid conjugate, pneumococcal), clean water and sanitation reduce the need for antibiotics.
  • Innovation: rapid point-of-care tests and incentives for new antibiotics.
  • Environment and farms: antibiotic limits in pharmaceutical effluent and veterinary stewardship.
  • Awareness: World AMR Awareness Week (18–24 November) and community campaigns.

AP angle: AP produces more than a quarter of India's fish, so curbing antibiotic use in shrimp and fish farms, through residue testing and farm biosecurity, protects both public health and seafood exports.

AMR is a silent pandemic. Only a One Health approach that combines rational use in people and animals, a cleaner environment and new drugs, implemented down to the district, can keep antibiotics working for the next generation.
free.g1m-2023-p5-8b:
Bio-pesticidesIntegrated Pest ManagementPesticide residuesSustainable agriculture

Bio-pesticides are pest-control agents derived from living organisms or natural materials: microbes (bacteria, fungi, viruses), plant extracts such as neem, and insect pheromones. They act more slowly than synthetic chemicals, persist for a shorter time and are sensitive to heat, sunlight and humidity. Yet the hidden costs of chemical pesticides to health, ecology and trade make a shift to bio-pesticides, within Integrated Pest Management (IPM), necessary.

1. Why the shift is needed despite their limitations

  • Human health: chemical residues reach food and water, and farmers spraying without protection are poisoned, as in Yavatmal (Maharashtra, 2017); endosulfan's toll in Kasaragod (Kerala) led to its ban in 2011. Bio-pesticides are largely non-toxic to people.
  • Target-specific: they spare pollinators, birds, fish and natural enemies of pests, whereas broad-spectrum chemicals kill them and trigger pest resurgence.
  • Breaking the resistance treadmill: repeated chemical use breeds resistant pests such as whitefly and pink bollworm, demanding ever stronger doses; microbes with several modes of action slow resistance.
  • Short persistence is a strength: the very "weakness" in the question means no long-lasting residues in soil and groundwater, and safer harvests.
  • Trade and markets: strict residue limits abroad (the EU's tricyclazole limit hit Indian basmati exports) and rising demand for organic and natural produce reward residue-free farming.
  • Policy fit: they suit IPM, organic farming (PKVY) and the National Mission on Natural Farming (2024), which plans 10,000 bio-input resource centres.

2. Overcoming the limitations

  • Better formulations: oil- and polymer-based carriers, UV protectants and microencapsulation extend shelf life and field persistence.
  • Smart use within IPM: apply early in the pest cycle and in the evening, alongside resistant varieties, crop rotation, light traps and pheromone traps.
  • Quality and regulation: faster registration by the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee under the Insecticides Act, 1968, and action against spurious products.
  • Local production and extension: village-level units run by women's groups and FPOs, Krishi Vigyan Kendra training and subsidies make them cheap and fresh.

AP angle: AP Community Managed Natural Farming (2016), with over 10 lakh farmers, replaces chemical sprays with farm-made botanical extracts such as neemastram and agniastram; heavy pesticide users, such as chilli and cotton growers, stand to gain most.

Bio-pesticides trade speed for safety and sustainability. With better formulations, IPM and farmer support, they can deliver lasting pest control that protects farmers, consumers and ecosystems, making Indian farm produce residue-free and export-ready.
free.g1m-2023-p5-9a:
Patent grantsR&D intensityExaminer capacityLab-to-market gap

India's rank in the Global Innovation Index (GII) has climbed from 81st in 2015 to 38th of 139 in 2026, and patent filings in India reached a record 1,10,375 in 2024-25. Yet grants remain a fraction of the leaders': China granted about 9.21 lakh patents and the USA about 3.15 lakh in 2023, against India's record 1,03,057 in 2023-24. The gap reflects research effort and patent-office capacity.

1. The gap in numbers

2. Why India's patent grants lag

  • Low R&D spending: India spends only 0.84% of GDP on R&D (DST, 2023-24); the 2% target of 2003 is still unmet, so fewer patentable inventions are produced.
  • Weak private and university research: business funds about 45% of research spending, most state universities do little research, and academics are rewarded for papers rather than patents or licences.
  • Too few examiners: India had only 1,383 patent examiners at the end of 2024-25, about a tenth of China's 13,704, so a large backlog of applications waits for examination. Grants are also uneven: they fell from a record 1,03,057 in 2023-24 to 33,504 in 2024-25.
  • Strict patentability: Section 3(d) (new forms of known substances), 3(k) (software per se) and 3(j) (plants and animals) keep out incremental claims that are patented elsewhere.
  • Low IP culture: MSMEs and start-ups lack awareness and money for drafting, foreign filing and litigation, and much frugal, process-based innovation is never patented. Even in India, only about 32% of patents granted in 2024-25 went to Indian applicants.

3. Why the innovation rank still rises

  • Broader yardstick: the GII also counts non-patent outputs; India ranks 25th on outputs but 49th on inputs (2026), and is first in ICT services exports.
  • Start-ups and digital public infrastructure: UPI, Aadhaar and a large start-up base reflect innovation that patents do not capture.
  • China's numbers were pushed up by state targets and subsidies, and not all its grants are of high value.

4. Way forward

  • Faster examination: recruit more examiners (525 more approved over three years) and digitise prior-art search.
  • More research money: move GERD towards 2% through the Anusandhan National Research Foundation and the ₹1 lakh crore RDI scheme for private R&D.
  • Lower barriers: 80% fee rebates for start-ups and educational institutions, IP cells and technology-transfer offices in universities, and IP literacy under the National IP Awareness Mission (2021).

AP angle: IIT and IISER Tirupati, Andhra University and the Amaravati Quantum Valley can set up patent cells and technology-transfer offices so that the State's research turns into filings.

India's rising rank shows a vibrant innovation ecosystem; turning ideas into patents now needs more R&D money, faster examination and a culture of IP protection.
free.g1m-2023-p5-9b:
IP commercialisationTechnology transferCIPAMNational IPR Policy 2016

A patent earns nothing until it is used. IP commercialisation turns protected inventions, designs, brands and geographical indications into products, licences, start-ups and royalties. It is one of the seven objectives of the National IPR Policy (May 2016), "Creative India; Innovative India". India now files over 1.1 lakh patent applications a year (2024-25), but universities and public laboratories licence few of them, so the tools of commercialisation matter as much as the grant itself.

1. Tools for successful commercialisation

  • Quality, timely IP titles: fast and sound examination tells investors exactly what is owned; expedited examination helps start-ups.
  • Valuation and IP audit: reliable pricing of patents and brands is needed for licensing, mergers and IP-backed loans, but valuation skills are scarce.
  • Technology-transfer offices: university TTOs, NRDC (1953) and BIRAC license public research to industry under clear revenue-sharing rules.
  • Finance: venture capital, the Fund of Funds for Start-ups (2016), the RDI scheme's ₹1 lakh crore for private R&D, and lending against IP.
  • Markets and enforcement: incubators (Atal Innovation Mission), patent pools and IP exchanges link inventors with buyers, while commercial courts and the Delhi High Court's IP Division (2021) make licences enforceable.

2. Role of CIPAM

The Cell for IPR Promotion and Management (CIPAM) was set up in 2016 under DPIIT (Ministry of Commerce) to implement the National IPR Policy.

  • Awareness: campaigns in schools, colleges, industry and MSMEs, and the National Intellectual Property Awareness Mission (2021), which aimed to reach one million students.
  • Simpler IP processes: works with the IP office on digitisation, fee rebates and faster examination, so that rights are granted in time to be used.
  • Linking inventors with industry: promotes licensing and technology transfer, and is the national focal point for WIPO's Technology and Innovation Support Centres (TISCs, from 2017), which help inventors with patent searches and IP advice.
  • Enforcement: coordinates with police, customs and courts and trains them against piracy and counterfeiting, which protects the value of licensed IP.
  • Promotion of GIs and brands: helps traditional producers market GI-tagged goods.

3. Gaps

Few university licences, scarce valuation expertise, limited venture capital for deep technology and slow dispute resolution still keep most Indian patents idle.

AP angle: GI tags such as Araku Valley coffee, Banaganapalle mango and Kondapalli toys earn more when backed by branding and authorised users, and the AP MedTech Zone, Visakhapatnam (India's first medical-devices park), shows how shared facilities move ideas to market.

India's IP system must move from filing to earning; CIPAM's awareness work, combined with TTOs, finance and quick enforcement, can turn "Creative India" into a true knowledge economy.
free.g1m-2023-p5-10a:
Food securityLoss and distributionGM cropsGenome editing

The world grows enough calories for everyone, yet hundreds of millions go hungry. FAO estimates that about a third of all food is lost or wasted, and hunger follows poverty, prices, conflict and poor access more than total output. Critics therefore call genetically modified (GM) crops a technical fix for a social and logistical problem. The statement is largely true, but it overlooks what GM and genome-edited crops can do for specific farm problems.

1. Why the statement is largely true

  • Access, not availability: India produces surplus grain and gives free foodgrain to about 81 crore people under PMGKAY, yet 35.5% of children under five were stunted (NFHS-5, 2019-21). Hunger is about income, diet and health, which new genes cannot fix.
  • Loss and waste: poor storage, cold chains, roads and markets waste grain, fruit, vegetables and fish between farm and plate.
  • Inefficient farming: small, fragmented holdings, wasteful irrigation, degraded soils and large yield gaps limit output far more than a lack of new traits.
  • Distribution: leakages in the public distribution system, weak rural incomes and unequal access to nutritious food keep the poor hungry even in surplus years.
  • GM risks: costly seed and corporate control, gene flow to related plants, and resistance (pink bollworm now resists Bollgard II cotton).

2. Why GM is not simply the "wrong answer"

  • Pest losses: Bt cotton (2002), India's only commercial GM crop, cut bollworm damage and insecticide sprays.
  • Climate stress: drought-, flood- and salt-tolerant traits help rainfed and coastal farms. India released the world's first genome-edited rice varieties in May 2025: DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) yields about 19% more and matures 15–20 days earlier, and Pusa DST Rice 1 does well on saline soils.
  • Hidden hunger: biofortified crops such as Golden Rice (vitamin A) target micronutrient deficiency.
  • Import substitution: GM mustard DMH-11 aims to raise edible-oil output, though its release is on hold after the Supreme Court's split verdict (2024).

3. A balanced view

  • Fix the system first: storage, cold chains, efficient irrigation, extension services and nutrition schemes.
  • Use genetics for targeted problems, under transparent, science-based biosafety regulation (GEAC) and a national GM policy, as the Supreme Court has asked.

AP angle: AP-bred rice lies behind the new varieties: Kamala was developed from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204, bred at Bapatla) and Pusa DST Rice 1 from MTU 1010 (Maruteru), while AP's natural farming (APCNF) shows how resilience can come from better practice.

GM crops are one tool, not the solution: hunger needs efficient farming and fair distribution first, with genetic technologies used selectively under strong biosafety rules.
free.g1m-2023-p5-11a:
DeepfakesGenerative AIInfodemicDigital trust

Generative AI can now produce realistic fake videos, cloned voices and images, called deepfakes, within minutes, and social media spreads them faster than any correction. The result is an infodemic: an overload of false and manipulated content that erodes trust in everything people see and hear. India, with hundreds of millions of social-media users, many languages and frequent elections, is especially exposed.

1. Impact on privacy

  • Non-consensual images: morphed and "nudified" pictures, mostly of women, are used for harassment and sextortion.
  • Voice and video fraud: cloned voices of relatives or officials trick victims into paying, and "digital arrest" scams use fake police videos.
  • Misuse of identity: faces and voices of celebrities are used in fake advertisements; Indian courts have protected personality rights against AI cloning.
  • Data scraping: personal photos posted online become raw material for fakes without consent.

2. Impact on democracy

  • Fake speeches and endorsements: a deepfake released days before polling leaves no time for rebuttal and can sway voters.
  • Liar's dividend: genuine evidence can be dismissed as "fake", which weakens journalism and accountability.
  • Polarisation: micro-targeted propaganda and bot networks deepen divisions and lower trust in elections and the media.

3. Impact on national security

  • Impersonation of leaders: a 2022 deepfake showed Ukraine's President "surrendering"; fake orders or statements can spread panic in a crisis.
  • Communal tension: fabricated videos can trigger riots within hours.
  • Hostile influence and fraud: foreign actors run AI-driven influence operations, and deepfakes can fool face- and voice-based verification.

4. Solutions to tackle the infodemic

  • Law: the IT Act 2000 (Section 66D on cheating by personation, 66E on privacy), the IT Rules 2021 as amended in February 2026 (mandatory labelling of synthetic content and takedown within three hours of an order), the DPDP Act 2023, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's provisions on false information and defamation.
  • Platform duties: watermarks and content-provenance tags, quick grievance redress and labelling of political advertisements.
  • Election safeguards: Election Commission advisories (2024) asked parties to remove deepfakes within three hours of notice.
  • Technology: deepfake-detection projects under the IndiaAI Mission's "safe and trusted AI" pillar, and testing by the AI Safety Institute.
  • Society: digital and media literacy in schools, independent fact-checkers, and reporting through the cybercrime portal and helpline 1930.

Deepfakes turn seeing into doubting; a mix of law, platform accountability, detection technology and an alert public can restore digital trust without curbing free speech.
free.g1m-2023-p5-11b:
Renewable capacityNon-fossil shareEnergy securityPanchamrit

India's power sector is in the middle of an energy transition. On 30 September 2026, installed renewable capacity stood at 299.25 GW (MNRE), led by 171 GW of solar, and non-fossil sources crossed half of installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of the 2030 target in India's NDC. India is now third in the world in renewable capacity (IRENA 2026), after China and the USA.

1. Current scenario

  • Solar boom: 125.65 GW ground-mounted and 33.41 GW rooftop; a record 55.3 GW of non-fossil capacity was added in 2025-26, of which 44.61 GW was solar.
  • Capacity is not generation: non-fossil sources gave only 29.2% of electricity in 2025-26, because solar works only by day and wind is seasonal; coal still dominates generation.
  • Leading states: Rajasthan in solar (45.1 GW), Gujarat in wind and total renewables; India is fourth in the world in wind.
  • Targets: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035 (NDC 3.0).

2. Factors behind the shift to renewables

  • Climate commitments: the Panchamrit (COP26, 2021), net zero by 2070, and NDCs that cut the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 and 47% by 2035 (from 2005).
  • Energy security: India imports nearly 90% of its crude oil and some of its coal; domestic sun and wind, with electric vehicles and green hydrogen, cut import bills and exposure to price shocks.
  • Falling costs: solar is now among the cheapest sources of new power, and module and battery prices keep falling.
  • Policy support: solar parks, PM-KUSUM (about 25 lakh pumps and 13.1 GW by March 2026), PM Surya Ghar (over 50 lakh homes by August 2026), Green Energy Corridors, and PLI with the ALMM list, which raised module-making capacity to about 172 GW.
  • Health, jobs and diplomacy: cleaner air, manufacturing and installation jobs, and leadership through the International Solar Alliance.

3. Challenges

  • Intermittency: a midday solar surplus and an evening peak force curtailment; storage and flexible plants are needed.
  • Grid and finance: transmission lags new plants, and weak DISCOM finances delay payments.
  • Land and imports: land conflicts, and dependence on imported polysilicon, wafers and critical minerals.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets 78.5 GW of solar, 35 GW of wind, 22 GW of pumped storage and 1.5 MMTPA of green hydrogen. The State hosts the Ananthapuram-I (1,500 MW) and Kurnool (1,000 MW) solar parks, Greenko's 1,680 MW Pinnapuram pumped-storage project and NTPC's green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka.

India has achieved scale; storage, stronger grids and domestic manufacturing must now turn capacity into reliable, round-the-clock clean power.
free.g1m-2023-p5-12b:
Technology–environment paradoxOver-exploitationRebound effectSustainable technology

Technology multiplies human power over nature. Since the Industrial Revolution, fossil-fuel engines, machines and chemicals have raised living standards, but they have also let people extract, burn and dump on a scale nature cannot absorb. Carbon dioxide in the air reached 423.9 ppm in 2024 (WMO), about 152% of the pre-industrial level. The fault lies less in technology itself than in human exploitation: technology used for profit and consumption without limits.

1. How technology became a medium of destruction

  • Scale and speed: machines let a few people clear forests, level hills or empty aquifers in years; ISRO's atlas found 97.85 million ha (29.7% of India) degraded in 2018-19.
  • Rebound (Jevons) effect: efficiency lowers cost, which raises consumption, so total resource use often grows.
  • Industrial hazards: chemical technology without a safety culture causes disasters, from Bhopal (1984) to the LG Polymers styrene leak at Visakhapatnam (2020), which killed at least 12 people.
  • Externalised costs: polluters keep the profits while society bears the health and clean-up costs.
  • New frontiers: energy- and water-hungry data centres, space debris and fast-growing e-waste.

2. Human drivers behind the misuse

  • Consumerism and growth at any cost: GDP is counted, but the loss of forests, soil and clean air is not.
  • Short-term profit and weak enforcement: under-staffed pollution control boards and post-facto clearances.
  • Inequality: the richest consume and emit far more, while the poor live closest to mines, dumps and factories.
  • Population and demand: more people and rising incomes need more land, water and energy, multiplying the impact of every machine.

3. Andhra Pradesh angle

Aquaculture technology turned parts of Kolleru Lake and delta paddy fields into fish and shrimp ponds, causing salinity and pollution; about 1,500 illegal tanks were removed in 2006, but many returned. The LG Polymers leak showed the cost of poor industrial safety.

4. Technology as the cure

  • Clean technology: about 299 GW of renewable capacity (September 2026), electric mobility and green hydrogen.
  • Smarter farming: drip irrigation, precision and natural farming, and bio-pesticides.
  • Monitoring: satellites track forest loss, mining and pollution in near real time.
  • Governance: EIA, the precautionary and polluter-pays principles, extended producer responsibility, the circular economy and Mission LiFE.

Technology is a double-edged sword: the same tools that degraded the planet can heal it if guided by regulation, restrained consumption and the goal of sustainable development.
free.g1m-2023-p5-13a:
1.5 °C thresholdParis AgreementTipping pointsClimate risk

The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming "well below 2 °C" and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. The IPCC (2018) showed that every fraction of a degree matters. 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 °C (about 1.55 °C, WMO). The Paris limit is a 20-year average, but UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2025 says that average will very likely cross 1.5 °C within a decade.

1. Why 1.5 °C matters

2. What happens if the world passes 1.5 °C

  • More extreme weather: hotter and longer heat waves, heavier downpours, longer droughts, and cyclones that intensify rapidly over warmer seas.
  • Oceans and ice: faster sea-level rise as Greenland and West Antarctic ice melts, more marine heat waves, ocean acidification and the near-loss of coral reefs.
  • Tipping points: a greater risk of crossing thresholds such as permafrost thaw, Arctic sea-ice loss, Amazon dieback and ice-sheet collapse, which could lock in further warming even if emissions fall.
  • Food, water and health: lower crop yields in the tropics, water stress as Himalayan glaciers shrink, and more heat stress and vector-borne disease.
  • Society and economy: migration, conflict over resources and rising loss and damage, with small islands and poor countries hit first as adaptation reaches its limits.

3. Where the world stands

  • Recent heat: 2025 was the second or third warmest year (about 1.44 °C), and 2015–2025 were the 11 warmest years on record.
  • Projections: about 2.3–2.5 °C of warming this century if all NDCs are implemented, and up to 2.8 °C under current policies (UNEP, 2025).
  • What 1.5 °C needs: a 43% cut in global greenhouse-gas emissions by 2030 from 2019 levels (IPCC).

4. India and Andhra Pradesh

  • India: warmed by about 0.7 °C in 1901–2018; longer heat waves, erratic monsoons, retreating glaciers such as Gangotri, and a sea that rose about 3.3 mm a year in 1993–2017.
  • AP angle: the 1,053 km coast and the low Krishna–Godavari deltas face sea-level rise, salinity and severe cyclones such as Montha (2025), while Rayalaseema faces harsher heat and drought.

Passing 1.5 °C need not be permanent if emissions fall fast, but every tenth of a degree costs lives; deep emission cuts this decade, adaptation and fair climate finance are urgent.
free.g1m-2023-p5-13b:
BlockchainFarm-to-fork traceabilitySmart contractsDigital agriculture

Blockchain is a tamper-evident digital ledger: records are grouped into blocks, chained by cryptographic hashes and copied across many computers, so no single party can quietly alter them. Indian agriculture, dominated by small and marginal farmers, suffers from middlemen, opaque prices, delayed payments, spurious inputs and poor traceability. A shared, trusted record can address these problems, which is why blockchain is seen as a doorway to transforming the sector.

1. How blockchain can transform agriculture

  • Farm-to-fork traceability: each step, from seed lot and farm to harvest, testing, storage and export, is recorded, so buyers can verify origin, organic status and pesticide-residue limits; this matters for GI products and exports.
  • Fair and fast payments: smart contracts release payment automatically when produce is delivered and graded, cutting delays and the share of intermediaries.
  • Genuine inputs: tracking seeds, fertilisers and pesticides from factory to dealer curbs spurious products.
  • Credit and insurance: a trusted record of land, crops and sales builds a farmer's credit history, and crop-insurance claims can be settled faster using weather and satellite triggers.
  • Land records and subsidies: tamper-proof records reduce title disputes and leakages in subsidy payments.

2. Indian initiatives

  • Coffee Board (2019): a blockchain-based e-marketplace pilot to connect coffee growers directly with buyers and make the bean-to-cup chain transparent.
  • Spices Board–UNDP pilot (2021): blockchain traceability linked to the Board's e-Spice Bazaar portal, using data from over 1,000 chilli and turmeric farmers in AP's Guntur and Prakasam districts.
  • Digital foundations: the National Strategy on Blockchain (2021), e-NAM (2016) linking mandis online, and the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024, ₹2,817 crore), whose AgriStack farmer registry and digital crop survey provide the data that blockchain services need.

3. Challenges

  • Digital divide: many farmers lack smartphones, connectivity and digital skills.
  • Garbage in, garbage out: the ledger is only as honest as the data entered at the farm gate; blockchain cannot verify physical quality by itself.
  • Cost and scale: fragmented holdings and informal trade raise costs, and pilots rarely scale up.
  • Standards and law: interoperability between platforms, legal recognition of smart contracts and data privacy are still unsettled.

AP angle: Guntur, home of the GI-tagged Guntur Sannam chilli, has already tested blockchain traceability; linking it with farmer producer organisations and e-NAM could raise export prices for AP's chilli and turmeric growers.

Blockchain is a doorway, not the destination: combined with AgriStack, FPOs and digital literacy, it can bring transparency and fair prices if it stays cheap, simple and farmer-centric.
free.g1m-2023-p5-14a:
NPTNSG waiver123 AgreementNuclear power

The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT, 1968) recognises as nuclear-weapon states only the five that tested before 1 January 1967. India has refused to sign it, yet it has kept a clean non-proliferation record. In 2008, after the Indo-US civil nuclear initiative, the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) granted India a special waiver (6 September), ending more than three decades of nuclear isolation.

1. Reasons for India's opposition to the NPT

  • Discriminatory: it divides the world into nuclear "haves" and "have-nots"; India could join only as a non-nuclear-weapon state by giving up its weapons.
  • No disarmament deadline: the nuclear-weapon states need only negotiate disarmament "in good faith" (Article VI), with no time-bound duty.
  • Security environment: two nuclear-armed neighbours, China (since 1964) and Pakistan, and their nuclear cooperation require a credible deterrent.
  • Strategic autonomy: India seeks universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable disarmament, as in the Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan (1988), not an unequal treaty.
  • Responsible conduct outside the treaty: a no-first-use doctrine (2003), a testing moratorium since 1998 and strict export controls.

2. Impact of the 2008 deal on nuclear power

  • Fuel security: imported uranium for safeguarded reactors ended the shortage that had kept many reactors running well below capacity, and load factors rose.
  • Slow growth: capacity roughly doubled in 18 years, mostly from indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs (Kakrapar 3 and 4, RAPP-7) and the Russian VVERs at Kudankulam; nuclear still gives only about 3% of electricity.
  • Stalled foreign projects: Jaitapur (France) and Kovvada (USA) stalled over the supplier-liability clause of the 2010 liability law and high costs.
  • Diplomatic gains: membership of the MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017) and Australia Group (2018), though full NSG membership is still blocked, mainly by China.
  • New push: the SHANTI Act 2025 repealed the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and the CLNDA 2010, admitted private Indian companies and graded operator liability; the goal is 100 GW by 2047, helped by a ₹20,000 crore mission for small modular reactors.

AP angle: Kovvada in Srikakulam is planned for 6 × 1,208 MW Westinghouse AP1000 reactors, but NPCIL–Westinghouse talks were still continuing in September 2026; Tummalapalle (YSR Kadapa) uranium supports the domestic fuel cycle.

Staying out of the NPT protected India's strategic autonomy, while the 2008 waiver opened access to fuel and technology; turning that access into power now depends on cost, legal clarity and indigenous capacity.
free.g1m-2023-p5-14b:
E-wasteInformal recyclingExtended Producer ResponsibilityE-Waste Rules 2022

E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment: phones, computers, televisions, appliances and solar panels. India generated about 17.78 lakh tonnes in 2023-24, up from 16.01 lakh tonnes in 2021-22 (MoEFCC), and is the world's third-largest generator after China and the USA. E-waste holds valuable metals but also lead, mercury, cadmium and flame retardants, so the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 are built on Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).

1. E-waste recycling practices in India

  • Informal sector dominates: kabadiwalas collect most discarded devices, and clusters such as Seelampur (Delhi) and Moradabad (Uttar Pradesh) dismantle them by hand.
  • Crude methods: open burning of cables for copper, acid baths to strip gold from circuit boards and dumping of residues poison soil, water and air, and expose workers, including women and children, to lead, mercury and toxic fumes.
  • Formal recycling: 322 CPCB-authorised recyclers with a capacity of about 22 lakh tonnes a year (2025) shred, separate and recover copper, gold, silver and rare metals; yet much of this capacity sits idle, partly because informal dealers pay more for scrap.
  • Reuse and refurbishing: repair shops extend product life, and "urban mining" can recover critical minerals.

2. Highlights of the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022

The Rules came into force on 1 April 2023, replacing the 2016 Rules.

  • Wider coverage: 106 types of equipment, and solar panels and cells are also covered.
  • EPR certificates: registered recyclers generate certificates for the quantity processed, and producers buy them to meet annual targets: 60% (2023-25), 70% (2025-27) and 80% from 2027-28.
  • Single online system: manufacturers, producers, refurbishers and recyclers must register on the CPCB portal; the older roles of dismantlers and producer responsibility organisations were dropped.
  • Polluter pays: environmental compensation for non-compliance, with verification and audits by CPCB.
  • Other duties: limits on hazardous substances in new products continue; solar-panel waste must be stored and processed as per CPCB norms; States must earmark industrial space for recycling and protect workers. A 2024 amendment fixed a price band for EPR certificates (30–100% of the environmental compensation), and several manufacturers have challenged the floor price in the Delhi High Court since late 2024.

3. Way forward

  • Bring informal workers in: cooperatives, training, safety gear and links with authorised recyclers.
  • Design for reuse: right to repair, eco-design and consumer take-back schemes.
  • Recover critical minerals from batteries and electronics to support clean-energy supply chains.

AP angle: AP's expanding electronics manufacturing (Sri City, Tirupati) and growing cities such as Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada will add to e-waste, so APPCB must license more recyclers and stop informal burning.

E-waste is both a hazard and a resource; strict EPR enforcement and an inclusive, formal recycling chain can make it the basis of a circular economy.
free.g1m-2023-p5-15a:
COP26 pledgesGlobal Methane PledgeForests and Land Use DeclarationClimate justice

At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021), over 100 countries joined two voluntary pledges: the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use, to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030, and the Global Methane Pledge, to cut global methane emissions at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. India signed neither. Instead it announced its own Panchamrit, including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.

1. Why India stayed out of the methane pledge

  • Farm-based methane: most of India's methane comes from livestock (enteric fermentation) and flooded paddy fields, the base of food security and of the incomes of small and marginal farmers.
  • Survival versus luxury emissions: methane from a poor farmer's cattle or rice field is not comparable to leaks from oil and gas operations in rich countries.
  • Shifting the burden: the pledge moves attention from carbon dioxide, the long-lived gas emitted mostly by developed countries, to a short-lived gas, against the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC).
  • Livelihoods and trade: India has about 536 million livestock (2019 census) and is the world's largest milk producer (247.87 million tonnes in 2024-25), so targets could hurt rural incomes and invite trade pressure.
  • No sectoral targets: India's NDC sets an economy-wide intensity goal and avoids sector-specific obligations, especially in agriculture.

2. Why India stayed out of the forest declaration

  • Trade linkage: the text tied forest goals to trade and commodity policies; India opposes bringing trade, a WTO matter, into climate pledges and fears non-tariff barriers.
  • Development space: a fixed 2030 halt to forest loss could restrict land for roads, railways, power lines, mining and housing that a developing country still needs.
  • Already a net gainer: forest and tree cover is about 25% of India's area (ISFR 2023) and rising, and the NDC promises an additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2030 (3.5–4 billion tonnes by 2035).

3. Assessment

  • Criticism: cutting methane is the fastest way to slow near-term warming, and staying out may weaken India's climate diplomacy.
  • India's answer: voluntary action without binding sector targets: direct-seeded rice and alternate wetting and drying in paddy, anti-methane feed, biogas from dung, compressed biogas plants, and afforestation under the Green India Mission and CAMPA.
  • Ambition remains: NDC 3.0 (March 2026) targets a 47% cut in emissions intensity and 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035.

AP angle: paddy in the Godavari–Krishna deltas and the livestock incomes of AP's small farmers would bear any methane target; natural farming (APCNF) and biogas from dung are better voluntary paths.

India's refusal reflects climate justice and food security, not climate denial; finance-backed, voluntary action on methane and forests fits its path to net zero by 2070.
free.g1m-2023-p5-15b:
Gene sanctuaryIn-situ conservationCrop wild relativesGenetic diversity

A gene sanctuary is a protected area set aside for the in-situ conservation of the wild relatives and traditional land races of crop plants in the habitats where they evolved. India lies in Vavilov's Indian centre of crop origin, the home of wild ancestors of rice, sugarcane, mango, citrus, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper. India's first gene sanctuary, for citrus, was established in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya (Nokrek) in the early 1980s.

1. Gene sanctuaries in India

  • Purpose: to keep wild relatives and land races growing in nature, not just as seeds in cold storage.
  • First example: Nokrek protects the wild Indian orange, Citrus indica (locally memang narang), the mother germplasm of cultivated citrus; Nokrek became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2009.
  • Regions rich in crop diversity: the North-East, the Western and Eastern Ghats, the Himalaya and the Jeypore tract of Koraput (a FAO Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System, 2012) hold wild rice, citrus, banana, mango, pepper and millets.

2. How they protect plant genetic diversity

  • Evolution continues: wild populations keep adapting to local pests, diseases and climate, generating new useful genes that frozen seed banks cannot.
  • Reservoir of resistance genes: an Indian wild rice, Oryza nivara, supplied resistance to the grassy stunt virus that threatened Asian rice in the 1970s; such traits are vital for climate-resilient breeding.
  • Shield against genetic erosion: high-yielding varieties, monocultures, shortened shifting-cultivation cycles, grazing and habitat loss are wiping out land races; sanctuaries protect them in place.
  • Complement to gene banks: NBPGR's National Gene Bank in New Delhi stores seeds ex situ, so the two together form a double safety net.
  • Community stewardship: farmers who conserve land races are rewarded under the PPV&FR Act 2001 (Plant Genome Saviour awards from the National Gene Fund), and the Biological Diversity Act 2002 provides for Biodiversity Heritage Sites and People's Biodiversity Registers.

3. Challenges

  • Few notified sites: gene sanctuaries have no separate legal category, so most wild relatives are protected only incidentally inside protected areas.
  • Pressures: land-use change, invasive weeds, fire and climate change threaten wild populations.
  • Weak documentation: many land races and wild relatives are not yet surveyed or linked to breeding programmes.

AP angle: the Eastern Ghats agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju district, next to the Koraput tract, still grow traditional rice and millet land races; community seed saving under natural farming can work like a farmer-run gene sanctuary.

Gene sanctuaries are living gene banks; more notified sites, rewards for conserving communities and close links with NBPGR can secure the genetic base of India's food security in a warming world.
free.g1m-2025-p2-2a:
Kalyani ChalukyasVesara styleSoapstone templesKannada literature

The Chalukyas of Kalyani (Western or Later Chalukyas, 973–1189 CE) were founded by Tailapa II, who overthrew the Rashtrakutas. Someshvara I made Kalyani (Basavakalyan, Bidar) the capital, and Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126) was the greatest ruler. Their two centuries of rule produced a refined temple style, often called the Kalyani Chalukya or Gadag style, and a golden age of Kannada and Sanskrit literature.

1. Architecture

  • Bridge between styles: their temples link the early Chalukya (Badami) and Rashtrakuta traditions to the later Hoysala style.
  • New material: fine-grained soapstone replaced sandstone, allowing sharper and more intricate work.
  • Plans and towers: stepped and star-shaped (stellate) plans, vesara towers mixing Dravida and Nagara features, and lathe-turned, bell-shaped pillars.
  • Major temples: the Mahadeva temple at Itagi (1112), praised as "Devalaya Chakravarti" (emperor among temples); the Kasivisvesvara temple and the Brahma Jinalaya (built by Attimabbe) at Lakkundi; the Doddabasappa temple at Dambal (stellate plan); the Siddhesvara temple at Haveri; and the Trikuteshwara temple at Gadag.
  • Stepwells: ornamental stepped tanks at Lakkundi show their skill in civic architecture too.

2. Sculpture

  • Ornate doorways and screens: richly carved doorframes, pierced window screens, makara toranas and kirtimukha (face of glory) motifs.
  • Figure sculpture: bracket figures of dancers (madanikas) and deities placed in miniature shrines on the outer walls.
  • Delicacy: the soft soapstone allowed jewellery-like detail, a delicacy later perfected by the Hoysalas.

3. Literature

  • Kannada: Ranna (Gadayuddha, Ajitapurana), one of the "three gems" of Kannada poetry; Nagavarma II (Kavyavalokana, Karnataka Bhashabhushana); Durgasimha's Kannada Panchatantra.
  • Sanskrit history and law: Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita, a biography of Vikramaditya VI; Vijnaneshwara's Mitakshara, a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti that became the basis of Hindu inheritance law in most of India.
  • Encyclopaedic works: Someshvara III's Manasollasa covers polity, arts, music, food and sports.
  • Religious ferment: the Vachana movement of Basavanna arose at Kalyani soon after, under the Kalachuri Bijjala, a former Chalukya feudatory.

AP angle: The Kalyani Chalukyas fought the Cholas for control of Vengi (coastal Andhra), and the Kakatiyas began as their feudatories; Kakatiya temples such as the Thousand Pillar temple at Hanamkonda carry forward their pillared, ornate style.

The Kalyani Chalukyas thus left a refined architectural idiom that shaped Hoysala and Kakatiya art, and a body of Kannada and Sanskrit learning; their Mitakshara shaped Hindu inheritance law into modern times.
free.g1m-2025-p2-2b:
SufismSilsilaKhanqahComposite culture

Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam that seeks union with God through love, devotion and self-purification rather than ritual alone. It reached India with the Ghaznavid and Ghurid conquests. Al-Hujwiri of Lahore (11th century) wrote the Kashf-ul-Mahjub, an early Persian treatise on Sufism, and Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer (died 1236) established the Chishti order in India. With the Bhakti saints, the Sufis shaped India's composite culture.

1. Characteristics of the Sufi movement

  • Love over ritual: God is reached through love (ishq), remembrance (zikr) and devotional music (sama), rather than through legalism alone.
  • Pir–murid bond: the master (pir) guides the disciple (murid), and spiritual succession runs through a chain called a silsila.
  • Khanqahs: hospices with open kitchens (langar) welcomed people of all faiths and classes.
  • Two streams: ba-shara orders followed the Sharia, while be-shara wanderers such as the qalandars did not.
  • Local idiom: Sufis used local languages and music, and some Chishtis adopted Indian practices such as yogic breathing exercises.
  • Attitude to the state: Chishtis refused state grants and avoided the court, while Suhrawardis accepted grants and posts.
  • Philosophy: Ibn Arabi's wahdat-ul-wujud (unity of being) was popular, though later opposed by Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi's wahdat-ul-shuhud.

2. Impact on Indian culture

  • Religious syncretism: Hindus and Muslims share veneration at dargahs and urs festivals; Sufis found common ground with Bhakti saints such as Kabir and Nanak, and Baba Farid's verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Music: sama gave rise to the qawwali; Amir Khusrau, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, blended Persian and Indian musical forms.
  • Language and literature: Khusrau enriched Hindavi; malfuzat literature such as Fawaid-ul-Fuad recorded Nizamuddin's conversations; Deccan Sufis like Gesu Daraz of Gulbarga helped develop Dakhni Urdu.
  • Social equality: khanqahs and langars attracted artisans and lower castes and gave Islam an Indian idiom.
  • Pilgrimage culture: dargahs such as those of Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi became pilgrimage centres for people of all faiths.
  • Limits: orthodox ulema opposed sama and syncretism, and the Naqshbandi revival under Sirhindi stressed strict Sharia.

AP angle: The Bara Shaheed Dargah at Nellore (famous for the Rottela Panduga), the Ameen Peer Dargah at Kadapa and Baba Fakhruddin's dargah at Penukonda draw devotees of all faiths, a living example of Sufi syncretism.

Sufism thus helped build India's composite culture; its message of love, tolerance and service remains a valuable resource for social harmony today.
free.g1m-2025-p2-3a:
East India CompanyFactories and farmansPresidenciesMasulipatnam

The English East India Company was chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600, giving a group of London merchants a 15-year monopoly of eastern trade. Pushed out of the Spice Islands by the Dutch (Amboyna, 1623), it turned to India's textiles, indigo and saltpetre. Over the next century it grew from a trading body dependent on Mughal farmans into a fortified and armed power.

1. Establishment: from factories to presidencies

  • Mughal permission: William Hawkins reached Jahangir's court (1609); after the English defeated the Portuguese at Swally (1612), they got a factory at Surat (1613), and Sir Thomas Roe (1615–19) won wider trading rights.
  • East coast: a factory at Masulipatnam (1611); the Golconda Sultan's "Golden Farman" (1632) allowed trade in his ports for 500 pagodas a year; Fort St. George at Madras (1639–40) was built on land from a local Nayaka.
  • West coast: Bombay, part of Charles II's dowry (1661), was leased to the Company (1668) and became its western headquarters (1687).
  • Bengal: a factory at Hugli (1651); Calcutta founded by Job Charnock (1690); the zamindari of Sutanuti, Govindpur and Kalikata (1698), protected by Fort William.

2. Early operations

  • Trade: exported cotton textiles (calicoes, muslins), indigo, saltpetre, silk and pepper to Europe, paying largely in bullion because there was little demand in India for English goods.
  • Organisation: factories were grouped into three fortified presidencies — Madras, Bombay and Calcutta — each under a President and council.
  • Rivalry and conflict: the Company competed with the Portuguese, the Dutch and later the French; its Child's War against Aurangzeb (1686–90) failed, and it had to seek pardon and pay a fine.
  • Reorganisation: rival English companies merged into the United Company (1708–09).
  • Privileges: Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717), the Company's "Magna Carta", allowed duty-free trade in Bengal for ₹3,000 a year; misuse of dastaks (free passes) for private trade later caused conflict with the Nawabs.

AP angle: The Masulipatnam factory and the Golconda farman make coastal Andhra the cradle of English trade on the east coast; the Northern Circars later passed to the Company in the 1760s.

In a little over 150 years, the Company changed from a commercial body seeking Mughal favour into a territorial power after Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764); trade, forts and privileges paved the way for empire.
free.g1m-2025-p2-3b:
Christian missionariesCharter Act 1813Modern educationSocial reform

Christian missionaries were active in India from the Portuguese period (Francis Xavier, 1542), but large-scale Protestant work began with the Danish mission at Tranquebar (1706) and the Baptist mission at Serampore (1800) led by William Carey. The Charter Act of 1813 opened British India to missionaries. Their schools, presses, hospitals and criticism of social customs had a deep but mixed impact on Indian society and culture.

1. Positive impact: education and print

  • Modern education: English schools and colleges such as Alexander Duff's institution at Calcutta (1830, now Scottish Church College), Wilson College in Bombay and Madras Christian College.
  • Women's education: girls' schools and boarding homes were opened at a time when society opposed female education.
  • Language and print: Carey's Serampore press printed in many Indian languages; missionary grammars, dictionaries and Bible translations aided the growth of modern vernacular prose.
  • Tribal languages: scripts in Roman letters were devised for several tribal languages of the North-East.

2. Positive impact: social reform and health

  • Social reform: campaigns against sati, female infanticide, child marriage and untouchability supported reform laws such as the abolition of sati (1829).
  • Health care: hospitals and nursing schools, for example CMC Vellore (Ida Scudder, 1900).
  • Marginalised groups: schools and a new sense of dignity for Dalits and tribals.
  • Indirect stimulus: missionary criticism pushed Indians to reform their own society through the Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Arya Samaj.

3. Negative impact

  • Social tension: conversions, often of the poor, created friction, and revivalist responses such as the Arya Samaj's shuddhi grew partly as a reaction.
  • Colonial link: missionaries were closely identified with colonial rule and often disparaged Indian religions; fear of conversion was among the grievances behind the 1857 Revolt.
  • Caste persisted: caste distinctions survived among converts, and Dalit Christians remained socially disadvantaged.
  • Cultural alienation: a Western curriculum sometimes devalued Indian knowledge and traditions.

AP angle: The London Missionary Society began work at Visakhapatnam (1805); Noble College, Machilipatnam (1843) and Andhra Christian College, Guntur (1885) grew from missionary schools; American Baptists drew large numbers of Dalits, chiefly Madigas, into the church around Ongole in the late 19th century.

Missionaries were agents of modern education, print and health care, and they indirectly spurred Indian reform, though conversion-related tensions remained; their schools, colleges and hospitals still serve India.
free.g1m-2025-p2-4a:
Permanent SettlementZamindari systemSunset lawAgrarian distress

The Permanent Settlement (zamindari system) was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, making the Decennial Settlement (1789–90) permanent. It was later extended to Banaras and the Northern Circars (1802–03) and covered about 19% of British India. It aimed at an assured revenue, a loyal landed class and investment in land, but it reshaped rural society in harmful ways.

1. Main features

  • Zamindars as owners: revenue collectors became hereditary, transferable owners of land.
  • Revenue fixed for ever: zamindars paid 10/11 of the rent to the Company and kept 1/11; the State demand could never be raised.
  • Sunset Law: an estate was auctioned if revenue was not paid by sunset on the due date.
  • Ryots as tenants: cultivators lost customary rights and became tenants without recorded rights.
  • Aims: an assured revenue for the Company, a loyal landed class as a social base for British rule, and the hope, modelled on English landlords, that owners would improve their estates.

2. Impact on Indian society

  • Peasants: rack-renting, illegal cesses (abwabs) and eviction left them indebted tenants-at-will, vulnerable to famine.
  • Old aristocracy: the high, rigid demand led to the auction of many old estates; merchants and moneylenders bought them and became absentee landlords.
  • Land as a commodity: land became freely saleable, encouraging speculation and the transfer of estates to urban moneyed classes.
  • Subinfeudation: layers of intermediaries, such as patnidars (legalised in 1819), arose between the zamindar and the cultivator, each taking a share.
  • Agriculture: stagnated because zamindars rarely invested in land; the State also lost the gains from rising land values and extended cultivation.
  • Gains for the rulers: stable revenue for the Company, and a loyal rentier class that funded education and culture in Bengal.
  • Unrest: peasant revolts such as Pabna (1873) led to the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885.

AP angle: Estates such as Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram and Venkatagiri were permanently settled; tenant oppression led to the zamin ryots' agitations of the 1930s under N.G. Ranga and others. The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 ended the system.

The settlement secured revenue at the cost of the peasantry and agricultural growth, and created a parasitic landlordism; its abolition after Independence opened the way for land reform.
free.g1m-2025-p2-4b:
Safety valve theoryA.O. HumeLightning conductorIndian National Congress

The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay (72 delegates; president W.C. Bonnerjee) with the help of A.O. Hume, a retired ICS officer. The "safety valve" theory holds that Hume, with Viceroy Dufferin's blessing, created the Congress as a harmless outlet for growing discontent, to prevent another revolt like that of 1857. Most historians now regard this as an incomplete explanation.

1. Meaning and basis of the theory

  • Hume's fears: William Wedderburn's biography of Hume (1913) said Hume had seen secret reports, in seven volumes, of growing unrest among the masses and wanted a constitutional outlet for it.
  • Official blessing: the theory assumes that the Viceroy encouraged a body to channel educated opinion, so that it would not join hands with mass discontent.
  • Used by critics: Lala Lajpat Rai (Young India, 1916) used it to attack the Moderates, and the Marxist R. Palme Dutt (India Today) saw the Congress as a British plan to forestall a popular revolution.
  • Apparent fit: the early Congress's loyalty, prayers and petitions seemed to match the idea of a safety valve.

2. Critique of the theory

  • No evidence: the seven volumes of reports have never been found, and Hume's motives appear largely liberal and humanitarian.
  • Official hostility: Dufferin soon turned hostile, dismissing the Congress as a "microscopic minority" (1888).
  • Indian roots: the Congress grew out of a decade of political activity by Indian associations.
  • Lightning conductor thesis (Bipan Chandra): Indian leaders used Hume as a "lightning conductor" to avoid official suspicion; Gokhale said in 1913 that no Indian could then have started such a body.
  • Uncomfortable demands: from its first session the Congress asked for expanded legislative councils, simultaneous ICS examinations and cuts in military spending, demands the government disliked.
  • Radical content: the Moderates' drain theory attacked the moral basis of British rule, hardly the work of a safety valve.

AP angle: P. Ananda Charlu, a founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha, attended the 1885 session and presided over the Nagpur Congress (1891), showing that Indian, including Telugu, initiative lay behind the Congress.

The theory may reflect part of Hume's intentions, but the Congress was the product of a maturing Indian political awakening; far from being a safety valve, it became the main vehicle of the freedom struggle.
free.g1m-2025-p2-5a:
ModeratesDrain theoryConstitutional methodsPolitical education

The first phase of the Congress (1885–1905) was led by the Moderates — Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, W.C. Bonnerjee, Badruddin Tyabji, M.G. Ranade, G.K. Gokhale and R.C. Dutt. Drawn from the Western-educated middle class, they believed in British justice and used constitutional methods. Though later mocked for "political mendicancy", they laid the ideological foundation of Indian nationalism.

1. Methods

  • Prayer, petition and protest: resolutions, memorials and petitions to the government, always within the law.
  • Lobbying in Britain: a British Committee of the Congress (1889) and its journal "India" tried to win over British opinion.
  • Political education: speeches, newspapers and annual sessions built public opinion in India.
  • Gradualism: they believed political change should come step by step, as Indians gained experience of self-government.

2. Contributions

  • Economic critique of colonialism: Naoroji's drain theory (Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901) and R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India exposed how British rule impoverished India (Naoroji estimated per capita income at only ₹20 a year in 1867–68); they demanded lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax, protection for Indian industry and cuts in military spending.
  • Constitutional reforms: expansion of legislative councils with elected Indians, partly met by the Indian Councils Act, 1892.
  • Administrative reforms: Indianisation of services through simultaneous ICS examinations (House of Commons resolution, 1893), separation of the judiciary from the executive and repeal of the Arms Act.
  • Civil rights: defence of freedom of speech and the press, for example protests against Tilak's arrest in 1897.
  • Nation-building: an all-India, secular platform, and evidence before the Welby Commission (1895) on Indian expenditure.

3. Limitations

  • Narrow base: the movement was confined to the urban educated elite and did not mobilise peasants and workers.
  • Faith in British fairness: reliance on petitions brought few concrete gains.
  • Social questions kept aside: the Congress avoided social reform, leaving it to Ranade's Indian National Social Conference, so political and social reform moved on separate tracks.
  • Result: growing frustration led to the rise of the Extremists and the split at Surat (1907).

AP angle: Telugu Moderates such as P. Ananda Charlu and Nyapathi Subba Rao Pantulu, a co-founder of The Hindu (1878), spread political awareness in Andhra.

The Moderates were the pioneers of nationalism; their economic critique of imperialism was their most lasting legacy, which later leaders turned into mass politics.
free.g1m-2025-p2-5b:
SatyagrahaMass movementNon-Cooperation to Quit IndiaConstructive programme

Between 1920 and 1947, Mahatma Gandhi turned the national movement from an elite affair into a mass struggle. His method of satyagraha, non-violent resistance based on truth, alternated phases of struggle with phases of constructive programme (khadi, communal unity, removal of untouchability). Peasants, workers, women and students were drawn in, and each movement widened the social base of nationalism.

1. Non-Cooperation–Khilafat Movement (1920–22)

  • Causes: the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and the Khilafat issue.
  • Programme: launched in August 1920 and endorsed at the Calcutta and Nagpur sessions; boycott of government schools, courts, councils, titles and foreign cloth; swadeshi and the Tilak Swaraj Fund.
  • Participation: students left government colleges, lawyers such as C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru gave up their practice, and national institutions such as Jamia Millia and Kashi Vidyapith were founded.
  • End: withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura violence (February 1922), but it made the Congress a mass party.

2. Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34)

  • Background: the Purna Swaraj resolution (Lahore, 1929).
  • Salt satyagraha: the Dandi March (12 March–6 April 1930) broke the salt law; boycotts and no-tax campaigns followed, with large participation of women.
  • Course: suspended after the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931) and the Second Round Table Conference, resumed in 1932 and withdrawn in 1934; after the Poona Pact (1932) Gandhi led a nationwide campaign against untouchability (Harijan Sevak Sangh).

3. Individual Satyagraha (1940–41) and Quit India (1942)

  • Individual Satyagraha: protested against India being dragged into the Second World War; Vinoba Bhave was the first satyagrahi and Nehru the second.
  • Quit India: launched at Bombay on 8 August 1942 with the call "Do or Die"; leaders were arrested at once, but a mass upsurge followed, with parallel governments at Satara, Ballia and Tamluk.

4. Final phase (1946–47)

  • Communal peace: Gandhi worked for peace in riot-hit Noakhali and Bihar and spent Independence Day in Calcutta, working to stop communal violence.

AP angle: The AICC met at Bezawada (1921), where Pingali Venkayya presented a flag design to Gandhi; Andhra saw the Chirala–Perala struggle led by Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya, the Pedanandipadu no-tax campaign and the Palnadu forest satyagraha (1921–22), salt satyagraha along the coast (1930) and the Tenali incidents during Quit India (1942).

Each movement drew in new sections of society and eroded the moral authority of British rule; together they made the Raj untenable and led to independence in 1947.
free.g1m-2025-p2-6a:
AP Reorganisation Act 2014Loss of HyderabadRevenue deficitDecentralised growth

Under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, the State was divided on 2 June 2014. Hyderabad went to Telangana and served as the common capital for up to ten years (Section 5), a period that ended on 2 June 2024. Residual Andhra Pradesh thus lost the centre of its administration, investment, services and culture of nearly six decades, and had to rebuild its institutions almost from scratch.

1. Administrative impact

  • A capital-less start: the government functioned from Hyderabad until 2016, then moved to an interim Secretariat at Velagapudi; a separate High Court began at Amaravati on 1 January 2019.
  • Division pains: the division of employees, assets and the Schedule IX and X institutions remained slow and partly disputed.
  • Relocation of staff: employees allotted to AP had to move their families from Hyderabad, and many offices first worked from temporary premises in Vijayawada and Guntur.
  • Rebuilding institutions: headquarters, offices and records had to be relocated; shifting capital plans (Amaravati, three capitals in 2020, Amaravati again from 2024) added uncertainty for officials and investors.

2. Economic impact

  • Loss of the growth engine: AP lost its main IT, pharma and services hub and much of its tax base, while taking about 58% of the population and of the debt.
  • Fiscal stress: it began with a large revenue deficit, depending on Finance Commission revenue-deficit grants and a central special assistance package (2016) in place of special category status.
  • Structural shift: the economy became more dependent on agriculture, and per capita income fell behind Telangana's.
  • New institutions: the Act brought national institutions such as IIT Tirupati, IIM Visakhapatnam and AIIMS Mangalagiri, and growth was spurred in Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati.

3. Socio-cultural impact

  • Institutions left behind: the Telugu film industry, media houses, leading hospitals and universities remained in Hyderabad, as did many Andhra families.
  • Identity and migration: a sense of loss and a search for a new identity followed; educated youth kept migrating to Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai.
  • Education: AP students lost easy access to Hyderabad's universities and coaching ecosystem; the Act kept existing admission quotas common for ten years (Section 95).
  • Regional sensitivities: debates on where the capital and new institutions should go revived old concerns of Rayalaseema and North Andhra.

The loss of Hyderabad imposed lasting fiscal and institutional costs, but it also pushed AP towards a multi-centred growth model; a stable capital and full implementation of the 2014 Act's promises are the way forward.
free.g1m-2025-p2-6b:
AmaravatiLand poolingGreenfield capitalFiscal sustainability

After losing Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh chose Amaravati, a greenfield capital on the Krishna between Vijayawada and Guntur. The Prime Minister laid its foundation stone on 22 October 2015, and the AP Capital Region Development Authority (APCRDA) plans it. The project was meant to give the residual State an administrative centre, an economic engine and a symbol of identity, but its cost and stop–start history raise serious financial questions.

1. The vision

  • A "people's capital": a world-class "blue-green" city of about 217 sq km, master-planned with Singapore, with nine theme cities (government, justice, finance, knowledge and others).
  • Land pooling instead of acquisition: about 34,000 acres from farmers of 29 villages, who receive developed plots and annuities; the scheme was meant to make the capital largely self-financing.
  • Growth engine and identity: jobs, investment and a new urban centre to replace Hyderabad's role, symbolising a fresh start after bifurcation.

2. Financial implications: a critical assessment

  • High cost: the State put core works at ₹64,721 crore (Assembly, March 2025), far beyond its own fiscal space.
  • Debt-led funding: World Bank and ADB loans of US$1.6 billion (about ₹13,400 crore) under the ₹15,000 crore support in Union Budget 2024-25, plus HUDCO (₹11,000 crore) and KfW (₹5,000 crore) loans, add to an already indebted State's liabilities.
  • Stop–start costs: after the three-capitals law (2020, repealed 2021), works stalled until 2024; half-built structures deteriorated and contracts had to be revised.
  • Tight fiscal space: large committed spending on salaries, pensions, interest and welfare leaves little room for capital outlay, so every rupee for the capital competes with other needs.
  • Land-based risk: repayment hinges on land sales and land values, while farmers' annuities and returnable plots are fixed obligations.
  • Opportunity cost: heavy investment in one region worries Rayalaseema and North Andhra, fertile farmland is lost and flood protection adds cost; the Sivaramakrishnan Committee (2014) had cautioned against a concentrated capital on fertile land and favoured decentralised development.
  • Positives: loans are long-term (World Bank repayment from 2031); land value capture, stamp duties and property taxes can repay them, and construction creates jobs; the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026, amending Section 5(2), ended legal uncertainty by making Amaravati the statutory capital.

The vision of Amaravati is sound, but its fiscal sustainability depends on phased, transparent execution, cost control and land monetisation, together with balanced investment in other regions.
free.g1m-2025-p2-8a:
Kakatiya SaivismKalamukhaAradhyaVirashaivism

The Kakatiyas of Warangal (c. 1163–1323), the first dynasty to unite most Telugu-speaking lands, began as Jains but became devoted Shaivites. Under Rudradeva, Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi and Prataparudra, Shaivism flourished in many forms, from ascetic orders and temple mathas to the socially radical Virashaiva movement. These sects shaped religion, literature, temples and society in the Telugu lands.

1. The major Saivite sects

  • Kalamukha and Pashupata: ascetic orders with mathas at Srisailam, Alampur and other centres; their acharyas managed temples, taught and received royal grants.
  • Shaiva Siddhanta (Golaki Matha): Visvesvara Sivacharya, rajaguru of Ganapatideva and Rudramadevi, headed this order; the Malkapuram inscription (1261) records his foundation of a matha with a school, a hospital and a feeding house.
  • Aradhya Shaivism: led by Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya (12th century), one of the Pancha Aradhyas; these Brahmin Shaivites worshipped the linga but kept Vedic rites and caste.
  • Virashaivism: Basavanna's movement from Kalyani rejected caste, ritual and priestly authority; it was popularised in Telugu by Palkuriki Somanatha (Basava Puranam, Panditaradhya Charitra) and attracted artisans and peasants.

2. Royal patronage and temples

  • Temples: the Thousand Pillar (Rudreswara) temple at Hanamkonda (1163) and the Ramappa temple at Palampet (1213, UNESCO World Heritage Site 2021) express Kakatiya Shaiva devotion in stone.
  • Temple and tank: Kakatiya temples were often paired with irrigation tanks, as the Ramappa temple with the Ramappa lake, linking religion with agrarian prosperity.
  • Grants: endowments went to great Shaiva centres such as Srisailam and Draksharamam, and mathas received land for teaching and charity.

3. Impact on literature and society

  • Literature: the "Shivakavi" age — Nannechoda (Kumarasambhavam), Panditaradhya (Sivatattvasaram) and Somanatha, who used the desi dwipada metre and brought Telugu literature to ordinary people.
  • Society: mathas became centres of learning, health care and charity; Virashaiva equality challenged caste rigidity.
  • Tolerance: Vaishnavism and Jainism coexisted, and Tikkana's Mahabharata honoured Harihara, the unity of Shiva and Vishnu.

AP angle: Srisailam and Draksharamam, both in present Andhra Pradesh, were among the Shaiva centres that received patronage in this age and remain major pilgrimage centres today.

Kakatiya-era Saivism, from Brahmanical Aradhyas to radical Virashaivas, enriched Telugu religion, literature and art; its legacy lives on in Ramappa and in the Shaiva centres of Andhra Pradesh.
free.g1m-2025-p2-8b:
Warangal FortKakatiya architectureKirti ToranasTelugu heritage

The Warangal Fort at Orugallu (Ekasilanagaram), the capital of the Kakatiyas, was begun by Ganapatideva (1199–1262) and completed by Rudramadevi and Prataparudra in the 13th century. Built around a single rock hill (Ekashila) that gave the city its name, it was one of the strongest forts of medieval South India. Today it is a symbol of Telugu political unity, military engineering and Kakatiya art.

1. Features of the fort

  • Concentric defences: an inner wall of large dressed granite blocks with bastions, a middle earthen wall and an outer earthen rampart, each with moats.
  • Kirti Toranas: four ornate stone gateways, facing the four directions, around the ruined Svayambhu Shiva temple.
  • Other remains: scattered sculptures and temple ruins, the Ekashila hillock and the later Khush Mahal.

2. Significance as a historical monument

  • Political: it was the capital of the first dynasty to unite the Telugu lands, from coastal Andhra (Motupalli port) to Telangana; Rudramadevi ruled from here, and Marco Polo, who visited Motupalli, praised her rule.
  • Military history: Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khalji's general, besieged it in 1309–10 and Prataparudra paid tribute; Ulugh Khan (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) captured it in 1323, ending Kakatiya rule; Amir Khusrau described its mud and stone walls.
  • Architecture: it is a fine example of medieval military engineering, and its toranas display the Kakatiya stone carving also seen at Ramappa.
  • Identity: the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam was placed in Telangana's State emblem in 2014.
  • Heritage status: the fort, with the Thousand Pillar and Ramappa temples, is on UNESCO's tentative list as "The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways" (Ramappa was inscribed in 2021); Warangal was selected under the HRIDAY heritage city scheme (2015).
  • Tourism: the fort is part of a Kakatiya heritage circuit with Hanamkonda and Ramappa, supporting local livelihoods.
  • Legacy: the fall of Warangal led to the Musunuri Nayakas' struggle for liberation and influenced the rise of Vijayanagara.

AP angle: For Andhra Pradesh, the fort recalls an age when coastal Andhra and Telangana formed one Kakatiya kingdom, with Motupalli on the Andhra coast as its port; it is a shared heritage of both Telugu States.

The fort, a shared heritage of all Telugu people, symbolises political unity, military engineering and Kakatiya art; scientific conservation and heritage tourism can preserve it for future generations.
free.g1m-2025-p2-9b:
Telugu renaissanceVeeresalingamWestern educationSocial reform

Social awakening in Andhra in the second half of the 19th century, often called the Telugu renaissance, challenged child marriage, the ban on widow remarriage, kanyasulkam (bride-price), the nautch system and superstition. It was led by a new educated middle class, with Kandukuri Veeresalingam as its central figure, and prepared the ground for later political consciousness. Several educational, economic and cultural factors came together to produce it.

1. Education and missionary influence

  • Western education: Madras University (1857), government colleges (Rajahmundry) and missionary institutions (Noble College, Machilipatnam) produced a new middle class exposed to liberal and rational ideas.
  • Missionary activity: schools for girls and Dalits, and criticism of social evils, prompted self-examination in Hindu society.

2. Economic change

  • Irrigation and prosperity: Sir Arthur Cotton's anicut at Dowleswaram (1852) on the Godavari and the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada (1855) brought prosperity to the deltas, and a landed middle class could now educate its children.
  • New professions: lawyers, teachers, clerks and journalists formed a new middle class in towns such as Rajahmundry, Machilipatnam and Guntur, ready to question old customs.
  • Communications: railways, the post and the telegraph linked Andhra towns with Madras and the rest of India, spreading new ideas.

3. Press, literature and reformers

  • Press: Veeresalingam's journal Viveka Vardhini (1874) attacked social evils and corruption.
  • Literature: his Rajasekhara Charitramu is regarded as the first Telugu novel; Gurajada Apparao's play Kanyasulkam (1892) satirised bride-price; Paravastu Chinnayasuri's Neeti Chandrika became a model of Telugu prose.
  • Reformers: Veeresalingam, "father of the Telugu renaissance", started a girls' school at Dowleswaram (1874), performed the first widow remarriage in Andhra at Rajahmundry (11 December 1881) and founded a social reform association; Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu led the anti-nautch and social purity movements.

4. Wider influences and patronage

  • Pan-Indian movements: the Brahmo and Prarthana Samajs, the Theosophical Society at Adyar (1882) and the early Congress carried new ideas to Andhra.
  • Cultural pride: the study of Telugu classics and history, helped by new printing presses, created pride in the Telugu language and a wish to modernise society.
  • Patronage: enlightened zamindars of Vizianagaram and Pithapuram supported education and literature.

These forces created a reform-minded Telugu middle class whose energy later flowed into the Andhra movement, the library movement and the freedom struggle.
free.g1m-2025-p2-10a:
Gentlemen's Agreement 1956Mulki rulesRegional CouncilTelangana safeguards

The Gentlemen's Agreement was signed at Delhi on 20 February 1956 by leaders of Andhra State (including B. Gopala Reddy and N. Sanjiva Reddy) and Telangana (including B. Ramakrishna Rao and K.V. Ranga Reddy). Its aim was to reassure Telangana, which feared domination by the more advanced Andhra region in education and jobs, so that the two could merge into Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

1. Background

  • SRC view: the States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1955) suggested keeping Telangana separate for some years, with a later merger if its legislature agreed by a two-thirds majority.
  • Push for Visalandhra: Andhra leaders and the Visalandhra movement pressed for an early merger of all Telugu areas, while many in Telangana were apprehensive, so safeguards became the price of unity.

2. Main provisions

  • Finance: common administrative costs shared proportionately; Telangana's surplus revenue to be spent on Telangana.
  • Education: existing educational facilities in Telangana reserved for Telangana students and improved.
  • Services: proportionate retrenchment if needed, recruitment on a population basis, and 12 years' residence (Mulki rules) for jobs in Telangana.
  • Language: Urdu to continue in administration and courts for five years.
  • Regional Council: a statutory Telangana Regional Council for development, education and local bodies, which would also control the sale of agricultural land in Telangana.
  • Cabinet: a 60:40 ratio; a Deputy CM from Telangana if the CM was from Andhra (and vice versa); two of the portfolios of Home, Finance, Revenue, Planning and Development, and Commerce and Industry for Telangana.
  • Prohibition in Telangana to be decided by its MLAs.

3. How far did it satisfy Telangana?

  • Initial reassurance: it satisfied Telangana leaders enough to make the merger possible; Article 371 (Seventh Amendment, 1956) and a 1958 Presidential Order created a Regional Committee of the Legislature.
  • Dilution: the Regional Committee had weaker powers than the promised Council, and the Deputy CM post was not filled consistently.
  • Grievances: complaints grew about the diversion of Telangana surpluses and the violation of Mulki rules in recruitment.
  • No enforcement mechanism: as a political understanding, the Agreement had no legal force, so implementation depended on the goodwill of successive governments.
  • Consequences: these grievances fuelled the 1969 agitation, the Six-Point Formula (1973), Article 371D (32nd Amendment) and the 1975 Presidential Order, and ultimately bifurcation in 2014.

The Agreement satisfied Telangana only partly, because it was a political understanding without legal force; the lesson is that regional safeguards need statutory backing, monitoring and faithful implementation.
free.g1m-2025-p2-10b:
Jai Telangana 1969Student agitationMulki rulesRegional equity

The 1969 "Jai Telangana" agitation was the first mass movement for a separate Telangana. It grew out of grievances that the safeguards of the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) on jobs, funds and education had been violated. Students of Khammam, Osmania University and colleges across the region started it, set its agenda and kept it alive in the face of police repression.

1. Raising the issues

  • Spark: in January 1969 a student, Annabhatula Ravindranath, began a hunger strike at Khammam demanding implementation of the safeguards; protests spread quickly to Osmania University and the rest of Telangana.
  • Mulki rules and jobs: students demanded the removal of non-Mulki employees from Telangana posts (an issue raised at the Kothagudem Thermal Power Station) and strict enforcement of the Mulki rules.
  • Funds and backwardness: they highlighted the alleged diversion of Telangana's surplus funds and the region's lag in irrigation, education and employment.
  • Legal uncertainty: court rulings in 1969 that weakened the legal basis of residence rules deepened students' anxiety about jobs.
  • From safeguards to statehood: the demand moved from enforcement of safeguards to a separate Telangana.

2. Methods and sacrifices

  • Mass action: strikes, boycotts of classes and examinations, rallies and bandhs paralysed the region.
  • Wider support: teachers, non-gazetted employees and political leaders joined the students, broadening the movement's base.
  • Organisation: student action committees joined the Telangana Praja Samithi, led by Dr. M. Chenna Reddy from mid-1969.
  • Repression: police firings killed many, mostly students (369 by the commonly cited count); the Gun Park memorial in Hyderabad honours them, and an academic year was lost.

3. Government response and outcome

  • Accords: an all-party accord (January 1969) and Indira Gandhi's Eight-Point Plan (April 1969).
  • Committees: the Wanchoo Committee on the legality of Mulki rules and the Bhargava Committee on Telangana surpluses.
  • Political result: the Telangana Praja Samithi won 10 of Telangana's 14 Lok Sabha seats in 1971 and then merged with the Congress.

AP angle: The Mulki issue also stirred the Andhra region: after the Supreme Court upheld the Mulki rules (1972), the Jai Andhra movement (1972–73) followed, and the Six-Point Formula (1973) ended both agitations.

Students turned administrative grievances into a political movement; the issues they raised, jobs, funds and regional equity, shaped Article 371D and resurfaced in the movement of 2009–14.
free.g1m-2025-p2-12a:
Agrarian economyClimate changeAgro-climatic zonesClimate-smart agriculture
