Agriculture is the backbone of Andhra Pradesh: the primary sector (crops, livestock and fisheries) contributes about 35% of GSVA (2025-26, State estimates), roughly double the national share. Its fertile deltas, long coast and dry interior support a wide range of crops and allied activities. But its key inputs, rainfall, temperature, irrigation and power, are all sensitive to climate change, making the sector both vital and vulnerable.

1. Background of agriculture in AP

  • Agro-climatic zones: the canal-irrigated Godavari–Krishna deltas (the "rice bowl"), the rain-fed north coastal tracts, the south coast (tobacco, chillies) and semi-arid Rayalaseema (groundnut, horticulture).
  • Crops and allied sectors: paddy is the main crop; AP leads India in chillies (Guntur), oil palm, fish and shrimp, and is a major producer of mango, banana and papaya.
  • Support systems: canal, tank and well irrigation, free farm power, and the APCNF natural-farming programme (since 2016).
  • Rainfall base: seasonal normals of 556 mm (south-west monsoon) and 296 mm (north-east monsoon); the coast benefits from both, while Rayalaseema gets low, erratic rain.

2. Climate change and key inputs: a critical examination

  • Rainfall: trends show erratic onset, long dry spells and extreme downpours (Vijayawada floods, 2024), meaning drought for rain-fed Rayalaseema and floods and cyclone damage in the deltas.
  • Temperature: heat waves cause stress at flowering, cut paddy and pulse yields, raise water demand and hit livestock, poultry and aquaculture.
  • Irrigation: canal supply depends on erratic Krishna and Godavari inflows from upstream States; groundwater is falling in hard-rock areas; higher evaporation reduces tank storage; and sea-level rise brings salinity into delta aquifers.
  • Power: heat raises pumping demand and strains free farm power, while low reservoir levels reduce hydropower; solar parks and solar pumps (PM-KUSUM) offer resilience.
  • Caveat: impacts are uneven and partly uncertain (some crops may gain from higher carbon dioxide), so district-level planning is needed.

3. Adaptation

  • Farm practices: natural farming, drought-tolerant varieties and micro-irrigation reduce water and input needs.
  • Water security: completion of Polavaram and river links such as Pattiseema can stabilise supply.
  • Risk cover and research: crop insurance and ICAR's NICRA programme support climate-resilient farming.

Climate-smart agriculture, built on water efficiency, crop diversification and solar irrigation, can make AP's farm sector resilient and sustainable.
free.g1m-2025-p2-15b:
APPCBPost-disaster pollutionPolluter paysChemical disaster preparedness

The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board (APPCB), constituted in 1976 under the Water Act, 1974, enforces the Water, Air (1981) and Environment (Protection) (1986) Acts and the waste-management rules. Cyclones, floods and industrial accidents suddenly release debris, sewage, chemicals and toxic gases, so the Board's regulatory powers become crucial after a disaster, alongside the disaster-management agencies.

1. Role of APPCB after disasters

  • Monitoring: checks air and water quality, drinking-water sources and effluents after floods and cyclones, and issues advisories to the public.
  • Industrial accidents: inspects units and issues closure or other directions under Section 33A of the Water Act, Section 31A of the Air Act and the EP Act.
  • Waste management: guides urban bodies on debris, solid waste and bio-medical waste from relief camps under the 2016 waste rules, as after Hudhud (2014) and the Vijayawada floods (2024).
  • Chemical disaster preparedness: under the Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, 1996, it supports emergency plans and mock drills with the Factories Department.
  • Coordination: works with the State Disaster Management Authority, collectors and the health and municipal departments.

2. Case study: LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam (2020)

  • The disaster: the styrene gas leak of 7 May 2020 killed at least 12 people and affected nearby villages.
  • Action: the plant was shut, the NGT directed the company to deposit an interim ₹50 crore, and a State high-power committee found lapses by the company and regulators.
  • Lesson: regular inspection of hazardous units matters more than action after an accident.

3. Assessment

  • Reactive approach: the Board is largely reactive, with staff and laboratory shortages.
  • Overlaps and enforcement: its work overlaps with the Factories Department; enforcement is weak, and the NGT often has to step in.
  • Gaps: there is no dedicated post-disaster pollution protocol and little real-time public data; the Atchutapuram pharma SEZ explosion (2024) showed continuing risks.

4. Way forward

  • Capacity: more scientists, mobile laboratories and joint training with the State Disaster Management Authority.
  • Right to know: public disclosure of emergency plans to residents living near hazardous units.
  • Reforms: disaster-specific SOPs in State and district plans, public real-time dashboards, risk mapping of industrial clusters and strict application of the polluter-pays principle.

APPCB's role is vital but under-equipped; making it proactive, technology-driven and well-coordinated is essential to "build back better".
free.g1m-2025-p3-2a:
State legislative procedureGovernor's reservationArticles 200–201Union primacy

A Union Bill becomes law once both Houses pass it and the President gives assent (Art 111). A State Bill (Art 196–201) passes through an extra Union filter: the Governor, appointed by the President (Art 155) and holding office during his pleasure (Art 156), who may reserve it for the President acting on the Union Cabinet's advice. This asymmetry reflects India's "holding together" federation, where national unity and uniform law take priority.

1. How the two procedures differ

2. Safeguards for Union interests

  • Discretionary reservation (Art 200): the Governor may reserve any Bill; reservation is compulsory if it would endanger the position of the High Court.
  • Absolute veto (Art 201): the President may withhold assent; a returned non-Money Bill must be reconsidered within six months, yet assent is still not obligatory, and no time limit is laid down.
  • Prior sanction or assent: Bills restricting inter-State trade need the President's previous sanction (Art 304(b)); a State law repugnant to a central law on a Concurrent subject prevails only with presidential assent (Art 254(2)); laws under Art 31A and 31C, and State taxes on water or electricity of Union authorities (Art 288), are protected only after reservation.
  • Financial Emergency (Art 360): State Money Bills may have to be reserved for the President.

3. Judicial balancing

  • Punjab Governor case (2023): the Supreme Court held that a Governor cannot sit on Bills indefinitely; withholding means returning the Bill to the House.
  • Tamil Nadu Governor case (8 April 2025): a two-judge Bench fixed timelines for the Governor and the President and, using Art 142, deemed ten re-passed Bills to have received assent; this led to a Presidential Reference.
  • Presidential Reference opinion (Art 143, November 2025): a five-judge Bench held that courts cannot fix timelines or grant "deemed assent", but prolonged, unexplained inaction is open to limited judicial review.

AP angle: The AP Disha Bill 2019, which amended central criminal laws on a Concurrent subject, was sent for the President's assent, showing how Art 254(2) brings State laws under Union review.

4. Assessment

  • Justification: uniform laws on Concurrent subjects, protection of the High Court, a single national market and a check on unconstitutional Bills.
  • Criticism: the Governor may act as an agent of the Union, and long delays over Bills have strained Centre–State relations.

These safeguards protect national uniformity, but, as the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions advised, reservation should be rare and decisions timely, so that cooperative federalism is not reduced to Union control.
free.g1m-2025-p3-2b:
Seventh ScheduleParliamentary supremacyArticles 249–253State autonomy

Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule divide legislative power among the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (originally 97, 66 and 47 subjects). States have exclusive power over the State List in normal times, but the scheme is tilted towards the Centre: Parliament can enter the State field in several situations, and its law prevails in a conflict. This reflects India's centralised federation built for unity and integrity.

1. Parliament's power over State subjects

  • National interest (Art 249): if the Rajya Sabha resolves by two-thirds of members present and voting, Parliament may legislate on a State subject for one year, renewable; the law lapses six months after the resolution ends.
  • Consent of States (Art 252): when two or more States request it, Parliament may legislate for them, and other States may adopt the law; only Parliament can then amend it. Examples: Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 and Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974.
  • International agreements (Art 253): Parliament can implement treaties even on State subjects, as in the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, which followed the Stockholm Conference (1972).
  • Emergencies: during a National Emergency (Art 250) and President's Rule (Art 356–357), Parliament can legislate on any State subject.

2. Supremacy in conflicts and structure

  • Federal supremacy (Art 246(1), 254(1)): the Union List prevails over the State List, and a central law prevails over a State law on a Concurrent subject; even when a State law gets assent under Art 254(2), Parliament can later override it.
  • Shifting the lists: the 42nd Amendment (1976) moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice from the State List to the Concurrent List.
  • Reservation of State Bills (Art 200–201): the Union can veto State laws through the President.
  • Reorganisation (Art 3): Parliament can alter State boundaries; the views of the State Legislature are not binding (Babulal Parate, 1960).

3. Limits on this overarching power

  • Doctrines: courts apply pith and substance and strike down colourable legislation, protecting the State field.
  • Federalism is basic structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994): Parliament cannot destroy the States' sphere.
  • Ratification: in Union of India v Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the 97th Amendment's provisions on State cooperative societies were struck down for lack of ratification by half the States.
  • Taxing powers: in Mineral Area Development Authority (2024), a nine-judge Bench held that States can tax mineral rights.

AP angle: The AP Reorganisation Act 2014 was enacted under Art 3 although the AP Assembly had rejected the draft Bill, showing that even a State's territory lies within Parliament's power.

State autonomy is thus real but subordinate to the national interest. Sparing use of Art 249 and 252, and consultation through a stronger Inter-State Council (Art 263), as the Punchhi Commission urged, can balance unity with diversity.
free.g1m-2025-p3-3a:
Fiscal federalismArticle 280Vertical & horizontal imbalanceDevolution

India's federation has a built-in fiscal imbalance: the Union collects the most buoyant taxes (income tax, corporation tax, a large share of GST), while the States carry most of the spending on health, education, police and agriculture. The Finance Commission (FC), a constitutional body under Article 280, corrects this vertical imbalance (Union vs States) and the horizontal imbalance (rich vs poor States) through rule-based devolution. That is why it is called the backbone of fiscal federalism.

1. Constitutional basis and composition

  • Constituted by the President every five years (or earlier), with a Chairperson and four members; qualifications are laid down by the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951.
  • Its recommendations are laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum (Article 281). The current 16th FC (Chairman Arvind Panagariya) covers 2026-27 to 2030-31.

2. Role of the Finance Commission

  • Vertical devolution (Art. 270): fixes the States' share of the divisible pool. The 14th FC raised it from 32% to 42%; the 15th FC fixed 41% after Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory; the 16th FC has retained 41%.
  • Horizontal distribution: shares each State's portion by a transparent formula that balances need, equity and efficiency.
  • Grants-in-aid (Art. 275): for States that need help beyond their tax share, such as disaster-management grants.
  • Local bodies (Art. 280(3)(bb) and (c)): suggests measures to augment State funds for panchayats and municipalities; the 16th FC recommended about ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies.
  • Fiscal discipline: advises on deficit and debt paths, for example a deficit limit of 3% of GSDP for States.

3. Significance: why it is the "backbone"

  • Predictability: formula-based, five-year transfers reduce discretion and political bargaining.
  • Equity with efficiency: poorer States receive more through income distance, while the new GDP criterion rewards States that contribute more to national output.
  • Cooperative federalism: an independent, expert body balances the Union's macro-stability needs with the States' development needs.
  • Strengthening the third tier: local-body grants deepen grassroots democracy under the 73rd and 74th Amendments.

4. Limitations

  • Recommendations are advisory, not binding.
  • Cesses and surcharges are outside the divisible pool, so the effective share of States is lower than 41%.
  • Large Centrally Sponsored Schemes and discretionary transfers bypass the FC, and GST has narrowed States' independent taxation.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's share of the divisible pool rises from 4.047% (15th FC) to about 4.22% (16th FC), but the 16th FC has discontinued revenue-deficit grants, which post-bifurcation AP received under the 14th and 15th FCs.

In conclusion, the Finance Commission keeps the Union and the States in financial balance through rules rather than discretion; bringing cesses into the divisible pool and ensuring timely transfers would make cooperative fiscal federalism stronger.
free.g1m-2025-p3-3b:
73rd AmendmentGram SabhaDemocratic decentralisationEleventh Schedule

The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, in force from 24 April 1993 (now National Panchayati Raj Day), gave constitutional status to panchayats by inserting Part IX (Art 243–243O) and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects. It turned Art 40, a Directive Principle, into a binding framework of democratic decentralisation, creating a third tier of government closest to the people.

1. Strengthening representative democracy

  • Uniform three tiers (Art 243B, 243C): village, intermediate and district panchayats, with members directly elected; States with a population under 20 lakh may skip the middle tier.
  • Regular elections (Art 243E): a fixed five-year term, and elections within six months of dissolution, ending the old practice of indefinite supersession.
  • Independent State Election Commission (Art 243K): removes elections from executive control.

2. Making democracy inclusive

  • Reservation (Art 243D): seats and chairpersons' posts for SCs and STs in proportion to population, and at least one-third for women; many States, including Andhra Pradesh, reserve 50%, and women now hold nearly half of all panchayat seats.
  • Tribal self-rule: the PESA Act 1996 gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth Schedule areas powers over minor forest produce, land alienation and local resources.
  • New leadership: Dalit, tribal and women representatives gain experience that feeds into higher politics.

3. Making democracy participatory and accountable

  • Gram Sabha (Art 243A): all voters of the village approve plans, select beneficiaries and conduct social audits, a form of direct democracy.
  • Planning (Art 243G): panchayats prepare plans for economic development and social justice on the 29 subjects, now through Gram Panchayat Development Plans.
  • Funds (Art 243H, 243I): power to levy taxes, and a State Finance Commission every five years; the 16th Finance Commission recommends ₹4.35 lakh crore for rural local bodies (2026-31).

4. Limitations

  • Partial devolution: the transfer of the "3Fs" (funds, functions and functionaries) is left to States and remains uneven; Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996) is an exception.
  • Proxy representation: "sarpanch-pati" culture undermines women's leadership.
  • Weak finances and capacity: low own revenue, dependence on grants, and bureaucratic control over panchayat staff.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh introduced panchayati raj in 1959, soon after Rajasthan. The AP Panchayat Raj Act 1994 provides gram panchayats, mandal parishads and zilla parishads, with 50% of seats reserved for women; village secretariats (2019) bring services to the panchayat level, and PESA applies in AP's Scheduled Areas.

The 73rd Amendment made panchayats institutions of self-government; real devolution of the 3Fs, capacity building under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan and digital tools such as eGramSwaraj can make grassroots democracy fully effective.
free.g1m-2025-p3-4a:
Legislative procedureThree readingsJoint sittingPresidential assent

Under Articles 107–111, a Bill becomes an Act only when both Houses pass it in identical form and the President gives assent. Bills may be government Bills (moved by ministers) or private members' Bills, and by content ordinary, Money, Financial or Constitution Amendment Bills, each with its own route. The detailed stages, known as the three readings, are laid down in the Rules of Procedure of each House.

1. Stages in the originating House

  • First reading: the member moves for leave to introduce the Bill; once introduced it is published in the Gazette. There is no discussion; if the Bill was published earlier with the Speaker's permission, leave is not needed.
  • Second reading, general discussion: the principles of the Bill are debated. The House may take it up at once, refer it to a Select Committee (one House) or a Joint Committee (both Houses), or circulate it for public opinion; many Bills also go to one of the 24 Department-Related Standing Committees.
  • Committee and consideration stages: the committee examines the Bill clause by clause and hears experts; the House then considers each clause and votes on amendments.
  • Third reading: the Bill is passed or rejected as a whole by a simple majority; only verbal or formal amendments are allowed.

2. In the second House

  • Same three readings. The second House may pass the Bill, pass it with amendments and return it, reject it, or keep it pending.
  • Deadlock: if it rejects the Bill, the Houses disagree on amendments, or six months pass without passage, the President may summon a joint sitting (Art 108), presided over by the Speaker, where a simple majority decides.
  • Rare use: only three joint sittings have been held: Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) (1978) and Prevention of Terrorism (2002) Bills.

3. Assent and enforcement

  • Presidential assent (Art 111): the President may assent, withhold assent, or return a non-Money Bill once; if re-passed, assent is obligatory. The absence of a time limit allowed a "pocket veto" of the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
  • Commencement: the Act is published in the Gazette and comes into force on the notified date; some Acts, such as the Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014, await notification for years.
  • Lapse: on dissolution of the Lok Sabha, a Bill pending in it, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses, unless a joint sitting has already been notified.

4. Special categories of Bills

AP angle: The Andhra Pradesh Legislature follows a similar process (Art 196–201), but its Legislative Council can only delay a Bill and there is no joint sitting; the Governor may also reserve a Bill for the President.

The three-reading process ensures deliberation and scrutiny. Wider pre-legislative consultation (2014 policy) and regular referral of Bills to parliamentary committees can further improve the quality of law-making.
free.g1m-2025-p3-4b:
Legislative CouncilArticle 169Rajya SabhaBicameralism

Under Article 169, Parliament may create or abolish a State's Legislative Council if the Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority. Only six States have one: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh. Both the Council and the Rajya Sabha are upper Houses and continuing chambers, but the Rajya Sabha is a federal chamber with near-equal powers, while the Council is a revising chamber with only delaying powers.

1. Existence and composition

  • Status: the Rajya Sabha is a permanent and essential House of Parliament. A Council depends on the Assembly's will, and the law creating or abolishing it is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Art 368. In both, members serve six years and one-third retire every two years.
  • Representation: the Rajya Sabha represents the States, elected by the elected members of State Assemblies by proportional representation (Art 80(4)). A Council has functional representation (Art 171): one-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth each by graduates and teachers, and one-sixth nominated by the Governor from literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service.

2. Legislative and financial powers

  • Ordinary Bills: the Rajya Sabha can reject a Bill, and a deadlock goes to a joint sitting (Art 108). A Council can only delay a Bill passed by the Assembly, for three months and then one month (Art 197); a Bill that originates in the Council and is rejected by the Assembly simply ends.
  • Money Bills: both can only make recommendations within 14 days (Art 109, 198).
  • Constitutional amendments: the Rajya Sabha must pass every amendment Bill by a special majority (Art 368(2)). The Council has no such role; it comes in only as part of the State Legislature when a federal amendment needs ratification by the Legislatures of half the States (proviso to Art 368(2)).

3. Federal, executive and electoral role

  • Federal powers: only the Rajya Sabha can let Parliament legislate on a State subject (Art 249) or create new All India Services (Art 312).
  • Executive control: in both cases ministers are collectively responsible only to the lower House (Art 75(3), 164(2)), but members of both upper Houses may ask questions and become ministers.
  • Elections: elected Rajya Sabha members vote in the President's election and all members in the Vice-President's; Council members vote in neither, nor in Rajya Sabha elections.

AP angle: In 2020, when the Council referred two Bills on decentralisation and the CRDA to a select committee, the Assembly re-passed them and they became law under Art 197; they were repealed in 2021. The episode showed both the Council's power to delay and its inability to block.

The Rajya Sabha is thus a co-equal federal chamber, while the Council is a chamber of second thought, useful for expert review but dependent on the Assembly for its very existence.
free.g1m-2025-p3-5a:
Fundamental RightsArticle 32Judicial reviewWrits

Part III of the Constitution (Art 12–35) guarantees Fundamental Rights, which, unlike the Directive Principles, are justiciable. Rights without remedies are hollow, so the Constitution also provides layered safeguards: courts, writs, independent institutions and limits on emergency powers. That is why Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies, the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

1. Judicial safeguards

  • Judicial review (Art 13): any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is void. The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) protects their core even from constitutional amendments.
  • Right to constitutional remedies (Art 32): a citizen can move the Supreme Court directly; the Court called itself the "protector and guarantor" of rights (Romesh Thappar, 1950), and this right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides.
  • High Courts (Art 226): can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and "for any other purpose", so their writ power is wider.
  • Public Interest Litigation: relaxed locus standi (S.P. Gupta, 1981) and letters treated as petitions brought justice to undertrials (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979) and bonded labourers (Bandhua Mukti Morcha, 1984).
  • Expansive interpretation: Maneka Gandhi (1978) required any law affecting life and liberty to be "fair, just and reasonable"; Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy under Art 21.

2. Institutional safeguards

  • Independent judiciary: security of tenure, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, contempt powers (Art 129, 215) and separation from the executive (Art 50); judicial review is a basic feature (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
  • Rights commissions: National Commissions for SCs, STs and Backward Classes (Art 338, 338A, 338B), and the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993.
  • Free legal aid (Art 39A): the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 provides legal aid and Lok Adalats through NALSA and State authorities.

3. Safeguards during emergencies

  • Non-suspendable rights: after the 44th Amendment (1978), Art 20 and 21 cannot be suspended (Art 359), and Art 19 is suspended only in war or external aggression (Art 358).
  • Correcting past error: ADM Jabalpur (1976), which allowed suspension of habeas corpus, was overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).

4. Enabling laws (Art 35)

Parliament has made laws to give effect to rights, such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (Art 17), the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 (Art 23) and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989.

AP angle: The High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati hears writ petitions under Art 226, and the AP State Legal Services Authority provides free legal aid and holds Lok Adalats.

Courts, laws and institutions thus protect rights together. Speedy justice, legal awareness and stronger commissions will make these rights real for every citizen, in keeping with the rule of law.
free.g1m-2025-p3-5b:
Judicial independence42nd Amendment99th AmendmentBasic structure

The judiciary's powers rest on judicial review and on Articles 32, 136 and 226. Parliament has often used its amending power under Article 368 to reshape these powers, and the Supreme Court has replied with the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973). Two amendments stand out: the 42nd (1976), which curtailed judicial review, and the 99th (2014), which sought to change how judges are appointed.

1. 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: curtailing judicial review

  • Limits on writ and review powers: inserted Art 32A (the Supreme Court could not examine State laws in Art 32 cases), Art 131A (exclusive Supreme Court jurisdiction over the validity of central laws), Art 144A (at least seven judges and a two-thirds majority to invalidate a law) and Art 226A, and narrowed the High Courts' writ jurisdiction.
  • Amendments beyond review: added Art 368(4) and (5), declaring that no amendment could be questioned in any court and that Parliament's amending power was unlimited.
  • Tribunals: inserted Art 323A and 323B, enabling tribunals to take over service, tax and other disputes from High Courts.
  • Impact: the judiciary's role as guardian of rights was weakened during the Emergency. The 43rd (1977) and 44th (1978) Amendments undid most changes; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art 368(4) and (5), holding limited amending power to be a basic feature, and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) brought tribunal decisions under High Court review.
  • Lasting effect: tribunals survive, and Art 39A (free legal aid), added by the same amendment, widened access to justice.

2. 99th Amendment Act, 2014: National Judicial Appointments Commission

  • Context: the collegium system, created by the Second Judges case (1993) and refined in the Third Judges case (1998), was criticised as opaque.
  • What changed: Art 124A–124C set up a six-member NJAC: the Chief Justice of India, the two senior-most judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons; any two members could block a recommendation.
  • Impact: in SCAORA v Union of India (2015), the Fourth Judges case, the Supreme Court struck it down 4:1 as violating judicial independence, a basic feature, and the collegium was restored. The Court asked for a revised Memorandum of Procedure to improve transparency.

3. Combined significance

  • Basic structure as a shield: both attempts failed because judicial review and judicial independence are basic features beyond Parliament's amending power.
  • Institutional dialogue: Parliament amends and the courts review, a balance that keeps both accountable.

AP angle: Art 371D, added for Andhra Pradesh by the 32nd Amendment (1973), allowed the State Government to modify or annul orders of the AP Administrative Tribunal; in P. Sambamurthy (decided December 1986, reported 1987) the Supreme Court struck down clause (5) and its proviso for denying effective judicial review.

Both episodes show that the basic structure doctrine protects judicial independence. Transparent appointments and timely filling of vacancies remain the way to keep the judiciary both independent and accountable.
free.g1m-2025-p3-6a:
Mauryan centralisationGupta decentralisationSamanta systemArthashastra

Mauryan administration (c. 321–185 BCE) is known from Kautilya's Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indica and Ashoka's edicts; Gupta administration (c. 4th–6th century CE) from inscriptions such as Harisena's Prayaga Prashasti, the Damodarpur copper plates and the account of Fa-Hien. The Guptas inherited the Mauryan framework of monarchy and territorial units, but ran a far less centralised and more feudal state.

1. Similarities

  • Monarchy: a hereditary king at the apex, assisted by ministers and a council (Mauryan mantriparishad; Gupta mantrins, the sandhivigrahika for peace and war, and the mahadandanayaka).
  • Territorial hierarchy: both divided the empire into provinces, districts and villages. Mauryan provinces were governed by princes (kumaras) at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri; Gupta provinces (bhuktis) by uparikas and districts (vishayas) by vishayapatis.
  • Village as base unit: the village headman (gramika) managed local affairs with village elders.
  • Revenue: land revenue (bhaga, usually one-sixth of produce) was the main source of income in both.
  • Dharma-based kingship: Ashoka's Dhamma and paternal ideal ("all men are my children") and the Gupta ideal of the king as protector of dharma and varna order.

2. Differences in structure and economy

  • Centralised vs decentralised: the Mauryas ruled through a vast bureaucracy; the Guptas ruled the Ganga valley directly and the rest through feudatories (samantas). Samudragupta's southern policy of capture and release (grahana-moksha-anugraha) shows this indirect control.
  • Officials and land: Mauryan officials were paid in cash (the Arthashastra lists salaries). Gupta land grants (agraharas) to brahmanas carried fiscal and administrative rights, and offices such as kumaramatya often became hereditary.
  • Economic role: Mauryan superintendents (adhyakshas) controlled agriculture on crown land, mines, trade and industry; the Gupta state was far less involved.

3. Differences in local administration, control and justice

  • Local participation: Megasthenes describes six boards of five members each for Pataliputra; Gupta district councils included the chief merchant (nagarashreshthi), chief caravan trader (sarthavaha), chief artisan (prathama-kulika) and chief scribe (prathama-kayastha).
  • Army: the Mauryas kept a huge standing army, managed according to Megasthenes by six boards; the Guptas relied partly on troops supplied by feudatories.
  • Control and justice: an elaborate Mauryan spy system and Dhamma Mahamattas; under the Guptas these were much lighter, and Fa-Hien noted mild punishments, mostly fines.

AP angle: Ashoka's rock edicts at Erragudi (Kurnool) show direct Mauryan presence in Andhra, while Samudragupta defeated and reinstated southern kings such as Mahendragiri of Pishtapura (Pithapuram) and Hastivarman of Vengi, reflecting indirect Gupta control.

Thus the Guptas kept the Mauryan framework but made it decentralised and feudal, a shift that shaped the early medieval Indian state.
free.g1m-2025-p3-6b:
Colonial legacySteel frameDistrict administrationRule-bound bureaucracy

India's administrative system is largely a colonial inheritance. Over nearly two centuries the British built a merit-based civil service, district administration, codified laws and a secretariat system, mainly to collect revenue and maintain order. The Government of India Act 1935 supplied much of the Constitution's administrative framework, and Sardar Patel retained the ICS model as the All India Services, India's "steel frame".

1. Civil services and personnel system

  • Merit-based permanent service: open competition began after the Macaulay Committee (1854); the Lee Commission (1924) led to a Public Service Commission in 1926, forerunner of the UPSC (Art 315). Cornwallis, the "father of civil services in India", had organised the covenanted service.
  • All India Services: the IAS and IPS (Art 312) continue the ICS model of officers recruited by the Union and serving the States, which Patel defended as essential to national unity.
  • Service values: political neutrality, anonymity, permanence and generalist leadership, with generalists heading departments, remain hallmarks of Indian bureaucracy.

2. Structures of administration

  • District administration: the Collector, head of revenue, magistracy and coordination, is still the pivot of field administration.
  • Secretariat system: Canning's portfolio system (1861) evolved into ministries; files, noting, hierarchy and rules of business still guide work.
  • Federal and local structures: the 1935 Act gave the three lists, provincial autonomy, the Governor's office and a Federal Court; Ripon's Resolution (1882) laid the base of local self-government.

3. Laws, police and finance

  • Codified laws: the IPC 1860 and Evidence Act 1872 governed criminal justice until 2024, when the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced them.
  • Police: the Police Act 1861 is still the basis of policing in many States, despite the Supreme Court's reform directions in Prakash Singh (2006).
  • Revenue and audit: land settlements (Permanent, Ryotwari, Mahalwari), the first budget by James Wilson (1860) and the Auditor General (1860), forerunner of the CAG (Art 148).
  • Secrecy: the Official Secrets Act 1923, now balanced by the RTI Act 2005.

AP angle: Thomas Munro, as Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema), developed the ryotwari system, extended across the Madras Presidency in 1820; he died at Pattikonda (Kurnool) in 1827. Sir Arthur Cotton's Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari (1852) reflects the public works tradition.

4. Assessment

These features gave India stability, unity and the rule of law, but also elitism, red tape, secrecy and a "ruler" mindset. Reforms such as Mission Karmayogi (2020), citizen charters and e-governance seek to make the steel frame citizen-centric and responsive.
free.g1m-2025-p3-7a:
NEP 2020Foundational learningMultidisciplinary higher educationViksit Bharat

Education builds human capital and turns India's demographic dividend into growth. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, the first since 1986, aims at universal access from pre-school to secondary level, a 50% Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education by 2035 and public spending on education of 6% of GDP. Most recent reforms in school and higher education flow from it.

1. School education

  • New structure: the 5+3+3+4 design replaces 10+2 and brings early childhood care into formal schooling; new National Curriculum Frameworks for the Foundational Stage (2022) and School Education (2023) guide textbooks.
  • Foundational learning: NIPUN Bharat (2021) aims at foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by Class 3; mother-tongue instruction is encouraged at least till Class 5.
  • School quality: PM SHRI (2022) is upgrading over 14,500 schools as NEP exemplars.
  • Assessment reform: PARAKH is the national assessment centre, and CBSE allows two Class 10 board examinations from 2026, reducing exam stress.
  • Digital learning: the APAAR student ID, DIKSHA and PM e-Vidya extend access.

2. Higher education and research

  • Flexible degrees: four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit, and the Academic Bank of Credits; CUET (2022) for central university admissions.
  • Internationalisation: UGC regulations (2023) allow foreign universities to open campuses in India.
  • Access and finance: PM Vidyalaxmi (2024) offers collateral-free education loans; One Nation One Subscription (2025) gives institutions access to journals.
  • Research: the Anusandhan National Research Foundation Act 2023 funds and coordinates research.
  • Umbrella regulator: the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill 2025, introduced in December 2025 to replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with one umbrella regulator, is pending before a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

3. Budget support

The Union Budget 2025-26 announced 50,000 Atal Tinkering Labs in government schools over five years and an AI Centre of Excellence for education.

AP angle: Talliki Vandanam (2025, replacing Amma Vodi) gives ₹15,000 a year per child (Classes 1–12) through the mother, ₹2,000 of it for school maintenance; the mid-day meal is now Dokka Seethamma Madhyahna Badi Bhojanam.

4. Concerns

  • Learning gaps: ASER surveys show many children lack basic reading and arithmetic skills.
  • Inputs: teacher vacancies, the digital divide and spending below the 6% target.
  • Federal friction: Centre–State differences over language policy and regulation.

Cooperative implementation and a sharp focus on learning outcomes can make education the engine of Viksit Bharat 2047.
free.g1m-2025-p3-7b:
Implementation gapStreet-level bureaucracyLast-mile deliveryOutcome monitoring

The policy–implementation gap is the distance between a policy's stated goals and its actual outcomes. In their classic study "Implementation" (1973), Pressman and Wildavsky showed how a well-funded programme failed as it passed through many agencies and decision points. In India, the gap was captured in the oft-quoted 1985 remark of Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi that only about 15 paise of every rupee reached the intended beneficiary.

1. Design-stage issues

  • Top-down design: policies made centrally without field consultation ignore local diversity; uniform norms and unit costs do not suit hilly, tribal or urban areas alike.
  • Rigid schemes: many Centrally Sponsored Schemes overlap and leave States little flexibility, which is why they were rationalised into core and optional schemes in 2016.
  • No piloting: schemes are scaled up nationwide without testing, so design flaws surface late.

2. Administrative and capacity issues

  • Weak field capacity: vacancies, poorly trained frontline staff and frequent transfers break continuity. Lipsky's idea of street-level bureaucrats shows that frontline staff, through their discretion, often decide what a policy becomes.
  • Silos: departments work in isolation, so convergence of schemes on the same household is rare.
  • Fund flow problems: delayed releases and unspent balances, now partly addressed through SNA-SPARSH.
  • Leakages and corruption: middlemen, ghost beneficiaries and inclusion-exclusion errors, as in the PDS before Aadhaar seeding.

3. Monitoring and participation issues

  • Output, not outcome: counting toilets built or money spent rather than toilets used or learning achieved.
  • Low citizen participation: beneficiaries are unaware of entitlements, and grievance redress is weak.
  • Political and legal hurdles: short-term priorities, litigation and land acquisition delays.
  • Information gaps: policy-makers lack timely field data, so problems surface only after damage is done.

4. Bridging the gap

  • Evidence-based policy: NITI Aayog's Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO) evaluates schemes.
  • Outcome tracking: the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) ranks districts on outcome indicators, and PRAGATI reviews stalled projects.
  • Accountability tools: Direct Benefit Transfer, social audits, citizen charters and capacity building under Mission Karmayogi.

AP angle: The long delays and cost escalation of the Polavaram project show how rehabilitation, funding and coordination problems widen the gap. Village and ward secretariats (2019), Real Time Governance dashboards and WhatsApp governance (Mana Mitra, 2025) aim to close last-mile gaps.

Expert design is necessary but not sufficient: participatory planning, capable field institutions and outcome monitoring turn plans into results at the citizen's doorstep.
free.g1m-2025-p3-8a:
Civil societyAssociational lifeParticipatory democracyAccountability

Civil society is the sphere of voluntary collective action between the family, the state and the market, where citizens associate to pursue shared interests and values. In India it includes NGOs, self-help groups, trade unions, cooperatives, community and faith-based bodies, professional associations and social movements. Alexis de Tocqueville saw such voluntary associations as schools of democracy.

1. Civil society in the Indian context

  • Reform roots: social reform bodies such as the Brahmo Samaj (1828) and Gandhian constructive work laid the foundation of voluntary action.
  • New social movements: Chipko (1973) and the Narmada Bachao Andolan raised issues of ecology and displacement.
  • Rights-based campaigns: the MKSS campaign of the 1990s led to the RTI Act 2005, and the Right to Food campaign shaped the National Food Security Act 2013.
  • Service partners: civil society runs schools, health camps and disaster relief, as during Covid-19.
  • Digital civil society: online petitions, fact-checking groups and citizen-science networks are newer forms.

2. Key features

  • Voluntary and autonomous: independent of the state and the profit motive, so it can criticise both.
  • Plural: reflects India's linguistic, religious and regional diversity.
  • Watchdog and advocacy: PILs, social audits and election watch keep power accountable.
  • Voice of the marginalised: bridges citizens and the state, deepening participatory democracy beyond voting.
  • Deliberation: creates public spaces for debate on policy.
  • Non-partisan: unlike political parties, it does not seek state power.

3. Limitations in a democratic system

  • Funding dependence: the FCRA (Amendment) Act 2020 capped administrative expenses at 20% of foreign contributions and barred their transfer to other organisations.
  • Accountability deficit: weak transparency and internal democracy; some NGOs misuse funds.
  • Urban and elite bias: uneven reach in rural and tribal areas.
  • Fragmentation and politicisation along caste, religious or ideological lines; some groups even promote hatred, the "uncivil" face of society.
  • Trust deficit: adversarial relations with the state reduce cooperation.
  • Dependence on government contracts: NGOs that implement state schemes may lose their independent watchdog voice.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's women self-help group movement, supported by SERP since 2000, and the independent Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (2009) show civil society partnering the state for empowerment and accountability.

A transparent, accountable and autonomous civil society, supported by an enabling framework (National Policy on the Voluntary Sector, 2007), is essential for a deliberative democracy.
free.g1m-2025-p3-8b:
Women's empowermentNGOsSelf-help groupsGender justice

NGOs are non-profit, voluntary bodies outside government. In women's empowerment they pioneered models later adopted by the state: SEWA (1972) for informal women workers, MYRADA's self-help groups that inspired NABARD's SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (1992), and Prajwala (Hyderabad, 1996) against trafficking. Naila Kabeer defines empowerment as expanding women's resources, agency and achievements, and NGOs work at all three levels.

1. Ways to enhance the role of NGOs

  • Economic empowerment: SHG formation, credit linkage, skilling and market access, partnering DAY-NRLM and the Lakhpati Didi initiative.
  • Legal awareness and support: legal literacy on the Domestic Violence Act 2005 and the PoSH Act 2013, and counselling at One Stop Centres under Mission Shakti.
  • Health and education: nutrition (Poshan Abhiyaan), menstrual hygiene and girls' retention in school.
  • Digital and financial literacy: narrowing the gender digital divide and building cyber-safety.
  • Political empowerment: training elected women in panchayats to counter proxy representation, and preparing women for the one-third reservation in legislatures under the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023).
  • Research and advocacy: gender data, audits of gender budgeting and feedback on policy.
  • Reaching the most excluded: Dalit, tribal, disabled and single women, who are often missed by mainstream programmes.

2. Key challenges

  • Funding constraints: dependence on short-term grants; stricter FCRA rules (2020) reduced foreign funding.
  • Patriarchal resistance: opposition from families and communities, and threats to field workers.
  • Credibility gaps: misuse of funds by some NGOs erodes trust; monitoring is weak.
  • Limited capacity and reach: concentration in urban areas, staff turnover and lack of professional skills.
  • Friction with government: delayed payments, bureaucratic procedures and short project-based partnerships.
  • Tokenism: success measured in numbers trained rather than change in women's agency.

3. Way forward

  • Transparent registration on NITI Aayog's NGO-DARPAN portal and regular audits.
  • Stable funding: long-term partnerships and corporate social responsibility funds (Companies Act 2013, Section 135).
  • Outcome-based partnerships that measure change in women's incomes, safety and decision-making.
  • Sustainability: helping SHG federations become self-managed institutions, so that gains outlast project funding.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's SHG movement (DWCRA groups, strengthened by SERP since 2000) and the Stree Nidhi credit cooperative show how community institutions and government together can build one of India's largest women's collectives.

With credibility and stable support, NGOs can be effective allies of the state in achieving SDG 5 on gender equality and turning welfare into genuine empowerment.
free.g1m-2025-p3-9a:
National Commission for WomenNCW Act 1990Statutory bodyWomen's rights

The National Commission for Women (NCW) is a statutory body established under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990, and constituted on 31 January 1992. The need for such a body was highlighted by the Committee on the Status of Women in India in its report "Towards Equality" (1974). The NCW acts as the national watchdog for women's rights, advising the government on policy and acting on complaints.

1. Composition and status

  • Members: a Chairperson committed to the cause of women, five members of ability and standing (at least one each from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes) and a Member-Secretary, all nominated by the Central Government for up to three years.
  • Funding and removal: it is financed by grants from the Central Government, and members can be removed by the Central Government on grounds laid down in the Act.
  • Consultation: the Central Government must consult the Commission on all major policy matters affecting women (Section 16).

2. Main functions (Section 10)

  • Review of safeguards: examines constitutional and legal safeguards for women, reviews laws and recommends amendments to remove gaps and discrimination.
  • Complaints and suo motu action: looks into complaints and takes notice of the deprivation of women's rights and non-implementation of protective laws.
  • Litigation and inspection: funds litigation on issues affecting large numbers of women, and inspects jails, remand homes and other custodial institutions for women.
  • Development role: advises on planning for women's socio-economic development and evaluates progress; undertakes studies and research.

3. Powers and reporting

  • Civil court powers: while investigating, it can summon persons, require documents, receive evidence on affidavit and requisition public records.
  • Reports: its reports are laid before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken, so its findings are publicly debated.
  • Initiatives: Parivarik Mahila Lok Adalats for quick settlement of family disputes, an NRI cell, a 24x7 helpline and online complaint registration.

4. Limitations

  • Recommendatory: it cannot enforce its findings or punish; governments may ignore its advice.
  • Limited autonomy: members are chosen by the Union Government without a selection committee, inviting charges of political appointments; it depends on the Ministry of Women and Child Development for funds.
  • No investigating machinery of its own; it relies on the police.
  • Statutory, not constitutional: unlike the National Commissions for SCs and STs (Art 338, 338A), it lacks constitutional status.
  • Capacity constraints: a heavy complaint load and limited staff; it is criticised for reacting to high-profile cases rather than structural issues.

AP angle: The AP State Commission for Women handles complaints within the State, complementing the NCW in matters such as domestic violence and dowry harassment.

Constitutional status, a transparent selection process, binding force for some recommendations and stronger State Commissions can make the NCW an effective guardian of women's rights.
free.g1m-2025-p3-9b:
Quasi-judicial bodiesTribunalsArticles 323A–323BNatural justice

Quasi-judicial authorities are bodies outside the regular court hierarchy that decide disputes or determine rights by applying law to facts and following natural justice, without being full courts. They offer speedy, expert and inexpensive adjudication in specialised fields such as service matters, taxation, environment and elections. The Constitution creates some of them directly and empowers Parliament and State Legislatures to create others through tribunals.

1. Specific constitutional provisions

  • Art 323A: Parliament may set up administrative tribunals for recruitment and service conditions of public servants, as in the Central Administrative Tribunal under the Administrative Tribunals Act 1985.
  • Art 323B: Parliament and State Legislatures may set up tribunals for taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, elections, rent and other matters. Both articles were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice.
  • Art 262: Parliament provides for adjudication of inter-State river water disputes, e.g. the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunals (Bachawat; Brijesh Kumar), vital for Andhra Pradesh.
  • Art 324 with Art 103 and 192: the Election Commission decides disputes over party recognition and symbols, and its opinion binds the President or Governor on disqualification of legislators.
  • Tenth Schedule: the Speaker or Chairman acts as a tribunal on defection, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).

2. General legislative competence

Under Art 245–246, legislatures can create quasi-judicial bodies on subjects in their lists. Examples include the National Green Tribunal (2010), consumer commissions (Consumer Protection Act 2019), Information Commissions (RTI Act 2005), the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the Competition Commission and electricity regulatory commissions such as the AP Electricity Regulatory Commission (1999).

3. Judicial control

  • Supervision: the Supreme Court (Art 136) and High Courts (Art 226, 227) review their decisions.
  • L. Chandra Kumar (1997): tribunal decisions are subject to High Court review, since judicial review is a basic feature.
  • Independence: the Madras Bar Association cases and the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 addressed appointments, tenure and qualifications of members.

AP angle: Art 371D(3), inserted by the 32nd Amendment (1973), let the President set up an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh's public-employment disputes, and in P. Sambamurthy (decided December 1986, reported 1987) the Supreme Court struck down the State Government's power to modify or annul its orders (clause (5) and its proviso).

4. Significance and concerns

They reduce court backlog and bring expertise, but vacancies, executive control over appointments and post-retirement postings raise questions of independence.

Quasi-judicial bodies are vital for speedy justice; independent selection, adequate staff and judicial oversight will keep them credible guardians of the rule of law.
free.g1m-2025-p3-10a:
Social auditCommunity monitoringGram SabhaAccountability

Social audit is the verification of a public programme by its intended beneficiaries and the community, comparing official records with ground reality and discussing the findings at a public hearing (jan sunwai). Pioneered by the MKSS in Rajasthan in the 1990s, it became mandatory for rural employment works under Section 17 of MGNREGA 2005. It narrows the gap between a scheme's vision on paper and its reality on the ground.

1. How social audit narrows the gap between vision and reality

  • Verifies outcomes: checks whether works exist, wages were paid and beneficiaries are genuine, exposing fake muster rolls and ghost works.
  • Accountability and recovery: officials answer in public; misused funds are recovered and erring staff face action.
  • Empowers citizens: Gram Sabhas (Art 243A) become active participants, and people learn their entitlements, deepening deliberative democracy.
  • Feedback and deterrence: reveals design flaws for correction, and the prospect of public scrutiny discourages corruption.
  • Builds social capital: repeated audits create informed communities and local leaders who go on to monitor other schemes.
  • Wider use: the National Food Security Act 2013 (Section 28) requires periodic social audits of fair price shops and the public distribution system.

2. Andhra Pradesh model

Andhra Pradesh was the first State to institutionalise social audits of rural employment works (2006), later through the independent Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT, 2009), with village resource persons and public hearings. The Mahatma Gandhi NREGA Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011 later required every State to have an independent social audit unit. Meghalaya enacted India's first social audit law in 2017.

3. Impediments to institutionalisation

  • Lack of independence: social audit units often depend on the implementing department for funds and staff, which softens findings.
  • Narrow legal backing: audits are mandatory mainly for rural employment and a few schemes; there is no general law.
  • Weak follow-up: action-taken reports and recoveries lag, so findings lose force.
  • Low participation: poor awareness, elite capture of Gram Sabhas and intimidation of resource persons.
  • Records and staff: delayed access to documents and few trained auditors.
  • Political resistance: local elites and contractors who benefit from leakages resist public hearings.

4. Current position

The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, which replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026, retains mandatory social audits.

An independent, well-funded, statutory system on the Meghalaya and AP models can make social audit a routine tool of good governance and participatory accountability.
free.g1m-2025-p3-10b:
Good governanceRTI Act 2005TransparencyAccountability

Governance is "the manner in which power is exercised in the management of a country's economic and social resources for development" (World Bank, 1992). Good governance is governance that is participatory, consensus-oriented, accountable, transparent, responsive, effective and efficient, equitable and inclusive, and follows the rule of law (UNESCAP's eight features). It shifts the focus from ruling citizens to serving them.

1. The RTI Act 2005

  • Constitutional root: the right to know is part of freedom of speech under Art 19(1)(a) (Raj Narain, 1975).
  • People's movement: the MKSS campaign in Rajasthan and State laws paved the way; the Act, in force from 12 October 2005, replaced the Freedom of Information Act 2002.
  • Judicial backing: in S.P. Gupta (1981) the Supreme Court linked open government to the right to know.
  • Scope: any citizen can seek information held by public authorities, including bodies substantially financed by government.

2. How RTI promotes good governance

  • Transparency: Section 4 requires proactive disclosure of functions, budgets, norms, subsidies and decisions, reducing the need to ask.
  • Accountability: replies within 30 days (48 hours where life or liberty is involved), appeals to Information Commissions, and penalties of up to ₹25,000 on erring officers (Section 20) make officials personally answerable.
  • Anti-corruption: RTI applications have exposed irregularities in ration distribution, rural works and housing allotments, such as the Adarsh Housing Society case in Mumbai.
  • Participation and equity: citizens, including the poor (BPL applicants pay no fee), can track entitlements, ration cards and pensions.
  • Rule of law and responsiveness: officials record reasons and follow rules, knowing decisions can be scrutinised; even the CJI's office is a public authority (CPIO v Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019).

3. Challenges

  • Institutional: vacancies and pendency in Information Commissions, so second appeals can take months or years, and weak Section 4 compliance.
  • Record management: poor record-keeping and low digitisation delay replies, though online filing has improved access.
  • Safety: attacks on RTI activists.
  • Legal changes: the 2019 amendment lets the Centre fix commissioners' tenure and salaries, and the DPDP Act 2023 widened the personal-information exemption in Section 8(1)(j).

AP angle: The Andhra Pradesh Information Commission hears appeals, and Real Time Governance dashboards aid proactive disclosure.

Filling vacancies and building a culture of openness can keep RTI the "master key to good governance", as the 2nd ARC's first report (2006) called it.
free.g1m-2025-p3-11a:
Ethical dilemmaConstitutional moralityPublic interestAccountability

An ethical dilemma arises when a public servant must choose between competing values, each with a moral claim. Personal values, such as family loyalty, religious belief, compassion or political preference, may clash with public duties of impartiality, legality and service to all. A strong ethical foundation, made of internalised values, knowledge of rules and the ability to reason, helps resolve such conflicts without sacrificing accountability.

1. How a strong ethical foundation helps

  • Constitutional morality: as Dr Ambedkar urged, the Constitution, not personal belief, guides public action; the Preamble's values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity are the reference point.
  • Primacy of public interest: the Nolan principles (1995) of selflessness, integrity, objectivity and accountability, and the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, as amended in 2014, require decisions solely in the public interest.
  • Ethical reasoning: Kant's duty ethics, the utilitarian test of the greatest good, Gandhi's talisman (recall the face of the poorest) and the Gita's nishkama karma (duty without attachment) help weigh choices.
  • Emotional intelligence: self-awareness to recognise one's own bias, and empathy to implement firm decisions humanely.
  • Moral courage: a settled conscience lets the officer resist pressure from family, community or superiors.
  • Inner check: officers who have internalised values do not need constant supervision; conscience works where rules and inspections cannot reach.

2. Procedures that preserve accountability

  • Disclose and recuse when a personal interest is involved.
  • Speaking orders: recording reasons makes the decision defensible before courts, auditors and RTI applicants.
  • Consultation: seeking guidance from seniors or a dissent note on file, rather than quietly disobeying.
  • Transparency: keeping records that can withstand scrutiny.

3. Balancing, not suppressing, personal values

Compassion can shape how a decision is carried out, for example clearing encroachments with rehabilitation, and faith can inspire honesty, provided the decision itself follows law and the public interest. An officer who disagrees with a policy on moral grounds may record dissent or seek a transfer, but must not sabotage a lawful decision.

AP example: S.R. Sankaran, an Andhra Pradesh-cadre IAS officer known for his simple life, used his office to champion bonded labourers, Dalits and tribals, showing that personal compassion can be channelled through lawful public action.

A strong ethical foundation does not erase personal values; it aligns them with constitutional duty, so that both conscience and accountability are satisfied.
free.g1m-2025-p3-11b:
Whistleblower protectionMoral couragePublic interest disclosureIntegrity

A whistleblower is a person, often an insider, who exposes corruption, fraud or abuse of power to the authorities or the public. The killings of Satyendra Dubey (NHAI engineer, 2003) and S. Manjunath (Indian Oil officer, 2005) after they exposed wrongdoing showed why such guardians of accountability need protection. Whistleblowing turns one person's conscience into an institutional check on misconduct.

1. Ethical importance

  • Moral courage and conscience: the whistleblower puts the public interest above personal safety and loyalty to colleagues, consistent with Kant's duty to truth and the utilitarian aim of preventing wider harm.
  • Higher loyalty: loyalty is owed to the Constitution and the public, not to a superior's wrongdoing; this upholds the Nolan principles of integrity, openness and honesty.
  • Ending complicity: silence makes honest employees accomplices; disclosure breaks the culture of collusion.
  • Public trust: citizens are assured that wrongdoing will not stay hidden.

2. Institutional importance

  • Early detection: insiders expose fraud that audits and inspections miss, saving public money.
  • Deterrence: the fear of disclosure discourages corruption at every level.
  • Feeding accountability bodies: the CVC, Lokpal, CAG and media act on credible information.
  • Organisational learning: vigil mechanisms required by the Companies Act 2013 (Section 177) and SEBI's listing rules improve corporate governance.
  • Global commitment: the UN Convention against Corruption asks States to protect persons who report corruption.

3. Legal framework and gaps

  • PIDPI Resolution (2004): issued after Dubey's death, it designated the CVC to receive complaints and protect complainants' identity.
  • Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014: provides for confidentiality, protection from victimisation and penalties for false complaints, but has not been operationalised; its 2015 Amendment Bill lapsed in 2019.
  • Gaps: retaliation and harassment, attacks on RTI activists, no anonymous complaints, and weak protection for private-sector employees.

4. Way forward

  • Operationalise the 2014 Act with an independent authority to receive complaints and protect complainants.
  • Safe channels: secure digital platforms that allow protected, even anonymous, disclosures.
  • Wider coverage: extend protection to private-sector and contract employees, and act on complaints within fixed timelines.

AP angle: The AP Lokayukta (Andhra Pradesh Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983) and State vigilance bodies depend on such disclosures to act against corruption.

An organisational culture that rewards ethical courage rather than punishing it is essential to make integrity the norm in public service.
free.g1m-2025-p3-12a:
Peaceful coexistenceToleranceFraternityUnity in diversity

Peaceful coexistence means people of different religions, languages, castes, regions and beliefs living together with mutual respect and without conflict. India, with 22 scheduled languages and followers of all major world religions, depends on shared ethical values rather than uniformity. The Preamble's promise of fraternity and the ideal of unity in diversity express this.

1. Essential values, with examples

  • Tolerance and mutual respect: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII urged respect for all sects, saying that one who honours his own sect by condemning others harms his own.
  • Empathy and compassion: feeling others' suffering, as when neighbours of different faiths shelter each other during riots or floods.
  • Fraternity and dignity: the Preamble promises "fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual"; Ambedkar saw liberty, equality and fraternity as an inseparable trinity.
  • Equal respect for all faiths: Akbar's sulh-i-kul (peace with all); Art 25–30 and the fundamental duty to promote harmony (Art 51A(e)).
  • Justice and fairness: equal treatment and affirmative action reduce resentment between groups (Art 14–17).
  • Non-violence and dialogue: Gandhi's ahimsa; resolving disputes through discussion rather than force.
  • Open-mindedness: the Jain idea of anekantavada, that truth has many aspects; Swami Vivekananda told the Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893) that India accepts all religions as true.

2. Why these values matter

  • Prevent conflict: shared values defuse communal and ethnic tensions before they turn violent.
  • Protect minorities: they secure the dignity of smaller groups, the true test of a democracy.
  • Build social capital: trust across groups supports cooperation, investment and development.
  • Constitutional vision: the framers chose secularism and fraternity partly because the violence of Partition had shown the cost of hatred.
  • Changing society: migration, urbanisation and social media bring diverse people into daily contact, making these values a civic necessity.

3. Role of institutions

  • Family and schools: value education teaches children to respect difference.
  • Media: responsible reporting avoids stereotypes and fake news.
  • Administration: impartial civil servants and district peace committees act quickly during tensions.
  • Law: Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita punishes promoting enmity between groups.

AP angle: Gurajada Apparao's line "Desamante matti kadoi, desamante manushuloi" (a nation is not its soil, a nation is its people) captures this spirit. The Ameen Peer Dargah at Kadapa, visited by people of all faiths, and Vemana's verses against caste discrimination reflect Andhra's composite culture.

Peaceful coexistence is not merely the absence of conflict but active respect for difference, the essence of "unity in diversity" and of a mature democracy.
free.g1m-2025-p3-12b:
Family socialisationConscienceMoral developmentEthical decision-making

The family is the first school of values. Through primary socialisation, children internalise honesty, empathy, respect, responsibility and fairness long before they meet formal rules. These early lessons form the conscience, habits and patterns of reasoning that shape how adults, including public servants, make ethical decisions under pressure.

1. How early value education influences adult decisions

  • Formation of conscience: early values become an inner voice. Gandhi credited his mother Putlibai's religious discipline, and the stories of Shravana and Raja Harishchandra, for his lifelong commitment to truth.
  • Role modelling: Bandura's social learning theory shows that children imitate parents; a parent who refuses a bribe teaches integrity better than any lecture.
  • Moral reasoning: families that explain why rules matter help children move, in Kohlberg's terms, from fear of punishment towards principled reasoning.
  • Habits and character: Aristotle held that virtues become habits through practice; sharing and truthfulness learnt young persist into adulthood.
  • Emotional intelligence: empathy and self-control learnt at home help adults handle conflicts calmly and resist impulsive decisions.
  • Attitudes to equality: families that reject caste and gender discrimination raise fair-minded adults; the reverse breeds prejudice.
  • Sense of duty: children given household responsibilities learn that rights come with duties, the basis of a public-service ethic.

2. Examples

  • Positive: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam wrote that he inherited honesty and self-discipline from his father.
  • Negative: children who see corruption or discrimination normalised at home may rationalise it later as "the way things work".
  • Public service: an officer brought up to value fairness is more likely to refuse an unfair transfer request or a gift, even when no one is watching.

3. Limitations

  • Other influences: school, peers, media and workplace culture can reinforce or dilute family values.
  • Adult reflection: adults can revise inherited values through education, experience and reflection; inherited prejudice can also be unlearnt.
  • Rigid upbringing: values imposed through fear alone may produce conformity rather than conscience.
  • Narrow loyalty: family loyalty can later clash with impartiality, as in nepotism; ethical maturity means going beyond the family's interest.

AP angle: Telugu families traditionally teach children Vemana's verses, the Sumati Satakam and Paravastu Chinnaya Suri's Neeti Chandrika stories, transmitting values of truth, humility and social justice.

Early value education lays the foundation of ethical decision-making; it must be sustained by value-based schooling, as NEP 2020 envisages, and by ethical organisational cultures.
free.g1m-2025-p3-13a:
AttitudePublic service orientationBehaviourTheory of Planned Behaviour

Attitude is a learned, relatively enduring tendency to evaluate a person, object, idea or situation favourably or unfavourably. Gordon Allport (1935) called it "a mental and neural state of readiness, organised through experience", which directs a person's responses. It has cognitive, affective and behavioural components, and in public servants it shapes how power is used towards citizens.

1. Nature and functions of attitude

  • Learned and changeable: attitudes form through family, education, experience and organisational culture, and can be changed through persuasion and training.
  • Three components: a belief (cognitive), a feeling (affective) and a readiness to act (behavioural), for example believing that tribal welfare schemes are underused, feeling concern, and organising enrolment camps.
  • Functions: Daniel Katz described attitudes as serving adjustment (seeking rewards), ego-defence, value expression and knowledge (making sense of the world).

2. How attitude affects the behaviour of public servants

  • Towards citizens: a service attitude makes an officer courteous, accessible and responsive; an elitist attitude produces arrogance and "babu culture".
  • Towards weaker sections: empathy leads to proactive outreach; caste, gender or class prejudice leads to discrimination and exclusion.
  • Towards work: commitment and result orientation encourage innovation; a status-quo attitude causes red tape and delay.
  • Towards rules and ethics: respect for the rule of law prevents corruption; cynicism encourages rule-bending.
  • Towards politics: political neutrality ensures impartial decisions whichever government is in office.
  • Towards change: openness supports reforms such as e-Office and Direct Benefit Transfer; resistance stalls them.
  • Towards colleagues and subordinates: a democratic attitude encourages teamwork and frank feedback; an authoritarian one breeds fear and passivity.

3. Theory and examples

  • Theory: Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour holds that attitudes, social norms and perceived control together shape intentions and actions, so organisational culture also matters.
  • Attitude–behaviour gap: situational pressures such as political interference or fear of vigilance action can stop even well-meaning officers from acting on their attitudes.
  • Examples: Armstrong Pame (Manipur) built a 100-km "People's Road" through community contributions; S.R. Sankaran, an Andhra Pradesh-cadre IAS officer, devoted his career to bonded labourers and Dalits, reflecting a pro-poor attitude.

4. Building the right attitudes

Value frameworks (Nolan principles; the 2nd ARC's 4th Report, Ethics in Governance, 2007), training at LBSNAA and under Mission Karmayogi (2020), role models and citizen feedback can nurture a service orientation.

Attitude is the bridge between values and behaviour; a positive, empathetic and impartial attitude turns a civil servant into a true public servant.
free.g1m-2025-p3-13b:
Tripartite modelCognitive componentAffective componentBehavioural component

The tripartite (ABC) model of attitude (Rosenberg and Hovland, 1960) holds that every attitude has three interrelated components: what we think (cognitive), what we feel (affective) and how we tend to act (behavioural). In public service, all three must point the same way for good intentions to become good governance.

1. Cognitive component

  • Meaning: beliefs, knowledge and thoughts about the attitude object, whether true or false.
  • Example: a District Collector believes, on the basis of NFHS-5 data showing that 23.3% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18, that child marriage harms girls' health and education.
  • Another example: an officer believes that helmets save lives in road accidents.

2. Affective component

  • Meaning: feelings and emotions towards the object, such as liking, sympathy, fear or anger.
  • Example: the Collector feels concern and compassion for girls at risk.
  • Another example: a revenue officer feels empathy for farmers who lost crops in a cyclone.

3. Behavioural (conative) component

  • Meaning: the tendency or readiness to act in a certain way towards the object.
  • Example: the Collector runs awareness drives, tracks school dropouts and stops child marriages with Child Marriage Prohibition Officers and the police.
  • Another example: the revenue officer speeds up crop-loss enumeration and input subsidy.

4. Interrelation and inconsistency

  • Mixed attitudes: an officer knows helmets save lives (cognitive) but feels indifferent (affective), so enforcement stays weak (behavioural).
  • Prejudice: a stereotype that tribal communities are "backward" (cognitive), dislike (affective) and neglect of their grievances (behavioural).
  • Cognitive dissonance: when components conflict, Festinger (1957) showed that people feel discomfort; an officer who values honesty but accepts a gift either rationalises the act or changes behaviour.

AP angle: Officers in the Agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju district who understand and respect tribal culture (cognitive and affective) design more participatory programmes (behavioural).

5. Why the distinction matters in public service

  • Training design: classroom lectures change beliefs, but field visits and village stays during induction training build empathy, and supervised practice builds habits of action.
  • Behaviour-change campaigns: Swachh Bharat combined information on health (cognitive), appeals to dignity and pride (affective) and incentives for building toilets (behavioural).
  • Attitude–behaviour gap: LaPiere's classic 1934 study found that people's stated attitudes did not always predict their actions, so officers must also change situations, not just minds.

Training must target all three components, knowledge, empathy and action, to build a citizen-centric civil service.
free.g1m-2025-p3-14a:
Code of ethicsConflict of interestEthical decision-makingEthics infrastructure

A code of ethics states broad values, such as integrity, impartiality and accountability, that guide public servants, while a code of conduct lays down specific rules of behaviour. A conflict of interest arises when an official's private interests could improperly influence the performance of public duties (OECD). Codes give officials a shared standard to recognise such conflicts and resolve them in favour of the public interest.

1. How a code of ethics helps resolve conflicts of interest

  • Disclosure: declaration of assets and liabilities (All India Services (Conduct) Rules 1968; Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013) and of private interests in a decision brings hidden conflicts into the open.
  • Recusal: officers step aside from matters involving relatives or personal stakes, such as a tender in which a family member has an interest.
  • Gifts and relatives: the CCS (Conduct) Rules 1964 regulate gifts and the employment of family members in firms having official dealings.
  • Post-retirement restrictions: cooling-off periods before commercial employment prevent "revolving doors" between regulators and the regulated.
  • Clear standards: since the 2014 amendment, the AIS (Conduct) Rules list values such as integrity, impartiality and accountability, and require officers to declare private interests and resolve conflicts in favour of the public interest.

2. How it promotes ethical decision-making

  • Guidance in grey areas where rules are silent, giving officials a reference point.
  • Consistency: similar cases are treated alike, reducing arbitrariness and favouritism.
  • Accountability culture: recorded reasons make decisions defensible before courts, auditors and RTI applicants.
  • Institutional support: ethics committees (Rajya Sabha, 1997), vigilance officers and ethics training make the code a living document.
  • Signal of values: a published code tells citizens and new recruits what the organisation stands for.

3. Recommendations and models

  • Nolan Committee (UK, 1995): seven principles of public life: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership.
  • 2nd ARC's 4th Report, Ethics in Governance (2007): recommended codes of ethics for ministers, legislators and civil servants.
  • Judiciary: the Supreme Court's Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997) guides judges' conduct.

4. Limitations

Codes can become box-ticking exercises if vague or unenforced; they need an ethics infrastructure of training, leadership example, protected whistleblowing and independent oversight.

AP angle: The AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964 and the AP Lokayukta apply these standards at the State level.

Codes work only with enforcement and the right culture; training, ethics audits and protected whistleblowing must back them so that ethical choices become institutional habit.
free.g1m-2025-p3-14b:
IntegrityTransparencyAccountabilityEthical leadership

Integrity is consistency between values, words and actions, including incorruptibility; transparency is openness about decisions, reasons and resources; accountability is answerability for actions and acceptance of responsibility for outcomes. Together they form the moral foundation of legitimate leadership: integrity guides the choice, transparency shows it, and accountability answers for it.
