1. Significance in leadership

  • Trust and legitimacy: citizens cooperate with, and comply with decisions of, leaders they trust; trust is the currency of democratic governance.
  • Checks misuse of power: openness and answerability limit arbitrary discretion and corruption.
  • Better decisions: scrutiny forces evidence-based, reasoned choices and exposes errors early.
  • Role modelling: leaders shape organisational culture; the Nolan Committee (1995) lists leadership among the seven principles of public life.
  • Efficiency: honest, open systems reduce leakages and delays, saving public resources.
  • Constitutional mandate: collective responsibility to the legislature (Art 75(3)), audit by the CAG (Art 148) and the RTI Act institutionalise these values.

2. How public leaders can demonstrate these values

  • Declare and recuse: disclose assets and interests, and step aside when conflicted.
  • Reasoned, recorded decisions: speaking orders, minutes, and selection criteria published in advance.
  • Consultation: pre-legislative consultation (2014 policy), public hearings and Gram Sabha participation.
  • Proactive disclosure: Section 4 of the RTI Act, open data dashboards and e-procurement through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM).
  • Merit and fairness in recruitment, transfers and contracts.
  • Owning failures: Lal Bahadur Shastri offered to resign as Railway Minister after the Mahbubnagar rail accident (1956) and resigned after the Ariyalur accident later that year.
  • Feedback: social audits, CPGRAMS and citizen charters.

3. Examples

T.N. Seshan enforced the Model Code of Conduct impartially as Chief Election Commissioner; E. Sreedharan delivered the first phase of the Delhi Metro ahead of schedule.

AP angle: Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari), the first Chief Minister of Andhra State (1953), is remembered for courage, integrity and simplicity in public life.

4. Challenges

Political pressure, a culture of secrecy and fear of vigilance action can make leaders avoid decisions, leading to "policy paralysis". The 2018 amendment to the Prevention of Corruption Act (Section 17A), which requires prior approval before investigating decisions taken in official functions, seeks to protect honest decisions taken in good faith, while critics fear it may shield wrongdoing.

Leaders who practise what they preach turn integrity, transparency and accountability into institutional norms, the essence of good governance.
free.g1m-2025-p3-15a:
CyberstalkingIT Act 2000Cyber offencesBharatiya Nyaya Sanhita

Cyberstalking is the use of the internet, email, social media, messaging apps or other electronic means to repeatedly follow, monitor, harass or threaten a person. It includes tracking someone's online activity or location, sending unwanted messages, creating fake profiles and threatening to publish private content. India's first reported case was Ritu Kohli (Delhi, 2001). With cheap smartphones, women and children are its most common victims.

1. Legal position of cyberstalking

  • No named offence in the IT Act: the Information Technology Act 2000 does not define cyberstalking.
  • Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Section 78 (earlier IPC Section 354D) punishes stalking, including monitoring a woman's use of the internet, email or electronic communication, with up to three years, and five years on repeat conviction.
  • Related provisions: criminal intimidation (BNS Section 351), and IT Act Sections 66E, 67 and 67A where private or sexual images are captured or published.
  • Gap: Section 78 protects women only; male victims rely on intimidation and IT Act provisions.

2. Other offences under the IT Act 2000 (amended 2008)

  • Offences against computer systems: tampering with source code (Section 65), hacking, data theft, virus attacks and denial of service (Section 66 read with Section 43), and cyber terrorism (Section 66F), punishable with up to life imprisonment.
  • Offences against persons: identity theft (66C), cheating by personation such as phishing, fake customer care and "digital arrest" scams (66D), and violation of privacy (66E).
  • Content offences: publishing obscene (67), sexually explicit (67A) and child sexual abuse material (67B).
  • Data offences: breach of confidentiality (72) and unlawful disclosure of personal information in breach of contract (72A); receiving stolen computer resources (66B).
  • Civil remedy: Section 43 also provides compensation for damage to computer systems, decided by adjudicating officers (Section 46).
  • Struck down: Section 66A (offensive messages) was invalidated in Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) for violating free speech.

3. Enforcement framework

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and helpline 1930 coordinate response, while CERT-In (Section 70B) handles cyber security incidents.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh police cyber crime units register and investigate such complaints, including those received through the 1930 helpline.

4. Challenges

Anonymity, cross-border servers, low reporting due to stigma and a shortage of trained investigators weaken enforcement.

Digital literacy, victim-friendly reporting, trained investigators and an updated digital law are needed as frauds like "digital arrest" scams and online harassment grow.
free.g1m-2025-p3-15b:
Goods and Services Tax101st AmendmentGST CouncilCooperative federalism

Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a destination-based indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, with input tax credit at each stage, so that tax falls only on value added. Launched on 1 July 2017, it subsumed 17 Central and State taxes (such as excise duty, service tax and VAT) and 13 cesses, creating "One Nation, One Tax" and a common national market.

1. Constitutional provisions (101st Amendment Act, 2016)

  • Art 246A: Parliament and State Legislatures both have power to tax supplies of goods and services; Parliament alone taxes inter-State supplies.
  • Art 269A: Integrated GST on inter-State supplies and imports is levied by the Union and shared between the Union and the States.
  • Art 279A: the GST Council of the Union Finance Minister (chair) and State Finance Ministers recommends rates, exemptions and model laws; decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes (Centre one-third, States two-thirds).
  • Art 270: CGST and part of IGST are shared with the States through the Finance Commission's divisible pool.
  • Seventh Schedule: the State List's sales-tax entry now covers only petroleum products and alcoholic liquor.
  • Art 366(12A): defines GST, excluding alcoholic liquor for human consumption; petroleum products await the Council's recommendation (Art 279A(5)).
  • Section 18 of the Amendment: compensation to States for five years for loss of revenue.

2. Statutory and administrative framework

  • Laws: the CGST, IGST, UTGST and GST (Compensation to States) Acts 2017, plus each State's SGST Act, such as the Andhra Pradesh GST Act 2017.
  • Technology: GSTN is the IT backbone for returns, e-invoicing and e-way bills; the CBIC and State tax departments administer the tax.
  • Dispute resolution: the GST Appellate Tribunal (Section 109, CGST Act) is the second appellate forum, above departmental appellate authorities.
  • Judicial view: in Union of India v Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, since both Parliament and States have equal power under Art 246A.

3. Recent reform

"GST 2.0", approved at the 56th Council meeting, moved from 22 September 2025 to two main slabs, 5% and 18%, plus 40% on luxury and sin goods, simplifying the earlier four-slab structure.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh received GST compensation until June 2022; its Finance Minister sits on the Council.

4. Concerns

The end of compensation, petroleum outside GST and reduced State fiscal autonomy remain concerns. Stable rates, faster refunds and cooperative federalism through the Council can make GST a truly "Good and Simple Tax".
free.g1m-2025-p4-2a:
Monetary policyFiscal policyInflation targetingResource mobilisation

Monetary policy is run by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934, amended in 2016 for flexible inflation targeting: a six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) aims at CPI inflation of 4% ±2%, a target the Government has retained for April 2026 to March 2031. Fiscal policy is run by the Government through the Budget (Article 112), using taxes, spending and borrowing. Together they mobilise resources for development and keep prices stable.

1. Instruments of monetary policy

  • Policy rates: the repo rate (raised by 25 bps to 5.50% in October 2026), with the Standing Deposit Facility (5.25%) as the floor and the Marginal Standing Facility (5.75%) as the ceiling of the corridor.
  • Reserve ratios: the Cash Reserve Ratio (3%) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (18%) control how much banks can lend.
  • Liquidity tools: open market operations, variable-rate repo and reverse-repo auctions, and forex swaps.
  • Qualitative tools: priority-sector lending norms, margin requirements, moral suasion and forward guidance.

2. Instruments of fiscal policy

  • Taxation: direct taxes and GST, rationalised mainly into 5% and 18% slabs from September 2025.
  • Expenditure: capital spending, subsidies and transfers, which redirect resources to priority sectors.
  • Borrowing and other receipts: market borrowing, small savings and disinvestment finance the Union's fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP (2026-27 BE).

3. Role in resource mobilisation

  • Fiscal: gross tax revenue of about ₹44 lakh crore (2026-27 BE) funds infrastructure and welfare, while borrowing finances capital spending.
  • Monetary: priority-sector norms direct bank credit to farmers and MSMEs, and stable prices encourage financial savings.

4. Role in inflation management: an evaluation

  • Monetary success: 250 bps of repo hikes (May 2022 to February 2023) brought inflation down; the October 2026 hike, with the stance changed to 'calibrated tightening', responds to CPI inflation rising to 4.8% (August 2026).
  • Fiscal and supply-side tools: excise cuts on fuel, export curbs and open-market sale of buffer stocks tackle food and fuel spikes.
  • Limits: monetary policy is weak against supply shocks (monsoon, crude oil), transmission to lending rates is slow, and high fiscal deficits can crowd out private investment.

AP angle: AP sells vegetables at subsidised rates through Rythu Bazaars during price spikes and raises resources through State Development Loans within FRBM limits.

A credible, coordinated policy mix, inflation targeting with fiscal consolidation, keeps prices stable while mobilising resources for growth.
free.g1m-2025-p4-2b:
Public debtInternal debtExternal debtDebt sustainability

Public debt is the total borrowing of the government to bridge the gap between its spending and receipts. The Union borrows under Article 292, while States may borrow only within India (Article 293). The Centre's outstanding liabilities are estimated at 55.6% of GDP in 2026-27 (Union Budget), with a target of 50±1% by March 2031. Whether debt is raised at home or abroad shapes its cost and its risks.

1. Internal and external debt: the difference

  • Legal framework: the Union's borrowing is disciplined by the FRBM Act, 2003; under Article 293(3), a State still indebted to the Centre needs its consent to borrow.
  • Debt management: the RBI acts as banker and debt manager to the Centre and the States, conducting their market borrowings through auctions.

2. Internal debt: advantages and risks

  • No exchange-rate risk: repayment is in rupees, which the government raises through taxes.
  • Money stays at home: interest is paid to domestic savers and institutions, so income circulates within the economy.
  • Deep market: the RBI manages a liquid government-securities market, and SLR norms ensure steady demand.
  • Risks: crowding out of private investment through higher interest rates; a heavy interest burden (about 40% of the Centre's revenue receipts in 2026-27 BE); inflation if the debt is monetised.

3. External debt: advantages and risks

  • Supplements low domestic savings: brings long-term, often concessional finance for infrastructure, along with technology and project expertise.
  • No crowding out of domestic borrowers.
  • Currency risk: rupee depreciation raises the repayment burden in rupee terms.
  • Sudden stops: foreign lenders can withdraw quickly; India's 1991 BoP crisis and Sri Lanka's 2022 default show the danger. Multilateral loans may also carry policy conditions.

4. India's position

  • Mostly rupee-denominated, long-maturity, domestically held public debt makes India relatively safe from external shocks.
  • India's total external debt (public and private) was US$736.3 billion, about 19.1% of GDP, at end-March 2025, and only 18.3% of it was short-term (RBI).
  • The inclusion of Indian government bonds in JP Morgan's emerging-market index (2024) brings foreign money into rupee debt, but also some volatility.

AP angle: AP's outstanding liabilities are about 36% of GSDP (2026-27 BE); since States cannot borrow abroad, its World Bank and ADB loans for Amaravati come through the Centre as externally aided projects.

A prudent mix of long-term domestic borrowing and limited, concessional external debt, on a declining debt-to-GDP path, best suits a developing country like India.
free.g1m-2025-p4-3a:
Human capitalInclusive developmentLearning outcomesOut-of-pocket expenditure

Education and healthcare build human capital, the foundation of inclusive and sustainable development (SDGs 3 and 4). They widen people's capabilities, in Amartya Sen's sense, and let the poor share in growth. Recognising this, NEP 2020 targets public spending on education of 6% of GDP, and the National Health Policy 2017 targets public health spending of 2.5% of GDP.

1. Role in inclusive and sustainable development

  • Productivity and jobs: education and skills raise employability and earnings, breaking the cycle of poverty across generations.
  • Demographic dividend: girls' education lowers fertility and maternal and child mortality, so a young workforce becomes an asset.
  • Financial protection: affordable healthcare prevents catastrophic out-of-pocket spending that pushes families into poverty.
  • Sustainability: educated, healthy citizens adopt cleaner technologies, better nutrition and small families, sustaining growth over the long run.
  • Social equity: schools and health centres in backward areas narrow gaps of caste, gender and region.

2. Current challenges

  • Learning crisis: many children lack foundational literacy and numeracy; dropouts rise at the secondary level, and teacher vacancies persist in poorer States.
  • Higher education: a gross enrolment ratio of only 28.4% (AISHE 2021-22), uneven quality and a digital divide between rural and urban students.
  • Health financing: government health expenditure is only 1.84% of GDP, and out-of-pocket spending is 39.4% of total health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2021-22).
  • Health system and nutrition: shortages of rural doctors and specialists, 35.5% of under-5 children stunted (NFHS-5), and a rising burden of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes.

3. Critical evaluation

  • Access has improved: near-universal enrolment at the elementary level, and insurance cover for the poor and the elderly.
  • Quality lags: learning outcomes remain weak, and PM-JAY covers hospitalisation but not outpatient care and medicines, which make up much of out-of-pocket spending.
  • Spending gap: public spending on both sectors remains below the NEP and NHP targets.
  • Inequity: private schools and hospitals serve those who can pay, while public institutions in poorer States remain understaffed.

AP angle: AP's Budget 2026-27 allocates ₹35,673 crore to education and ₹19,630 crore to health; Talliki Vandanam gives mothers ₹15,000 a year per school-going child, alongside the Dokka Seethamma mid-day meal scheme and Dr NTR Vaidya Seva.

Higher public spending, a focus on learning outcomes and primary care, and convergence of schemes can make education and health true drivers of inclusive and sustainable growth.
free.g1m-2025-p4-3b:
Own tax revenueCentral transfersCommitted expenditureDebt burden

Andhra Pradesh's Budget 2026-27, presented on 14 February 2026, has a gross size of ₹3,32,205 crore (including ₹22,147 crore of debt repayment). It is financed by revenue receipts of ₹2,34,140 crore and borrowings of about ₹97,315 crore (PRS). Since bifurcation in 2014, the State has struggled to raise enough resources for its large welfare and capital needs.

1. Major sources of budgetary resources (2026-27 BE)

  • Own tax revenue, ₹1,25,846 crore (about 54% of revenue receipts): State GST ₹45,078 crore, State excise ₹30,067 crore, sales tax/VAT (mainly on petroleum and liquor) ₹24,126 crore, stamps and registration ₹18,701 crore, and motor vehicle tax.
  • Own non-tax revenue, ₹11,474 crore: mining royalties, forest receipts, and fees and user charges.
  • Share in central taxes, ₹64,362 crore: AP's share of the divisible pool rises to 4.22% under the 16th Finance Commission (from 4.05%).
  • Grants from the Centre, ₹32,458 crore: for centrally sponsored schemes and Finance Commission grants.
  • Borrowings: State Development Loans and other loans, including capex loans from the Centre (₹11,000 crore, outside the borrowing ceiling).

2. Key challenges in mobilising resources

  • Bifurcation legacy: the loss of Hyderabad's revenue base left AP with a largely agrarian economy of low tax buoyancy.
  • Committed expenditure: interest (16% of revenue receipts) and pensions (10%), plus large welfare commitments, leave little room; the revenue deficit was 2.3% of GSDP in 2025-26 (RE).
  • Debt: outstanding liabilities of about 36% of GSDP, guarantees of ₹1.77 lakh crore, and off-budget borrowings (₹1.28 lakh crore as of March 2023, CAG).
  • Tighter federal transfers: GST compensation ended in 2022; the 16th FC discontinued revenue-deficit grants and capped States' fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP.
  • Narrow own base: reliance on liquor and petroleum taxes, which are volatile, while GST rates are set by the GST Council, leaving little rate autonomy.

3. Way forward

  • Widen the tax base: better GST compliance through data analytics, revision of land values for stamp duty, and more non-tax revenue from mining and user charges.
  • Rationalise spending: target subsidies better and bring off-budget borrowings onto the budget.
  • Mobilise outside the budget: monetise idle assets, use PPPs, and seek central and multilateral support for Polavaram and Amaravati.

Restoring fiscal space needs both higher own revenue and disciplined spending, so that AP's borrowings build assets rather than fund consumption.
free.g1m-2025-p4-4a:
Annual Financial StatementRevenue vs capital expenditureCharged expenditureOutcome Budget

A Government Budget is the annual statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March). The Constitution calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement' (Article 112 for the Union, Article 202 for the States). It is the main instrument of fiscal policy, serving Musgrave's three functions of allocation, distribution and stabilisation. The Union Budget 2026-27 provides for a total expenditure of ₹53.47 lakh crore.

1. Structure of the Budget

  • Revenue budget: revenue receipts (tax and non-tax revenue) and revenue expenditure on the day-to-day running of government.
  • Capital budget: capital receipts (borrowings, recovery of loans, disinvestment) and capital expenditure.
  • Parliamentary control: expenditure is presented as Demands for Grants, voted by the Lok Sabha and authorised by the Appropriation Act; taxes are approved through the Finance Act.

2. Types of public expenditure

  • Revenue expenditure: does not create assets or reduce liabilities, e.g., salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants to States and interest (₹14.04 lakh crore, about 26% of total spending in 2026-27 BE).
  • Capital expenditure: creates assets or reduces liabilities, e.g., roads, railways, defence equipment and loans to States (₹12.22 lakh crore in 2026-27 BE).
  • Developmental vs non-developmental: spending on economic and social services (education, health, irrigation) vs administration, defence, pensions and interest.
  • Charged vs voted: charged items such as the President's emoluments, the salaries of Supreme Court judges and debt charges are not put to vote (Article 112(3)); the rest is voted as demands for grants.

3. Classification in the government budget

  • End of Plan/non-Plan: the distinction was abolished from 2017-18, when the Railway Budget was also merged; expenditure is now shown as revenue vs capital.
  • By function: major heads under General, Social and Economic Services, following the standard list of heads of account.
  • By scheme: the Centre's establishment expenditure, Central Sector Schemes (fully Union-funded) and Centrally Sponsored Schemes (cost shared with States), plus Finance Commission transfers.
  • By results: the Outcome Budget and the Gender Budget statement (since 2005-06) link spending to results and to gender equity.

AP angle: AP's Budget 2026-27 (₹3,32,205 crore) raises capital outlay by 47% to ₹48,698 crore, and the State also presents a separate Agriculture Budget.

A rising share of capital and outcome-linked spending improves the quality of public expenditure and makes the Budget a tool for growth, not just an account of receipts and payments.
free.g1m-2025-p4-4b:
Fiscal deficitRevenue deficitPrimary deficitFiscal consolidation

A deficit in government finance is the excess of expenditure over receipts (other than borrowings); it measures how much the government must borrow in a year. Deficits are regulated by the FRBM Act, 2003. The Union Budget 2026-27 targets a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP, down from 4.4% in 2025-26 (RE) and from 9.2% in the COVID-19 year 2020-21.

1. Types of deficits

  • Union position (2026-27 BE): revenue deficit 1.5% of GDP, fiscal deficit 4.3% (about ₹16.96 lakh crore) and primary deficit 0.7%.
  • Effective revenue deficit was introduced from 2011-12, because many grants to States create assets such as roads and school buildings.
  • Monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997; the FRBM Act now bars the RBI from subscribing to primary issues of government securities except in special circumstances.

2. Economic implications

  • Positive: deficits provide counter-cyclical support in downturns, as in 2020-21; capex-led deficits build infrastructure with strong multiplier effects on growth and private investment.
  • Debt and interest burden: interest takes about 40% of the Centre's revenue receipts, crowding out spending on health and education.
  • Crowding out: heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces funds for private investment.
  • Inflation and external balance: a monetised deficit is inflationary, and a high fiscal deficit adds to the CAD ('twin deficits').
  • Quality matters: a revenue deficit is more harmful than a fiscal deficit driven by capital expenditure, because it borrows for consumption.

3. Fiscal consolidation

  • Debt anchor: following the N.K. Singh Committee (2017), debt is now the anchor; the Centre targets 50±1% of GDP by March 2031.
  • Finance Commission path: the 16th Finance Commission advises a Union deficit of 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31 and a cap of 3% of GSDP for States.
  • Better quality: a higher share of capital spending, rationalised subsidies, asset monetisation and buoyant GST and direct taxes.
  • Transparency: the Union now discloses its extra-budgetary borrowings, and the 16th Finance Commission wants States' off-budget borrowings brought onto their budgets.

AP angle: AP's fiscal and revenue deficits are budgeted at 3.8% and 1.1% of GSDP in 2026-27, down from 4.6% and 2.3% in 2025-26 (RE).

Deficits are not bad in themselves; they help when they fund investment on a credible, declining debt path.
free.g1m-2025-p4-5a:
State Finance CommissionArticle 243-IFiscal decentralisationLocal finances

The State Finance Commission (SFC) is a constitutional body under Articles 243-I and 243-Y, added by the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992). The Governor constitutes it every five years to review the finances of panchayats and municipalities and to recommend how resources should be shared with them. In Andhra Pradesh it works under the AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 and the municipal laws, and is the key to fiscal decentralisation within the State.

1. Role of the SFC

  • Sharing State revenue: recommends how State taxes, duties, tolls and fees are divided between the State and local bodies, and among the three tiers of panchayats (gram panchayat, mandal parishad and zilla parishad).
  • Assigning taxes: identifies taxes and fees that local bodies may levy or keep, e.g., property tax and the surcharge on stamp duty (transfer duty) in AP.
  • Grants-in-aid: recommends grants to local bodies from the State's Consolidated Fund.
  • Better finances: suggests measures to raise local bodies' own revenue and improve budgeting and accounts.
  • Link with the Union FC: its report, with an action-taken memorandum, is laid before the State Legislature, and guides the Union Finance Commission under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c).

2. Significance for local finances and fiscal decentralisation

  • Funds to match functions: formula-based, predictable transfers give local bodies the 'funds' to perform the 29 subjects of the Eleventh Schedule and 18 of the Twelfth, matching 'functions' and 'functionaries' (the 3Fs).
  • Less discretion: rule-based devolution reduces dependence on ad hoc grants and political bargaining.
  • Unlocks central funds: the 15th FC made constituting SFCs and acting on their reports a condition for local-body grants. Under the 16th FC (2026-31), AP is to receive ₹16,627 crore (rural) and ₹12,158 crore (urban).
  • Deeper democracy: money in the hands of gram panchayats makes them real 'institutions of self-government' (Article 243G).

3. Issues observed

  • Delays: SFCs are often constituted late, and their reports are acted on slowly or partly; local data on finances are weak.
  • Low own revenue: property tax is under-assessed and user charges are low, so local bodies depend heavily on State transfers.
  • State fiscal stress: AP's high debt and committed spending limit how much it can devolve.

Timely SFCs, faithful implementation and stronger own revenue (for example, GIS-based property tax) will make AP's local bodies true institutions of self-government.
free.g1m-2025-p4-5b:
Fifteenth Finance CommissionVertical devolutionHorizontal criteriaFiscal roadmap

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (Chairman N.K. Singh), constituted under Article 280 in November 2017, gave an interim report for 2020-21 and a final report for 2021-26, tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2021. Working through the COVID-19 shock and the creation of the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, it shaped Union and State budgets for six years.

1. Key recommendations

  • Vertical devolution: 41% of the divisible pool to the States, 1 percentage point below the 14th FC's 42%, to adjust for the new Union Territories.
  • Horizontal distribution: a formula weighted towards equity (income distance) that also rewarded States for lower fertility (demographic performance) and tax effort; AP's share was 4.047%.
  • Grants: revenue-deficit grants of about ₹2.95 lakh crore to 17 States (including AP); local-body grants of ₹4.36 lakh crore; disaster-management funds with a separate window for mitigation; sector-specific and performance-based grants.
  • Fiscal roadmap: States' fiscal deficit at 4% of GSDP (2021-22), 3.5% (2022-23) and 3% (2023-26), plus 0.5% extra linked to power-sector reforms; the Centre's deficit to come down to 4% of GDP by 2025-26.

2. Influence on budgeting at the Centre and in the States

  • Centre: devolution and grants fix the large 'transfers to States' item and limit the Union's fiscal space; the Union set itself a 4.5% deficit target for 2025-26 and reached 4.4% (RE).
  • States: the tax share is a large, untied receipt that States can spend on their own priorities; revenue-deficit grants helped AP bridge its post-bifurcation gap.
  • Borrowing: the deficit path and the power-sector incentive shaped States' capital spending and pushed reforms in DISCOMs.
  • Local bodies: grants were tied to audited accounts, property-tax floor rates and SFC compliance, pushing State budgets towards better local finance.

3. Assessment

  • Strengths: it balanced equity with efficiency, kept transfers predictable during COVID-19, rewarded States that had controlled population growth, and gave local bodies and disaster management larger, assured funds.
  • Concerns: cesses and surcharges stayed outside the divisible pool, and the use of 2011 population worried southern States.
  • Latest position: the 16th Finance Commission (2026-31) retained 41% but discontinued revenue-deficit grants; AP's share rose to 4.217%.

The 15th FC balanced equity, efficiency and fiscal discipline, strengthening cooperative federalism through a period of great uncertainty.
free.g1m-2025-p4-6a:
Gender gapWomen-led developmentFemale labour force participationNari Shakti

Women form nearly half of India's population, yet deep gender gaps persist in work, health, safety and political voice: India ranked 131st of 148 countries in the WEF Global Gender Gap Report 2025. Recognising that growth cannot be inclusive without women, government policy has moved from 'women's development' to 'women-led development'.

1. Challenges faced by women

  • Economic: female labour force participation of only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), concentration in unpaid care and informal work, wage gaps, and low ownership of land and assets.
  • Health and nutrition: 57% of women aged 15-49 are anaemic (NFHS-5), and maternal mortality remains high in some States.
  • Social: son preference (a sex ratio at birth of 929, NFHS-5), child marriage, dowry and domestic violence.
  • Safety: crimes against women and harassment at work and in public spaces limit mobility, education and jobs.
  • Political: women are only about 14% of Lok Sabha members (2024), and proxy representation weakens women's voice in local bodies.

2. Recent programmes for women's empowerment

  • Political voice: the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for women, to take effect after the next delimitation.
  • Safety and support: Mission Shakti (2022) combines 'Sambal' (One Stop Centres, Women Helpline 181, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao) and 'Samarthya' (PM Matru Vandana Yojana, Shakti Sadan and creches).
  • Livelihoods and credit: Lakhpati Didi aims at 3 crore SHG women earning over ₹1 lakh a year; Namo Drone Didi gives drones to SHGs; Stand-Up India and Mudra provide loans to women entrepreneurs.
  • Reducing drudgery and building assets: PM Ujjwala (LPG), the Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water) and PMAY houses registered in women's names.
  • Work: the Labour Codes (in force from November 2025) guarantee equal remuneration and allow night-shift work for women with consent and safeguards.

3. Evaluation

  • Gains: the SHG movement under DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women) has built women's financial agency; Ujjwala and tap water have reduced drudgery; Jan Dhan accounts brought many women into banking.
  • Gaps: women's reservation awaits delimitation; care infrastructure, safe transport and skilling remain weak, so participation in paid work is still low.
  • Approach: many schemes still treat women as beneficiaries rather than decision-makers; gender budgeting and gender-disaggregated data can sharpen targeting.

AP angle: Stree Shakti free APSRTC bus travel for women (from August 2025), Talliki Vandanam for mothers, Deepam-2 free LPG refills and the pioneering DWCRA/SHG movement give AP a strong base for women's economic empowerment.

Women-led development needs safe workplaces, care infrastructure and skills, so that women's work is counted, valued and rewarded.
free.g1m-2025-p4-6b:
Inclusive growthEquality of opportunitySocial protectionRegional equity

Inclusive growth is growth that is broad-based across sectors, regions and social groups, creates productive jobs and gives everyone equality of opportunity and access to basic services. The 11th Five Year Plan (2007-12) made 'faster and more inclusive growth' its central aim, and the goal of Viksit Bharat@2047 carries it forward. Unlike mere GDP growth, it asks who benefits from growth and who is left out.

1. Meaning in the Indian context

  • Gains: NITI Aayog estimates that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23 (headcount 29.17% to 11.28%); the World Bank estimates that extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011-12) to 5.3% (2022-23).
  • Gaps: about 46% of workers are still in agriculture (PLFS 2023-24); most jobs are informal, women's participation is low, and regional and rural–urban disparities and concentration of income and wealth persist.
  • Dimensions: inclusion means productive jobs, capabilities (health and education), access (finance, markets, infrastructure), protection (social security) and voice (participation in decisions).

2. Key strategies and instruments

  • Employment-intensive growth: MSMEs, labour-intensive manufacturing, PLI schemes and the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (2025) to create jobs for a young workforce.
  • Human capital: NEP 2020, Ayushman Bharat, POSHAN 2.0 and PMKVY skilling build the capabilities people need to benefit from growth.
  • Financial inclusion and DBT: the JAM trinity, PMJDY, Mudra and UPI bring the poor into the formal system and deliver benefits directly.
  • Social protection: free foodgrains for over 80 crore people (PMGKAY), pensions, e-Shram and the Code on Social Security for gig and unorganised workers.
  • Rural and regional equity: DAY-NRLM SHGs, PM-KISAN and the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (125 days of wage work from July 2026, replacing MGNREGA); the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Blocks (2023) programmes; progressive taxes and the Finance Commission's income-distance criterion.

3. Ensuring that benefits reach all

  • Structural transformation: moving workers from farms to higher-productivity jobs in manufacturing and services is the most durable path to inclusion.
  • Last-mile delivery: DBT, doorstep services and a unified social registry reduce leakages and exclusion errors.
  • Gender lens: gender budgeting, creches, safe transport and skilling to raise women's participation in paid work.
  • Local institutions: empowered panchayats, municipalities and SHGs give the poor a voice in planning and monitoring.
  • Sustainability: climate-resilient farming and green jobs protect the poor, who are hit first by climate shocks.

AP angle: AP's P4 (Public–Private–People Partnership) initiative, launched in 2025 under the Swarna Andhra@2047 vision, aims at zero poverty by linking well-off 'Margadarshis' with poor 'Bangaru Kutumbam' families.

Growth becomes truly inclusive when jobs, skills and social security reach the last person, in line with the goal of Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2025-p4-7a:
Poverty alleviationWage employmentSelf-employmentRural and urban poverty

India's anti-poverty strategy has moved from 'trickle-down' growth to direct wage-employment, self-employment, food-security and social-security programmes, now delivered largely through Direct Benefit Transfer. The World Bank estimates that extreme poverty (at its new US$3-a-day line) fell from 27.1% in 2011-12 to 5.3% in 2022-23, though vulnerability, informality and urban deprivation remain serious concerns.

1. Major programmes

  • Wage employment: MGNREGA (2005) guaranteed 100 days of work on demand; since 1 July 2026 it has been replaced by the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (125 days; Centre–State funding of 60:40).
  • Self-employment and livelihoods: IRDP (1978) gave way to SGSY (1999) and then DAY-NRLM (2011), which organises about 10 crore women in SHGs; PMEGP (2008) and Mudra (2015) fund micro-enterprises.
  • Skilling: DDU-GKY for rural youth and PMKVY link the poor to wage jobs.
  • Urban: DAY-NULM (2013), PM SVANidhi for street vendors (2020) and PMAY-Urban 2.0.
  • Food and housing security: the NFSA, 2013 and PMGKAY (free grains for over 80 crore people), and PMAY-Gramin.

2. Effectiveness against rural poverty

  • Safety net: MGNREGA cushioned rural households during droughts and the COVID-19 lockdown, raised rural wages and created water and land assets.
  • Women's gains: women did over half of MGNREGA person-days, and NRLM SHGs improved women's incomes and access to credit.
  • Outcome: at the World Bank's older US$2.15 line, rural extreme poverty fell from 18.4% to 2.8% between 2011-12 and 2022-23.

3. Effectiveness against urban poverty

  • Outcome: urban extreme poverty fell from 10.7% to 1.1% over the same period (same line).
  • Formal credit: PM SVANidhi brought street vendors into formal credit and digital payments.
  • Gaps: informal jobs, slums, high rents and the lack of an urban employment guarantee leave many urban poor vulnerable.

4. Limitations

  • Delivery problems: delayed and low wages, fake job cards and poor quality of assets.
  • Exclusion: authentication failures and missing documents keep some of the poorest out.
  • Weak graduation: skill–job mismatch and small, low-productivity enterprises mean many families stay just above the poverty line and slip back after shocks such as illness or crop failure.

AP angle: AP's Velugu/Indira Kranthi Patham (2000) SHG model inspired NRLM; NTR Bharosa pensions (₹27,719 crore, 2026-27 BE) and the P4 zero-poverty initiative (2025) target the poorest families.

Convergence of schemes, non-farm skills, urban livelihood support and outcome monitoring can end extreme poverty and reduce vulnerability.
free.g1m-2025-p4-7b:
Social welfareDirective PrinciplesTargetingInclusive growth

Social welfare schemes are State interventions, rooted in the Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39, 41, 46 and 47), that protect vulnerable groups — the poor, women, children, SCs, STs, the elderly and persons with disabilities — and help them share in growth. By providing a floor of food, health, housing and income security, they convert economic growth into inclusive growth.

1. Significance

  • Safety net: protection against illness, drought, job loss and old age, which otherwise push families into debt and poverty.
  • Human capital: food, health care and schooling raise the future productivity of poor children.
  • Empowerment: assets and services in women's names, and targeted support for SCs, STs and other weaker sections, reduce social inequality.
  • Demand support: transfers raise consumption and rural demand, helping to stabilise the economy in downturns.

2. Major schemes: objectives and features

  • Common design features: most schemes now use Aadhaar-based identification, DBT into bank accounts and online dashboards, and many register assets in women's names.

3. Effectiveness in reaching the vulnerable and reducing inequality

  • Positive: NITI Aayog's multidimensional poverty headcount fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23); the World Bank puts India's consumption Gini at 25.5 (2022-23); DBT through JAM has cut leakages and duplicate beneficiaries.
  • Exclusion errors: migrants, people without documents and those facing authentication failures miss out.
  • Inclusion errors and quality: ineligible people get benefits, while the quality of services in public hospitals and schools varies widely.
  • Limits: rising fiscal cost, and income inequality that is higher than consumption inequality, show that transfers alone cannot close gaps.

4. Improving reach and impact

  • Unified social registry: a dynamic, family-based database can reduce both exclusion and inclusion errors.
  • Portability: One Nation One Ration Card shows how benefits can follow migrant workers; health and welfare benefits need the same portability.
  • Graduation: linking transfers with skilling, SHG credit and jobs helps families move out of dependence.
  • Social audits: Gram Sabha audits and grievance redress keep schemes accountable to the people they serve.

AP angle: NTR Bharosa pensions (₹4,000 a month for the elderly; ₹27,719 crore in 2026-27 BE) are delivered at the doorstep by village and ward secretariats; Annadata Sukhibhava gives farmers ₹20,000 a year, including PM-KISAN.

Well-targeted, portable and outcome-audited welfare can make growth inclusive while keeping the welfare system fiscally sustainable.
free.g1m-2025-p4-8a:
Financial inclusionJAM trinityRangarajan CommitteeDigital payments

The Rangarajan Committee (2008) defined financial inclusion as ensuring access to financial services, and timely and adequate credit, for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable cost. It covers savings, credit, insurance, pensions and payments. The RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose to 67.0 in March 2025 from 64.2 a year earlier, showing steady progress.

1. Role in inclusive growth

  • Savings and credit: mobilises household savings and channels credit to farmers, MSMEs and women, reducing dependence on moneylenders.
  • Risk protection: insurance and pensions protect poor households against illness, death and old age.
  • Efficient welfare: Direct Benefit Transfer into bank accounts cuts leakages and delays.
  • Formalisation: digital payments bring small businesses into the formal economy and build credit histories for future loans.
  • Women's empowerment: accounts, insurance and SHG credit in women's names increase their control over income and their say in household decisions.

2. Key initiatives

  • PMJDY (2014): over 55 crore basic accounts, a majority held by women; with Aadhaar and mobile phones it forms the JAM trinity.
  • Jan Suraksha schemes (2015): low-cost life cover (PMJJBY), accident cover (PMSBY) and the Atal Pension Yojana.
  • Credit: PM Mudra Yojana (2015), Stand-Up India (2016) and PM SVANidhi (2020).
  • New institutions: payments banks and small finance banks, and the India Post Payments Bank (2018) using the postal network.
  • Digital public infrastructure: UPI (2016), Aadhaar-enabled payments and Account Aggregators, with the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2019-24 and financial literacy centres.

3. Impact: an evaluation

  • Access: account ownership rose from 53% (2014) to 78% (2021) (World Bank Global Findex), and women's access improved sharply.
  • Payments: DBT and UPI made India a world leader in real-time digital payments.
  • Usage gaps: many accounts are dormant; credit and insurance penetration remain low, especially for small farmers and informal workers; women use accounts less than men.
  • New risks: rising digital fraud and continuing dependence on moneylenders in rural areas show that the 'underbanked' still need attention.

AP angle: AP leads in SHG–bank linkage through its DWCRA network, and Stree Nidhi (2011) provides quick credit to SHG women.

The next phase must move from 'access' to 'usage and credit', backed by financial literacy, affordable insurance and strong consumer protection against digital fraud.
free.g1m-2025-p4-8b:
Sustainable agricultureSoil healthNatural farmingClimate resilience

Sustainable agriculture is farming that meets present food and livelihood needs without degrading soil, water and biodiversity for future generations: it must be economically viable, ecologically sound and socially just. The Green Revolution raised output but left falling water tables, degraded soils and heavy chemical use in many regions. India institutionalised the shift through the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (2014-15) under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008).

1. Key objectives

  • Food and income security: stable yields and higher farm incomes through lower costs and better prices.
  • Resource conservation: protect soil health, groundwater and biodiversity, including pollinators and local seed varieties.
  • Climate resilience: adapt to droughts, floods and heat, and cut emissions such as methane from flooded paddy and nitrous oxide from fertilisers.
  • Lower input dependence: reduce the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides and their health effects.
  • Equity: reach small and marginal farmers, who hold 86% of holdings (Agriculture Census 2015-16).

2. Common practices in India

  • Diversification: shifting from water-guzzling paddy and sugarcane to millets, pulses and oilseeds in water-stressed areas.
  • Integrated farming systems: combining crops, livestock and fish recycles nutrients and spreads risk.
  • Rainwater harvesting and watersheds: farm ponds, check dams and watershed development recharge groundwater in rain-fed areas, which make up about half of the net sown area.
  • On-farm bio-inputs: compost, vermicompost and other farm-made preparations used in natural farming cut cash costs and improve soil organic matter.

3. Challenges

  • Transition costs: yields may dip in the first years of organic or natural farming, and certification and premium markets are limited.
  • Distorted incentives: subsidised urea and free power encourage overuse of fertiliser and groundwater.
  • Weak extension: knowledge-intensive practices need trained field staff and farmer-to-farmer learning.
  • Market linkages: without certification, aggregation and price premiums, farmers have little reason to give up familiar input-intensive methods.

AP angle: AP Community-managed Natural Farming (APCNF, 2016), run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, promotes chemical-free farming and pre-monsoon dry sowing and won the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity in 2024; AP was also an early leader in drip irrigation through the AP Micro Irrigation Project (2003).

Scaling up these practices through FPOs, extension and fair prices can raise incomes while protecting natural resources, in line with SDG 2 and SDG 13.
free.g1m-2025-p4-9a:
APMC ActPrice discoveryMinimum Support Pricee-NAM

Agricultural marketing in India is regulated by State Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts, enacted mostly in the 1960s and 1970s to protect farmers from exploitation by traders and moneylenders. 'Markets and fairs' is a State subject (Entry 28, State List); Andhra Pradesh's law is the AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966. With MSP and procurement, the APMC system forms the backbone of India's agricultural price policy.

1. Role in price policy and market regulation

  • Regulated markets: notified market areas and yards ensure open auctions, correct weighing and prompt payment, replacing distress sales in villages.
  • Licensing and fees: traders and commission agents are licensed, and market fees pay for yards, roads and storage.
  • Price discovery: competitive bidding in mandis reveals prices, and mandi data on arrivals and prices guide policy.
  • Fair practices: APMC rules fix commission charges and payment deadlines and provide for settling disputes between farmers and traders.
  • MSP and procurement: mandis are the main channel through which the FCI and State agencies buy at the Minimum Support Price, recommended by the CACP for 22 crops.

2. Issues observed by policymakers

Committees such as the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) and the Ashok Dalwai Committee on doubling farmers' income, and the Model Acts, highlighted:

  • Monopoly: farmers had to sell in notified mandis; licensing barriers and trader cartels limited competition.
  • High costs: market fees, cesses and commissions exceed 8% in some States.
  • Too few markets: about 7,000 regulated markets, each serving far more than the 80 sq km suggested by the National Commission on Farmers.
  • Poor infrastructure: inadequate storage, grading and cold chains, and delayed payments, which force farmers into distress sales at harvest.
  • Limited MSP reach: the Shanta Kumar Committee found that only about 6% of farmers sold to procurement agencies.
  • Fragmented markets: State-wise rules and fees hinder 'One Nation, One Market'.
  • Capture by intermediaries: market committees are often dominated by traders and commission agents rather than farmers, defeating the purpose of the Act.

3. Reforms undertaken

  • Wider choice for farmers: Model Acts allow private markets and direct purchase, while e-NAM links mandis online for transparent bidding across markets.

AP angle: AP's Rythu Bazaars (1999) let farmers sell directly to consumers without middlemen, and several of the State's market yards trade on e-NAM.

Reforms built on Centre–State consensus, with more mandis, e-NAM integration and FPO-led marketing, can give farmers fair and stable prices.
free.g1m-2025-p4-9b:
Agricultural creditProductivityAgricultural marketingFarmer Producer Organisations

Agriculture employs about 46% of India's workforce (PLFS 2023-24) but contributes only around 18% of GVA, reflecting low productivity. Finance, production and marketing are linked pillars of agricultural development: credit buys inputs, production creates a surplus, and markets turn that surplus into income that can be reinvested. A weakness in any one breaks the chain, so reforms must address all three together.

1. Significance

  • Finance: timely, cheap credit funds seeds, fertiliser, irrigation and machinery, and frees farmers from moneylenders.
  • Production: ensures food and nutrition security, supplies raw material to agro-industries and earns export income.
  • Marketing: fair prices, value addition and fewer post-harvest losses raise incomes and give farmers the right signals on what to grow.
  • Interdependence: without remunerative markets, loans cannot be repaid; without credit, farmers cannot adopt new seeds and technology, so the three must improve together.

2. Challenges

  • Finance: 86% of holdings are small and marginal; tenant farmers lack land records and collateral; 50.2% of agricultural households were indebted (NSO SAS 2019), with AP the highest at 93.2%; credit is skewed to short-term crop loans rather than investment.
  • Production: low yields, fragmented holdings, about half the net sown area still rain-fed, soil degradation and climate shocks.
  • Marketing: too few mandis, many intermediaries, poor storage and cold chains, and volatile prices for perishables such as tomato and onion.
  • Risk: delayed insurance claims, and a regional skew in farm credit towards a few States, leave many farmers exposed to a single bad season.

3. Opportunities and measures

  • Digital agriculture: the Digital Agriculture Mission (AgriStack) with farmer IDs and digital crop surveys can enable quicker, collateral-light credit and better-targeted insurance.
  • Collectives: FPOs give small farmers scale in buying inputs, accessing credit, storing produce and bargaining with buyers and processors.
  • Technology: drones, precision farming and climate-resilient seeds can raise yields while cutting costs.
  • Allied activities: dairy, fisheries and poultry give steadier incomes, and Kisan Credit Cards now extend to animal husbandry and fisheries.

AP angle: the AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019 helps tenant farmers get crop loans, and Rythu Seva Kendras (formerly Rythu Bharosa Kendras) provide village-level inputs, advice and procurement.

Integrating credit, technology and markets through FPOs and digital platforms can make Indian agriculture productive, remunerative and sustainable.
free.g1m-2025-p4-10a:
Blue economyAquaculturePMMSYSeafood exports

India is the world's second-largest fish producer (about 8% of global output), with a record production of about 198 lakh tonnes in 2024-25 (Department of Fisheries). The sector supports about 3 crore fishers and fish farmers, supplies affordable animal protein and is a leading agricultural export. It is rightly called a 'sunrise sector' of the blue economy.

1. Key drivers of growth

  • Resources: a coastline of about 11,099 km (re-measured), an Exclusive Economic Zone of 2.02 million sq km, and vast rivers, reservoirs, tanks and brackish waters.
  • Aquaculture boom: inland fisheries now provide about three-fourths of production; shrimp farming in coastal ponds has expanded rapidly.
  • Export demand: record seafood exports of ₹62,408 crore in 2024-25 (MPEDA), led by frozen shrimp for the US, China, the EU and South-East Asia.
  • Rising domestic demand: higher incomes and urbanisation raise demand for affordable protein.
  • Technology and institutions: hatcheries, cage culture, recirculating aquaculture, cold chains and fishing harbours; a separate Department of Fisheries (2019) and Kisan Credit Cards for fishers.

2. Schemes of the Department of Fisheries

  • PMMSY is the flagship: it funds fishing harbours and landing centres, cold chains and markets, brood banks and hatcheries, and insurance and welfare for fishers.
  • Infrastructure finance: FIDF provides concessional loans to States and cooperatives for harbours and processing.
  • Formalisation: the PM Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana registers fishers and enterprises on a digital platform to link them to credit and insurance.
  • Others: group accident insurance, seaweed and ornamental fisheries, and transponders on vessels for safety at sea.

3. Challenges

  • Disease and quality: shrimp diseases and antibiotic residues cause losses and export rejections.
  • Overfishing: bottom trawling and juvenile catch threaten marine stocks.
  • Market risk: heavy dependence on a few export markets, as US tariffs in 2025 showed.
  • Post-harvest losses from weak cold chains, and low incomes of traditional fishers.

AP angle: AP is India's largest fish producer (over a quarter of national output) and the hub of shrimp aquaculture in the Godavari–Krishna deltas; marine products formed 18% of AP's exports in 2025-26. The State supports fisher families during the annual fishing ban and is building new fishing harbours.

Disease control, traceability, market diversification and sustainable marine fishing can sustain this 'sunrise sector' and raise fishers' incomes.
free.g1m-2025-p4-11a:
IndustrialisationStructural transformationLinkagesIndustrial policy

The industrial sector (manufacturing, mining, electricity and construction) accounts for roughly a quarter of India's GVA and workforce; manufacturing alone is about 17% of GVA. Development economists such as Lewis and Kaldor treat industrialisation as the engine of structural transformation: it moves workers from low-productivity farming to higher-productivity jobs and raises incomes across the economy.

1. Income generation

  • Productivity and value addition: output per worker is far higher than in agriculture, with strong backward and forward linkages (steel, auto components, automobiles).
  • Exports and foreign exchange: engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and electronics; smartphone exports were about US$24 billion in 2024-25.
  • Tax base: GST and corporate tax from industry fund development spending.
  • Multiplier effects: factory investment creates demand for transport, banking, trade and other services.

2. Employment

  • Absorbing surplus labour: industry draws workers out of disguised unemployment in agriculture.
  • Labour-intensive sectors: textiles, leather, food processing and construction employ large numbers; MSMEs employ over 11 crore people (NSS 73rd round).
  • Formal jobs: organised industry offers regular wages and social security, though most industrial jobs are still informal.

3. Modernisation of the economy

  • Technology and skills spread from factories to suppliers and workers; industry drives urbanisation and infrastructure.
  • Modern agriculture depends on industrial inputs such as tractors, fertilisers and pumps.
  • Strategic autonomy: self-reliance in defence, energy and electronics.

4. Policy references

  • Planned era: the 1948 and 1956 resolutions and the Mahalanobis model put the public sector at the 'commanding heights', building steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur, while licensing and the MRTP Act controlled private industry.
  • Liberalisation (1991): the New Industrial Policy abolished licensing for most industries, removed MRTP restrictions on expansion, opened the door to FDI and began disinvestment.
  • Recent push: Make in India, PLI schemes, PM Gati Shakti, the National Manufacturing Mission and the Labour Codes aim to raise manufacturing's share and create jobs at scale.

AP angle: the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (RINL; ₹11,440 crore revival package, 2025), the Sri City industrial hub, Kia Motors at Anantapur and the pharma cluster at Parawada (Visakhapatnam) show industry's role in the State.

Concerns: manufacturing's share has stagnated (premature deindustrialisation), growth is increasingly capital-intensive, and jobs are concentrated in small, informal units.

Labour-intensive, export-oriented and green manufacturing, backed by skills and infrastructure, is essential for Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2025-p4-11b:
Startup IndiaEntrepreneurshipFund of FundsInnovation ecosystem

Startup India, launched on 16 January 2016 with a 19-point Action Plan and anchored in DPIIT, aims to build an ecosystem for innovation and entrepreneurship, so that young Indians become job creators rather than job seekers. A startup recognised by DPIIT gets easier rules, funding and tax benefits. India is now the world's third-largest startup ecosystem.

1. Major features of the programme

  • Easier compliance: DPIIT-recognised startups can self-certify compliance with several labour and environmental laws.
  • Funding: the Fund of Funds for Startups (₹10,000 crore through SIDBI, plus a new ₹10,000 crore fund announced in Budget 2025-26), the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (2021) and the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (2022).
  • Tax: an income-tax holiday for 3 out of 10 years under Section 80-IAC; the 'angel tax' was abolished in 2024.
  • IPR support: fast-tracked patent examination and an 80% rebate on patent fees.
  • Ease of doing business: relaxed public-procurement norms, quick exit under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the Startup India Hub, the States' Startup Ranking and Atal Innovation Mission incubators (2016).

2. Contribution to industrial and economic growth

  • Scale: over 2.2 lakh DPIIT-recognised startups (a record 55,200 recognised in 2025-26), creating over 23 lakh direct jobs (DPIIT, April 2026); nearly half come from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
  • Unicorns and new sectors: over 100 unicorns, with leadership in fintech built on UPI, and growth in SaaS, edtech, healthtech, space and drones.
  • Innovation for industry: startups supply EV, electronics, agritech and logistics solutions to established firms.
  • Inclusion: more women entrepreneurs and wider regional spread of enterprise.
  • Global reach: Indian SaaS and fintech firms sell to customers abroad, adding to services exports.

3. Limitations

  • Funding winter: venture funding slowed after 2022, and many startups shut down.
  • Concentration: activity clusters in Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Mumbai.
  • Few hard-tech firms: most startups are in consumer services rather than manufacturing and R&D-intensive fields.
  • Governance lapses: a few high-profile failures exposed weak corporate governance and inflated valuations.

AP angle: AP's Innovation and Startup Policy (2024-29) is building the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub at Amaravati with regional spokes to spread entrepreneurship across districts.

Deeper risk capital, deep-tech support and university–industry links can make startups a key engine of Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2025-p4-12b:
Industrial sectorDIPP/DPIITEase of Doing BusinessMake in India

The industrial sector drives structural transformation by shifting workers from low-productivity agriculture to higher-productivity jobs; manufacturing contributes about 17% of India's GVA. The Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion (DIPP), set up in 1995 under the then Ministry of Industry and now under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, was renamed the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) in January 2019, when internal trade (retail trade and traders' welfare) was added to its mandate.

1. Role of the industrial sector

  • Growth: higher value addition and strong linkages with agriculture and services raise national income and exports.
  • Employment: industry absorbs surplus farm labour; MSMEs are the second-largest employer after agriculture.
  • Modernisation: industry spreads technology, drives urbanisation and infrastructure, and builds self-reliance in defence and energy.
  • Revenue: a broad tax base (GST, corporate tax) funds public investment.

2. DPIIT as policy-maker and promoter

  • Policy: formulates industrial policy and FDI policy, and promotes investment through Make in India (2014) and Invest India.
  • Manufacturing push: coordinates PLI schemes, public-procurement preference for local goods (2017 order) and quality control orders.
  • Investor outreach: Invest India, the national investment promotion agency set up under the department, guides domestic and foreign investors.
  • Infrastructure: develops industrial corridors through the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation and leads PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy.

3. DPIIT as facilitator and regulator

  • Ease of Doing Business: Business Reforms Action Plan rankings of States, the National Single Window System (2021) and decriminalisation of minor offences under the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023.
  • Startups: runs Startup India (2016), including recognition, the Fund of Funds and the Seed Fund.
  • Intellectual property: the National IPR Policy (2016); administers patents, designs, trade marks and copyright.
  • Data: its Office of the Economic Adviser compiles the Wholesale Price Index and the Index of Eight Core Industries, used in policy-making.
  • Internal trade: since 2019, the welfare of traders and the growth of retail trade.

AP angle: AP's strong BRAP rankings and the Orvakal and Kopparthy industrial nodes show DPIIT–State cooperation in attracting investment.

DPIIT's shift from licensing control to facilitation mirrors India's journey from the 1956 policy to post-1991 liberalisation; its success now depends on State-level reforms, since land, power and many approvals lie with the States.
free.g1m-2025-p4-13a:
Transport infrastructureLogistics costModal shiftPM Gati Shakti

Transport infrastructure is the lifeline of the economy, linking producers, markets and people. India has the world's second-largest road network and fourth-largest railway network, and rising public capital spending has rapidly expanded highways, railways, ports and airports over the last decade. Yet high logistics costs, a road-heavy freight mix and weak last-mile links still limit India's competitiveness.

1. Current state

  • Roads: national highways expanded to about 1.46 lakh km (2024) under Bharatmala, with new access-controlled expressways; PMGSY links villages to markets.
  • Railways: near-complete electrification of the broad-gauge network; the Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor is complete; Vande Bharat trains and the Kavach safety system modernise services.
  • Ports and waterways: capacity and turnaround time improved under Sagarmala; 111 National Waterways were declared in 2016.
  • Aviation: operational airports grew from 74 in 2014 to over 150, helped by the UDAN regional connectivity scheme (2016).
  • Logistics: India ranked 38th in the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index 2023.

2. Contribution to economic development

  • Lower costs, wider markets: faster movement of goods integrates the national market and makes Indian products competitive.
  • Growth sectors: manufacturing, exports, tourism and farm produce all depend on cheap and reliable transport; quicker transport cuts post-harvest losses.
  • Jobs and multiplier: public capex in roads and railways has a high multiplier and creates construction jobs.
  • Regional balance: roads, rail and air links integrate the North-East, hill areas and remote tribal regions.

3. Key challenges

  • Modal imbalance: heavy dependence on roads; railways carry only about 27% of freight.
  • Road safety: about 1.7 lakh road deaths a year.
  • Execution: land acquisition, cost and time overruns, and slow PPP financing.
  • Gaps: weak last-mile rural links, urban congestion, poor maintenance and rising emissions.

4. Policy measures

  • Integrated planning: PM Gati Shakti (2021) and the National Logistics Policy (2022).
  • Modal shift: the National Rail Plan targets a 45% rail share in freight by 2030; multimodal logistics parks, coastal shipping and inland waterways.
  • Finance: asset monetisation, the Hybrid Annuity Model and InvITs, with sustained public capex (₹12.2 lakh crore in 2026-27).
  • Safety: better road engineering, enforcement under the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019, and trauma care.

AP angle: AP's coastline of about 1,053 km, Visakhapatnam port, new ports at Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam and Mulapeta, and the Bhogapuram airport can make the State a gateway to South-East Asia.

Integrated, safe and green multimodal transport is key to lower logistics costs and to Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2025-p4-13b:
Solar energyPanchamritEnergy securityStorage and grid

With about 300 sunny days a year and a solar potential of about 748 GWp (NISE), solar power is the backbone of India's renewable-energy strategy and of its COP26 'Panchamrit' pledges: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070. Solar serves three goals together: energy security, climate action and affordable, decentralised access to power.

1. Significance

  • Energy security: cuts dependence on imported coal, oil and gas, and shields the economy from price shocks.
  • Climate: decarbonises power in line with the updated NDC (2022), which targets about 50% of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030.
  • Cheapest new power: record-low tariffs below ₹2.5 per unit make solar cheaper than new coal plants.
  • Decentralised access: rooftop systems, solar pumps for farmers and mini-grids reach remote areas and create green jobs.
  • Industrial opportunity: domestic manufacturing of modules and cells can make India a supplier to the world.

2. Major initiatives

  • National Solar Mission (2010): its target was raised in 2015 to 100 GW by 2022.
  • Solar Parks scheme (2014-15) and PM-KUSUM (2019) for solar pumps and solarisation of farm feeders.
  • PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024): rooftop solar for 1 crore households, with up to 300 free units a month.
  • Domestic manufacturing: PLI for high-efficiency modules and the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM).
  • Grid and storage: Green Energy Corridors and viability gap funding for battery storage; the International Solar Alliance (2015), launched with France.

3. Achievements

  • Capacity: solar capacity crossed 100 GW in January 2025 and reached about 162 GW by June 2026 (MNRE).
  • NDC goal met early: non-fossil sources exceeded 50% of installed power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of the target.

4. Challenges and responses

  • Storage gap: solar generation peaks at midday while demand peaks in the evening, so storage decides how far solar can grow.
  • Supply chain: module assembly has grown fast, but upstream polysilicon, wafers and cells still depend on imports.

AP angle: AP hosts the Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park (1,000 MW), the Ananthapuramu solar parks and the Pinnapuram pumped-storage project, under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy (2024).

Storage, grid expansion and a domestic supply chain can make solar the foundation of India's energy transition.
