The Smart Cities Mission (SCM), launched on 25 June 2015 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, aimed to develop 100 cities, chosen through a challenge (2016-18), with core infrastructure, a clean environment and a decent quality of life through 'smart solutions'. It was India's first attempt at competitive, technology-driven urban renewal.

1. Objectives and design

  • Area-based development: retrofitting, redevelopment or greenfield development of a chosen part of each city as a model for the rest.
  • Pan-city solutions: ICT-based services such as intelligent traffic management, e-governance and smart water and power metering.
  • Institutional model: implementation through city-level Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) set up as companies.
  • Funding: central assistance of ₹48,000 crore (about ₹100 crore per city per year for five years), matched by States and urban local bodies; convergence with AMRUT, PMAY and Swachh Bharat.

2. Implementation progress

  • Projects: about 8,000 projects worth about ₹1.64 lakh crore were taken up; over 90% were completed by the mission's extended end-date of 31 March 2025 (MoHUA).
  • Timeline: the original five-year schedule was extended several times, reflecting slow early implementation.

3. Key achievements

  • Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) in all 100 cities, used for traffic, policing, disaster response and COVID-19 management.
  • Visible infrastructure: smart roads, water SCADA systems, rooftop solar, revived public spaces and heritage areas.
  • New capacity: cities gained experience in data-driven planning and project management.
  • Mobility and safety: smart traffic signals, CCTV networks and public bicycle sharing in several cities improved urban mobility and policing.

4. Major challenges

  • 'Islands of excellence': area-based development covered only a small part of each city.
  • Governance: SPVs bypassed elected municipal bodies, diluting the spirit of the 74th Amendment.
  • Finance and capacity: weak PPP interest, low own revenue and limited technical capacity of urban local bodies.
  • Scope: flooding, affordable housing and public transport, which matter most to ordinary citizens, were largely outside the mission.

AP angle: AP's four smart cities, Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Tirupati and Amaravati, gained ICCC-based civic services and urban-renewal projects.

The mission modernised urban management but did not transform whole cities; integrating ICCCs into municipal governance and using the Urban Challenge Fund (₹1 lakh crore, Budget 2025-26) for citizen-centred, climate-resilient planning should guide the next phase.
free.g1m-2025-p4-15a:
Sixteenth Finance CommissionDivisible poolContribution to GDPFiscal federalism

The Sixteenth Finance Commission (Chairman Arvind Panagariya), constituted under Article 280 on 31 December 2023, covers 2026-27 to 2030-31. Its report was tabled on 1 February 2026, and the Union accepted its devolution recommendations. As the latest Finance Commission, it sets the rules for sharing central taxes, about ₹15.26 lakh crore in 2026-27, and shapes Union–State fiscal relations for five years.

1. Resource allocation and revenue sharing

  • Vertical devolution: the States' share of the divisible pool is retained at 41%.
  • Horizontal criteria: income distance 42.5%, population (2011) 17.5%, demographic performance 10%, area 10%, forest and ecology 10%, and a new 'contribution to GDP' criterion (10%) in place of tax effort. AP's share rises from 4.047% to 4.217%.
  • Grants: about ₹9.47 lakh crore, mainly ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies and ₹1.56 lakh crore for disaster management; revenue-deficit grants are discontinued.
  • Fiscal discipline: the Union's deficit to come down to 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31; States capped at 3% of GSDP; off-budget borrowings to be brought onto budgets.
  • Cesses and surcharges: the Commission noted that they shrink the divisible pool and suggested folding them into regular taxes over time.

2. Significance for Union–State fiscal relations

  • Predictability: formula-based transfers for five years reduce discretion and bargaining.
  • Efficiency: the GDP criterion rewards States that contribute more to national output, addressing the concerns of southern and western States.
  • Equity: income distance remains the largest criterion, so poorer States still receive more.
  • Decentralisation: larger local-body grants strengthen the third tier of government.
  • Transparency: bringing off-budget borrowings onto budgets gives a truer picture of State debt and builds trust between the Union and the States.

3. Concerns

  • Fiscally stressed States: ending revenue-deficit grants hurts States such as AP, Kerala and Punjab.
  • Shrinking pool: cesses and surcharges remain outside the divisible pool for now.
  • Capex squeeze: tight borrowing caps may limit States' capital spending.
  • Balance of criteria: a GDP-based criterion tends to favour richer States, so the balance between rewarding performance and supporting need will remain under debate.

AP angle: AP gains a higher tax share and local-body grants of ₹16,627 crore (rural) and ₹12,158 crore (urban), but loses revenue-deficit grants.

Cooperative fiscal federalism must balance national fiscal discipline with the States' development needs.
free.g1m-2025-p4-15b:
Public-Private PartnershipRisk allocationKelkar CommitteeHybrid Annuity Model

A Public-Private Partnership (PPP) is a long-term contract under which a private partner finances, builds and/or operates public infrastructure, sharing risks and rewards with the government. After a boom in the 2000s, especially in roads, power, ports and airports, India's PPP model ran into stalled projects and bank NPAs, prompting the Kelkar Committee (2015) on revisiting and revitalising the PPP model to recommend restructuring.

1. Flaws in the existing model

  • Poor risk allocation: private partners bore land, traffic and clearance risks they could not control, as in BOT-toll road projects.
  • Aggressive bidding: bids based on optimistic traffic forecasts were followed by demands for renegotiation.
  • Rigid contracts: there was no framework for renegotiation, and dispute resolution was slow.
  • Delays: land acquisition and clearances held up projects, causing cost overruns.
  • Financing mismatch: long-gestation projects funded by short-tenure bank loans fed the twin balance-sheet problem.
  • Weak institutions: few independent regulators, poor project preparation and officials' fear of vigilance action.

2. Key points for restructuring

  • Balanced risk sharing: the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016), Toll-Operate-Transfer, InvITs and asset monetisation (National Monetisation Pipeline, 2021; a ₹10 lakh crore plan for 2025-30).
  • Kelkar Committee reforms: a renegotiation framework, an Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal, independent sector regulators, a '3P India' institution, protection for honest decisions (the Prevention of Corruption Act was amended in 2018) and avoiding the Swiss Challenge method.
  • Long-term finance: NaBFID (2021), deeper bond markets and Viability Gap Funding.
  • Better preparation: land and clearances before bidding, standard concession agreements, and three-year PPP project pipelines by ministries (Budget 2025-26).
  • Service focus: transparent tariffs and payments linked to service quality rather than only to construction.

3. Lessons from recent practice

  • Risk sharing works: the Hybrid Annuity Model revived highway PPPs by sharing risks, though it adds to the government's long-term annuity commitments.
  • New sectors: PPPs are spreading to hospitals, urban water and waste, where user charges are low and contracts must focus on service quality.
  • Fiscal transparency: contingent liabilities from guarantees and annuities should be disclosed in budgets so that PPPs do not hide public debt.

AP angle: AP's Infrastructure Development Enabling Act, 2001 was among India's first PPP laws; Krishnapatnam and Gangavaram ports and the Bhogapuram airport are PPP projects.

A fair, flexible and transparent PPP framework can crowd in private capital for Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2025-p5-2a:
Raman effectInelastic scatteringNobel Prize 1930Raman spectroscopy

When light passes through a transparent substance, a tiny part of it is scattered with a changed wavelength. This inelastic scattering of light, discovered by C.V. Raman and his co-worker K.S. Krishnan at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), Calcutta, and confirmed on 28 February 1928, is the Raman effect. It won Raman the Nobel Prize in Physics, 1930, Asia's first science Nobel, and 28 February is observed as National Science Day.

1. The discovery

  • A question at sea (1921): on his return voyage from Europe, Raman doubted the accepted view that the sea is blue only because it reflects the sky, and argued that water molecules themselves scatter light.
  • Patient experiments: at IACS he and his students studied light scattering in many liquids, gases and solids. Using sunlight passed through colour filters, and later a mercury lamp and a spectrograph, they found faint new lines in the scattered light that were absent in the incident light.
  • Announcement: the result appeared in the journal Nature in 1928 as "A New Type of Secondary Radiation". Landsberg and Mandelstam in Moscow saw a similar effect in quartz the same year, but Raman's clear demonstration and explanation won the credit.

2. The physics

  • Most scattered light keeps its frequency; this elastic Rayleigh scattering explains the blue sky.
  • A very small fraction exchanges energy with the vibrations of molecules and comes out shifted: lower in frequency (Stokes lines) or higher (anti-Stokes lines).
  • The shift equals the molecule's vibrational energy, so every substance has a unique "fingerprint". The effect also supported the photon (quantum) nature of light.

3. Impact on the global scientific community

  • A new tool: Raman spectroscopy became a standard method to identify molecules and study chemical bonds and crystals; after lasers arrived in the 1960s it became fast, sensitive and portable.
  • Wide applications: quality control of medicines, forensic and airport screening of drugs and explosives, gem and art authentication, cancer diagnosis, research on graphene and semiconductors, and Raman amplifiers in optical-fibre networks. NASA's Perseverance rover carries Raman instruments to look for signs of past life on Mars.
  • Recognition for Asian science: the first science Nobel for an Asian showed that world-class research could be done in a colonial country with modest, largely home-made equipment. The American Chemical Society named the discovery an International Historic Chemical Landmark in 1998.

4. Legacy in India

Raman became the first Indian Director of IISc (1933), founded the Indian Academy of Sciences (1934) and the Raman Research Institute (1948) in Bengaluru, and trained a generation of physicists. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1954.

The Raman effect turned a simple observation into a universal molecular fingerprint; its story still inspires India's push for curiosity-driven research and scientific temper.
free.g1m-2025-p5-3a:
E-governanceNeGPDigital IndiaCitizen engagement

E-governance is the use of ICT to deliver services and exchange information between government and citizens (G2C), businesses (G2B), employees (G2E) and other governments (G2G). Its goal, in the words of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2008), is SMART governance: simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent. India has moved from computerising back offices to a population-scale digital public infrastructure (DPI).

1. Evolution in four phases

  • Computerisation (1970s–1990s): the National Informatics Centre (1976) computerised ministries and district offices; the Railways' computerised reservation (1986) showed what IT could do for citizens.
  • State experiments (late 1990s): AP's CARD land registration and eSeva centres, and Karnataka's Bhoomi land records, offered single-window, kiosk-based services.
  • Planned scale-up (2006): the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) launched Mission Mode Projects (passports, income tax, MCA21, e-Courts) with State Wide Area Networks, State Data Centres and Common Services Centres.
  • Digital India and DPI (2015 onwards): Digital India (1 July 2015) and e-Kranti made services mobile-first and paperless, built on Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker.

2. Key initiatives

  • Identity and payments: Aadhaar (over 145 crore numbers), Direct Benefit Transfer through the JAM trinity, and UPI (about 242 billion transactions in 2025-26).
  • Documents and services: DigiLocker (72 crore+ users), UMANG (about 2,575 services, July 2026), Passport Seva and e-Courts.
  • Business and procurement: the GST Network, MCA21 and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM).
  • Health and welfare: CoWIN (220 crore+ vaccine doses), eSanjeevani telemedicine and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.

3. Transformation of public service delivery

  • Speed and convenience: certificates, passports, tax refunds and bill payments now take minutes or days instead of weeks, anytime and anywhere.
  • Less leakage and corruption: DBT pays money straight into bank accounts, removing ghost beneficiaries and middlemen; GeM makes public purchases transparent.
  • Last-mile reach: CSCs and, in AP, about 15,000 village and ward secretariats bring services to the doorstep.
  • Data-driven administration: dashboards and AP's RTGS command centre track schemes, assets and grievances in real time.

4. Enhanced citizen engagement

  • Voice and feedback: MyGov (2014) invites ideas on policies and CPGRAMS tracks grievances online; apps collect citizens' ratings.
  • Conversational governance: AP's Mana Mitra (30 January 2025) offered 1,126 services on WhatsApp by July 2026.
  • Transparency: online RTI, open data and social audits let citizens watch how government works.

Gaps: the digital divide (only about half of women used a mobile phone of their own, NFHS-5), authentication failures, cyber fraud, privacy risks and language barriers.

E-governance has turned the citizen from a petitioner into a participant; assisted access, Indian-language interfaces, DPDP safeguards and quick grievance redress can make it truly inclusive.
free.g1m-2025-p5-3b:
CybercrimeFinancial fraudDigital arrestIT Act 2000

Cybercrime is any unlawful act in which a computer, mobile phone or network is either the target (hacking, ransomware, data theft) or the tool (fraud, stalking, child sexual abuse material). In India it is dealt with mainly under the IT Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It is growing fast: NCRB's Crime in India 2024 report recorded 1,01,928 cyber crime cases, up 17.9% over 2023, about 73% of them with fraud as the motive.

1. Categories

  • Against individuals: stalking, harassment, sextortion and identity theft.
  • Against property and money: online fraud, hacking of accounts, crypto and investment scams.
  • Against organisations: ransomware, data breaches and insider theft.
  • Against the State: cyber terrorism, espionage and attacks on critical infrastructure.

2. Major types prevalent in India today

  • Financial fraud dominates: UPI and card frauds, fake KYC updates and predatory loan apps target new and elderly users; stolen money moves through rented "mule" bank accounts.
  • "Digital arrest": fraudsters in fake uniforms keep victims on video calls for hours and extort their savings; in December 2025 the Supreme Court asked the CBI to investigate such scams across India.
  • Attacks on institutions: ransomware hit AIIMS Delhi (2022) and power utilities in AP and Telangana, exposing the risk to critical infrastructure.
  • Crimes against women and children: cyber stalking, morphing, deepfake pornography and sextortion are rising with social media and generative AI.

3. Why it is growing

Rapid digital adoption (over 111 crore internet subscribers, TRAI, June 2026) with low digital literacy, cheap SIMs and mule accounts, cross-border gangs, anonymity through VPNs and crypto, under-reporting and low conviction rates.

4. Response

  • Law: the IT Act (Sections 43, 66 to 66F, 67, 67B), the BNS, which brings large cyber-fraud syndicates under organised crime, and the DPDP Act, 2023 for data protection.
  • Institutions: the Home Ministry's I4C runs helpline 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in, whose fraud-reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026; CERT-In requires incidents to be reported within 6 hours; Sanchar Saathi blocks lost phones and fake SIMs.
  • AP angle: the State's 2026-27 budget provides for a cybercrime police station in every district.

Cybercrime is now organised and transnational; digital literacy, quick reporting, bank–telecom coordination and trained cyber police are the best defence for a digitally secure India.
free.g1m-2025-p5-4a:
National Policy on IT 2012Global IT hubE-literacyDigital empowerment

The National Policy on Information Technology (NPIT), 2012, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2012, aimed "to strengthen and enhance India's position as the Global IT hub and to use IT and cyber space as an engine for rapid, inclusive and substantial growth in the national economy". It shifted the focus from IT as an export industry to IT as a tool of inclusive development that reaches every household.

1. Key objectives

  • Industry growth: raise IT-ITeS revenue from US$100 billion to US$300 billion, and exports from US$69 billion to US$200 billion, by 2020, and win global market share in emerging technologies.
  • Skills and literacy: create 10 million additional skilled ICT workers and make at least one person in every household e-literate.
  • E-governance: mandatory delivery of, and affordable access to, all public services in electronic mode, with transparency, accountability and decentralisation.
  • Inclusion: use ICT in education, health, rural development and financial services; develop language technologies for all Indian languages; make content accessible to differently-abled people.
  • Security and openness: a secure, legally compliant cyberspace, and open standards and open-source technologies.

2. Key features (strategies)

  • Competitive ecosystem: spread the IT industry to Tier-II and Tier-III cities and give fiscal benefits to SMEs and start-ups that adopt IT.
  • Innovation and R&D: cloud computing, mobile value-added services, location-based services, localisation and social media.
  • ICT for productivity: IT adoption in key economic and strategic sectors to raise competitiveness.
  • New services: internet- and mobile-driven services, e-governance delivery and GIS-based services.
  • Cyber security: a framework for a secure cyberspace, followed by the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013.

3. Towards a digitally empowered society

  • Digital literacy: the one-e-literate-person-per-household goal led to rural programmes such as PMGDISHA (2017), aimed at 6 crore rural households.
  • Services as a right: the e-delivery goal became Digital India's "governance and services on demand", seen in UMANG, DigiLocker and DBT.
  • Language and access: the Indian-language goal lives on in Bhashini (2022).
  • Trust: cyber-security institutions and later the DPDP Act, 2023 protect users.

4. Assessment

  • Gains: internet subscribers rose from about 25 crore (March 2014) to over 111 crore (June 2026), and India's digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker) has become a global model.
  • Gaps: the industry targets were met years late; the digital divide, skill mismatch and cyber fraud remain; hardware was left to a separate electronics policy.

AP angle: AP's IT & GCC Policy 4.0 (December 2024), AP Fibernet and Mana Mitra apply the same idea of IT-led inclusive growth at the State level.

NPIT 2012 was the bridge between the e-governance plan of 2006 and Digital India (2015); its people-centred goals of e-literacy and online services remain the core of a digitally empowered society.
free.g1m-2025-p5-4b:
DRDOSelf-relianceDefence technologySpin-off technologies

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) was formed on 1 January 1958 by merging the Army's Technical Development Establishments and the Directorate of Technical Development and Production with the Defence Science Organisation. It works under the Department of Defence R&D, Ministry of Defence, through about 41 laboratories and 5 Young Scientist Laboratories, with a budget of about ₹29,100 crore (2026-27). It is the backbone of India's quest for self-reliance (Aatmanirbharta) in defence.

1. Vision and mission

  • Vision: "Empowering the nation with state-of-the-art indigenous Defence and Security technologies and systems."
  • Mission (design): design and develop state-of-the-art sensors, weapon systems, platforms and allied equipment for the land, air, sea, space and cyber domains.
  • Mission (production): facilitate production and induction of systems developed through its R&D ecosystem, and provide technological solutions that raise the combat effectiveness of the Services.
  • Mission (capacity): strengthen defence R&D in Indian industry, S&T institutions and academia, and build test facilities, design certification and skilled manpower.

2. Contribution to national security

  • Strategic deterrence: the IGMDP (1983), led by Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, overcame technology denial and built the missile backbone of India's nuclear deterrent.
  • Combat edge: the DRDO-developed Akash air-defence system was among the indigenous systems credited in Operation Sindoor (2025).

3. Role in national development

  • Industrial base and jobs: Development-cum-Production Partners, transfer of technology and the Technology Development Fund for MSMEs and start-ups spread capability. Defence production reached a record ₹1.78 lakh crore and exports a record ₹38,424 crore in 2025-26; DRDO-designed BrahMos (Philippines) and Akash (Armenia) are among the systems exported.
  • Import substitution: indigenous systems save foreign exchange and guard against supply cut-offs in war.
  • Civilian spin-offs: bio-digester toilets used by Indian Railways; during COVID-19, oxygen plants based on fighter-aircraft oxygen technology and the anti-COVID drug 2-DG.
  • Human capital: DRDO trains scientists and funds research in IITs and universities, building a high-technology workforce.
  • Internal security and disasters: bomb-disposal and NBC-protection equipment, body armour, avalanche forecasting and high-altitude farming serve the police and civilians.

AP angle: DRDO's NSTL (Visakhapatnam) develops underwater weapons; the National Open Air Range, Kurnool, hosted the laser-weapon test of April 2025; and the foundation stone of a missile test range at Nagayalanka (Krishna district, about ₹1,460 crore) was laid in May 2025.

Challenges: delays (Tejas, the Kaveri engine), cost overruns, continued import of engines and chips, and, until recently, weak partnership with private industry.

DRDO has turned technology denial into self-reliance; focusing on frontier research while industry takes over production can make it a true engine of national development.

Remote sensing means collecting information about the Earth from a distance by recording the radiation reflected or emitted by its surface. India's Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme began with IRS-1A on 17 March 1988, after the experimental Bhaskara satellites (1979 and 1981). It has grown into one of the world's largest civilian Earth observation constellations, whose data is received and distributed by ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad.

1. How remote sensing works

2. The IRS programme and its role

  • Data backbone: NRSC supplies the data, and ISRO's Bhuvan geoportal (2009) offers free maps and thematic layers to departments, researchers and citizens.
  • Planning tool: natural-resource census maps, wasteland and land-degradation atlases (29.7% of India's land degraded in 2018-19) and urban master plans use IRS data.
  • Disaster management: flood, cyclone-damage and drought maps; ISRO is a member of the International Charter "Space and Major Disasters".
  • Commerce and security: NSIL sells data abroad, and high-resolution imagery supports mapping for security.

3. Natural resource management

  • Agriculture and soil: FASAL crop forecasts by the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre, drought assessment, support to crop insurance, and soil and land-degradation maps.
  • Water: groundwater-prospect maps guide well-drilling; reservoirs, snow, glaciers and glacial lakes are monitored; watershed and command-area plans use IRS data.
  • Forests and biodiversity: the Forest Survey of India maps forest cover from IRS imagery for its biennial ISFR (forest cover 21.76% in 2023); forest-fire alerts and mangrove and wetland maps follow.
  • Oceans and fisheries: INCOIS issues Potential Fishing Zone advisories from satellite ocean-colour and sea-temperature data, cutting fuel use and search time for fishers.
  • Minerals and land: geological and lineament maps aid mineral exploration, and land-use change and illegal mining can be tracked.

AP angle: the AP Space Applications Centre maps land use, crops and water bodies for the State, and NRSC's flood maps of the Godavari and Krishna deltas guide relief.

Limits: cloud cover (partly overcome by radar), costly very-high-resolution data, and the loss of EOS-09 and DRDO's EOS-N1 in the PSLV failures of May 2025 and January 2026.

The IRS programme turned space technology into a tool of development; combining its data with AI, State GIS systems and village planning can make resource management more precise and timely.
free.g1m-2025-p5-6a:
Induced seismicityRock burstStress redistributionMine safety regulation

Most earthquakes are natural, caused by sudden slip along faults as tectonic stress builds up. Human activity can also trigger them; this is called induced seismicity. Mining removes huge volumes of rock, ore, water or gas and changes the balance of stresses in the crust, producing tremors that range from small rock bursts in deep mines to rare shocks strong enough to damage buildings. The deep Kolar Gold Fields (Karnataka) were notorious for rock bursts.

1. How mining causes earthquakes

  • Stress redistribution: in deep hard-rock mines the weight of the overlying rock concentrates around the openings; brittle rock then fails violently as a rock burst, as in Kolar and South Africa's deep gold mines.
  • Fault reactivation: mining close to an already stressed fault can make it slip, releasing more energy than the mining alone could.
  • Collapse and subsidence: old, unfilled underground workings, as in the Jharia and Raniganj coalfields, cave in, causing tremors and land subsidence.
  • Fluid changes: dewatering mines or extracting oil and gas alters pore pressure; gas extraction at Groningen (Netherlands) caused hundreds of quakes and led to the field's closure.
  • Blasting: opencast blasting shakes the ground and cracks nearby houses, though it is not an earthquake in the geological sense.

2. Assessing the link

  • Most mining tremors are small and shallow, but a shallow focus means strong shaking close to the mine.
  • The main victims are miners, through rock bursts and roof falls, and villagers whose houses crack.
  • Risk rises with depth, hard and brittle rock, fast extraction, nearby faults and location in a higher seismic zone.

3. Regulating mining to minimise seismic risk

  • Before mining: geotechnical and seismic-hazard studies in the EIA, avoiding active faults, and approved mining plans with safe pillar and stope design.
  • During mining: microseismic monitoring networks that detect stress build-up and warn workers; backfilling (stowing) of voids; controlled extraction rates; and controlled blasting within DGMS vibration limits.
  • Law and institutions: the Mines Act, 1952 with DGMS rules (Coal Mines Regulations, 2017; Metalliferous Mines Regulations, 1961); the MMDR Act, 1957 with mine closure plans; research support from CSIR-CIMFR (Dhanbad) and CSIR-NGRI.
  • After mining: sealing and filling old workings, subsidence monitoring and buffer zones around villages.

AP angle: AP lies on the stable Peninsular shield, but blasting in the limestone quarries of the Kurnool–Kadapa–Palnadu belt and the granite quarries of Chimakurthy (Prakasam), and underground uranium mining at Tummalapalle (Kadapa), call for vibration monitoring and structural audits of nearby homes.

Mining-induced tremors are usually small and largely preventable; science-based mine design, continuous monitoring and strict DGMS enforcement can keep mineral development safe for miners and communities.
free.g1m-2025-p5-6b:
Sustainable developmentBrundtland ReportIndustrialisationDecoupling

The Brundtland Report (Our Common Future, 1987) defined sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs". It rests on three pillars, economic, social and environmental, and is now framed by the 17 SDGs of the 2030 Agenda (2015). Modern industrialisation drives growth and jobs but also causes much of today's pollution, resource depletion and greenhouse-gas emissions.

1. Core principles

  • Equity: fair shares for future generations (intergenerational) and for the poor today (intragenerational).
  • Precaution and polluter pays: prevent harm and make polluters bear its cost, both upheld by the Supreme Court in the Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum case (1996).
  • Carrying capacity: use renewable resources within their rate of regeneration.

2. Relevance to modern industrialisation

  • Environmental limits: industry, power and transport drive air and water pollution and climate change; under NCAP only 14 cities met the PM10 standard in 2025-26.
  • Resource security: India imports nearly 89% of its crude oil and most critical minerals, so efficiency and recycling reduce risk.
  • Trade: buyers demand clean supply chains, and the EU's CBAM (definitive phase from January 2026) taxes the carbon in imported steel, aluminium and cement.
  • Safety and social licence: disasters such as Bhopal (1984) and the LG Polymers leak in Visakhapatnam (2020) show the cost of ignoring safety.
  • Economic gains: cheap solar power, energy efficiency and green jobs make clean growth profitable.

3. Critical evaluation

  • Development first: India's per-capita emissions are low and developing countries need carbon space; under CBDR-RC, rich countries must lead and pay.
  • A vague goal: "sustainable" is easily used for greenwashing, and GDP still ignores the loss of natural capital.
  • Costs: clean technology is costly for MSMEs, and promised climate finance (US$300 billion a year by 2035) falls short of needs.
  • Weak enforcement: poor EIA reports and attempts at post-facto approval; in the Vanashakti case (July 2026) the Supreme Court held that prior clearance is the rule.
  • Yet decoupling is possible: India's emissions intensity of GDP fell 36% between 2005 and 2020, and non-fossil sources passed half of installed power capacity in June 2025.

4. Tools for sustainable industrialisation

PAT and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023), ZED certification for MSMEs, EPR rules for plastics, e-waste and batteries, SEBI's BRSR disclosures, the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) and Mission LiFE.

AP angle: the Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, NTPC's green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka and the green ammonia complex at Kakinada link industrial growth with clean energy.

Sustainable development is not anti-industry; it asks industry to grow cleaner, circular and fairer, so that today's factories do not borrow from tomorrow's generations.
free.g1m-2025-p5-7a:
Zoonotic spilloverDeforestationDilution effectOne Health

About 60% of known human infections and some 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic, that is, they jump from animals to people (UNEP, 2020). Deforestation and other land-use change are among the strongest drivers of such spillover: clearing and fragmenting forests brings wildlife, livestock, disease vectors and people into new and closer contact. Outbreaks of Ebola and Nipah have made this link a global concern.

1. How deforestation leads to new infections

  • More edges, more contact: fragmentation creates long forest edges where people, cattle and wildlife meet, while loggers, miners, hunters and settlers move deep into forests.
  • Vectors thrive: sunlit clearings, pits and puddles favour mosquitoes, and scrub and grazing land favour ticks and mites; "frontier malaria" follows forest clearing in the Amazon.
  • Loss of the dilution effect: in diverse forests a pathogen is spread across many poor hosts; when diversity falls, efficient carriers such as rodents and bats dominate.
  • Stressed, displaced animals: bats and monkeys that lose habitat move into orchards, farms and villages, bringing their viruses closer to people.
  • Bushmeat and wildlife trade: new roads make hunting and trade easier, multiplying human exposure.

2. Examples

3. Indian and AP context

  • India's forest-fringe and tribal districts carry a large share of its malaria burden, including the agency areas of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Mining, road building and podu clearing in the Eastern Ghats increase contact with ticks, mites and mosquitoes; scrub typhus, spread by mites of scrubland, is widely reported in rural South India.
  • Nipah outbreaks in Kerala (since 2018) and West Bengal (2001, 2007, 2026) show the bat–human link.

4. Response: a One Health approach

  • Protect forests: halt the clearing of intact forests, restore degraded land, curb wildlife trade and include health impacts in EIA.
  • Integrated surveillance: link human, animal and wildlife disease data (IHIP, ICMR-NIV Pune's BSL-4 laboratory), as the WHO Pandemic Agreement (May 2025) urges.
  • Local protection: tick repellents and protective clothing for forest workers in KFD areas, bed nets and early diagnosis in forest villages.
  • Prediction: satellite maps of forest loss can flag spillover hotspots before outbreaks.

Healthy forests are a public-health shield; protecting them is far cheaper than fighting the next epidemic, which makes One Health the logical policy frame.
free.g1m-2025-p5-7b:
Environmental Impact AssessmentEIA Notification 2006Public hearingPrecautionary principle

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a process that predicts the environmental and social effects of a proposed project before it is approved, and designs ways to avoid, reduce or offset the harm. It puts the precautionary principle into practice. In India it was first made mandatory in 1994 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; today the EIA Notification, 2006 governs it, and applications are handled online on the PARIVESH portal.

1. Objectives

  • Build environmental concerns into project planning at the start, when changes are cheapest.
  • Compare alternatives of site, technology and scale.
  • Prepare an Environmental Management Plan (EMP) to reduce harm.
  • Give affected people a voice and make decisions transparent.

2. Categories under the 2006 Notification

3. Key stages

  • Screening: decides whether a project needs an EIA, and whether a Category B project is B1 or B2.
  • Scoping: the expert committee fixes the Terms of Reference: the issues, study area and studies the EIA must cover.
  • Baseline study and impact prediction: accredited consultants collect data on air, water, soil, noise, biodiversity and people, predict impacts and prepare the draft EIA report with an EMP.
  • Public consultation: a public hearing at or near the site, conducted by the State Pollution Control Board, plus written comments from others with a stake.
  • Appraisal: the EAC or SEAC scrutinises the final report and the hearing record and recommends clearance or rejection.
  • Decision: the MoEFCC or the SEIAA grants environmental clearance with conditions, or rejects the proposal.
  • Monitoring: the project submits six-monthly compliance reports, which regional offices check.

The 2006 Notification itself names four core stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal.

4. Issues and reforms

  • Weaknesses: reports paid for by project proponents, copied or one-season baseline data, hearings in technical language, weak monitoring and attempts at post-facto clearance; in the Vanashakti case (July 2026) the Supreme Court held that prior clearance is the rule.
  • Reforms: cumulative and Strategic Environmental Assessment of whole river basins or regions, an independent EIA authority, summaries in local languages and real-time compliance data on PARIVESH.

AP angle: large projects such as Polavaram and the Visakhapatnam industrial cluster show both the need for EIA and the cost of weak monitoring, which the LG Polymers styrene leak (2020) exposed.

EIA is India's main preventive environmental safeguard; making it independent, participatory and well monitored will turn it from a formality into a real tool of sustainable development.
free.g1m-2025-p5-8a:
Natural resourcesRenewable and non-renewableConservationSustainable use

Natural resources are materials and energy found in nature that people use: land, soil, water, forests, wildlife, fisheries, minerals and energy sources. India has about 2.4% of the world's land and 4% of its freshwater but about 18% of its people, so pressure on resources is intense. Their conservation rests on sustainable use: taking no more than nature can regenerate, using finite stocks efficiently, and sharing the benefits fairly.

1. Types of natural resources

  • Renewable is not inexhaustible: aquifers, fish stocks and forests behave like non-renewable resources when used faster than they recover.

2. India's resource base

  • Land and soil: fertile alluvial, black and red soils, but 29.7% of land was degraded in 2018-19 (ISRO atlas).
  • Water: large rivers and monsoon rain, but groundwater extraction stands at about 61% of recharge (CGWB, 2025), with about 11% of assessment units over-exploited.
  • Forests: forest and tree cover on 25.17% of the area (ISFR 2023).
  • Minerals and energy: about 95 minerals, with strength in iron ore, bauxite, chromite, limestone and barytes; coal output above 1 billion tonnes (2024-25); but nearly 89% of crude oil and most critical minerals are imported.
  • Fisheries: the world's second-largest fish producer (about 198 lakh tonnes, 2024-25).
  • Biodiversity: one of 17 megadiverse countries, with 7–8% of recorded species and four of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots.

3. Conservation through government initiatives

  • Legal approach: laws such as the Forest Rights Act, the Biological Diversity Act and the MMDR Act regulate use and protect local rights.
  • Economic approach: auctions, royalties, compensatory afforestation and tradable certificates put a price on resource use.
  • Community approach: Joint Forest Management, water-user associations and Gram Sabha consent under PESA make local people custodians.
  • Technology approach: satellite monitoring, drip irrigation and recycling ("urban mining") stretch resources further.

AP angle: AP's natural farming programme (APCNF) restores soil and saves water, WALTA (2002) regulates groundwater, sand and trees, and Mangampet holds the world's largest single barytes deposit.

Gaps: groundwater over-extraction, illegal sand mining, shrinking wetlands and monoculture plantations show that enforcement still lags behind policy; perverse incentives such as free farm power also encourage waste.

Conserving resources does not mean locking them away but using them wisely and fairly; natural-resource accounting in planning and community stewardship are the way forward.
free.g1m-2025-p5-8b:
Integrated Solid Waste ManagementWaste hierarchySource segregationCircular economy

Integrated Solid Waste Management (ISWM) treats waste as one connected system, from generation and segregation to collection, transport, processing and disposal, choosing the best mix of methods for each waste stream and involving all stakeholders. It replaces the old "collect and dump" approach with resource recovery. In India, the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 (in force from 1 April 2026) and Swachh Bharat Mission–Urban 2.0 put this approach into practice.

1. Key principles of ISWM

  • Waste hierarchy: preventing waste comes first and landfill last (see below).
  • Integration: all stages, from generation to final disposal, and all streams (wet, dry, sanitary, special-care, plastics, e-waste, construction debris) are planned together.
  • Source segregation: the foundation of ISWM; the 2026 Rules require four-stream segregation into wet, dry, sanitary and special-care waste.
  • Polluter pays and EPR: user fees and fines for generators, and Extended Producer Responsibility for plastics, e-waste and batteries.
  • Decentralisation: wet waste is treated close to the source; bulk generators must process it on-site or buy certificates.
  • Inclusion and participation: citizens, resident associations, informal waste pickers, recyclers and private operators all have roles.
  • Sustainability: systems must be financially viable, environmentally safe and socially fair.

2. Role of the waste hierarchy in ISWM

  • Sets priorities: it tells cities to invest first in reduction and segregation, not in incinerators for wet waste that burns poorly.
  • Shrinks landfills: under the 2026 Rules landfills take only inert rejects, cutting methane, leachate and dump fires.
  • Drives the circular economy: compost returns to farms and recyclables to industry, while solid-fuel industries such as cement plants near an RDF plant must replace part of their fuel with refuse-derived fuel, rising to 15% within six years.
  • Shapes policy: the plastic ban (prevention), EPR (recycling) and RDF rules (energy recovery) each target one level of the hierarchy.

3. Indian progress

Under SBM-Urban 2.0, about 1,048 of 2,476 legacy dumpsites had been cleared by November 2025, and Indore remains the model of segregation-led management.

AP angle: the monthly Swachh Andhra–Swarna Andhra day, waste-to-energy plants at Visakhapatnam and Guntur, and the entry of Vijayawada, Guntur and Tirupati into the Super Swachh League (2024-25).

Challenges: poor segregation at home, weak municipal finances, an unorganised recycling sector and resistance to user fees.

ISWM succeeds only when the hierarchy guides every rupee: reduce and segregate first, recover what is left, and use the landfill as a last resort.
free.g1m-2025-p5-9a:
Plant-derived biopharmaceuticalsMolecular farmingGreen pharmacyPharmaceutical lifecycle

Plant-derived biopharmaceuticals are medicines taken from plants or produced inside them. They include classic plant drugs such as artemisinin and paclitaxel and, through molecular farming, therapeutic proteins, antibodies and vaccines made in genetically engineered plants or plant cells. Green pharmacy applies green chemistry and sustainability to every stage of a medicine's life, from design to disposal, so that curing people does not poison rivers, soils and wildlife.

1. Potential for sustainable healthcare

  • Low cost, easy scale-up: plants need only light, water and nutrients; more greenhouse space replaces costly steel bioreactors and mammalian cell culture.
  • Safety: plants do not carry human or animal viruses and prions, a risk with mammalian cell lines.
  • Proven products: taliglucerase alfa, an enzyme for Gaucher disease made in carrot cells, became the first plant-made protein drug approved by the US FDA (2012); the ZMapp antibodies against Ebola (2014) were grown in tobacco leaves; Canada approved a plant-made COVID-19 vaccine, Covifenz, in 2022.
  • Renewable small molecules: plant-cell fermentation now makes the anticancer drug paclitaxel without felling slow-growing yew trees; artemisinin from Artemisia annua anchors malaria treatment.
  • Limits: low yields, costly purification, plant-type sugars on proteins, and gene flow from open-field GM crops, so contained greenhouses or cell cultures are preferred.

2. Green pharmacy at each stage of the lifecycle

3. Green-pharmacy principles in practice

  • Principles: waste prevention, atom economy, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks and design for degradation (Anastas and Warner's twelve principles of green chemistry, 1998).
  • Lesson from vultures: the painkiller diclofenac in cattle carcasses wiped out more than 95% of India's Gyps vultures before its veterinary use was banned in 2006; drugs must also be judged for ecological safety.
  • Antibiotic pollution: effluents from bulk-drug clusters such as Patancheru (Telangana) were found to carry very high antibiotic levels; India's NAP-AMR 2.0 (2025–29) follows One Health, linking factory effluents to drug resistance.
  • Sustainable sourcing: good agricultural and collection practices, the National Medicinal Plants Board (2000) and benefit-sharing under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 protect wild medicinal flora and collectors.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's bulk-drug belt around the Jawaharlal Nehru Pharma City, Parawada (Anakapalli) needs strict effluent treatment, solvent recovery and APPCB monitoring, while tribal collectors of medicinal plants in the Eastern Ghats need sustainable-harvest rules.

Plant-based production and green pharmacy together can deliver affordable, low-impact healthcare; India, a global generic-drug supplier, should pair molecular-farming research with binding effluent standards and drug take-back schemes.
free.g1m-2025-p5-9b:
Conventional energyNon-conventional energyEnergy securityEnergy transition

Conventional energy sources, namely coal, oil, natural gas, large hydro and fuelwood, have long been in use and mostly run large, centralised plants; the fossil ones are exhaustible. Non-conventional sources, namely solar, wind, small hydro, biomass, geothermal, tidal and green hydrogen, are renewable, cleaner and often decentralised. India, the world's third-largest energy consumer, needs both: conventional energy for reliable supply today and non-conventional energy for security and net zero by 2070.

1. Differences

  • Technology, not only renewability: "conventional" means mature, long-used technology; large hydro is renewable yet counted as conventional.
  • Classification varies: NCERT lists nuclear energy as non-conventional, but official power statistics count nuclear and large hydro with conventional capacity and treat only MNRE's renewables as "non-conventional".
  • Overlap: fuelwood and dung are conventional but non-commercial, still used for cooking in poor households.

2. Relevance of conventional energy

  • Backbone of supply: coal and lignite are 41.6% of installed capacity (August 2026) but generate about 70% of electricity, because they run round the clock and carry the evening load; peak demand hit a record 270.8 GW on 21 May 2026.
  • Industry and transport: coal for steel and cement, oil for transport and petrochemicals, gas for fertiliser and city gas; India mined about 1,040 million tonnes of coal in 2025-26.
  • Vulnerabilities: 88.7% of crude oil was imported in 2025-26, and the 2026 Hormuz crisis exposed this risk; coal drives air pollution and most CO₂ emissions.

3. Relevance of non-conventional energy

  • Rapid growth: renewables (solar 168 GW, wind 58.5 GW) are now the largest block of capacity; with large hydro and nuclear, non-fossil sources crossed 50% of capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of the NDC target; India is 3rd in renewable capacity (IRENA 2026).
  • Climate goals: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, and a 60% non-fossil share of installed capacity by 2035 (NDC 3.0).
  • Access and livelihoods: PM-KUSUM solar pumps (about 13.1 GW by March 2026), rooftop solar, biogas, and module manufacturing under PLI.
  • Limits: non-fossil sources gave only 29.2% of electricity in 2025-26; intermittency needs storage, Green Energy Corridors and imported critical minerals.

AP angle: AP's Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets 78.5 GW solar, 35 GW wind and 22 GW pumped storage; the Ananthapuram-I (1,500 MW) and Kurnool (1,000 MW) solar parks and Greenko's 1,680 MW Pinnapuram pumped storage lead, while coal plants such as NTPC Simhadri still provide base supply.

India's path is not "either-or" but a managed transition: conventional plants for reliability now, non-conventional sources for a clean, secure future, linked by storage, grids and a just transition for coal regions.
free.g1m-2025-p5-10b:
Water Act 1974Air Act 1981Environment (Protection) Act 1986Pollution control boards

India's pollution laws rest on Article 21 (read by the Supreme Court to include a clean environment), Articles 48A and 51A(g), and Parliament's powers under Article 252 (the Water Act was passed at the request of States) and Article 253 (the Air and EP Acts implement the Stockholm Conference, 1972). The framework is a command-and-control system run by pollution control boards and, since 2010, backed by the National Green Tribunal.

1. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

  • Institutions: created the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs).
  • Consent system: no industry may be set up or discharge effluent without the SPCB's consent to establish and consent to operate; boards set standards and inspect.
  • Enforcement: boards can order closure or cut power and water; the 2024 amendment replaced jail with penalties of ₹10,000 to ₹15 lakh for many offences, and applies first to Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and the UTs.

2. Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981

  • Same boards: States declare air pollution control areas, where industries need consent and must meet emission standards.
  • Wider scope: noise was added as an air pollutant in 1987; ambient standards (2009) cover 12 pollutants.
  • Recent changes: the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 replaced imprisonment with penalties for many offences; the Commission for Air Quality Management Act, 2021 created an airshed body for Delhi-NCR.

3. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the NGT

  • Umbrella law after Bhopal: gives the Centre wide powers to set standards, restrict industrial locations and order closure; the EIA Notification and the waste, CRZ and GM rules are made under it.
  • Citizen's suit: any person may complain to a court after 60 days' notice to the authorities.
  • National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: speedy civil remedies and compensation under the Water, Air and EP Acts, applying polluter pays and the precautionary principle.

4. Limitations

  • Weak boards: SPCBs are understaffed and short of experts; monitoring relies heavily on industries' own reports.
  • Point-source bias: the Acts target factories, while vehicles, dust, crop-residue burning, farm runoff and untreated town sewage, the largest water polluter, escape effective control.
  • Deterrence: penalties are small and prosecutions slow.
  • Fragmentation: airsheds and rivers cross State boundaries that boards cannot; courts and the NGT often fill executive gaps.
  • Results: only 14 of 130 NCAP cities met the PM10 standard in 2025-26; CPCB lists 296 polluted river stretches.

AP angle: the APPCB grants consents and monitors industries; the LG Polymers styrene leak at Visakhapatnam (2020), where the NGT imposed an interim ₹50 crore under absolute liability, and aquaculture effluents in Kolleru show both the reach and the gaps of the law.

The legal framework is sound, but enforcement capacity lags; independent, well-staffed boards, continuous monitoring and airshed and river-basin management can turn the Acts into clean air and water.
free.g1m-2025-p5-11a:
Global warmingClimate changeEnhanced greenhouse effectHuman influence

Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature, caused mainly by greenhouse gases (GHGs) that strengthen the natural greenhouse effect. Climate change is broader: lasting shifts in temperature, rainfall, extremes, sea level, ice and ocean chemistry, whether natural or human-caused. Warming is thus one driver and one symptom of climate change. 2024 was the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C (about 1.55 °C) above pre-industrial levels (WMO).

1. Global warming vs climate change

  • Cause and effect: warming melts ice, expands sea water and lets air hold about 7% more moisture per °C, producing many of the changes called climate change.
  • Not uniform: land warms faster than the ocean and the Arctic fastest; some regions get wetter, others drier.
  • Legal usage: the UNFCCC (1992) defines climate change as change attributed directly or indirectly to human activity, over and above natural variability.

2. Natural causes

  • Solar output: the Sun's 11-year cycle varies heat input slightly; solar activity shows no rising trend since about 1980, while temperatures rose.
  • Volcanoes: large eruptions put sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere and cool the Earth for a year or two (Pinatubo, 1991).
  • Orbital (Milankovitch) cycles: changes in Earth's orbit and tilt drive ice ages over tens of thousands of years, too slow to explain recent warming.
  • Internal variability: El Niño years are warmer and La Niña years cooler; oceans move heat around but do not add it.

3. Human-induced causes

  • Fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas for power, transport and industry are the largest CO₂ source; CO₂ reached 423.9 ppm in 2024, about 152% of pre-industrial.
  • Land-use change: deforestation releases stored carbon and removes sinks.
  • Methane and nitrous oxide: paddy, livestock, landfills and gas leaks (methane, GWP about 27–30); nitrogen fertilisers (N₂O, about 273).
  • F-gases and soot: HFCs and SF₆ trap heat strongly; black carbon darkens snow and ice.
  • Aerosols: sulphate pollution reflects sunlight and masks part of the warming.

4. Dominant factors today

  • Human influence is unequivocal (IPCC AR6): practically all observed warming is human-caused, and natural drivers added almost nothing.
  • CO₂ leads, methane second: fossil CO₂ is the single largest driver; the 3.5 ppm rise in 2024 was a record.
  • Natural factors only modulate: the 2023–24 El Niño helped push 2024 above 1.5 °C, but the trend is set by GHGs; the Paris limit refers to about 20-year averages.

AP angle: the warming already shows on AP's 1,053 km coast through erosion at Uppada, rapidly intensifying Bay of Bengal cyclones and severe heat waves in Rayalaseema.

Global warming is the thermometer reading; climate change is the whole illness. Since humans dominate the cause, deep cuts in CO₂ and methane, as in India's 500 GW non-fossil target and net zero by 2070, are the cure.
free.g1m-2025-p5-11b:
Remote sensingPollutant dispersionAerosol optical depthExposure mapping

Remote sensing means gathering information about the Earth from satellites, aircraft or drones by measuring reflected or emitted radiation. Gases such as nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone, and particles (aerosols), absorb or scatter particular wavelengths, so sensors can map their amounts and follow pollutant plumes from fires, factories and cities across regions and borders, something scattered ground monitors cannot do.

1. Tracking dispersion from space

  • Gases: ESA's Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI, 2017) maps NO₂, SO₂, CO, ozone, formaldehyde and methane every day at a few kilometres' resolution; it showed NO₂ falling sharply over Indian cities during the 2020 lockdown.
  • Aerosols and smoke: the US MODIS and VIIRS sensors and ISRO's INSAT-3D/3DR give aerosol optical depth and fire counts; IARI's CREAMS laboratory uses such data to count paddy-residue fires in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh as smoke drifts towards Delhi.
  • Water and coasts: ocean-colour sensors (Oceansat-3) detect algal blooms and sediment plumes, and radar satellites spot oil slicks even through clouds.
  • Greenhouse gases: methane plumes from landfills, coal mines and gas leaks can now be detected from space, helping target controls.

2. Implications for human health

  • Exposure maps: satellite-based PM2.5 estimates, calibrated with ground monitors, cover rural areas and small towns without monitors; the ICMR-led study (Lancet Planetary Health, 2020) that linked about 16.7 lakh deaths in 2019 to air pollution used such satellite-based exposure estimates.
  • Source attribution: tracing stubble smoke, power-plant SO₂ and dust storms shows who is exposed and supports regional airshed action instead of city-only plans.
  • Early warning: plume forecasts allow health advisories, school closures and curbs on construction (as under GRAP in Delhi-NCR), protecting children, the elderly and heart and lung patients.
  • Epidemiology: linking maps to hospital data reveals pollution-related asthma, pneumonia, heart disease and low birth weight; bloom maps protect fishers and drinking-water intakes.
  • Vulnerable groups: overlaying plume maps on population data shows which slums, schools and hospitals lie in the worst-affected zones, so that protection and clean-air measures can be targeted there first.

3. Limitations and future improvements

AP angle: Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada are among AP's NCAP non-attainment cities; satellites can map their aerosol and NO₂ plumes, but the LG Polymers styrene leak (2020) shows why sensors around factories remain essential.

Remote sensing turns pollution from a point reading into a regional picture; combined with ground networks, AI models and geostationary satellites, it can drive health-based air-quality management.
free.g1m-2025-p5-12a:
GMO regulationRules 1989GEACGenome editing

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) are regulated in India under the Rules, 1989 for hazardous micro-organisms and genetically engineered organisms, framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The system works through six competent authorities, from institutional committees to the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC), and follows the precautionary principle and the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000), which requires the importing country's advance informed agreement before living modified organisms meant for release into the environment cross borders.

1. The regulatory framework

  • Six authorities: RDAC (advisory), the IBSC at each institution, RCGM under DBT, GEAC under MoEFCC (renamed from "Approval" to "Appraisal" in 2010), State Biotechnology Coordination Committees and District-Level Committees.
  • Other laws: FSSAI regulates GM food under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; the PPV&FR Act, 2001 protects farmers' seed rights; the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 governs access to bio-resources.
  • Genome editing: since 30 March 2022, SDN-1 and SDN-2 edited plants free of foreign DNA are exempt from the 1989 Rules once an IBSC certifies them; SDN-3 still follows the GEAC route.

2. Record so far

  • Bt cotton (2002): the only commercial GM crop; it cut bollworm attacks, but pink bollworm now resists it and herbicide-tolerant (HTBt) cotton is sown illegally.
  • Bt brinjal: under moratorium since 2010 after public consultations.
  • GM mustard DMH-11: cleared by GEAC in 2022; the Supreme Court gave a split verdict (23 July 2024) and asked the Centre for a national GM-crop policy; release remains on hold.
  • Genome-edited rice: Kamala and Pusa DST Rice 1, released on 4 May 2025, took the lighter SDN route.

3. Adequacy for modern challenges

  • Strengths: a tiered, science-based and precautionary system, aligned with Cartagena; the editing exemption has already enabled innovation.
  • Weaknesses: slow, opaque decisions often overruled politically; DBT both promotes and regulates biotechnology; States, which control agriculture, have only a limited role.

4. Way forward

  • Statutory regulator: an independent, transparent biotechnology regulator with time-bound decisions.
  • National GM policy: prepared after consulting States, farmers and scientists, as the Supreme Court asked.
  • Risk-based rules: product-focused assessment for edited crops, strong post-release monitoring, liability and labelling.

AP angle: as a major cotton and rice State, AP has a stake in both routes: its cotton farmers grow Bt hybrids, and India's genome-edited rice varieties were bred from AP-developed parents, Samba Mahsuri (Bapatla) and MTU 1010 (Maruteru).

The 1989 framework has kept India cautious and safe, but it is outdated for gene editing and synthetic biology; a transparent, statutory system can balance biosafety with innovation.
free.g1m-2025-p5-12b:
NBDSDBT and BIRACBioeconomyBioE3 Policy

The National Biotechnology Development Strategy (NBDS) is the Department of Biotechnology's roadmap for turning India's biological science base into products, jobs and a bioeconomy. Since DBT was set up in 1986, three strategies (2007, 2015–2020 and 2021–2025) shifted the focus from building research capacity to manufacturing and commercialisation, a path now carried forward by the BioE3 Policy (2024).

1. Evolution

  • NBDS 2007: after two decades of public investment, it aimed to build human resources, research infrastructure and public–private partnership, and proposed a single biotechnology regulator (later the lapsed BRAI Bill, 2013).
  • NBDS 2015–2020: aimed to make India a "world class bio-manufacturing hub" and a US$100 billion industry by 2025, through four missions (healthcare, food and nutrition, clean energy, education) and a translation network of 5 new clusters, 40 incubators, 150 technology transfer offices and 20 bio-connect centres.
  • NBDS 2021–2025: continued the push for start-ups, bio-manufacturing and translation.
  • BioE3 (24 August 2024): biomanufacturing hubs, biofoundries and Bio-AI hubs in six areas; Bio-RIDE (₹9,197 crore) merged DBT's schemes.

2. Key objectives

  • Human capital: skilled scientists and entrepreneurs; a Life Sciences and Biotechnology Education Council.
  • Research base: genomics, vaccines, stem cells, agri-biotech, marine biotechnology, bioprospecting.
  • Translation: incubators, technology transfer offices and BIRAC grants and equity for start-ups.
  • Inclusive development: affordable healthcare, food and nutrition, clean energy and environment.
  • Enablers: transparent regulation and global partnerships.

3. Impact: a critical evaluation

  • Growth: the bioeconomy grew nearly twentyfold to US$195.3 billion in 2025 (about 4.8% of GDP), well past the 2015 strategy's US$100 billion goal, with about 11,800 start-ups.
  • Health products: India makes nearly 60% of the world's vaccines; Covaxin, ZyCoV-D (the first human DNA vaccine), the HPV vaccine CERVAVAC (DBT-BIRAC), NexCAR19 CAR-T therapy (2023) and BIRSA 101 for sickle cell disease (2025).
  • Agriculture and genomics: genome-edited rice (2025) and the 10,000-genome Genome India Project.
  • Shortfalls: national R&D spending is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24); much output is biosimilars, generics and services rather than new discoveries; regulatory delays have stalled agri-biotech beyond Bt cotton; reagents and equipment are largely imported; start-ups cluster in a few States.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's bioeconomy was US$13.74 billion in 2025, fifth among States; the AP MedTech Zone, Visakhapatnam (2016), and AP-bred rice parents of the genome-edited varieties show its potential.

The NBDS turned biotechnology from a laboratory pursuit into a US$195 billion sector; reaching US$300 billion by 2030 needs higher R&D spending, a modern regulator and bio-manufacturing spread beyond a few clusters.
free.g1m-2025-p5-13a:
AntigenAdjuvantImmunological memoryHerd immunity

A vaccine is a biological preparation that trains the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease. It contains a harmless form, part or genetic blueprint of the microbe, the antigen, plus ingredients that make it safe, stable and effective. By creating memory cells it gives long-lasting active immunity, and when enough people are vaccinated, herd immunity protects those who are not.

1. Components of a vaccine

  • Antigen (active ingredient): a weakened live microbe, a killed microbe, a purified protein or sugar, an inactivated toxin (toxoid), or genetic code (mRNA, DNA or a viral vector) that makes the body's cells produce the antigen.
  • Adjuvant: boosts and prolongs the immune response so that less antigen is needed; aluminium salts (alum) are the commonest.
  • Stabilisers: sugars, amino acids or gelatin keep the vaccine potent during storage and transport.
  • Preservatives: such as 2-phenoxyethanol or thiomersal, prevent contamination in multi-dose vials.
  • Other contents: a diluent (sterile water or saline), buffers, and traces of production materials reduced to safe limits; a cold chain of 2–8 °C protects potency.

2. How a vaccine works

  • Innate alarm: the antigen and adjuvant cause mild local inflammation; antigen-presenting cells carry the antigen to the lymph nodes.
  • Adaptive response: helper (CD4) T cells activate B cells, which become plasma cells making specific antibodies (humoral immunity); cytotoxic (CD8) T cells learn to kill infected cells (cell-mediated immunity).
  • Memory: memory B and T cells persist for years; on real exposure they respond within days, before disease sets in. The first dose gives a slow, mainly IgM response; boosters give a rapid, high IgG response.
  • Herd immunity: above a threshold, about 95% for highly contagious measles, transmission chains break; India was certified polio-free in 2014.

3. India's vaccination effort

  • Programmes: the Universal Immunisation Programme (1985) offers free vaccines against 12 diseases; Mission Indradhanush (2014) reaches left-out children; U-WIN keeps digital records; HPV vaccination for girls aged 14 began on 28 February 2026.
  • Production: India makes nearly 60% of the world's vaccines, including indigenous Covaxin, ZyCoV-D and CERVAVAC.
  • Challenges: vaccine hesitancy, zero-dose children in urban slums and remote areas, and cold-chain gaps.

A vaccine combines an antigen with adjuvants and stabilisers to build immune memory safely; wider coverage, new platforms such as mRNA and a strong cold chain keep it the most cost-effective tool of public health.
free.g1m-2025-p5-13b:
Genetic engineeringRecombinant DNAGM cropsGene therapy

Genetic engineering is the direct alteration of an organism's genes using biotechnology: cutting, joining and moving genes between organisms through recombinant DNA technology (Cohen and Boyer, 1973), or changing a gene precisely in place through genome editing such as CRISPR-Cas9 (2012). Because the genetic code is universal, a bacterial gene can work in cotton and a human gene in bacteria, opening wide uses in farming and medicine.

1. How it works

  • Tools: restriction enzymes ("molecular scissors", e.g., EcoRI), DNA ligase ("molecular glue"), vectors such as plasmids, the Agrobacterium Ti plasmid for plants and viral vectors for gene therapy, and PCR to copy genes.
  • Gene transfer: gene gun for plants, microinjection for animal eggs, electroporation for cells.
  • Genome editing: a guide RNA leads Cas9 to a target sequence; India exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 edits without foreign DNA from GM rules in 2022.

2. Applications in agriculture

  • Pest resistance: Bt cotton (2002) carries cry genes of Bacillus thuringiensis that kill bollworms, cutting insecticide use; it is India's only commercial GM crop.
  • Yield and stress tolerance: the genome-edited rice varieties released in May 2025: Kamala (about 19% more yield, maturing 15–20 days earlier) and Pusa DST Rice 1 (9.7–30.4% more yield on saline and alkaline soils).
  • Hybrid seed: GM mustard DMH-11 uses a barnase–barstar male-sterility system to make high-yield hybrids, though its release is on hold.
  • Nutrition and animals: Golden Rice carries beta-carotene genes against vitamin A deficiency; transgenic animals give medicines in milk and faster growth (AquAdvantage salmon).

3. Applications in medicine

  • Recombinant proteins: insulin (1982) from engineered E. coli or yeast, growth hormone, clotting factors and erythropoietin.
  • Vaccines and antibodies: recombinant hepatitis B and HPV vaccines, Corbevax, the DNA vaccine ZyCoV-D (2021), mRNA vaccines and monoclonal antibodies for cancer.
  • Gene and cell therapy: NexCAR19 (2023), India's first CAR-T therapy; a haemophilia A gene-therapy trial at CMC Vellore that ended bleeds in all five patients (2024); BIRSA 101 (2025), an indigenous CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease.
  • Diagnosis and research: PCR and RT-PCR tests, DNA fingerprinting and knock-out mice as disease models.

AP angle: Kamala was edited from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), bred at ANGRAU's Bapatla station, and Pusa DST Rice 1 from MTU 1010, bred at Maruteru, so AP germplasm underpins the world's first genome-edited rice.

Genetic engineering offers precise solutions for food and health security; its promise is best realised under strong biosafety and ethical oversight.
free.g1m-2025-p5-14a:
Poultry bacterial diseasesMolecular diagnosticsVaccines and probioticsOne Health

Poultry is a major source of cheap protein and rural income; India produced about 149 billion eggs in 2024-25, second in the world. Crowded flocks spread bacterial diseases quickly, and some, such as Salmonella and Campylobacter, also cause human food poisoning. Heavy antibiotic use worsens antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Biotechnology therefore offers an integrated strategy to detect, prevent and control outbreaks with fewer antibiotics.

1. Monitoring and early detection

  • Molecular diagnostics: PCR and real-time PCR identify Salmonella, Mycoplasma and E. coli within hours; LAMP tests work on farms without costly machines.
  • Serology: ELISA and rapid plate agglutination tests screen breeder flocks for antibodies to Salmonella Pullorum and Mycoplasma, so infected parents are removed before they pass infection through eggs.
  • Genomic surveillance: whole-genome sequencing traces an outbreak to its source, separates strains and detects resistance genes; ICAR's INFAAR network monitors AMR in animals and fish.
  • Reporting and mapping: notification under the Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009 and GIS maps of farm clusters allow quick ring control.

2. Prevention

  • Vaccines: live fowl-typhoid vaccine, inactivated fowl-cholera and coryza vaccines, and Mycoplasma vaccines; recombinant and vector vaccines and in-ovo vaccination at hatcheries are newer tools.
  • Healthy stock and genetics: pathogen-free breeder flocks; marker-assisted selection for disease resistance; hardy native breeds conserved as gene pools.
  • Biosecurity: all-in-all-out batches, disinfection, chlorinated water, clean feed, and control of rodents and wild birds.

3. Control with fewer antibiotics

  • Probiotics and competitive exclusion: beneficial Lactobacillus and Bacillus strains, or defined gut cultures, crowd out Salmonella and Clostridium.
  • Bacteriophages: viruses that kill only target bacteria are used in water, feed or on carcasses.
  • Other alternatives: prebiotics, organic acids, essential oils, antimicrobial peptides and egg-yolk antibodies (IgY).
  • Prudent use: treatment guided by culture and sensitivity tests; India banned colistin as a growth promoter (2019), and NAP-AMR 2.0 (2025–29) follows One Health.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh is India's largest egg producer, with about 18% of output (BAHS 2025), so a single outbreak in its dense layer clusters hits lakhs of birds; Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University, Tirupati, and district diagnostic laboratories can anchor PCR-based surveillance.

Combining rapid diagnostics, vaccines, biosecurity and antibiotic alternatives protects farmers' incomes, consumers' health and the fight against drug resistance.
free.g1m-2025-p5-15a:
Respiratory tract infectionsDroplet and aerosol spreadUrban crowdingPublic health strategy

Respiratory tract infections (RTIs), such as influenza, Covid-19, tuberculosis, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), pneumococcal pneumonia and measles, spread through the air from person to person. In densely populated cities, crowding, poor ventilation, constant movement and air pollution raise the number of contacts per case, so one infection can spark a large outbreak. India carries about 25% of the world's TB cases, a reminder that airborne diseases thrive where people are packed together.

1. Transmission dynamics

  • Routes: large droplets travel a metre or two when people cough or talk; fine aerosols linger in closed rooms (TB, measles, Covid-19); hands and surfaces carry influenza and RSV.
  • Reproduction number: the average number infected by one case rises with contact rate, duration of exposure and infectiousness; measles (12–18) spreads far faster than seasonal influenza (below 2).
  • Silent spread: pre-symptomatic and mild cases keep moving; "super-spreading" events occur in crowded indoor venues.
  • Seasonality: influenza peaks during the monsoon and winter in much of India, when people crowd indoors.

2. Urban amplifiers

  • Crowding: one-room slum homes, packed buses and suburban trains, schools, offices, malls and hospital waiting areas.
  • Poor ventilation: sealed, air-conditioned rooms recirculate air, and small-windowed tenements trap it.
  • Air pollution: PM2.5 damages airway defences and raises pneumonia risk; air pollution was linked to about 16.7 lakh deaths in 2019.
  • Host factors: malnutrition, diabetes, smoking and HIV raise TB and pneumonia risk, while migrants and the urban poor delay care.

3. Public health strategies

  • Make buildings breathe: ventilation norms for schools, hospitals and public transport, and decongested housing under PMAY-Urban.
  • Behaviour and communication: masks in crowded transport during surges, cough etiquette, staying home when sick, and clear, local-language risk messages.
  • TB-specific steps: short regimens such as BPaLM and Ni-kshay nutrition support; TB incidence fell 21% between 2015 and 2024.
  • Clean air: NCAP measures against dust and vehicle exhaust reduce susceptibility to infection.

AP angle: during Covid-19, ASHAs and village and ward volunteers in AP ran door-to-door surveys for influenza-like illness and logged symptomatic people on a mobile app for testing; with Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, a similar network can track influenza-like clusters in fast-growing cities such as Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada.

Urban RTIs are driven by contacts, crowding and dirty air; layered action, from surveillance and vaccination to early TB detection, ventilation and better housing, can make dense cities healthy cities.
free.g1m-2025-p5-15b:
Intellectual property rightsAcademia–industry collaborationTechnology transferLicensing and royalties

Intellectual property rights (IPR), such as patents, copyrights, designs, trade secrets and plant-variety rights, give creators exclusive rights for a limited time. In academia–industry collaborations, universities bring knowledge and talent while firms bring money, scale and markets. Clear IP terms decide who owns the results, who may use them and how gains are shared; without them, inventions stay in laboratories and partnerships end in disputes. India's National IPR Policy, 2016 makes commercialisation of research a priority.

1. Why IPR matters in collaborations

  • Clarity and trust: agreements define background IP (what each partner brings) and foreground IP (what is created), so partners can invest without fear of losing control.
  • Incentive for industry: firms fund research only if they can secure exclusive or preferred rights; a patent also attracts investors to start-ups and spin-offs.
  • Revenue for universities and public labs: licence fees and royalties fund further research; ICMR, for instance, received royalties on sales of Covaxin, which it co-developed with Bharat Biotech.
  • Credit for researchers: inventors are named on patents and share income, rewarding applied work.
  • Openness with protection: a short review period before publication lets patents be filed without blocking academic freedom.

2. Key clauses of a collaboration agreement

3. Indian initiatives

  • Policy: the National IPR Policy, 2016 ("Creative India; Innovative India") with CIPAM under DPIIT; the National IP Awareness Mission (2021) for colleges; an 80% patent-fee cut for educational institutions (2021 rules).
  • Funding and institutions: IPR cells and technology transfer offices in IITs and CSIR laboratories; BIRAC and Atal Innovation Mission incubators; ANRF (2023) and the ₹1 lakh crore RDI scheme (2025) to draw private money into research.
  • Success story: NexCAR19 (2023), India's first CAR-T cell therapy, was developed by IIT Bombay and Tata Memorial and commercialised through the IIT Bombay-incubated ImmunoACT.

4. Challenges

  • Weak commercialisation: few university patents are licensed; many institutions lack clear IP policies and trained IP managers.
  • Low R&D base: national R&D spending is 0.84% of GDP (2023-24), and industry funds little university research.
  • Legal gaps: no law like the US Bayh–Dole Act (1980) on publicly funded IP; the 2008 Bill on it was never passed; patent backlogs persist.

AP angle: newer institutions such as IIT Tirupati and IISER Tirupati, the AP MedTech Zone in Visakhapatnam and ANGRAU need model agreements and technology transfer offices to link research with local industry.

IPR is the bridge between laboratory and market; model agreements, professional transfer offices and fair benefit-sharing can turn India's rising innovation (Global Innovation Index rank 38th, 2026) into products and jobs.
